engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed it at. The
pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.

I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going. I built a small custom
language for describing scenes (the name for that is a domain-specific language, a
DSL), then a program that read the language and caught my mistakes in it (a linter),
then a way to type commands at the whole thing from a terminal (a command-line
interface, a CLI). The night the engine first ran a program declaratively, meaning I told
it what should happen and let it work out the how without my spelling out each step,
I told my wife, Julie, I thought I was onto something. She said okay.

Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Z3 could settle
the small questions and fell over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me
staring down an infinite hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of
it, ever. One night, not even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old
story about a creature living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third.


                                           59
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


And it landed on me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said
it out loud: I get it now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees
what it can read and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind
to. It isn’t broken. It was just never built with an eye that points that way. The two
computers on the first pages of this book are my attempt to show you that blindness
with something you can hold. I opened a new repo that same night and called the
thing in it the Thiele Machine. The name began as a working title and became the
name of the model. It carries the larger claim plainly: the machine treats structural
state as part of computation.

What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the code. Not one line of it.
By the time the Coq proofs finally landed, every line of that first renderer had been
thrown out and rewritten at least twice, probably more, and good riddance to all of it.
What survived was a single architectural commitment I made early and never once let
anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the actual thing the machine runs on.
It is no metaphor laid over some realer state underneath. Category theory was the first
language I found for that structure. It is not what the model is. The model asks for a
state, a step, a record, a ledger, and a window, and category theory appears nowhere
in that list. It lived on for a while in a bigger machine I built on the way here, a
fifty-one-instruction virtual machine with its own chip design, whose partition graph
(groups, and arrows between them) was, in different words and different syntax, the
same object as the category structure that came together in that first week and first ran
morphisms correctly at two in the morning. That machine was useful for building and
confusing for everything else, so it’s set aside now, kept but out of this book. What
building it showed me is that six instruction kinds were enough for everything this
book needs, and that the big one was mostly in the way. I did not write that code,
not then and not now. I directed the models and refused everything they handed me
until the morphisms composed the way the shape said they had to. The morphisms
in that early code were objects that remembered where they came from; the records
in the small machine I ended up with remember where they came from too, and you
can walk up to one and challenge it. The receipt grew teeth. But the shape itself
never moved. The shape was the substrate the entire time, and everything else, every
renderer and language and proof, was me slowly learning to see what I had already
built. By the shape I mean structure held as state. Not category theory. Category
theory was just the first language I had for it.

Formal verification was a graveyard of dead ends further on. The hardware came
after that, in the bigger machine I set aside, and none of it is in this book. Every step
pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known was there, and I
mean that plainly: I did not know what a Turing machine was when I started, I did
not know what Coq was, I did not know most of the words in this document existed.
I learned each one the same way, by walking face-first into a wall that needed it and
not being let past until I had it. The needing always came first. The learning came



                                            60
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


after, dragged along behind the needing because it had no say in the matter.

Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want the divi-
sion of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong about work
like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference implementation, no
prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the direction, the demand that the
thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk. The symbol-pushing, the actual
Coq and the actual math, the models produced and the proof checker judged. The
proofs compile or they do not. I refused every one that did not. Coq is an obedient
idiot. It checks the proof matches the statement. It does not check that the statement
means what you think it means. A theorem can claim “every cat that is also a prime
number has whiskers” and the proof can be three characters long and Coq will nod
and stamp it. So I read every statement. The proofs you can’t fake. The statements
you can fake by accident, which is the more dangerous failure mode. I refused both
kinds. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable by
reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had typed
it. The monkeys could not have refused.

A word on what I actually do, because it runs under everything after it. I do not write
code or math by hand. I do not pick constants. I do not grind through derivations. I
have never written a line of code on paper or in a notepad in my life. What I do is
see, and direct, and refuse. When I take hold of an idea it does not stay a point. It
opens up. It becomes a shape I can blow up and turn over and take apart, lay across
another shape to find where the two of them touch, run forward and then back to
where it started, zoom into until it is the only thing in the world and pull back until
it is one dot in a field of other dots, and the whole time it stays wired to everything I
have ever connected it to, the right connections and the wrong ones both, all of them
live at once. I am not reading that field neutrally, the way a search would. The thing
doing the looking is me, the whole of me, my gut and my mood and my stubbornness
picking what lights up and which way I move through it, and that is the part you
cannot lift out without turning me back into a search engine. So I see where a thing
has to fit, the shape it is obligated to have, usually well before I could write it down in
a single symbol. Then the model gives me the symbols, the proof checker takes them
or throws them back, and I refuse anything that will not compile or does not match
the shape I am holding. That refusal is the one thing in this entire document that is
mine and only mine: the demand that it be true, and the throwing-out of everything
that wasn’t.

I am telling you all of this because it’s the engine. I did not come up through anywhere
that hands you a foundation and says trust us, this part is settled. No professors, no
colleagues, no field full of authority to lean back on when a claim got heavy. From
the outside that is a deficit. From the inside it is the whole reason any of this is solid:
when I meet a claim I either find the proof or I do not believe it, and that goes double
for my own, because my own are the ones I most want to wave through. It is how I


                                            61
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


am built. It is the only way I know to hold a thing and actually trust that I am holding
it.

So everything in here gets built from the ground up. It isn’t a courtesy to you. I build it
because I do not believe I understand a thing until I have built it with my own hands,
watched it stand up on its own, and tried to knock it over. I built this document the
exact way I built the machine, brick by brick, refusing each brick until it held weight.
That includes the parts you already knew cold before you opened this. I did not skip
them for you, and I could not skip them for me.

The vocabulary I had to go look up to do any of this sits at the back of the book, so
the argument comes first. If a word stops you, it is there. If you already know this
material, you never have to open it. But if you catch something in the basics that is
wrong, I want to know, and I mean that as a real ask. It isn’t politeness. Nothing in
here is correct just because I wrote it. Especially the parts I wrote.

On the name. I wanted to call it the meta machine. Then, in October 2021, Facebook
renamed its company Meta: a company taking a term for self-reference as its name
and draining the word of meaning in the same motion. So I went one level up, where
this machine already lives. The most meta move available, for a machine that runs on
meta-level reasoning, was to put my own name on the cover and take the word back.
That’s the whole of it, a meta move on a meta machine. It happens to be my dad’s
name too, and my wife’s now. So I asked them before I did it. They said go ahead.

2 What structure is
One word. That’s this whole section. Here’s the word, and you can decide whether to
stay. Structure.

I used that word for most of my life without once looking at it, which I suspect is
true of most people and most words, and it’s fine, right up until you do something
stupid. The stupid thing I did was build a machine that keeps a running bill, and the
bill has one rule I couldn’t talk it out of. You can arrange things however you like
for whatever price you name, including free. But the moment you ask the machine to
vouch for an arrangement, to put its own name on the claim that these things belong
together, there’s a charge, and it isn’t zero. How much, charged in what, why I picked
that one, and whether I had any business picking it at all: that’s all later, and some of
it I’m still not sure of. What I was sure of, standing there with the thing built, was that
I’d made something that charges for standing behind structure and I could not have
told you what structure was. It didn’t care. It can’t nod along the way a person does.
It needed the word to hold still, and the word had never held still for anyone, least of
all me. (The machine itself stays off the page until Part IV, on purpose. Until then, the
one rule is all of it that matters, and I want you to meet the rule in a toy you can hold.
A machine you’d have to take on trust can wait.)



                                            62
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


So I went looking at the people who’d wrestled it before me. Some of them have
been dead two thousand years and are still, I’d bet money, better at this than I am.
I used everything I had: language models, more than one, books, libraries, my own
gut, anything in reach. I don’t know if I found enough. I never do. There’s always
another shelf behind the one I was reading. And being dead and famous is not the
same as being right, so I pushed on each of them, and what follows is what I could
reach, pushed on as hard as I know how. The one thing I’m asking is that you push on
it with me, out loud, at your own kitchen table, because the first time through I was
the only one checking, and that’s not enough people.

The order I ran into them was a mess. Category theory came first, because I’d built
one by feel before I knew it had a name, and everything else came in whatever order
the next question dragged it in. I’m going to put them in the order where each one
leans on the last, which is mostly the order they happened. And none of it is an oracle.
History is where I start digging. It gets retold, smoothed over, and now and then made
up outright (there’s a drowning coming up that nobody can place), so every piece of
it is a lead to check, and I check the parts I lean on.

2.1 A string, a square, and a drowning nobody can place
Start with the oldest one, and start by doing it. Take a string. A guitar string, a rubber
band over an open box, anything that twangs. Pluck it. Now press it down exactly at
the middle and pluck half. That’s the same note, an octave up, the one that makes a
round sound like a round. Press at a third of the way along and pluck the long side:
that’s the fifth, one of the handful of intervals a bugle can play at all, which is why you
hear it all through bugle calls. Half. Two thirds. Small whole numbers, and your ear
says yes before your brain does. About twenty-five hundred years ago, in the south of
Italy, the followers of a man named Pythagoras are credited with finding exactly that,
and it’s as true in your kitchen tonight as it was on their hillside.

Here’s what they did with it, as best anyone can tell. Nothing survives that’s surely
from Pythagoras’s own hand. The earliest fragments are from a later member, Philo-
laus, and scholars argue over those. Mostly what’s left is Aristotle, one to two centuries
later, writing in his Metaphysics about them the way you’d write about the neighbours’
religion, and he says they took the elements of numbers to be the elements of all things:
everything is number. Not that everything can be counted. That the parts of numbers
are the parts of all things.

Stop and ask what I asked. What does that even mean? Is a chair a number? Does
a chair have a number tucked inside it somewhere? Aristotle doesn’t say, and he’s
reporting a belief he doesn’t hold. So don’t take it on his word, or theirs, or mine.
But before you push on it, know what it was holding up, because you can’t test a
load-bearing wall without knowing what sits on it. These weren’t people doing math
for fun on weekends. They were a brotherhood, with rules about what you could eat
and when you had to keep quiet, and that plucked string was their scripture. Halve


                                            63
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the string, hear the octave: to them that was proof that under the mess of the world
there were whole numbers in clean ratios, that the cosmos was a chord and they’d
heard it. “Everything is number” wasn’t a slogan. It was what they’d organized their
lives around. Which is exactly the kind of sentence you should be suspicious of, mine
included.

Now push, and push where they loved most: the square. Draw one, with a side
one unit long, any unit you like, and draw the line from one corner to the opposite
corner. Call that the diagonal. If everything is number, then the diagonal is some
whole number of parts long when the side is some whole number of parts, so the
diagonal divided by the side is a fraction, a whole number over a whole number.
Cancel anything the top and bottom share, the way four-sixths becomes two-thirds,
until they have no common factor left. I’ll call the top p and the bottom q, and the
letters are purely so I don’t have to keep writing “the top” and “the bottom.”

You need one fact about squares, and it’s the one Pythagoras is famous for. The square
built on the diagonal has exactly twice the area of the square built on the side. If you
want to see it for yourself, cut out two identical squares, cut the second one along both
diagonals into four triangles, and lay one triangle against each side of the first, its long
edge on that side. The outline is the square on the first one’s diagonal, and it’s made
of exactly two of the small squares; it’s a five-minute job with scissors. So p times p
is twice q times q. People write “times itself” as a small raised two, so that’s p2 = 2q2 ,
and that is the only piece of notation in this argument.

Twice anything is even. So p times p is even. An odd number times itself is always
odd (three times three, five times five, try a couple), so p itself must be even: it’s two
times something, and I’ll call that something r. Put it back in. Two r times two r is four
times r times r, and that equals twice q times q. Halve both sides: two times r times r
equals q times q. So q times q is even, so q is even too, by the same step as before. But
you already cancelled everything the top and bottom had in common, so they can’t
both be even. The argument has eaten itself, and when an argument eats itself the
thing you supposed at the start is false. There is no such fraction. The diagonal of a
square can’t be named by any ratio of whole numbers, ever. Aristotle reaches for this
very argument in his Prior Analytics as his example of proof by contradiction (suppose
the diagonal can be measured, and odd numbers come out equal to even ones), and
you just did it with a pencil.

There’s a story that a member of the brotherhood named Hippasus let this secret out,
and his brothers took him to sea and drowned him for it. I went and checked, because
it’s a good story and good stories are the ones to check. The oldest drownings I could
find are in Iamblichus, writing around AD 300, seven or eight hundred years after
Hippasus. In Iamblichus the man drowned by name is Hippasus, and what he gave
away was how to fit twelve pentagons together into a ball, the dodecahedron. A few
pages on, Iamblichus tells it again about whoever first let out the incommensurable,


                                            64
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


and that time he names nobody. Carl Huffman, who wrote the Stanford Encyclopedia
of Philosophy’s entry on Pythagoreanism, follows the historian Walter Burkert there
and finds no ancient writer who connects Hippasus to this discovery at all. So the
version with Hippasus drowned for the diagonal looks like two old stories stitched
together later. It’s a legend. But notice that the legend exists. Somebody, long after,
felt that a man should have been drowned for this. That’s how much was riding on it.
To whoever stitched the story together, the diagonal wasn’t a math problem. It was
the end of the world.

So the claim is dead, and you killed it. I only handed you the pencil. Now the question
that matters: what’s left? Look at your square again. The diagonal is still there. It still
stands in a perfectly definite relation to the side; you drew it, and nobody drowned.
That relation was real before anyone tried to put a number on it, and it stayed real after
the number failed. The relation came first. The number, when there is one, is a name
for the relation, and sometimes there isn’t a name. I’m going to keep that, and I want
you to keep it too, because you’re going to watch the same move get made again and
again as this book goes on: somebody says “everything is X,” and it’s true enough to
do real work with, and it sounds right when you pluck it, and then somebody draws
the diagonal. I don’t know yet whether the thing I built survives its own diagonal.
That’s a real question, and I’ll get to it.

2.2 Shapes poured into nothing
About a century and a half after the brotherhood, Plato, in a dialogue called the
Timaeus, tried to build the whole physical world out of geometry. Fire, air, water and
earth were four regular solids (the pyramid, the eight-faced one, the twenty-faced one,
and the cube), and the faces of those solids were built from exactly two kinds of right
triangle. You can make one of each in a minute: cut a square from corner to corner for
the first, and cut an equilateral triangle from a corner to the middle of the opposite
side for the second. Everything else, in Plato’s story, was a receptacle, a featureless
medium that takes on shape the way wax takes a seal. Structure, for Plato, is shape
laid into something that has no shape of its own.

Why did he care? He wanted a world made on purpose, by a craftsman working from
a plan, and triangles were the plan. Is it true? No, but not for the cheap reason. You
can’t refute a claim about what things are made of at the smallest scale by picking
one up; the smallest scale is exactly where your hands don’t reach, and Plato knew
that. What sank it is that it made no prediction anyone could check, and the people
who eventually did reach that scale, two thousand years on, found atoms, and atoms
aren’t triangles. The idea was a guess with no way to lose, until it lost. But push on
it and two things survive. One: structure is something laid in, and the stuff it’s laid
into doesn’t carry it by itself. That’s a real idea, and I’d ask you to keep it loosely for
now, because later I’ll have to ask whether the state a machine holds is the wax or the
seal. Two: Plato broke his own claim, in a later dialogue called the Parmenides, with an
objection that Aristotle later nicknamed the third man, and it’s the most useful mistake

                                            65
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


in this section. Take all the large things. Plato says they share one thing, Largeness.
But Largeness is itself large, so now there’s a further thing that all the large things and
Largeness share, and that one is large too, and it never stops. Try it with any property
you like; it runs away every time. The lesson, and I think it’s right though Plato never
quite accepted it himself: the structure of a collection is not one more member of the
collection. The plan isn’t a brick. Hold on to that one. It’ll come back in a place you
won’t expect.

2.3 Prove it from what you and I both accept
Around 300 BC, in Alexandria, Euclid wrote the Elements, and the thing to take from
it is not the geometry. It’s the method, and the method is the whole reason I trust
anything in this book, so give me a paragraph on it. He starts with definitions (“a
point is that which has no part”), five postulates (things he asks you to grant, like
“to draw a straight line from any point to any point”), and five common notions
(things nobody argues with, like “things which are equal to the same thing are also
equal to one another”). Then he derives everything else, four hundred and sixty-five
propositions, from only those, in order, each meant to use nothing but what came
before (he sometimes leans on things he never stated, and later geometers filled those
in). Not “trust me.” Not “it’s well known.” Here are the rules you and I both accept;
now watch. If you’ve ever been in an argument that ended with “well, that’s just
your opinion,” Euclid is the man who found a way out of that room, and I’m not
embarrassed to say I learned the way out from someone dead for two thousand three
hundred years. Four hundred and sixty-five times he does the same trick, and the
trick is everything.

And then there’s the one rule Euclid seems almost embarrassed by, and it’s a hole
worth falling into. His fifth postulate, the one about parallel lines, is long and awkward
next to the others, and for two thousand years people tried to prove it from the rest
so it wouldn’t have to be assumed. Proclus, the fifth-century philosopher who wrote
a commentary on Euclid’s first book, tried. Mathematicians in Persia and the Arab
world tried. In 1733 an Italian priest named Girolamo Saccheri spent a whole book
assuming it was false so he could watch the contradiction arrive, and he got pages deep
into what is now a perfectly good geometry before declaring that it was repugnant and
stopping. A century later three people, separately, took the step he wouldn’t: drop the
postulate, and what you get is other geometries that hold up just as well. Nonsense
never arrives. Farkas Bolyai begged his son János to stay away from the problem,
warning that it had swallowed years of his own life; the son went in anyway and came
out with one of those geometries. Here’s the part I keep: they found something real by
refusing to believe one of the rules everyone accepted, and checking what happened
without it. That’s the push, two thousand years long.

What is structure, to Euclid? Whatever the starting rules force. And when are two
shapes the same? Here’s the one you can do: cut out two paper triangles and lay one
on the other. If they coincide, they’re equal. That’s his fourth common notion, and it’s

                                            66
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


how he proves his fourth proposition, by picking up one triangle and setting it down
on another. Sameness is coinciding under a move. Keep that; it’s about to get very
general, and I didn’t see that coming either.

2.4 The statue and the bronze
Aristotle, Plato’s student, pulled the forms down out of heaven and put them inside
things, which was a bit rude to his teacher and also, I think, correct. His example, from
the Metaphysics: a bronze statue is bronze plus a shape, and being made of bronze is
no part of what it is to be a statue. The same shape in marble makes a different statue
with the same form. Matter and form, and form is what the thing is.

Push on it. Is that true? Take anything on your desk. Could the same thing be made
of something else? A coffee cup, sure. A sandwich, no; a sandwich made of wood is a
sculpture of a sandwich, and if you’ve ever tried to eat one you know the difference
matters. So the claim doesn’t hold everywhere. It holds exactly where the material
was never doing the work, and that’s a sharper thing than Aristotle said: structure
is what survives a change of material, in the places where the material didn’t matter.
Why do I care? Because this whole book bets that the record is a form. The material
shouldn’t matter: the same rule whether it sits on a tape, on a table of counters or on a
lambda term. I don’t get to just say so. Section 10 is where that bet gets checked, over
any base at all, and Part IV builds it once, on the smallest base I could find (Section 16).
Aristotle is the one who told me what the bet means.

2.5 Where things are, without numbers
In 1679 Gottfried Leibniz, who co-invented calculus and had opinions about every-
thing, wrote to the physicist Christiaan Huygens asking for something that didn’t
exist: a way to reason about where things are directly, the way algebra reasons about
how much, without ever laying down coordinates. He called it the analysis of situation.
Try it yourself. Describe where the furniture is in the room you’re sitting in without
using a single number. “The couch is against the wall. The table is between the couch
and the window. The lamp is next to the chair.” You just did it, and what you used was
relations between places and nothing else. Huygens wrote back that November and
was not impressed. It took roughly two hundred years for Leibniz’s idea to become a
field, and the field is called topology, and Huygens is remembered for other things.

What survives the push is the same thing that survived the square, coming at you
from the other side. Position is a relation among places. The numbers you lay on top
are a convenience, and they’re a convenience you can take away and still have the
room. I’ll be honest about why this one landed for me: the thing I built keeps track
of which things belong together, and I spent a long time thinking that was a list of
numbers before I understood it was a relation that the numbers were merely naming.
Leibniz had that in 1679. Huygens told him no. I’d like to think I’d have sided with
Leibniz. I probably would have sided with the famous guy.



                                            67
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


2.6 Naming a thing by saying when two are the same
In 1884, in a short book called The Foundations of Arithmetic, Gottlob Frege noticed
something you can check in your head right now. “Line a is parallel to line b” and “the
direction of a is the direction of b” say exactly the same thing. There is no fact in one
that isn’t in the other. But the second sentence has a new object in it, a direction, that
the first one doesn’t. Where did it come from? From the sameness. Once you can say
when two things count as the same, you’ve earned the right to name the thing they
share. Frege used exactly this move to say what a number is: the number of things
in a pile is whatever every pile you can match up with it, one to one, has in common.
That’s a residue with teeth: a sameness relation lets you name a new object.

Now push, because Frege pushed too hard, and it cost him. In his big system he
also assumed that any condition you can state picks out a collection, the collection of
everything that satisfies it. In June of 1902, a young British philosopher and logician,
Bertrand Russell, wrote him a short letter. Consider the collection of all collections
that are not members of themselves. Is it a member of itself? If it is, then by its own
rule it isn’t. If it isn’t, then it qualifies, so it is. Do it in your head; it flips every time
you look at it, like one of those drawings that’s a vase and then two faces and then a
vase. Frege’s floor had a hole in it, and he knew it the day he opened the letter, and
his second volume was already at the printer. The repair came from Ernst Zermelo in
1908 and it’s the one mathematics still stands on: you may only cut a collection out of
a collection you were already given. You don’t get to sort “everything.” You sort a pile.
I’ll tell you now that this rule shows up again, later, in a place where I had to obey it
or fall through the same hole, and I’ll point at it when the book gets there.

Frege’s reply is worth hearing, because it’s the best example I know of how to lose.
He wrote back within days. He didn’t hide it or argue around it. He said, more or
less, that arithmetic was tottering, and in an appendix to the volume that was about to
come out he wrote that hardly anything worse can happen to a scientific writer than
having a foundation give way right after the work is finished. Then he tried to fix it.
If I’m wrong about something in this book, and I’d bet I am somewhere, that’s how
I’d like to take it.

2.7 Choose the changes, keep what survives
By 1872 there were too many geometries. Euclid’s, and ones where parallel lines meet,
and ones with no such thing as distance, and nobody could say what made them all
geometry and kept them from being a pile of unrelated hobbies. Felix Klein, twenty-
three years old and taking up a professorship at Erlangen, published an answer in
a program paper that people still call the Erlangen program. Pick a set of allowed
changes: rotations, stretches, whatever you decide. Then a geometry is the study of
the properties that stay the same under those changes. Pick a different set of changes
and you get a different geometry on the very same page. Euclid’s is the one where
you may slide and turn a shape, and stretching it is off limits. And here’s the part I’d



                                              68
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


underline if this were my book, which it is: in Klein’s scheme any group of changes
can define a geometry. The choice is free. Nobody tells you which changes to allow.

You can do this one at your desk. Take any drawing and ask what’s still true after you
turn it upside down (lengths, angles), after you stretch it (lengths are gone by then;
which lines cross which is still there), after you crumple it (almost nothing but what
touches what). Three answers, three structures, one drawing. The residue: structure
is what survives a chosen set of changes, and “chosen” is doing real work in that
sentence. There’s no structure of a thing from nowhere. You have to say what you’re
allowed to do to it first. I didn’t know that when I started, and I’d been saying “the
structure of” things for years.

2.8 An invariance comes with a bill
In 1918 Emmy Noether, who at the time wasn’t allowed to qualify for a university
teaching post because she was a woman, and for a while taught courses advertised
under David Hilbert’s name, proved something that physicists still treat as close to
holy. Take a physical system whose laws can be written the way most of physics is
written, as “of all the paths the system could take, it takes one that makes a certain
total stationary” (the total is called the action, and stationary means a small change
to the path doesn’t change the total to first order; the path needn’t make it smallest,
and that’s all I’ll say about it here). For such a system, every continuous symmetry
that leaves the action unchanged comes with a quantity that is conserved. If the
action doesn’t change when you shift everything in space, momentum is conserved.
If it doesn’t change when you shift everything in time, energy is. A symmetry isn’t
decoration. It has a consequence downstream that you can measure with instruments.
I can’t hand you this one to do at the table; the proof needs calculus I’d have to build
first and I’d lose you and probably me, and the “written as an action” condition is
doing real work that I’m not going to unpack here. What I can hand you is the shape.
Structure, once it’s really there and the setting is the right kind, has consequences you
can measure. I’ll admit that’s the sentence that made me think a machine could carry
a bill for structure in the first place, and I’ll also admit I don’t yet know whether that
hope was reasonable. Noether makes it reasonable to ask. She doesn’t make it true,
and nothing I build in this book is a system with an action.

2.9 All of mathematics as structures
Starting in the 1930s, a group of young French mathematicians began publishing a
vast treatise under one made-up name, Nicolas Bourbaki, as if he were a single person.
He wasn’t. In 1948 he also applied for membership in the American Mathematical
Society, and the application was quietly turned down, which I find comforting. (The
historian Michael Barany has gone through that application, a second one a year later,
and the letters they set off.) Their goal was to rebuild all of mathematics on one idea:
a structure is a set of elements “whose nature has not been specified,” together with
one or more relations on them that satisfy stated axioms. They believed three kinds of



                                           69
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


structure were the mothers of all the rest: algebraic, order, and topological.

Push on it, and here’s what the historian Leo Corry found when he went through the
entire treatise looking for the place where this formal definition of structure actually
does any work: it “plays no actual role in the presentation of theories within the trea-
tise.” Outside the chapter that defines it, almost nowhere. And I found no argument
in their writing for why the mother structures number three. And the chapter on
category theory, which they promised their readers, never appeared; Corry is where
I found that too, and Ralf Krömer’s 2006 history of Bourbaki and categories in the
1950s follows the attempt. Why did the definition sit idle? Here’s my reading: the
thing their definition left out was the maps, the ways of carrying a structure from one
set to another, and the maps were where the weight was. So I keep two things from
Bourbaki. The right thing: relations on elements whose nature doesn’t matter, which
is Aristotle’s bronze in different words. And the warning: a structure stated without
its maps won’t carry the work. I learned that one the slow way, and the origin story
you just read tells it.

2.10 A set with some named relations
What mathematical logic eventually settled on, with the logician Alfred Tarski giving
the field its name, “the theory of models,” in 1954, is almost boring, and the boring
ones are the ones that last. A structure is a set, called the domain, plus whatever
relations and functions a chosen vocabulary names on it. Pick the vocabulary (Klein
again: you choose), and a structure is anything that gives those names a meaning.
Now I want to say “the smallest one,” and the word “smallest” has no meaning until I
say what I’m measuring, so here is the ruler: count the vocabulary. One name, taking
one thing at a time, with two possible answers. That’s a domain with one yes-or-
no property named on it. One question, put to each thing. Two honest limits, and
I’ll give them to you now, so you don’t have to find them. A vocabulary with one
named constant (“this one, here”) is exactly as small by my ruler and it doesn’t sort
anything, so the claim is “smallest that sorts.” Plain “smallest” would be false. And
one question only splits the domain into two groups when some things answer yes
and some answer no; if they all agree there’s one group and nothing was sorted. With
those limits said, and with the ruler said: by the count of names, the smallest structure
that sorts anything is one question. Someone with a different ruler (fewest symbols to
write down, say, or least information) might land somewhere else, and I’d want to see
where. Keep it. It’s about to turn into the whole section.

2.11 The structure is in the arrows
This is the one I met first, backwards. I’d built it by feel, in a rendering engine, as
“digital DNA,” and only went looking for its name after the thing already ran. In 1945
two mathematicians, Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane, published a paper
that founded a field now called category theory, and they said in plain words that it
was a continuation of Klein, which I’d have loved to know at the time. The move:



                                           70
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


stop asking what a thing is, and ask how it’s carried. A category is some objects and
some arrows between them, where arrows can be followed one after another and
every object has a do-nothing arrow to itself, plus two rules that make the following
dependable: following three arrows in a row gives the same result whether you pair
up the first two or the last two, and the do-nothing arrow really does nothing when
you tack it onto either end. That’s the whole definition. Two rules, and on the page
they look like nothing. The two rules are the part people skip, so slow down on them
for a second, because each one is there for a reason you can see.

Picture three dots in a row, A, B and C, an arrow f hopping from the first to the second
and an arrow g from the second to the third. Composition says there’s an arrow taking
the whole stride from A to C in one, g after f. Without it, every multi-hop path has to
be named on its own, and the structure falls apart into a pile of unconnected pairs, a
phone book without a search function. Associativity says that with a third arrow h on
the end, pairing up the first two and then adding h gives the same arrow as adding h
to the last two first. Both spell the same three-hop path, and if they came out different,
two people who built the same chain in different orders would hold two different
arrows, which is a bug: the chain is the thing, and how you assembled it isn’t. The
identity laws say that tacking the do-nothing loop onto either end of an arrow gives
back the arrow. If the loop changed things, it wouldn’t be the loop. Six terms, objects,
arrows, composition, identities, associativity, identity laws, and that’s all of Eilenberg
and Mac Lane’s definition.

Composing relations is older than the definition, too. Who put a name on that move
first? I went looking. Augustus De Morgan, writing on the logic of relations around
1860, took the “is” out of the old syllogism, put a general relation in its place, and
composed two relations to get the conclusion. The example that gets quoted from
that tradition is “x is the lover of a servant of y,” which is relational composition with
better gossip. When exactly he read that paper to the Cambridge Philosophical Society,
and on which pages it was printed, the sources disagree, which is a small reminder
that history is where you start digging. Then in 1870 Charles Sanders Peirce, the same
Peirce from the opening chapter, carried George Boole’s algebra of logic (the arithmetic
of true and false that Part IV comes back to, along with the story of Boole himself, a
largely self-taught schoolmaster) over to relations, with composition as one of its basic
operations, and he’s usually counted as the real founder of the theory. So following
one arrow after another is older than computers, older than categories, older than
Turing’s clerk: a nineteenth-century logician’s product of relations.

And where did they get the word? Not from mathematics. They borrowed category
from the philosophers, from Aristotle and Kant, and functor (a map from one whole
category to another) from the philosopher Rudolf Carnap, and then gave both words
exact meanings none of those philosophers had in mind. So Aristotle walks back into
this chapter without being asked: the man who put the form inside the bronze lent his
word to the field that keeps track of forms by their arrows. Does that change the laws?


                                           71
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


No. It’s a reminder that a word can start in philosophy and arrive in mathematics with
a precise meaning bolted on, which is the thing I’ve been trying to do with established
since the first page.

What a thing is is how it maps. For now the residue is the one Bourbaki missed:
structure lives in the maps. Nothing later in this book needs more category theory
than that sentence, and the latch of Section 10, where a record is pinned down by the
maps between a machine and the base it extends, is where the sentence does its work.

2.12 Structure is the part that compresses
Play this one with me. I write “th” and you guess the next letter. You said “e,” and
you were right. Now “the q”: you said “u.” Congratulations, you just measured
the structure of English. In 1948 Claude Shannon measured it properly, in a paper
that founded information theory, and found that about half of written English is
“determined by the structure of the language.” It’s the reason a zip file of a long letter
is so much smaller than the letter. Be careful what that says. It does not say that
every other letter is fixed by the ones before it; you just guessed “e” after “th” and you
could have been wrong (think “than”). It says that, on average and over long stretches,
about half of what’s written could be rebuilt from the rest: the text is roughly twice
as long as the choices in it. And he said why that matters in one line that I’d frame
if I framed things: the structure “allows one to make a saving in time” (he added “or
channel capacity”). The more you can predict, the less you have to read.

Thirty years later Jorma Rissanen, a Finnish information theorist at IBM’s research lab
in San Jose, turned that saving into a price. His idea is called the minimum description
length principle, and it says: the best model of some data is the one that makes the total
description shortest, where the total is the length of the model plus the length of the
data once the model has explained what it can. A model is paid for in bits. It’s worth
stating only if it saves more than it costs. Peter Grünwald, a statistician who leads
a machine learning group at CWI, the Dutch national institute for mathematics and
computer science in Amsterdam, in a tutorial you can find online, adds the footnote
that keeps this honest: the price of a model depends on the code you chose to write it
in, so the price itself needs a principle behind it, and nobody hands you that principle
for free.

That’s a lot of “length of” to swallow in one paragraph, so do one with me, with
numbers small enough to check on the back of an envelope. Every number in it comes
from a code I’m about to make up on the spot, and I’ll say every rule of the code out
loud, because Grünwald’s footnote is the whole point: change the rules and every
number moves.

Here’s the data. A row of thirty-two digits, each a 0 or a 1, and you and I agree in
advance that the row is thirty-two long, so nobody has to spend anything saying so:




                                           72
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele




                     0101010101010101 0101010101010101

(The space is only there to rest your eyes.) Now the code. Every description starts
with one digit that says which kind of description follows: 0 means “here’s the row,
written out,” 1 means “here’s a pattern, then the exceptions to it.” Each digit is one
yes-or-no answer, one bit, which is what Shannon’s unit is. Written out, the row costs
that first digit plus the thirty-two digits themselves: thirty-three bits, and there’s no
model in it at all. A pattern description goes like this. First five digits giving the length
of a little block, anything from 1 to 32, because five yes-or-no answers can pick out
one of thirty-two lengths. Then the block itself. The rule is “repeat the block until you
have thirty-two digits.” Then five digits for how many places the row disagrees with
the pattern (up to thirty-one, which is plenty here), and five more digits for each of
those places, saying which of the thirty-two it is.

Do it for the row above. The block is 01, two digits long. So the model costs 1 (which
kind) plus 5 (the block’s length) plus 2 (the block): eight bits. Then what’s left to say
about the data once the model has said its piece: the row disagrees with “repeat 01”
nowhere, so that’s five digits saying “zero exceptions” and nothing else. Five bits.
Total, thirteen, against thirty-three for writing it out. The pattern pays for itself, with
twenty bits to spare. That’s Rissanen’s sentence happening on paper: a model is worth
stating when it saves more than it costs.

Now spoil the row. Flip two of its digits anywhere you like. The model doesn’t change,
eight bits, but now the leftover says “two exceptions, here and here”: five plus five
plus five, fifteen. Total twenty-three. Still cheaper than thirty-three; the pattern still
pays, it just pays less, because the data has more to say that the model can’t. Flip
four, and the total is 8 + 5 + 4 × 5 = 33, a dead tie. Flip five and it’s thirty-eight, and
now writing the row out is cheaper than explaining it, and by Rissanen’s rule you
shouldn’t state the pattern at all, even though it’s still sort of there if you squint. So
“is there structure here?” has turned into a question with a number on each side, and
a break-even point you can find yourself: somewhere between four and five spoiled
digits, in this code.

And now change the code, because I promised you’d see the numbers move. Say I’d
used six digits for each exception’s place (wasteful, but nobody stopped me). Then
four spoiled digits cost 8 + 5 + 4 × 6 = 37, and the tie is gone; the pattern stopped
paying one spoiled digit sooner. Same row, same pattern, different verdict, and the
only thing that changed was a convention I chose. That’s Grünwald’s footnote, and
it’s why I won’t let you take any of those numbers anywhere else. They’re the price of
a description in one made-up code, a length of a written-down message, and nothing
more. They are not the charge I opened this book with. That charge, when the book
finally states it, is on one step a machine takes. How long anybody’s description is
doesn’t enter it, and if the two ever turn out to be related, that has to be shown. Both


                                             73
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


of them being counted in whole numbers doesn’t get to stand in for the showing.

Now push, because this is where “structure means information” gets born, and it’s
wrong, and it’s an easy thing to believe. Flip a fair coin two hundred times and write
down the string. Almost always, there’s no shorter way to say that string than to
say the whole thing. You can watch it happen in the little code above, cut to thirty-
two digits: a coin-flip row disagrees with “repeat 01” in about sixteen places, which
would cost eighty-odd bits to list, and even the one block guaranteed to fit with no
exceptions, the whole row used as its own block, costs 1 + 5 + 32 + 5 = 43. The written-
out row at thirty-three wins, and no pattern earns its keep. Nikolai Vereshchagin, a
mathematician at Moscow State University, and Paul Vitányi, a computer scientist at
CWI in Amsterdam, in a 2004 paper on exactly this question, put it without mercy:
every bit of a string like that is “meaningless information, random noise.” Maximum
information. Zero structure. So in this sense structure is the part that compresses, the
part where the “th” tells you about the “e,” and most information and most structure
are different things. Hold that one tightly, because if you built something that charged
for information, you’d be charging for the wrong thing, and for a while I wasn’t sure
which one I’d built.

And now notice that the word just changed meaning on you, and on me. I’m pointing
at it so it doesn’t slide past. Shannon and Rissanen and Vereshchagin mean regularity: a
pattern that lets you say something shorter. Tarski, a few pages back, and Paul Halmos,
a Hungarian-American mathematician whose short textbook on sets is coming up,
mean a set with named relations on it, and those two are not the same thing. Here’s
the test, and you can run it: number a thousand objects, flip a coin for each, heads goes
in group one, tails in group two. That’s a perfectly good sorting in the set theorist’s
sense, every object in exactly one group. And the list of who went where is a thousand
coin flips, which is to say it compresses about as well as a thousand coin flips, which is
to say not at all. Feed it to a code built like the little one, with the fields widened to fit
a thousand, and you get the coin-flip row again, only longer: no block earns its keep,
the written-out list wins, and by Rissanen’s rule there’s no pattern worth stating. By
the set theorist’s rule, the sorting is the structure, and it’s every bit as much a sorting
as “evens in one group, odds in the other,” which compresses to almost nothing. Same
kind of object, wildly different description lengths. So the two meanings don’t even
rank things the same way: one asks “is there a sorting?” and the answer is yes for
both; the other asks “does a short rule say who went where?” and the answer is yes
for evens and odds and no for the coins. Structure in the set theorist’s sense, none in
Rissanen’s. I’ll keep both meanings, and I’ll try to say which one I’m using, and when
I slip you’ll know what to look for.

2.13 The four parts of every computer
In 1936 Alan Turing described the machine that every computer you’ve ever touched
is a version of, and he did it before any of them existed. It’s the clerk with the pencil
from the opening chapter, written down as a machine. Write down its parts; there

                                             74
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


are four. A tape, divided into squares. A head that reads one square at a time and
can write on it and move left or right. A finite list of states the head can be in. A
table of rules: in this state, reading this symbol, do this. That’s all, and two different
things are true about it that get run together. Every other recipe anyone has proposed
as a general formalization of “a procedure,” before or since, computes exactly what
this one does; those are theorems, proved one pairing at a time, and Turing himself
sketched one of them, the pairing with the logician Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus,
in an appendix to the 1936 paper. That it also captures everything a person could
ever carry out by rote, everything “computable” in the plain-English sense, is a claim,
called the Church-Turing thesis, and nobody has proved it, because the plain-English
side isn’t a mathematical object. Turing himself kept those two apart in the 1936 paper,
and so will I. There’s a third claim that gets stacked on top, and it’s a different kind
again: the physical Church-Turing thesis, that every device you could build out of real
stuff computes no more than this machine does. That one is a claim about physics. No
mathematical proof can settle it. Nobody has built a device that breaks it. Your laptop,
your phone, every server in every data center compute nothing a Turing machine
can’t; what differs between them is speed, space, energy, and cost. Hold on to that last
word. Cost is where this book lives.

Now do the thing I did, and do it honestly. Look through those four parts for a place
that says “these squares belong together.” I couldn’t find one. Any grouping has to
live in the table, as a rule, or on the tape, as marks, which is to say as bytes like any
other bytes. Maybe you can find a slot I missed. I’d want to know. I looked for a long
time and I kept not finding it, and not finding something is weaker than proving it
isn’t there, so I’ll be careful about what I claim from that.

In 1972 David Parnas, a software engineer, wrote a short paper that every programmer
should be made to read and most haven’t, on how to cut a program into modules.
He took one small program and cut it two ways. Both worked. But one was easy
to change later and the other wasn’t, and the easy one could be “much less efficient”
if talking between modules cost anything. His point: a module is “a responsibility
assignment,” a decision about who answers for what, and how you cut decides what
every later change costs. If you’ve ever maintained someone else’s code, you’ve paid
Parnas’s bill, probably at two in the morning. What survives the push: a division is
a commitment. It changes what the work costs. It is no caption, no label stuck on
afterwards. I’d like to say the thing I built understood that from the beginning. It
didn’t. I did, eventually.

2.14 Laying them all down
Now lay every one of those on top of the others and see what shows through. Here
are the seven things I think I see. They’re my overlay, the places where I see the
sources agreeing. The sources never proved it together; some of them never met,
and some of them disagree (Bourbaki left out the maps that Eilenberg and Mac Lane
built everything on; Shannon’s structure and Tarski’s are two different words, as I just

                                           75
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


showed you). You’ve pushed on each source yourself by now, so you’re in a position
to tell me if I’m seeing things.

A list of seven slogans would be easy to nod at and impossible to check, so I’m going
to carry one thing through all seven and let you watch each one add to the one before
it. The thing is the square you drew for the Pythagoreans, side, diagonal and all. Draw
a few more on the same sheet: one small, one big, the small one again but tilted, and
one stretched out into a long rectangle. You’ll want a pile.

Structure is about relations among things. The things themselves aren’t it. The di-
agonal, the bronze, Leibniz’s room, Bourbaki’s unspecified elements, Tarski’s named
relations, the arrows. On your sheet, what makes a square a square was never the ink.
It’s that the four sides match and the corners are square, and that the diagonal stands
to the side the way it does whether or not any number names it. Every one of those
is a relation among parts. But on its own this first thing is too loose to use, because a
sheet of paper is drowning in relations: this square is left of that one, this one is nearer
the coffee ring. Which relations count?

Structure is what stays the same under a chosen set of changes. Euclid’s triangles laid
together, Klein’s allowed moves, Noether’s symmetry, Frege’s direction that every
parallel line shares. That’s the answer the first thing was missing. The relations that
count are the ones that survive the moves you’ve decided to allow. Slide the small
square across the sheet, turn it, and the diagonal still stands to the side exactly as
before; “left of the coffee ring” doesn’t make it across. The second thing is a filter on
the first.

The same structure can be carried by different stuff. The statue in marble. Two sets
that answer the same vocabulary the same way. This is the second thing again with
one more change allowed: swap the material. Cut the square out of cardboard, or lay
it out in string on the table, and if the relations survive, it’s the same square in every
way you agreed to care about. Aristotle’s bronze is one more thing you agreed not to
look at, and the wooden sandwich is what happens when the material was never on
that list.

The first act of structure is a sameness that sorts a pile you were already given. Euclid’s
first common notion, Frege’s direction, Tarski’s one question, and Russell’s letter, with
Zermelo’s repair that you must start from a pile. This is where the overlay stopped
being a list for me and turned into a shape, so slow down here with me. Look at
your pile of drawings and say: two of them count as the same when an allowed
move carries one exactly onto the other. Watch what happens to the pile. It falls into
groups. The small square and its tilted twin go together; the big one sits on its own;
the rectangle sits on its own. And it falls cleanly, nothing half in one group and half in
another, for a reason you can check. Klein’s allowed moves always come with three
guarantees: doing nothing counts as a move, every move can be undone, and two
moves in a row is again a move. Those three are, in different clothes, “everything is


                                            76
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


the same as itself,” “if this matches that, then that matches this,” and “if this matches
that and that matches a third, then this matches the third.” Put the last two together
and you get Euclid’s first common notion, “things which are equal to the same thing
are also equal to one another.” So the second thing, sameness under chosen moves, is
a sorting of the pile the moment you ask which drawings it calls the same. Frege did
it with lines and parallels. Tarski’s one question does it in the crudest way there is, by
cutting the pile in two. And the pile has to be there first, because a sameness has to be
a sameness among something; that’s Russell’s letter, and Zermelo’s repair.

Adding structure rules possibilities out. Every one of Euclid’s postulates is a door
closed. Half of English is already decided. A conserved quantity limits where a
system can go. On your sheet: once the small square and its tilted twin are in one
group, you’ve given up the right to answer any question the moves respect differently
for the two of them. Tell me the side of one and the diagonal of the other isn’t an open
question any more. A sorting is a bundle of doors closed at once.

Held structure gets used without re-deriving it. Shannon’s saving in time. Rissanen’s
compression. Parnas’s one-module-at-a-time. Leibniz’s analysis of situation, reason-
ing about where things are straight from their relations, with no coordinates laid down
first. This is the fifth thing paying out. The doors you closed are doors you never
have to check again: know which group a drawing is in and you know everything the
group shares without getting the ruler out, the same way the row of 01 never needed
writing out. With one catch that I’ll need a whole section for: it only pays if you kept
the sorting somewhere you can read it back.

And structure is always relative to a chosen frame. Klein’s group. The vocabulary. The
code you compress against. Parnas’s criteria. Nobody gets to say “the” structure of a
thing without saying from where, and I do it constantly, so watch me for it. On your
sheet: allow stretching as one of the moves and the rectangle walks over and joins
the squares; allow only slides and turns and it doesn’t. Same pile, same ink, different
groups, because I chose different moves. The groups were never in the paper. They
were in the paper and the choice, together.

So here’s how I think they hang together. Relations are what structure is made of. The
chosen moves pick which relations count, and a change of material is just one more
move. Asking which things the moves call the same sorts the pile. The sorting closes
doors, and closed doors are what you get to skip later. And because the moves were
chosen, all of it is relative. Read that way, the fourth thing sits in the middle: it’s where
the first three turn into something you can write down, and where the last three get
their start.

That’s my reason for starting the next subsection with a sorting, and I want to be exact
about what kind of reason it is, because it’s mine. None of these people said “start
with a partition.” Klein would tell you to start with the moves, Eilenberg and Mac
Lane with the arrows, Shannon with the probabilities. What I can actually point at


                                             77
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


is narrower. In the framings about when two things are the same shape or the same
kind (Euclid laying one triangle on another, Klein’s moves, Frege’s directions, Tarski’s
question) there’s a moment where somebody decides what counts as the same, and
that decision, written down, is a sorting of a pile. In Shannon, Rissanen and Noether I
can’t find that moment as cleanly, and I’m not going to bend them until I do. So the
overlay doesn’t prove that a sorting comes first. It shows me where the framings I
trust most keep putting their first foot down, and I’m putting mine there too.

I looked for a framing that denies any of the seven and didn’t find one, which could
mean there isn’t one or could mean I didn’t look where it lives. If you know of one,
I’d like to see it.

2.15 The smallest piece
Now the sentence I wanted to say at the top and had no right to until here, and even
here I have to split it in two, because half of it is a textbook fact and the other half is
me. The piece of structure I’m going to start from is a partition.

The textbook half: a partition and an equivalence relation are the same object. That’s
Paul Halmos, Naive Set Theory, 1960, section seven, and you could read that section
before dinner. Here it is in words. Take any pile of things. An equivalence relation on
it is a way of saying “these two count as the same” that behaves the way sameness
should: everything is the same as itself; if a is the same as b then b is the same as
a; and if a is the same as b and b the same as c, then a is the same as c. Every such
relation sorts the pile into groups, the things that count as the same go together, and
every sorting into groups hands you back a relation, “same group.” Do one and then
the other and you land where you started, in both directions. So a partition and an
equivalence relation are one object seen from two sides, and that’s the fourth thing on
the overlay, the sorting of a given pile, now with a name and a page number.

Here it is in the exact form, since this is the first place the book uses one. A set is a pile,
x ∈ X means “x is in the pile X,” and a relation on X is any rule ∼ that, for each pair
of things, says whether x ∼ y holds. A few more marks show up below, and each is
a word in disguise. The buckets are written S j , with j saying which bucket (finitely
many buckets in every example here, though nothing below needs that). A cap, S j ∩ Sl ,
is “what the two buckets share,” and ∅ is the empty pile. And curly braces with a
colon, { y ∈ X : y ∼ x }, mean “the pile of every y in X for which y ∼ x holds”; the
theorem writes that pile [ x ], the things that count as the same as x.


Definition 2.1 (Equivalence relation, partition). A relation ∼ on a set X is an equiv-
alence relation when it is reflexive (x ∼ x), symmetric (x ∼ y implies y ∼ x), and
transitive (x ∼ y and y ∼ z imply x ∼ z). A partition of X is a collection of non-
empty subsets of X, the blocks, such that every member of X lies in exactly one block.
Spelled out, with the blocks written S j : each S j is non-empty, no two share a member
(S j ∩ Sl = ∅ when j ̸= l), and together they cover everything (every member of X lies


                                              78
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


in some S j ).


Theorem 2.1 (Sameness and sorting are one object). Every equivalence relation on X
determines a partition, whose blocks are the classes [ x ] = { y ∈ X : y ∼ x }; every partition
determines an equivalence relation, “x and y lie in the same block”; and the two constructions
undo each other.

Proof. The classes are non-empty (x ∈ [ x ] by reflexivity) and cover X. If z lies in [ x ]
and in [y], then z ∼ x and z ∼ y, so x ∼ y by symmetry and transitivity, and then
[ x ] = [y] by transitivity again; so the blocks don’t overlap. “Same block” is plainly
reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Going relation to partition to relation returns
x ∼ y exactly when x and y share a class, which is the original relation; going partition
to relation to partition returns the original blocks.

This is textbook mathematics (Halmos, section 7), and the book uses it as a foundation.
I’m claiming nothing new in it. Checked as nec_t_rel_of_partition_equiv, n
ec_t_blocks_of_equiv_partition, nec_t_rel_round_trip and nec_t_b
locks_round_trip (NecTPartition.v).

And the smallest structure that sorts, by my ruler in Tarski’s setup, the one question,
is the same object a third time. Put a yes-or-no question to every thing in the pile. The
ones that say yes are one group and the ones that say no are the other. Going the other
way, a two-group partition becomes a question the moment you point at one group
and call it “yes.” The only thing a question has that the partition doesn’t is which
group got the label. So the set theorist’s first step and the logician’s first step are the
same step, and nobody has to pick a side, which is a relief, because it’s an argument
you can lose with yourself for a long time.

That’s the textbook half. Now mine, and hold it looser, because Halmos says nothing
about “smallest” or “first” and I’d be lying if I let his page number carry my sentence.
In what I’m going to build, the order goes: a pile, then groups in the pile, then
whatever connects one group to another, and the groups come first because a question
needs something to be about and a connection needs somewhere to land. That’s an
order for my construction. It is not a law that every account of structure has to start by
sorting. You could start with an ordering instead (“this one comes before that one”),
or with arrows between the things themselves and no groups at all, and people do,
and nothing I’ve shown you rules that out. So the honest sentence is: a partition is
where I chose to start, it is the smallest start by the ruler I gave you, and I chose it
because it’s the first thing that can be right or wrong about a pile and the last thing I
could take away without everything I build on it coming down. If you have a smaller
start by a ruler you can state, I want to see it. It would change this book.




                                              79
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


2.16 Buckets
So here’s the smallest piece, done once, for real. Take everything in front of you
and sort it into buckets: nothing in two buckets, nothing left on the floor. That’s the
whole of the definition. It’s the thing you do with a kindergartner and a pile of blocks,
and I am aware that I’ve just marched you past Pythagoras, Plato, Euclid, Frege and
Noether to arrive at a pile of blocks. Keep the blocks anyway. They’re about to cost
you something.

Ten blocks. Red ones in one bucket, square ones in another, everything else in a third.
Now a red square turns up, as they do, and you’ve got your first crisis: it belongs
in two buckets and the rule says one. So this isn’t a partition yet, and you have to
decide which bucket wins. That decision is the whole thing. A partition is a pile of
small rulings like that one, and once you’ve made them all, the pile is holding a fact
it wasn’t holding a minute ago. The formal version says the same thing with fewer
words and more squiggles, and you’ve already seen it: it’s the definition of a partition
a few pages back (Definition 2.1). Non-empty buckets, nothing in two, nothing on the
floor.

Here’s the part that isn’t kindergarten. Why would that fact cost anything? Watch
what it does to one question. Before the buckets, “are these two in the same group?”
means working it out: go find the first one, go find the second one, apply the rule to
each, compare. After the buckets, it’s a glance: read the first one’s bucket, read the
second one’s bucket, done. And the glance costs the same when the pile goes from ten
blocks to a billion. That’s Shannon’s saving in time and Parnas’s one-module-at-a-time,
the sixth thing on the overlay, showing up in a kindergarten.

Now push on it, because that paragraph sells more than it should, and I want you to
see where. The partition didn’t give you the glance. A table gave you the glance: a
written-down line for each block saying which bucket it went in. The partition is the
fact; the table is one way of holding the fact so it can be read back fast, and you had
to build the table, and you have to store it, and it has to be the kind of thing you can
read in one look (a bucket number, say; a list of every block in the bucket would have
you searching through it again). Anybody who’s used a database has met this table;
it’s what an index is, and an index is a thing you build, store, and keep up to date,
and none of that comes free. Take the table away and keep the partition and you’re
back to working it out. And sometimes there was never a search to save: if the rule is
“evens here, odds there,” you can answer “same group?” by looking at the last digit of
each, no buckets needed. So here’s what survives: holding a sorting in a form you can
read back is worth something, and building that form cost something, and those are
already two different events. Building the table, storing it, checking that it’s right, and
deciding to rely on it are four different things. The question this book is about lives in
the gap between the third and the fourth, and nothing in the kindergarten has shown
you yet that there’s a charge in that gap. It’s shown you there might be a place for one.



                                            80
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


So who, in everything I read, says what the bill is? I found three answers that come
close, and I’ll be exact about how close, because this is the edge of what I know.
Rolf Landauer, in 1961, and Charles Bennett after him, say that any step which takes
two possible situations and makes them one, erasing a bit or merging two paths a
computation could have taken, has to push some disorder out into the world, which in
a real machine means heat. I mean that literally. It’s the place, of all I’ve found, where
a fact about information turns into a fact about heat, though at room temperature the
amount for one bit is far too small to show up on anybody’s electricity bill. In 2012
a lab in Lyon erased one bit, held in a single tiny bead, and measured the average
heat it gave off coming down toward Landauer’s floor as the erasing was slowed, and
other labs have found the same since. Not everyone accepts the principle in general,
and I’ll come back to the people who don’t. Is sending blocks to buckets a step of
that kind? Push, because it depends on what you keep. If you keep each block and
write its bucket next to it, you’ve lost nothing; you can read the block right back off
the pair, and Bennett’s whole point in his 1973 paper was that a computation which
keeps its inputs can be run without any such step at all. If instead you throw the block
away and keep only the bucket label, then two different blocks can leave the same
label behind, and that is a many-to-one step, the kind Landauer charges for. Both are
things people call “sorting into buckets.” Only the second loses a distinction. So the
bucket by itself doesn’t hand you a Landauer bill. The forgetting does, when there is
forgetting, and whether a given machine forgets is a question about that machine. It
has to be answered on the page, and I won’t wave at it here. Rissanen says a model
is paid for in the bits it takes to state, and Grünwald says the price depends on the
code. Parnas says a bad cut is paid for later, at two in the morning. And that’s where
it stops. Rovelli, back in the opening chapter, prices a choice that sticks, and his choice
is one nobody could predict, which Section 5 shows is a different act. I couldn’t find
anyone who says that the moment you vouch for a grouping, the moment you stand
behind “these belong together,” has a price of its own. Just arranging them that way is
a different act. That could mean nobody says it. It could mean I didn’t find the person
who does. I honestly can’t tell you which.

So that’s where I am at the end of one word. Holding a sorting in readable form is
worth something and cost something, forgetting where things came from costs heat,
and standing behind a sorting is a different act from either, and nobody I found has
priced it. (Rovelli’s price is on a choice nobody could predict, and that’s a different
act again.) You can walk back through all of that and tell me where it breaks. Maybe
there’s no such bill. Maybe I’m about to spend a book chasing a charge that nobody
owes, which would be an extremely me thing to do. The next two sections are me
trying to find out whether that charge is real on any machine at all, mine or anybody’s,
and if the answer comes back no, you should stop reading there. I would have stopped
writing there too.

Part II

The axiom
3 A record and a toll
I left you with a question I couldn’t answer: something pays for the glance, and I
couldn’t find anyone who says the moment of vouching for a grouping has a price of
its own. Before I go looking for that price in anything complicated, I want to try the
opposite. Build the smallest thing that could possibly carry such a bill, on paper, with
a pencil, write the bill into its rules, and see what follows from it. If nothing follows in
something with five parts, nothing is going to follow in something with five thousand.
I want to find that out on page one. Page four hundred is too late.

One thing about where the buckets went, because you’ll notice they vanish for a while.
Part I ended on vouching for a grouping, and what I’m about to build prices vouching
for anything at all: a flag goes up, and the rule doesn’t ask what the flag is standing
behind. A sorting is the first kind of claim I care about. It isn’t the only kind, and
the book comes back to what a flag stands behind in Section 8, and on a machine in
Section 16, where a flag stands on a checked claim. Until then nothing leans on the
buckets. The floor in this section, the reason for it in the next, and the latch in Part III
all work for any yes-or-no reading whatsoever, partition or no partition.

But first the word, because I’ve got a new one and I don’t trust it either. Record.
Receipt. Certificate. Vouch. People have been making marks that other people are
supposed to rely on for a very long time, and I wanted to know what they thought
they were doing, and what it cost them, and whether any of them ever said the thing
I need said. So, same deal as before: here’s what I could reach, pushed on with you,
and I’ll tell you where the search ran out.

3.1 Clay, seals, and seven witnesses
Start a little over five thousand years ago, in the Near East, with people who counted
sheep with little clay tokens. To send a count across a distance without the courier
changing it, they put the tokens inside a hollow clay ball, pressed the shapes of the
tokens onto the outside while the clay was soft, and sealed it. The archaeologist Denise
Schmandt-Besserat has spent a career on these, and she puts the practice at around
3300 BC; the ball is called a bulla. Here’s the push, and you can do it with a cookie tin:
what makes it a record is the outside. It shows what’s inside, and you have to break it
to get in. Opening it destroys it. Tampering shows. That’s a real idea and it will show
up again in a form you won’t expect: a record is worth something only if it can’t be
silently undone.

Now law, which is where people get serious about who’s allowed to say what hap-
pened. The book of Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen: nobody is convicted on the word


                                            82
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


of one witness; it takes “two or three.” The Roman jurist Gaius, writing in the second
century, says a will the praetor will honour is one sealed by seven witnesses. Seven.
Why seven? Gaius doesn’t say. The legal historian Henry Maine, in 1861, had an
answer: the older Roman will was a mock sale, done in front of five witnesses, a man
holding the scales, and the buyer of the estate, seven people in all, and when the
ceremony fell away the seven seals kept the count. Maine’s is the only account of it I
found, so treat it as his. Gaius’s own text does show they kept those old formalities
around a will, and it isn’t hard to see why anyone would: one person can lie, and
a will moves a fortune, and the dead man can’t object. So the record isn’t the paper.
It’s the number of independent people who have put their own seal, their own name,
their own risk, next to the claim. Try it: write “paid five dollars, signed A” on a napkin
and ask a friend to forge it. Takes them ten seconds. Now require two other people
to initial it at the moment of payment and each keep a copy. Your forger needs two
accomplices or has to match two copies held in two other pockets. The claim didn’t
change. What stands behind it did.

Which brings me to seals, and the medieval historian Michael Clanchy, whose book
is called From Memory to Written Record. England between the Norman Conquest and
the early 1300s was learning to trust writing. Until then it had trusted people who
remembered. The lesson was painful: seals were forged, charters were forged, and
historians today have a whole craft of telling real charters from fake ones because the
fakes are so many. A seal is only as good as whoever holds the stamp. Keep that one
too, because in 2011 a certificate authority called DigiNotar found out, at the cost of its
existence, that a mathematically perfect signature is worth exactly what the custody
of the key is worth, and intruders had taken control of the machines that signed. Nine
