hundred years, same failure. I find that oddly comforting.

And then the obvious next question: if seals could be forged, what caught the forgeries?
Not the seals. The most famous forged record in European history is the Donation
of Constantine, a document in which the emperor Constantine supposedly handed
rule over Rome and the western empire to the Pope. It was most likely written in the
eighth century, some four hundred years after Constantine died, and it was leaned on
for centuries. Around 1440 a scholar named Lorenzo Valla took it apart by its Latin:
the language belonged to a much later age, and it used words, “satraps” among them,
that no Roman of Constantine’s day would have used for his officials. (Valla wasn’t
even first. Nicholas of Cusa, a German churchman and philosopher who later became
a cardinal, had already called it a forgery in 1433, in De concordantia catholica, a long
book on how the Church and the empire ought to hang together. I know that from the
reference works, and I haven’t read the book. Valla’s is the version people remember,
which is a pattern that keeps turning up.) Look at what kind of check that was. The
question wasn’t “is the stamp real.” It was “could these words have been written
when they say they were.” A record can pass the first and fail the second, which is a
hint that what I keep calling one thing, a record, is doing more than one job.



                                            83
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


3.2 Two columns and a stamp
Here’s the one I’d never have guessed mattered. Bookkeeping. Around 1300, the
ledger of a Florentine company called Farolfi, kept at its branch in Provence, shows
the earliest complete example anyone has found of a trick merchants were working
out: write every transaction twice, once where the money came from and once where
it went, and the two columns have to balance. The treasurers of the city of Genoa kept
their ledger for 1340 that way, and accounting historians still count it among the most
famous government account books of the Middle Ages kept in double entry. And
in 1494 a friar named Luca Pacioli printed the method in a mathematics book, and it
spread. That’s double-entry bookkeeping, and it’s easy to take it for just a tidy habit.

Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them
at night. Now have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals
disagree; you catch it. Now have them change the matching entry in both columns.
The totals agree. You’ve caught nothing. Push on that and you’ve found what double
entry actually is: a trap for slips. A careful liar walks straight through it. Did Pacioli
see that? I can only get at it secondhand. The scholar Forrester, in a paper on the
University of Strathclyde’s accounting-history pages, reads him as reporting that in
many places the books were taken to the local consul to be authenticated before a
single entry went in. The stamp is a witness again, from outside. The two columns are
the discipline; the stamp is the claim that someone other than you will stand behind
the fact that these are the books. No other set gets that stamp. Keep both halves
separate in your head. One is a method. The other is a commitment.

And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society,
founded in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto Nullius in verba: take
nobody’s word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody’s words, naturally. It’s
half a line of the Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying he isn’t
bound to swear by the words of any master. So the society that takes nobody’s word
for it took its motto from a poet and cut the line to fit. That’s not a contradiction, and
it’s a nice picture of the method: borrow what’s useful, say whose it was, and don’t
swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about what that meant in
practice, and the answer is more interesting than the slogan. Robert Boyle, pumping
the air out of a glass globe to see what happens to a candle or a bird, had three
problems: the machine, the report, and the witnesses. He solved the third by having
gentlemen present who’d sign their names, and the second by writing the report so
richly that a reader who wasn’t there could picture the scene and count as a witness
anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he notes, dryly, that the air pump
was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So there was a cost. It just wasn’t
a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the instrument and of getting enough
people into the room. Hold on to that distinction. The rest of the book hangs on it.




                                           84
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


3.3 A demon, and the step that pays
Now the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James Clerk
Maxwell, in a letter to his friend the Scottish physicist Peter Guthrie Tait, imagined a
“very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at a tiny door between two halves of
a box of gas, letting fast molecules through one way and slow ones the other, so that
one side heats up and the other cools with no work done, which is supposed to be
impossible. The being got called Maxwell’s demon, and physicists have been arguing
about it for a hundred and fifty years, which should tell you something.

In 1929 Leo Szilard, a young Hungarian physicist working in Berlin, cut the demon’s
box down to a single molecule, and that made information part of the accounting.
The tempting move, and the one Szilard’s own accounting made, is to put the whole
bill on finding out which side the molecule is on. Bennett separated finding out
from restoring the memory for another round: measuring onto a blank record can,
in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting an unknown record is a
different operation. That does not make a real measuring device free to build or run. It
says that learning and resetting do not carry the same unavoidable entropy cost, and
I’m about to pick a step to charge, so I need that distinction before I do.

Bennett’s version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost is
“the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.” Erasing, or taking
two possible situations and making them one. And in the same paper he lists copy-
ing unknown data onto a blank place to write among “the most important logically
reversible operations,” the kind he says can, at least in principle, be run thermodynam-
ically reversibly. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is priced by physics,
the unavoidable erasure charge belongs to forgetting the unknown record. Making a
record carries no such charge of its own. Read that twice. It’s not what I expected
either.

I’ll put the rest of the lineage quickly, because it all points the same way. Regulators
who make brokers keep records on media that can’t be rewritten (the SEC required
exactly that, write once and read many, from 1997 until 2022, when it allowed an audit
trail as the other way to comply) are pricing the hardware. The act itself stays free.
Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the timestamping that Bitcoin’s footnotes lead back to
in the opening chapter, chained time-stamped records together with hashes so that
changing an old entry breaks every entry after it (and Ralph Merkle’s hash tree, from
his 1979 Stanford thesis on secrecy and authentication, lets one short value vouch for
a great many records); try it with five lines and a made-up sum, change line two, and
watch every number below it move. That makes a change visible. It doesn’t make it
cost. Proof-of-work, which the computer scientists Cynthia Dwork and Moni Naor
proposed in 1992 to make junk mail expensive and which Bitcoin later chained, is the
one framing where a record genuinely costs, and what it charges for is a search: how
many tries it took to find a lucky number. An empty block costs the same work as
a full one. So the work prices the search. The moment anything becomes certified

                                            85
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


costs nothing extra. Robert Floyd and Tony Hoare, two computer scientists asking
how you’d prove a program does what it’s supposed to, attached claims to points in
a program in 1967 and 1969 (“whenever you get here, this is true”), and the claim is
backed by a proof that’s paid for off the machine. And the certificates of complexity
theory, which go back to Stephen Cook’s 1971 work on NP, are strings designed to be
cheap to check: hand me the certificate and I can confirm the claim quickly. Whether
they’re also expensive to find is the famous open question of the field, P versus NP,
and nobody knows; what’s settled is only the cheap half. That’s the opposite of a
price on vouching: the whole design goal is that checking a claim costs nearly nothing.
And from statistics, a ledger that runs the other way: Dean Foster and Robert Stine’s
alpha-investing (2008) runs a long string of tests against a budget of allowed false
alarms, where every test spends some of the budget and every discovery, a rejection
that stands, pays some back. That’s the other way round from a toll on vouching: the
test pays, and a discovery that stands gets paid.

3.4 What they all agree on, and who they rule out
Lay them down, and this time what shows through is not one thing. It’s five different
jobs that the word “record” has been doing, and I’d been letting one word carry all
five. Each has a corpse next to it, and the corpses are different too.

Durability: the record can’t be silently undone. The bulla, the write-once disk, the
hash chain, Bennett’s card that has to be wiped. The corpse is the editable log, and
the company that kept its debts off the books: Enron hid its debt in side entities set
up to keep it off the balance sheet, which is how the Justice Department described the
scheme in 2002, and its auditor, Arthur Andersen, shredded the paper. Andersen was
convicted for the shredding that year, and the Supreme Court threw the conviction
out in 2005 over how the jury had been instructed; either way, those books recorded
nothing. But notice this job doesn’t need a witness at all. A copy will do: a hash chain
nobody signed is still hard to change quietly, so long as somebody else holds the latest
link, because a chain with no copy anywhere can be rewritten from end to end and
recomputed, and nobody would know.

Authenticity: the record came from who it says it came from. Seals, the signature
only a key-holder can make, the consul’s stamp. The corpse is the forged charter and
DigiNotar. This job is about custody of a stamp, and it’s a different job from durability;
a perfectly authentic entry can still be erased, and a perfectly durable one can still be
a forgery.

Evidence: enough independent people stand behind the claim that lying is expensive.
Two witnesses, seven seals, Boyle’s gentlemen. It rules out anonymous assertion, and
it rules out “the universe keeps the receipt”: information spread into the environment
is not a record anyone can read or rely on. This one is about numbers of people and
their risk. Paper has nothing to do with it.

Accounting: the record checks itself for slips. The two columns. And here’s a thing to

                                           86
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


keep straight: the second column is not an outside witness. It’s you, checking you. It
catches a dropped digit. A careful liar gets past it, as you saw. It belongs on this list as
its own job, separate from the seven seals.

Cheap checking: a record whose correctness can be confirmed for much less than it
cost to make. Cook’s certificates, the signature, the hash. This one isn’t universal, and
I thought it was. Whether checking needs to be cheaper than making depends on who
you’re worried about and how much a wrong record costs you; plenty of records are
checked by redoing the whole thing, and that’s fine when the thing is small.

Now the thing none of them says. Not one of these jobs is pricing the act of certifying.
Bennett prices merging and erasing, which a certifying step might or might not be.
Proof-of-work prices a search the designer chose. Bookkeeping prices a discipline.
Witnesses and seals price showing up and guarding the stamp. I looked, with every-
thing I had, and that’s where it ran out. If the bill exists, nobody in this lineage wrote
it down, and that’s either because it isn’t there or because the one person who did
write it down is on a shelf I never found. So I’m going to have to try it myself, on the
smallest thing I can build, and let you watch. And I’ll have to be honest about which
of the five jobs the small thing even attempts, because the answer is going to be none.

3.5 The smallest thing that could carry the bill
Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. That’s the reading,
a single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I’m going to be careful about what
the question is, because after five thousand years of seals and witnesses the word
“vouch” is carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none of it. The question is only:
“has the designated flag been set.” Not “is some claim about a grouping true.” Not
“did anyone check.” There is no claim in this toy, no evidence, no checker, nobody
standing behind anything. There is a flag. Whether a flag can ever be made to mean
that something was checked and can be relied on is a real question, and it’s not this
section’s; I’ll build toward it later, and until then please read YES as “the flag is up”
and nothing more. Where the state is: which box you’re in. That’s the whole state, one
bit. Then draw a line under the boxes for tally marks. The marks sit outside the state.
They’re the running total you keep beside it as you play, the way you’d keep score
beside a board game.

Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don’t move, no mark. WORK: you don’t
move either (it’s a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine takes), no mark. VOUCH:
from NO you move to YES; from YES you stay in YES; either way you make one tally
mark, because in this toy the price belongs to the move’s name; where you were
standing doesn’t enter into it. Play. Start in NO, make any sequence of moves you like,
and stop in YES. Count the marks. Now try to reach YES with zero marks. You can’t,
and you can see exactly why: the only move that crosses from NO to YES is VOUCH,
and VOUCH makes a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH’s rule and play again.
YES for free, every time. That’s the entire content of what I’m about to call a rule, and


                                            87
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


I want you to see how little it is before I dress it up: I’ve decided that the move which
crosses the line makes a mark, and nothing else about the machine forces that. It’s a
choice. The next section is about whether I had to make it.

Why tally marks, by the way? Because they’re about the oldest receipt there is. The
real ones, the English treasury’s notched sticks split down the middle, get their own
story in Part III (Section 6), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing like those.
Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you could rub a mark
out and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the end of this section
it’s the reason the toy does none of the five jobs a record does.

Here is the same toy, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the book
where I state it and everything later points back here. The thing on your paper has
five parts.

A set of states. (Here: NO and YES, and nothing else.)

A set of move names. (STAY, WORK, VOUCH.)

A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.

A cost for each move name: a whole number of marks, zero or more. (Zero, zero, one.)

A reading: for each state, yes or no.

That’s it. Add the one rule below and I’ll call it a certification system; in the checked
record the rule is a sixth field, so nothing counts as one without it. And I want to be
exact about what’s not in it. There’s no counter stored inside the state that’s forbidden
from going down; the marks are the side tally from the board game, and the tally only
ever grows because the costs are whole numbers, zero or more. (A machine could
keep the total inside its state too; that’s an extra part beyond the five, and Section 6
builds it.) There’s no window, no observer who sees only part of the state; that’s a
later question and it gets its own section. And the cost depends only on the move’s
name; where you are when you make it doesn’t matter, which is a real simplification,
and I’ll flag it where it counts.

One rule, which I’ll call the toll. For every state and every move: if the reading is NO
before the move and YES after it, the move’s cost is at least one mark. That’s all. It says
nothing about any other move. It says nothing about how big a mark is in anything
you could measure. One mark is one mark; what a mark is worth, why the smallest
charge is one (why not two, or a half?), and whether I had any right to decide that,
come next, and I’m not sure of all of it.

And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you’ve already
proved it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and ends in a YES
state. Then the marks it made add up to at least one. Here’s the argument in words,
and it’s short enough that you can hold the whole thing. Walk the run move by move,


                                            88
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


reading the box at each step. It read NO at the start and YES at the end, and every
move either leaves the reading alone or flips it, so at some move it went from NO to
YES. The toll says that move cost at least one. Every other move cost zero or more.
Add them up: at least one. Notice what the argument did not need. It didn’t need
the reading to stay YES afterward; if a later move flipped it back to NO and another
flipped it to YES again, that’s two tolls, and the argument still goes through. It didn’t
need the machine to be finite. It didn’t need to know what any move does besides
what the reading says before and after. It needed exactly one thing: the toll.

That’s the whole theorem. Here it is once more in the exact form, because from here
on the book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and what’s stated
and checked, in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. N is the whole
numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. S and I are just names for “the set of states” and “the set
of move names.” Writing step : S × I → S means “hand it a state and a move name
and it hands back a state.” A run is a list of move names, t = [i1 , . . . , in ], played from
a start s0 , one after another. The double arrow =⇒ reads “then”: the thing on its left
forces the thing on its right. And “by induction on the run,” in the proof, is the formal
name for the way you’d check it by hand: settle the empty run, then show that one
more move at the front can’t break what you’ve settled.


Definition 3.1 (Certification system). A certification system consists of a set S of states,
a set I of move names, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a
reading cert : S → {no, yes}, subject to one rule, the toll: for every state s and move i,

                cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes =⇒ cost(i ) ≥ 1.

The run of t = [i1 , . . . , in ] from s0 ends at run(t, s0 ), the result of applying the steps
in order, and its total cost is cost(t) = cost(i1 ) + · · · + cost(in ), with the empty run
costing 0.


Defined as the record CertificationSystem (UniversalCertificationCost.v).


Theorem 3.1 (The universal floor). In any certification system, every run that starts at a
state reading no and ends at a state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if cert(s0 ) = no and
cert(run(t, s0 )) = yes, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. By induction on the run. If t is empty, the run ends where it starts, at a state
reading no, so the hypothesis “ends at yes” can’t hold and there’s nothing to prove.
Otherwise t = i :: t′ (the first move, then the rest); let s1 = step(s0 , i ). If cert(s1 ) = yes,
the first move is a crossing, the toll gives cost(i ) ≥ 1, and the rest cost at least 0, so
cost(t) ≥ 1. If cert(s1 ) = no, the rest of the run starts at no and ends at yes, so by the
induction hypothesis cost(t′ ) ≥ 1, and cost(t) = cost(i ) + cost(t′ ) ≥ 1. Nothing else
is used: not finiteness, not that the reading stays yes, not what any move does beyond


                                               89
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the reading before and after.

Where to check it: the record’s six fields are cs_state, cs_instr, cs_step, cs_c
ost, cs_cert, and the toll cs_cert_costs; the theorem is universal_nfi_an
y_substrate, in the same file; and the checked proof is the induction above, step
for step. One honest edge: the theorem does not assume that a YES state exists. If no
state ever reads YES, no run meets the theorem’s hypothesis, so it’s true of every run
and tells you nothing about any of them, which is a mathematician’s way of saying
it’s true and useless. The toy on your paper has a YES box, so it isn’t useless there.
It would be natural to assume the system has to have at least one NO state and one
YES state; the checked statement has no such clause, and that’s on purpose, because a
theorem that applies to no run is still a theorem and the toy is where you supply the
runs.

The theorem also runs backwards, and that direction is one line. Suppose every run
from a state reading no to a state reading yes costs at least one, whichever state you
start from. A single move is a run of length one, so a move that takes no to yes costs at
least one, which is the toll. The floor from every start and the toll are the same rule (ne
c_f_floor_iff_a2), and nobody has to choose between them. From one fixed start
that reads no, the floor asks for the toll only at the crossings you can reach without
paying anything (nec_f_floor_at_iff_free_reach); a crossing you can only
reach by paying has already cost at least one by the time you get there.

And the bound of one is the smallest case of a count. Under the toll a run costs at
least the number of times it takes the reading from no to yes, with no permanence
assumed (nec_f_cost_ge_rises). That bound for every run is again the same rule
as the toll (nec_f_rises_iff_a2). And it is reached for every count: on a one-bit
machine whose set costs one and whose reset is free, setting and resetting k times from
no takes the reading from no to yes k times and costs exactly k (nec_f_bit_rises_
exact). All of these are in NecFFloor.v.

And one more edge, because it’s the first thing to bite when you ask a machine to
stand behind more than one thing. The definition has one reading in it. One question,
one flag, one toll on its crossing. Once the flag is up, a second claim has nowhere to
go: raising a flag that’s already up doesn’t move anything. So a second claim needs a
reading of its own, and a third claim a third: one reading per claim, each with its own
crossing. Part III builds that properly, as a family of flags, one per threshold, with a
step that raises any of them charged at least one (Theorem 10.10). A step that raises
three at once still owes at least one, and nothing in the toll makes the charges add
up flag by flag. Charges that add need the composition assumptions for independent
machines. The same theorem sends the bill for finiteness: a record held in k bits that
only ever turns bits on can take at most k + 1 different values, so it can go up at most
k times. A finite machine can keep only so many things up for good in its whole life.
That’s the opening chapter’s “you can’t keep all of it,” turned into a count.


                                            90
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


3.6 What this does and doesn’t buy
I want to be very plain about how small this is, because the temptation is to look at the
word “theorem” and feel something has been established about the world. Nothing
has. What’s been established is that if you adopt the toll, then the flag can’t be raised
for free, in any system with those five parts that obeys it, no matter what the states
and moves are. The “if” is doing all the work. I chose the rule. A reasonable person
could ask why, and the only honest answer right now is “because that’s the thing I
wanted to be true,” which is not a reason.

Notice also what it doesn’t ask about how strong the thing is, in either direction. A
system is Turing-complete when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger than
one when a Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither. Stronger than a
Turing machine, weaker, dead even: none of it reaches the floor. Bring the five parts,
charge the toll on the crossing, and you’re in scope. The floor doesn’t check what you
can compute, because it was never about what you can compute. It’s about what a
move is allowed to do for free.

Which brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I’ll make it
first. The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one mark for every move,
whatever it does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every crossing
is a move and every move costs one. So any computer with a step counter beside
it, and any yes-or-no question at all about its state, is a certification system. A clock
passes. Nothing about that is a loophole. It’s what the definition says, and it means
the definition, on its own, doesn’t tie the marks to certifying anything. It only says a
crossing can’t be free. (It’s also why “a base that can compute anything plus a flag that
obeys the toll” would be a cheap thing to call Thiele-complete, and why the definition
that gets that name, in Part IV, asks for free computing and an earned record, which
no clock meets; Section 16.) Two things later in the book do the tying. One is a ceiling:
demand that a run’s total never exceed the number of times the flag went up, and
together with the floor exactly one bill survives, one mark per raise and nothing on
any other step (Section 7); a clock fails that the first time it charges a step that raised
nothing. The other is order, on the smallest machine I build: there, from a clean start,
the flag can’t go up unless a passing check of a claim came first, then a commitment to
that same claim, and a clock can’t fake that, because it’s about which moves happened,
and a clock only makes marks (Theorem 16.9).

And the other side of that: nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A Turing
machine’s run isn’t an instance of this theorem because it’s a run. It becomes one when
somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and proves the toll
for that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I won’t pretend it does.

That’s also where the other axis from the Flatland night ended up, once I checked it. It
isn’t a direction an ordinary computer can’t reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading,
charge the toll on its crossing, and it’s in scope like anything else. The possibility was


                                            91
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


always there. What the usual rules leave out is the price.

The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers “is the flag
up,” then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to be relied
on. Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by somebody
who signs their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled entitlement
isn’t entitlement for the system, no matter whose name is on it. Be careful which way
that cuts, though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly entitled on their own
account; that’s what an auditor has, and it’s honest as long as it’s called the auditor’s.
It isn’t the system’s. On the smallest machine I build later, the reason to believe its
checker says yes only when the claim is true is exactly that kind: a proof, checked
outside any record the machine keeps, and I’ll say so when I get there (Section 16).
What outside entitlement never is, is something the system itself earned.

And here’s a question I’ll only start on here: bolt two certification systems together,
and do you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the
other, and add up the marks. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a
reading that can only go up when one of the parts’ readings goes up, like “either flag
is up” or “both are”: then any crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that part’s
toll charged it, and the pair obeys the toll. Take “the first flag is up and the second is
down,” and it doesn’t: that reading turns on when the second flag falls, and nothing
charges a fall. The first two readings are checked: read through “either flag is up”
the pair is a certification system whose floor is one. Read through “both are,” a run
that starts with both flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two
is reached when each part can raise its own flag for one (Section 18). From a start
with one flag already up, one raise is enough, so two is a floor for the clean start only.
The third is still an argument on this page. A related composite is checked too, a host
machine running a guest, read through “the host’s own flag or its copy of the guest’s”
(Theorem 16.35). Whether every way of building one machine out of others keeps the
toll is a bigger question, and Section 18 takes it as far as I could: some ways do, some
provably don’t, and it says which.

So why bother with the toy at all? Not because the lineage was looking for it. The
bulla was after durability, the seven seals after evidence, the consul’s stamp after
authenticity, the two columns after catching slips; none of them was trying to put a
price on the moment a flag goes up, and I shouldn’t pretend they were. The reason is
narrower. Everywhere in that lineage where somebody did locate a cost, it sat on a step
next to the flag. The flag itself went unpriced: Szilard on the measurement, Bennett on
the wiping, proof-of-work on the search, Boyle on the instrument and the room, Foster
and Stine on the test. The toy is the first thing I could build where the cost sits on the
crossing itself, and it proves that if you price that step, the floor follows everywhere,
for any machine with the five parts. That’s not an answer. It’s the question made
exact enough to be wrong. And of the five jobs a record does, the toy attempts none
of them. Not even durability: the flag can be lowered by any move you care to write,


                                           92
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


and the marks that don’t go away are kept by you, the scorekeeper, beside the board.
The machine keeps none of them. What the toy has is a scorekeeper’s receipt for
the crossing. Whether the machine can be made to keep that receipt itself, where
a step could reach in and change it, is Section 6’s question. Authenticity, evidence,
accounting, cheap checking: none of them is in here, and I’ll say so again when it’s
tempting to forget.

And here’s what I’ll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a necessity:
the next section, and I’ll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What a mark is
worth in anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer who sees only a
window can and cannot recover, including whether they can even tell which step paid:
its own section. And whether a full-size machine, the kind you could actually run a
program on, can be made to obey the toll without cheating, and what that machine
looks like, and what it costs to vouch for structure in it: that waits for Part IV, on
purpose, and takes most of the rest of the book, and I’m still not sure I pulled it off.

For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule you were
handed without a reason, and one theorem you proved yourself in about a minute.
Don’t let go of it. It’s the smallest version of everything that follows, and if it’s wrong
here, it’s wrong everywhere.

4 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary
I handed you a rule without a reason. The move that raises the flag makes a mark,
because I said so. If that’s all it is, this book is a long way of describing a preference,
and you should treat it the way you’d treat someone telling you their favourite colour
is a law of nature. So this section is me trying to find out whether I had to pick it.
I’ll tell you the shape of the answer up front, because I don’t want you reading forty
paragraphs to find out whether there’s a point: on a machine with a finite memory,
where the flag once raised stays up, the step that raises it has to forget something, and
forgetting is the one step Landauer’s principle puts a price on, when what’s forgotten
wasn’t already known (that last clause takes a lot back, and I’ll show you exactly how
much). Three “ifs” in that sentence. Every one of them is a door you can walk out of,
and I’m going to show you each door, because the doors are where the actual content
is.

4.1 A closed room with no spare chair
Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it’s about ninety
seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the certified room. Put three
chairs inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair;
the people are the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the ones
whose flag is already up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once: each
person stands up and goes to the chair the rule sends them to. Two rules. First: nobody
inside the room may end up outside, because the flag, once up, stays up. Second: the


                                            93
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


person by the door must end up inside, because this move is the one that raises their
flag.

Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.

You can’t. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the three
inside chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave. The
person from the door has to come in. There is no fourth chair inside. Somebody shares.
Two of the machine’s possible states land on one state, and after the move you can no
longer tell, from where everyone is sitting, which of the two it was. The move forgot
something.

That’s the whole argument, and I want to name the piece of mathematics that did the
work, because it’s old and it’s not mine. If you put things into fewer boxes than there
are things, some box gets two. People call it the pigeonhole principle; it’s the one from
the opening chapter, where Jean Leurechon used it in 1622 to argue that two people
somewhere have the same number of hairs, and the first name for it I could find came
from Dirichlet, who used it in 1842 and later called it the drawer principle. It’s the
kind of fact a child accepts and a mathematician spends a career finding new uses for.
Here the use is: a step that forgets nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a one-to-one shuffle
of a finite set of chairs hits every chair, so the inside chairs are all taken by insiders, so
there’s no room for the newcomer. Finite. Permanent. Flip. Those three and nothing
else, and the conclusion is “two states became one.”

The checked version of the chairs is a theorem a few lines down, and it needs one
word first. “Injective” is the mathematician’s word for “forgets nothing”: a step is
injective when two different starts always give two different ends. The theorem says
exactly what the chairs said and takes exactly the three premises: a duplicate-free list
that names every state (finite), a reading that no step ever turns off (permanent), and
one state that reads NO before the step and YES after it (the flip). There is no price in
it anywhere. It is pure counting. I’ll come back to what counts as physics, but notice
that nothing so far has been.

Here are the words, exactly. For this whole section the setting is the five parts from
Section 3 without the toll: states S, move names I, a step, a reading, and (later) a cost.


Definition 4.1 (Finite, permanent, injective). The machine is finite when there is a list
of states with no repeats that contains every state. The reading is permanent when
no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all s and i, cert(s) = yes implies
cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is injective (forgets nothing) when different starts give
different ends: step( a, i ) = step(b, i ) implies a = b. A move that is not injective merges.


Defined as finite_states, permanent and step_injective (PermanentCertifi-
cation.v).


                                             94
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Theorem 4.1 (A permanent flip merges). On a finite machine with a permanent reading,
if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then the move i merges.

Proof. Suppose i were injective. Let C be the list of states that read yes; it is finite
and has no repeats. By permanence, step(·, i ) sends every member of C into C. Being
injective, it sends the members of C to members of C with no two landing on the same
one, so its images are as many as C itself, and a list of that many distinct members of
C is all of C. So the yes-state step(s, i ) equals step(c, i ) for some c in C, and injectivity
gives s = c, so s reads yes. It reads no. That’s the contradiction, and it’s the chairs.

Checked as permanent_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentCertification.v).
The proof there uses the standard-library fact that a duplicate-free list of n mem-
bers inside a list of n is the whole list, which is the pigeonhole in the form Leurechon
would recognise.

Is that new? No. It has been sitting in two places for a long time, one in physics and
one in the theory of automata, and a physicist will recognise it on sight, so start there.
In 1876 Josef Loschmidt pointed out, against Ludwig Boltzmann’s account of how
a gas settles down, that the laws of mechanics run just as well backwards: reverse
every molecule’s velocity and the gas retraces its steps, so mechanics alone can’t make
entropy only ever climb. Twenty years on, in 1896, a young assistant of Max Planck’s
in Berlin pushed harder. He took Henri Poincaré’s recurrence theorem of 1890, which
says a bounded mechanical system comes back as close as you like to wherever it
started, again and again, and used it to argue that nothing in such a system can climb
forever: give it time and it comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo, the
same Zermelo who’d patch Frege’s floor twelve years later. Boltzmann answered
the same year, not very politely, that the times you’d have to wait for a return are
so enormous that nobody would ever see one. (Jos Uffink, who wrote the Stanford
Encyclopedia’s entry on Boltzmann’s statistical physics, calls that reply drenched in
sarcasm and bitterness, and calls Zermelo’s own paper a careful logical argument.)

Now look at the chairs again. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a reshuffle:
it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where it started. A
flag that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and never comes back
down. So a reshuffle can’t carry one, which is Zermelo’s objection with the infinities
taken out. On a finite set the loops are enough, and Poincaré’s theorem isn’t needed.
And the wait is at most as many steps as there are chairs. Nothing enormous. Zermelo
was aiming it at the second law. Flags never came into it. The quantum version
came in 1957, when P. Bocchieri and A. Loinger proved the same return for a closed
quantum system whose energies come in separate levels, so going quantum isn’t a
way out of the room either, not for a closed system that never sheds anything.

The second place stings more, because it’s in computer science. Somebody got here
first, again. Picture a finite machine that reads letters, one move per letter. If every


                                              95
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


letter just reshuffles the states one for one, automata theorists call it a permutation
automaton, and the sets of inputs such machines can pick out are called group lan-
guages. Jean-Éric Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata, machines whose letters act
as one-to-one maps, sorts out exactly which languages those machines recognise, and
in that world the chairs are folklore. Here’s the short version. Start at a state that reads
no, and collect every input that ends at a yes. Because yes is permanent, adding letters
to the end of a collected input keeps it collected. A group language with that property
is either empty or everything, and everything would include the empty input, which
ends where it started, at no. So it’s empty: no run of reshuffles raises the reading.
That’s Theorem 4.1 with the moves as letters. Pin’s paper is where I’d send you to
check the automata side. It isn’t about flags or prices, and I’m not claiming it says
anything about them.

And if you like your facts in the most general clothes going, category theorists have
this one too. Treat the moves as a monoid acting on the states, and a permanent
reading as a set of states the moves never leave. In the topos of that monoid’s actions,
the truth value of “reads yes” at a state is the set of move sequences that carry it into
the yes-states. Every move can be undone exactly when the monoid is a group, and
exactly then is that topos Boolean, which makes every such truth value all or nothing.
Morgan Rogers lays out that fact in his 2019 and 2021 papers on toposes of monoid
actions. On a finite set, a move that merges nothing can be undone, so it’s the chairs
again, in a third language. Does it change anything here? No. It’s the same fact
wearing a bigger coat, and I mention it so nobody thinks the chairs are mine.

Going quantum doesn’t get around the automata version either. Alex Brodsky and
Nicholas Pippenger (2002) showed that a quantum finite automaton that measures
only once, at the very end, accepts with bounded error exactly the group languages,
the reshuffle kind. One that’s allowed to measure after every letter, and to stop on
what it sees, does better: it accepts every piecewise testable language, and “has seen a
b somewhere” is one of those. A measurement that can stop the machine is a record
that stays, and it’s the extra thing that lets the bigger class in.

The third place is the closest, and it isn’t old at all. In 2023 Thomas Ouldridge and
David Wolpert derived the thermodynamics of a finite automaton built the way real
computers are: the same physical step run again and again, each time touching only
the part of the machine that changes. They sorted languages into two kinds by the
smallest automaton that recognises each one. If that automaton has a letter that sends
two states to one, every automaton for the language has such a letter too, and on their
derivation recognising the language on a device like that produces entropy, waste no
cleverer design gets back, unless the inputs are so finely arranged that only one of the
merged states ever actually turns up. If the smallest automaton only reshuffles, they
find the language can be recognised with no entropy produced at all. One of their
worked examples is the strings with no b in them, which is my flag turned inside out:
the runs that raise it are exactly the strings that have seen a b. So the chairs, a real


                                            96
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


price on them, and the escape when you already know which chair you’re in are all in
their paper, three years before this book. Their price is derived from the physics of the
device. Mine is assumed.

There’s a fourth neighbour, and I’d call it a cousin, because it speaks another language.
Constructor theory is David Deutsch and Chiara Marletto’s programme for stating
physics as which transformations a device that runs in a cycle can and can’t bring
about, and in it a task is irreversible when it’s possible and its inverse isn’t. Mar-
letto’s version of thermodynamics (posted in 2016) leans on exactly that: tasks that
are possible while their transposes aren’t. Marletto, the physicist Vlatko Vedral and
coauthors (2022) made an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser, a ma-
chine of reservoir qubits that interact by partial swaps, and ran it with photons. Maria
Violaris and Marletto (2022) then argued that the same machine, run in a cycle, can
turn a pure qubit into a mixed one and can never turn a mixed qubit back into a pure
one, even though every interaction in it is reversible, and that this suggests erasure
may cost something beyond Landauer’s bound. The chairs are a classical, finite, exact
cousin of that sentence: a set of states a step can’t leave, a task that’s possible, and no
way back. Theirs is quantum and approximate and aimed at physics’ price; mine is
counted, and assumes its price. Deutsch and Marletto’s paper on information (2015)
has a neighbour of the chairs argument in its section 8.6: measuring one observable
disturbs another irreducibly, and nothing can undo the disturbance afterwards while
the outcome stays in an information variable. That’s a second, theory-independent
way of saying that a record that stays makes the step irreversible.

So what I can claim here is narrower again, and I’d rather say exactly how. Is even the
pricing form Ouldridge and Wolpert’s? In physics, on their derivation, yes: a merge
the language can’t avoid costs entropy. What I didn’t find in their paper is the price
as a named rule about a move, one a machine charges on a ledger whether or not
anybody’s physics is right (put a price on merging and the flip has to pay it, which is
the next subsection), and what I get out of that rule: the toll, as a theorem about the
ledger, the merge-or-revoke split for a single move, the exact match between “forced to
be priced” and “merges,” the squeeze bound counted in whole marks and its entropy
form, a built machine walking out of each door, and all of it checked. The core move
is older than the computer, it had two homes before it got to mine, and its physical
price had a third.

4.2 Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out
Here’s the step I’d been circling since the kindergarten buckets. In the last section I
told you Bennett’s rule as he states it: what has to cost is erasing a bit or merging two
paths a computation could have taken. I didn’t ask you to believe it. I’m not going
to ask you now either. I’m going to write it down as a rule you can accept or refuse,
in the smallest form that does any work: any move that forgets something costs at least
one mark. Any move that is not injective has cost at least one. That’s it. Note what it
does not say. It says nothing about certifying. It says nothing about flags. It’s a price

                                            97
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


on forgetting and only on forgetting.

Put the two together. The room says: on a finite machine with a permanent flag,
the move that raises the flag forgets something. The price says: a move that forgets
something costs at least one. So the move that raises the flag costs at least one. That
is the toll, the rule I handed you without a reason, and now it has one. The proof is
two lines: the first theorem says the flipping move merges, the premise says merges
are priced, done. I’ll keep saying “premise,” because that’s what it is, and because the
next section of this book is about what happened to some very smart people who put
a price where a premise goes and then treated it as a law of nature, and about half of
this one is me trying not to do that.


Premise 4.2 (Merge pricing). Every move that merges costs at least one: for all i, if i is
not injective then cost(i ) ≥ 1. (Checked name: merging_steps_priced.)


Theorem 4.2 (The toll from finiteness, permanence, and merge pricing). On a finite
machine with a permanent reading whose cost satisfies merge pricing, every move that turns
the reading from no to yes costs at least one. That is, the machine with that cost is a certification
system in the sense of Definition 3.1, and the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) applies to it.

Proof. A move that flips the reading merges, by Theorem 4.1; merge pricing charges it
at least one.

Checked as a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence; the packaging of such
a machine as a certification system is certification_system_from_merging_p
rice, and the run-level floor for it is permanent_certification_trace_floor
(PermanentCertification.v).

The theorem asks for more than it uses. Only the yes-states need to be finitely many:
with a permanent reading and finitely many states reading yes, the rest of the machine
as large as you like, merge pricing still gives the toll (nec_f_toll_from_merg
es_yes_finite). And merge pricing asks for more than the toll needs. Under
those same two conditions the toll holds exactly when every move that flips the
reading somewhere and merges is priced (nec_f_a2_iff_flipping_merges_p
riced). Merge pricing gives that (nec_f_merging_priced_weakens), and the
eight-state machine described later in this section, with its jump made free, meets the
toll without merge pricing (nec_f_a2_without_merge_pricing). All four are in
NecFMerge.v.

One more way to see the same thing, because it answers a rival I’d otherwise owe
you. The rival says: leave certification alone. Price erasure, and keep an honest flag
that reports when something was erased. Fine; but a system can set its certificate at
cost zero with its erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly because the certifying move
merged two states and the flag didn’t say so (commit_without_erasure_syst

                                                 98
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


em_is_not_honest). Make the erasure flag honest, so that it reports every move
that forgets, and on a finite machine with a flag that stays up the erasure law sends
the same bill the toll does (honest_erasure_accounting_implies_a2). The toll
isn’t a rival to honest erasure accounting. It’s what honest erasure accounting says
about the certifying move.

So, is the toll arbitrary? Here’s the honest version. The toll is a consequence of three
things: a finite memory, a flag that stays up, and a charge on forgetting. If you accept
all three, you don’t get to refuse the toll; it’s forced. If you refuse any one of them, the
toll goes back to being my preference. So the question “did I have to pick it” has turned
into three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: a better set of
things to argue about. Let me take the three doors in order, and for each one, build the
thing that walks out through it, because a premise you can’t see the counterexample
to is a premise you’re taking on faith.

4.3 Door one: keep everything, and nothing ever has to merge
Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine’s whole state is the
strip. Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any
box has a 1 in it. Check the three premises. Permanent: once there’s a 1, there’s always
a 1. Flip: the empty strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. Forgets nothing:
every move can be undone by erasing the last 1, so two different strips never become
the same strip. So here is a machine that raises a flag, keeps it up, and never merges
anything. The room argument has no grip on it, and the toll doesn’t follow. The
checked version is unbounded_history_escapes, and its state is a list of bits of
any length, which is the formal way of saying the strip has no end.

If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it’s a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture
course in the winter of 1924–25, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many rooms,
every one of them taken, where a new guest still gets a room: everybody moves from
room n to room n + 1, and room 1 comes free. That’s the chairs argument losing its
grip, told as a joke about a front desk. And here’s the part worth checking: Hilbert
never published it. The hotel became famous because George Gamow put it in a
popular book in 1947, and for a long time it wasn’t clear Hilbert had told it at all. The
historian of science Helge Kragh first guessed that Gamow had made it up. Then
Tilman Sauer, a historian of science who had co-edited a volume of Hilbert’s lectures
on the foundations of physics, pointed him to Hilbert’s lecture notes, which had just
been printed in 2013, and in 2014 Kragh took his guess back in a paper called “The
True (?) Story of Hilbert’s Infinite Hotel.” Keep the question mark. Even Kragh’s
own paper puts the lecture in January 1924 in one place and January 1925 in another.
Still, this time a story everybody repeated turned out to have a real lecture behind it.
I’ve learned not to count on that happening. Bring it back to the table. In the room,
the person from the door had nowhere to sit because the chairs ran out. In Hilbert’s
hotel they never do, so everybody shifts one over and nobody has to share. The strip
machine is that hotel. The argument stays the same. What the hotel shows you is that

                                            99
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


it was about running out of chairs all along.

What walked out the door is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight boxes
and run it for real: eight boxes, nine moves. On the ninth move there’s nowhere to
write. To keep going you have to reuse a box, and the moment you reuse a box two
different histories end on the same strip, and you’re back in the room with a shared
chair. Keeping the whole history is exactly the move Bennett made in 1973, when he
showed that any computation can be done without forgetting if you let it keep a copy
of everything it did; Landauer, back in 1961, had already written that for a machine
able to run a program that doesn’t stop, the space to hold every intermediate result
“cannot be there.” The history escape is real. It costs you a memory that never fills.
Every machine you can buy has a memory that fills.

One thing I have to say plainly, because the file is more careful than I’d like to be. The
theorem shows the strip machine has the other two properties and forgets nothing.
The sentence “and this machine is infinite” is a second theorem, nec_f_history_
infinite (NecFPaperToys.v): no finite list holds every state of the strip. The first
theorem contains no cost at all. “Certifies for free” is written in a second theorem, hi
story_escape (AxMerge.v): there the strip is counted as a number, each move adds
one at a cost of zero, nothing merges, merge pricing holds, and the toll fails. So the
words and the files line up, in three theorems.

Which state is being counted. Whether a move merges depends on what the state keeps.
The strip keeps its history, so nothing merges; cut it to eight boxes and the reuse
merges. Section 21 proves the general form (Theorem 21.3): keep the previous state
alongside the current one and every fixed-instruction step is one-to-one. So a merge
price is a fact about a move on a stated state space. Each price derived in this book is
derived on the whole state its definition gives, and three things go with it: which state
that is, what lies outside it (nothing outside it is charged), and whether the move is one
primitive instruction or a composite run of several. Relabelling the states one-to-one
changes no price, since it sends merges to merges and one-to-one moves to one-to-one
moves. Adding history to the state, or projecting part of the state away, changes the
machine being modelled, and the price can change with it.

4.4 Door two: let the flag come back down
Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is
undoable (turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads: that’s a
flip, NO to YES. And heads goes to tails: the same move takes the flag back down
somewhere else. Two states, finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag forgets
nothing, so a schedule that charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it nothing.
The file states that the one move forgets nothing (it is injective) and its on-then-off
behaviour (revocable_certificate_escapes); that the coin is finite and that the
price may be zero are written in toggle_escape (AxMerge.v), which prices the turn
at zero, meets merge pricing, and fails the toll. The thing that walked out the door is


                                           100
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


permanence.

Now here’s a fact that I think is sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the
thing in this section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely. Keep only finiteness.
Take any move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the move
forgets something, or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There’s no
third option, and the proof below is a search: go through the finitely many YES states
looking for one this move turns to NO. Find one, and that’s the revocation; find none,
and the move is permanent at least for itself, which is all the room argument needs. So
a flag that goes up for free is a flag the same move can take back. A flag that nothing
takes back is paid for. You can’t have a free raise that stays raised, not on any finite
machine, not with any price schedule that charges for forgetting. That’s a narrower
sentence than “every certificate costs.” It’s true, and I’ll take it. The broad one would
only be mine.


Theorem 4.3 (Merge or revoke). On a finite machine (no permanence assumed), if
cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then either i merges, or there is a state t with
cert(t) = yes and cert(step(t, i )) = no.

Proof. Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that i sends to no. If there is
one, that is the second alternative. If there is none, then i keeps every yes-state at
yes, which is permanence for the single move i; the argument of Theorem 4.1 uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and i merges.

Checked as flip_merges_or_revokes, with the single-move form of the room
argument as permanent_at_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentRecordPric-
ing.v).

I’ll give you the three-card version too, because it shows that a move can be forced
to be priced without writing anything permanent, and I don’t want you to think the
picture is tidier than it is. Three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star on T1. The rule: T0 goes
to T1, T1 goes to T2, T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the star (a flip). T1 loses it (a revocation).
T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this move is priced, by the forgetting rule, and
yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a star away in the same breath. “The priced
moves are exactly the permanent records” is false, and the file proves it false with
these three cards. What’s true is one direction: on a finite machine whose move names
can be decided equal or different, every permanent raise is a priced move. The other
direction has the three cards standing in it. And “priced” here has an exact meaning
worth one sentence: a move is forced to be priced when every schedule that charges for
forgetting charges it, and that holds exactly when the move forgets something, with
no finiteness needed at all. A way to tell two move names apart is enough.


Definition 4.3 (Forced to be priced). A move i is forced to be priced when every cost


                                            101
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


function satisfying merge pricing (Premise 4.2) charges i at least one.


Defined as forced_priced (PermanentRecordPricing.v).


Theorem 4.4 (Forced price is merging). If any two move names can be decided equal or
different, then a move is forced to be priced exactly when it merges. No finiteness is needed.

Proof. If i merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function. If i
does not merge, define the cost that is 0 on i and 1 on every other move (this is where
telling move names apart is used). It satisfies merge pricing, since every merging
move is some move other than i and costs one, and it charges i nothing, so i is not
forced.

Checked as forced_priced_iff_merges (PermanentRecordPricing.v).


Corollary 4.5 (Permanent records are forced). On a finite machine whose move names can
be decided equal or different, a move that never turns the reading off and turns it on somewhere
is forced to be priced. (By Theorem 4.3 it merges; by Theorem 4.4 it is forced.) The converse
fails: the three cards are forced, because they merge, and they revoke.


Checked as forced_priced_iff_merges, permanent_record_write_is_fo
rced_priced, and the three-card counterexample forced_price_without_per
manent_record (PermanentRecordPricing.v).

4.5 Door three: forget for free
The third door is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I’ll describe
it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take two sheets of paper,
one blank and one stamped. One move: stamp whatever you’re handed. Finite, two
states. Permanent: stamped stays stamped. Flip: blank goes to stamped. Forgets: both
sheets end up as the same stamped sheet. Everything the room argument needs is
here, and the move merges. Now set the price of that move to zero. The toll fails, and
you can watch it fail: the flag went up for nothing. That’s free_merge_escapes
(PermanentCertification.v), and what walked out the door is the charge on forgetting.
(The same file shows that a price of one on that move satisfies all three premises, pri
ced_reset_satisfies_premises, so the premises can hold together; door three
is about whether they must.) Nothing in counting stops you from setting that price to
zero. Only a claim about the world does. The nearest such claim is Landauer’s, and I
have to be exact about the gap between the two: the premise as written charges every
forgetting move, whether or not you knew which state you were in, and Landauer’s
own heat, as the coin under the cup below will show, is owed only for what you
didn’t know. So the premise is Landauer’s claim taken in its worst case over what the
machine might be holding, and that’s the version the counting needs.


                                              102
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it. I went past the sum-
maries and read the paper itself. A logical operation with no single-valued inverse (a
step that forgets, in this book’s words) must produce heat, “typically of the order of
kT” per operation, where k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature; and for
the specific case of resetting one bit whose value you don’t know, the minimum is kT
times the natural log of 2, about 0.69 kT. I want you to hear two things in that. First,
“of the order of”: he was not handing out a number to three decimals. Second, and this
surprised me, he did not measure anything. The paper is argument, with models. He
writes that he can “show, or at least very strongly suggest” the conclusion, and that
his reasoning gives “no guarantee that this minimum is in fact achievable.” That’s the
founding paper of the whole subject, and it’s a careful man saying “I think this is right
and here’s why.” I like him more for it.

Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École
Normale Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto’s lab working with
Eric Lutz, trapped a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a double
well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many times
over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat came
down toward Landauer’s kT ln 2 and sat there as the erasure got slower. On average.
Single runs went under it; the bound is about the average, and any one erasure can
beat it. And if you only succeed in erasing half the time you owe nothing, which the
paper’s formula shows and which I think is the most honest line in it. Others have
done it since with different devices. So: predicted in 1961 by argument, seen in a
laboratory fifty-one years later.

And is it settled? No, and I’d be lying by omission if I left that out, because the people
who doubt it are not cranks. John Norton, a philosopher of physics, has argued since
2005 that the usual proofs of the principle quietly assume what they’re trying to prove,
and that the kinds of process they assume, combined, could be made to break the very
law the principle is supposed to guard. An earlier objection, made in 1999 by Norton
and his Pittsburgh colleague John Earman, also a philosopher of physics, was that
the principle can’t be independent of the second law. Charles Bennett, who did more
than anyone to build the subject, rated that one “in my opinion the one of greatest
merit,” and then disagreed with it. Others replied to Norton; Norton replied back. The
Stanford Encyclopedia entry on the topic, written by a philosopher of physics who
works on exactly this, ends without a verdict. I’ve read what I could of both sides and
I’m not qualified to referee them, and I’m not going to pretend the laboratory settles
a question about what the principle means in general, because measuring one bead
doesn’t do that.

So here’s what I did with it, and I think it’s the only honest thing to do. The charge
on forgetting is written into the checked work as a named premise. It’s a definition the
theorems take as an assumption, and nowhere is it proved as a general fact, because


                                           103
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


it isn’t provable from counting; for particular machines with particular price lists it’s
checked (the stamp at cost one, above), which is a different thing. If Norton turns
out to be right, every theorem in this section still holds; they just have one premise
fewer that the world agrees to. If Landauer’s side turns out to be right, the premise is
physics. Either way, nothing in this section says a device does anything until someone
measures the device. The counting is mine to prove. The physics is a door I’ve labelled,
and what opens it is a measurement. A proof can’t.

Labelled, though, isn’t the same as unplaced, and a hedge isn’t a position, so here’s
mine. Earman and Norton’s objection is a dilemma. Either an information-theoretic
exorcism of the demon assumes the second law, which they call the sound horn, and
then it adds nothing the second law didn’t already give; or it rests on a new principle
tying information to entropy, the profound horn, and nobody has given that principle
independent grounds. A named premise is the sound horn, on purpose. That’s where
Bennett ended up in 2003, and Norton’s “Too Good to Be True” (written in 2025,
published in 2026) says the careful literature almost always accepts that horn, and
argues that whatever succeeds there is ordinary thermodynamics relabelled. I’ll take
that. Ordinary thermodynamics, relabelled onto a ledger, is all this section asks of
the physics. And on the counting I’m on Norton’s side outright. His 2018 paper
“Maxwell’s Demon Does Not Compute” exorcises the demon with Liouville’s theorem
and nothing else, no information and no computation: dynamics that keeps every
patch of states the same size can’t crowd a big set of states into a small one. The
counting core of this section, that a step losing nothing can’t carry a no-state into a
set that stays up, is that point in finite, discrete form. And if you want the best case
for the premise itself, the one I found is James Ladyman, Stuart Presnell, Anthony
Short and Berry Groisman (2007): from one of the standard statements of the second
law, the one named for Kelvin, they derive that a logically irreversible operation can’t
be carried out thermodynamically reversibly by any of their L-machines. That’s the
merge-pricing premise with an argument under it, and if you want to argue with the
premise, that’s the paper to argue with.

One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it’s a good one: the laws under-
neath never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state forward to
exactly one next state and could carry it back again, and Liouville’s theorem adds that
a patch of states keeps its size as it moves; quantum mechanics is unitary, which is
one-to-one too. So when this section says a step merged two states, where did the
difference go? Out of the machine. The merge is in the machine’s own description, the
states its reading is about. The machine together with everything around it still runs
one-to-one, and the distinction the machine forgot survives. It gets pushed out into
the surroundings, mostly as heat. The surroundings are door one’s endless strip. That
door is always open for the universe as a whole and shut for the machine, because the
machine isn’t the universe and its memory fills. Read that way, Landauer’s premise is
the claim that pushing a distinction out of a finite machine into its surroundings costs



                                          104
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


heat, and that’s all it claims. Which also means the bill is heat handed over. None of
it has to be heat wasted. Takahiro Sagawa’s 2014 analysis says that a step that forgets
can, in principle, be run slowly enough that no entropy is produced overall: the heat
leaves the machine, the room’s entropy goes up by what the machine’s went down,
and nothing is lost that didn’t have to be. So on the premise the forgetting step can’t
be free, but it doesn’t have to be wasteful. When I call it a cost, I mean a transfer you
can’t avoid. None of it is a loss you could have engineered away.

4.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze
The toll says “at least one mark.” That’s a floor for raising one flag. The room argument
says more if you let it. Say there are m people already inside and k more come in
through the door in one move. (That’s a different k from the one in Landauer’s kT;
when the two meet, below, Boltzmann’s constant gets a little B hung under it, k B , so
you can tell it from a head count.) All m plus k of them end up in m chairs. That’s a
squeeze, by a factor of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a slightly stronger version
of the forgetting price, that each mark pays for at most one halving of the number
of distinguishable states, then the move costs at least the number of halvings in that
squeeze, which is the base-two logarithm of (m + k)/m.

Back to door three’s stamp, with four sheets this time: three blank, one stamped, and
the stamp-everything move. Four states go to one. Before the move, to say which
sheet you had took two yes-or-no questions (is it one of the first two? then which of
those two?); after the move, it takes none. Two bits gone. Two halvings. So that move
costs at least two marks, and two marks is enough: a cost of exactly two satisfies the
halving rule (both facts are checked for these four sheets, quad_stamp_needs_two
and quad_stamp_cost_two_is_priced). The general statement is m + k at most
2 to the cost times m, and next to it in the file sits a logarithm form that rounds both
logarithms up and is weaker for it (three states and one newcomer round to the same
two bits on both sides, and the rounded form says nothing). The halving premise, like
the one before it, is a definition used as an assumption. The units are halvings. To
turn a halving into joules of heat you multiply by k B T ln 2, and that multiplication is
physics; the counting stops before it.

That little k B deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where counting
turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann’s grave
in Vienna has S = k log W carved on it (that k is the same k B , before anyone hung a B
under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways the parts
could be arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written that way,
came from Max Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. In his Nobel lecture in
1920 Planck said the constant “is frequently termed Boltzmann’s constant, although
to the best of my knowledge Boltzmann himself never introduced it,” and guessed
that Boltzmann never believed anyone could measure it accurately. I’d assumed
Planck named it after Boltzmann. His own words point the other way: it was other
people calling it that. Who first did, I couldn’t pin down; one recent paper points to

                                          105
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Paul Ehrenfest in 1906, the year Boltzmann died, and I haven’t checked that myself.
Ehrenfest was an Austrian physicist who had done his doctorate under Boltzmann in
Vienna. So the most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the name of a
man who didn’t write it down. Does that change the bill? No. But look at the job the
constant does in that equation. Take it away and what’s left is the logarithm of a count,
which is a number of halvings, which is what the squeeze bound hands you. The
constant is the exchange rate, and whether the world honours that rate for a merge is
the premise. No theorem here settles it.

Exactly, with one new piece of notation: for a list D of states, write | D | for how many
it has, and imgi ( D ) for the number of different states the move i sends them to.


Premise 4.4 (Halving price). Each mark pays for at most one halving: for every move
i and every list D of states with no repeats, | D | ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ( D ). (Checked name: c
ompression_priced. It implies merge pricing, since a merge sends two different
states to one and so needs cost(i ) ≥ 1.)


There’s a plainer way to read that premise, and it’s worth having because it says what
the premise is about. Look at one landing spot of move i and count how many states
land there; call the biggest such count the move’s worst pile-up. The premise holds
exactly when every pile-up has at most 2cost(i) states in it, which is to say the cost is
at least the base-two logarithm of the worst pile-up. One direction: take D to be one
whole pile, which lands on a single spot, and the premise says the pile has at most
2cost(i) members. The other: any list D splits by where its members land, each part fits
inside one pile, so | D | is at most the number of landing spots times the worst pile-up,
which is the premise. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the worst it could
ever do, whichever state it’s actually handed. That’s worst case on purpose, and it
has a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices a single run that
has to succeed every time, with no averaging over many runs, Philippe Faist, Frédéric
Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner derived in 2015, in that framework,
what they give as the least work any logical process needs, and when every input
might occur and no error is allowed, their bound comes to k B T ln 2 times exactly that
logarithm. Take an AND gate as the example: three inputs land on 0, so it needs at
least log2 3, about 1.6, halvings’ worth of work (two marks, in whole numbers). The
premise asks for that bound of a device that has to work whatever it’s handed, and it
counts it in marks. Joules don’t come into it.


Theorem 4.6 (The squeeze bound). On a finite machine with a permanent reading and a
cost satisfying the halving price, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i
turn k different no-states to yes. Three numbers, then: m counts every yes-state of the machine,
reachable or not; k counts a list of distinct no-states that the move turns to yes, and the move




                                              106
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


may turn others too; and cost(i ) is the price the cost assigns to the move. Then

                                                                               m+k
         m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · m,       and, when m ≥ 1,        cost(i ) ≥ log2       .
                                                                                m
The counting inequality holds as stated. When m ≥ 1, it is equivalent to the displayed
logarithmic lower bound.

Proof. Put the m yes-states and the k newcomers in one list; it has m + k different
members. By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis
every newcomer does too, so all m + k land among the m yes-states: imgi ≤ m. The
halving price gives m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ≤ 2cost(i) · m.

The four sheets are the case m = 1, k = 3, where the bound is reached. With k = 1
the bound says cost(i ) ≥ 1, which is the toll again (a2_from_compression_price
_and_permanence). Checked as permanent_flips_compression_bound, with
the rounded-logarithm form permanent_flips_log_bound and the counting-only
cousin permanent_flips_collapse_at_least (at least k states collapse, with no
price premise at all).

The bound is reached for every m ≥ 1 and every cost c. Whenever m + k ≤ 2c m, a
finite machine with a permanent reading and the halving price has m yes-states and
a move of cost exactly c that turns a listed k distinct no-states to yes. The move turns
every other no-state of that machine to yes as well, (2c − 1)m of them in all. No cost

least whole-number cost that meets the bound is exactly ⌈log2 mm+k ⌉ (nec_f_least_

Four more facts about the halving price, all checked, and the last one is a limit. First,
the plainer reading above is a theorem on a finite machine: the halving price holds

squeeze bound is met with equality there: its stamp turns on the four states whose flag
is down, beside the four whose flag is already up, and 4 + 4 = 21 · 4 (ent2_frag_bo
und_attained). Fourth, and this is the limit, the small machine of Part IV as a whole
does not meet the halving price, whatever procedure you use to decide whether two of

the machine holds, lands two different states of the whole machine on the same state
(ent2_small_not_compression_priced; the pair is in Theorem 16.38). So on

that machine the toll is the rule I chose, as I said it was; that the halving premise fails
