4.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero
There’s one more way to say all this, and I include it because it’s the way physicists
say it and because it hands you the one case where the bill is exactly zero, which I find
more instructive than any case where it isn’t.

Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to “how much you don’t know”: if something
could be in any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty is log base
two of n bits, and that’s the most it can be for n states. If you push your uncertainty
through a step that forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a step that merges
two states you might have been in, it drops. Now run the room. Before the move,
you might be in any of the m + k states in play. After it, you’re in one of m. So
your uncertainty afterward is at most log2 of m, whatever you believed before. If you
started with no idea at all, every one of the m + k states equally likely, your uncertainty
was exactly log2 of (m + k), and the move removed at least log2 of (m + k)/m bits: the
same number as the halving count, now in Shannon’s units. Landauer’s principle, in
the form physicists write it, then says a step that removes that many bits from the state
gives off at least k B T ln 2 of heat per bit. Put the two together and the flip gives off
heat, and the exact statements below say how much and under which side conditions,
one of which (the temperature has to be taken as zero or above) is easy to skip and
shouldn’t be.

Why does Shannon’s number share a name with the physicists’ entropy at all? There’s
a story about it. Shannon wanted to call it uncertainty, and the mathematician John von
Neumann told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the same formula already
lived in statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody really knows what entropy
is, so in an argument he’d always have the upper hand. It’s a great story. It comes
from Myron Tribus, who spent years tying information theory to thermodynamics,
who said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and who printed it, with Edward McIrvine, in
Scientific American in 1971. Then in 1982 an interviewer, Robert Price, asked Shannon
about it, and Shannon said he didn’t think von Neumann had told him any such thing.
So it’s a legend with one witness, and the person the witness quoted doesn’t remember
saying it. What doesn’t hang on the story: the two formulas really do have the same
shape, and it still takes Landauer’s premise, a named assumption, to turn a count of
bits into heat.

Exactly, with the notation built first. A spread (probabilists say distribution) is a way
of giving each state a chance p( x ) ≥ 0, with the chances adding to 1. Its Shannon
entropy, in bits, is
                          H ( p) = − ∑ p( x ) log2 p( x ),
                                       x: p( x )>0

where the big sigma means “add up, over every state x with a chance above zero,”


                                            108
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


and each term is a state’s chance times the bits it would take to single that state out.
That comes to log2 n when n states share the chance evenly and less when the chance
is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move i gives the spread of where you land:
q(y) = ∑ x: step(x,i)=y p( x ). The bits the move removes are H ( p) − H (q).

Start with the half of the claim that costs nothing, Bennett’s half. A move that forgets
nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances just get carried to new
addresses, one for one. Nothing piles up and nothing spreads out. The uncertainty is
the same number before and after.


Theorem 4.7 (A move that forgets nothing removes no bits). Let the states be finite,
listed once each, and let f send states to states with f ( a) = f (b) only when a = b. Then for
every assignment of chances p, the pushed spread q has H (q) = H ( p).

Proof. An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list: every
state is hit exactly once. So q( f ( x )) = p( x ) for every x, and the sum defining H (q) is
the sum defining H ( p) with its terms in a different order.

Checked as step_entropy_invariant_if_injective (PermanentCertificatio-
nEntropy.v). That’s why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move free,
which is the shape the toll needs: the bill lands only where something was forgotten.


Theorem 4.8 (Entropy after a permanent flip). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i turn k ≥ 1 different
no-states yes. For any spread p whose chance lies on those m + k states, the spread after the
move has H (q) ≤ log2 m. For the even spread on the m + k states, the move removes at least
log2 mm+k bits.

Proof. After the move, all the chance sits on the m yes-states (permanence for the old
ones, the hypothesis for the new). There is at least one yes-state: the image of a state
that flips. Thus m ≥ 1. Write q1 , . . . , qr for the positive output probabilities, where
r ≤ m and their sum is 1.

For y > 0, ln y ≤ y − 1: the derivative of y − 1 − ln y is 1 − 1/y, so its minimum is 0 at
y = 1. Apply this with y = 1/(mq j ), multiply by q j , and add:

                            r               r
                 − ln m − ∑ q j ln q j ≤ ∑ (1/m − q j ) = r/m − 1 ≤ 0.
                           j =1            j =1


Dividing by ln 2 > 0 gives H (q) ≤ log2 m. The even input spread has m + k probabili-
ties each 1/(m + k ), hence H ( p) = log2 (m + k ). Subtracting the output bound gives
the claimed loss log2 ((m + k)/m).




                                                109
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Checked as permanent_step_entropy_ceiling and, for the even spread, perm
anent_flip_uniform_entropy_drop (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).


Premise 4.5 (Landauer’s principle, as a premise). A step that lowers the entropy of
the machine’s state by ∆H bits, at temperature T, gives off heat Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H,
where k B is Boltzmann’s constant. (Checked name: landauer_heat, with k B T as
one variable.)


Corollary 4.9 (Heat floor of a permanent flip). Under Premise 4.5, with k B T ≥ 0, the
flip of Theorem 4.8 from the even spread gives off at least k B T ln mm+k ; with k B T > 0 that is
strictly positive.

Proof. Theorem 4.8 gives an entropy loss of at least log2 ((m + k )/m) bits. Multiply
by the nonnegative factor k B T ln 2 and use Premise 4.5. The identity ln 2 log2 x = ln x
gives the displayed floor. Here m > 0 and k > 0, so (m + k )/m > 1 and its logarithm
is positive; if k B T > 0, the heat floor is strictly positive too.

Checked as permanent_step_entropy_ceiling, permanent_flip_uniform
_entropy_drop, entropy_le_log_support, permanent_flip_heat_floor,
and permanent_flip_heat_positive (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in beside
one that was already yes, so m = k = 1 and the floor is k B T ln 2. At room temperature,
about 300 kelvin, that’s roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth of
a billionth of a joule. And that’s the biggest bill a single flip gets from this corollary.
With k = 1 the floor is k B T ln mm+1 , and it shrinks as more states already read yes: with
a thousand of them it’s about a thousandth of k B T, some seven hundred times less
than the case of two. So one mark is not one halving. It’s one halving exactly when
the squeeze is two; for any thinner squeeze the physics asks for less than a halving,
and the toll still charges a whole mark, because marks come in whole numbers (that’s
the rounding the entropy road to the toll leans on, a little further down). Whatever the
size, it’s a bill only if you grant the premise; nothing on this page measured anything.
And even granted, it’s a bill nobody will ever see on a meter: real logic gates spend
many thousands of times more than this on every switch, even the frugal ones. One
2023 tally of the numbers puts switching a single CMOS gate at a hundred attojoules
at the low end, over thirty thousand times this. The point of the number isn’t that
certifying is expensive. It’s that, on the premise, it isn’t zero.

Physicists have a name for a step with no way back, and that logarithm has turned up
in their work before. Yûto Murashita, Ken Funo and Masahito Ueda (2014) studied
processes where some histories of the reversed process have no forward history at all.
They call that absolute irreversibility, and they derived that the entropy such a process
produces averages at least − ln(1 − λ), where λ is the chance of those orphaned


                                               110
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


reverse histories. Their first example is a gas let out of a box that held a fraction l of
the room, where the bound comes to ln(1/l ). Now picture the even spread of my flip
played backwards: the chance sitting on the m yes-states spreading back out over all
m + k, a gas let out of a box holding m/(m + k ) of the room. Their bound for that is
ln mm+k , the same logarithm as the heat floor, in units of k B T. So is my squeeze a special
case of their bound? No, and the reason is worth a minute, because the match is a
good trap. The even spread gives a real chance to every state the flip starts from, so no
forward history is missing: the flip itself isn’t absolutely irreversible at all, and their λ
for it is zero. The heat floor is ordinary Landauer heat, the bill for squeezing a spread
over m + k states into m of them, the same kind of bill as any reset into a smaller
set. The two logarithms match because a squeeze’s Landauer heat equals the entropy
produced by the free expansion that undoes it, and that free expansion, the flip played
backwards, is the process their bound is about. A mirror. Neither result descends
from the other. Their idea does reach the flip, just somewhere else: on a device whose
rates never change, raising the flag from a state it knows, which turns up at the end
of this section. Gonzalo Manzano, Gülce Kardeş, Édgar Roldán and David Wolpert
(2024) carried absolute irreversibility over to computations, with one-way transitions
and machines that stop at random times, worked on finite automata, and the same
− ln(1 − λ) term sits in their second-law bounds.

The even spread is the easy case, and you might worry the heat depends on picking it.
It doesn’t. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to the state that
flips will do.


Corollary 4.10 (Positive heat for any full spread). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, let move i turn a no-state s yes. Take any spread p that gives positive chance to s and
to every yes-state. Under Premise 4.5 with k B T > 0, the heat the move gives off is strictly
positive.

Proof. After the move, s and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there is
one more of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive chance
land on the same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits (Theorem 4.13
below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of bits is positive heat.

Checked as permanent_flip_full_support_entropy_drop_positive and
permanent_flip_full_support_heat_positive (PermanentCertificationEn-
tropy.v).

There’s a third road to the toll here too, and it’s the same shape as the merge road,
with bits in place of marks for forgetting.


Definition 4.6 (Entropy-priced). On a finite machine, a cost is entropy-priced when, for
every move i and every spread p, the cost of i is at least the bits the move removes:


                                              111
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


cost(i ) ≥ H ( p) − H (q), where q is p pushed through i.


Theorem 4.11 (The toll from entropy pricing). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at
least one. So the machine with that cost is a certification system (Definition 3.1), and every
run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least one.

Proof. Let move i turn s yes, and let m be the number of yes-states; m ≥ 1, since
step(s, i ) is one. Take the even spread on the m yes-states and s. By Theorem 4.8
with k = 1, the move removes at least log2 mm+1 > 0 bits, so the cost of i is a whole
number above a positive number, which makes it at least one. The run-level floor is
the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) applied to that system.

Checked as a2_from_entropy_price_and_permanence, with the packaging ce
rtification_system_from_entropy_price and the run-level floor entropy_
priced_trace_floor (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

Now the zero. Put a coin under a cup without looking. Rule: set it heads up. You
might have had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn’t know is gone,
and that’s the bit the principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads, put the cup
back, and apply the rule again. Nothing you didn’t know changed. No bit was lost.
And the principle, applied to a state you already knew, demands nothing: the premise
holds exactly when the heat is zero or more, which is to say it sets no floor at all. The
principle charges for uncertainty removed. The shape of the move doesn’t enter. This is
the generalized form of Landauer’s principle, worked out by Owen Maroney in 2009,
in a paper he wrote at the Perimeter Institute in Canada (he has been a philosopher of
physics at Oxford since 2011), and by Sagawa in 2014, and Landauer himself had the
seed of it in 1961: for a row of bits all already ONE, he wrote, there’s no need to carry
out any operation, so no entropy changes and no heat is given off, and resetting a row
all ZERO to ONE involves no entropy change either, because neither row carries any
information.


Theorem 4.12 (A known state gets no heat floor from the premise). On a finite machine,
if the spread puts all its chance on one state s, then any move removes zero bits, and Premise 4.5
for that move holds exactly when Q ≥ 0.

Proof. A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on
one state. So ∆H = 0 and the premise reads Q ≥ 0.

Checked as known_state_step_removes_no_entropy and known_state_fli
p_forces_no_heat (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).




                                               112
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Be careful with that one, because it’s easy to overread. “The premise sets no heat floor
for a known state” does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank sheet
gives off no heat. A fixed device that merges states dissipates on known input too;
Bennett calls that wasteful, because entropy goes out into the room with nothing taken
from the data. What the theorem says is only that the premise sets no floor there. The
floor comes from what you didn’t know. That’s a sentence about the bill. The device
is a separate matter. And notice that the toll still charges the known-state stamp one
mark, because the toll is a rule about the move, and the move doesn’t know what the
observer knows. That’s the worst-case gap from door three showing up again, and it’s
the price of having a rule a machine can follow without asking who’s watching.

There’s a second piece of fine print on that theorem, and it’s about who works the
controls. The generalized principle can charge a known state nothing because it lets
the step be driven by a protocol that changes in time: lower this barrier, tilt that well,
raise the barrier again, each at the right moment. Something outside the step keeps
that time, an outside clock or an outside hand, and the premise doesn’t bill it. Take the
hand away and the bill changes. Paul Riechers, Alexander Boyd, Gregory Wimsatt and
James Crutchfield (2020) analysed what happens when the control is time-symmetric,
the same played forwards or backwards, which covers a clocked pulse and any device
whose rates never change. On their analysis, every move that doesn’t come back to
where it started when you apply it twice, which they call nonreciprocal, costs at least
k B T ln(1/ε) on top of the change in free energy, to run with error at most ε. A flip that
stays up is always nonreciprocal: apply it twice from the no-state and you’re still at
yes. So, if they’re right, under that kind of control the known-state stamp isn’t free
after all, and the more reliable you want it, the more it costs. Their class is bigger than
mine, though. Erasure is nonreciprocal, and so is a counter of three or more values
that steps forward and wraps around, which merges nothing, so their bound is about
what the controls are allowed to do, records or no records. So read Theorem 4.12 with
its control written in: Landauer’s premise sets no positive heat floor for a known state
when the step can be driven by a protocol timed from outside it. The same goes for
Theorem 4.4. On a machine whose move names can be decided equal or different,
the moves every merge-pricing schedule must charge are exactly the merging moves,
and that’s true against merge pricing; measured against time-symmetric control, the
forced moves would be, on this argument and unchecked, the nonreciprocal ones, the
wrapping counter included. Which moves the physics forces a price on depends on
what the controls can do.

A deterministic run from a known start has a known state at every step. For such a run,
the adopted entropy-loss premise reduces to Q ≥ 0: it supplies no positive heat lower
bound. That does not establish that a particular device attains zero heat. The chairs
guarantee a collision among the already-yes states together with the entering no-state.
They do not guarantee that the entering state takes part in the collision (a four-state
machine where it doesn’t is nec_f_collision_avoids_s, NecFMerge.v). For an



                                           113
The Thiele Machine                                                                            Devon Thiele


input distribution supported only on no-states, this counting argument alone therefore
forces no positive entropy loss. Whether other states in that support merge depends
on the move. The operation-level ledger toll still follows under merge pricing.

So here’s what this section actually earns. A device with finitely many states that has
to raise a flag and keep it up correctly from every state it might be in, including states
where it can’t tell whether the flag is already up, can’t do it for free at any temperature
above zero, on Landauer’s premise; that’s the design envelope, the worst case. A
particular run from a start it knows can, on the same premise, as long as something
outside the step does the timing. What stays forced in every case is the toll as a rule
about the move, because the rule can’t ask what the run knows. Wherever this book
says that settling something for good can’t be free if Landauer’s right, it means the
device sentence. It never means the run sentence.

Here’s the general case, and it’s the one that shows you where the bits go. Split the
bill state by state. Each state x you might be in carries its chance p( x ) along to where
it lands, step( x, i ), and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If nobody else
landed there, its term is zero. If others did, its term is the difference between how
crowded its landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.


Theorem 4.13 (The bits removed, one term per state). On a finite machine, for any move
i and any chances p( x ) ≥ 0, with q the pushed spread,

                                     ∑
                                                                                         
              H ( p) − H (q) =                  p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )) − log2 p( x ) .
                                  x: p( x )>0


Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states x ̸= x ′ , both with
positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.

Proof. Group the sum for H (q) by where things land: the chance q(y) at a landing spot
is the sum of the p( x ) that land there, so H (q) = − ∑ x: p(x)>0 p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )).
Subtract from H ( p) term by term. Each term is non-negative because the landing spot
holds at least what x brought, q(step( x, i )) ≥ p( x ), and the logarithm keeps order. If
x and x ′ share a landing spot, that spot holds at least p( x ) + p( x ′ ) > p( x ), so the term
for x is strictly positive.

Checked as entropy_drop_as_point_sum, entropy_drop_nonneg, and entr
opy_drop_pos_of_support_merge (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

4.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not
Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and what is still a door?

You’ve earned this: on any machine with finitely many states, a move that raises a
flag either forgets something or takes a flag down somewhere else. Pure counting, no
physics, no premise beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down


                                                    114
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


is the four chairs. You’ve earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up,
then raising it forgets something, and a move that raises k states collapses at least k
of them. Counting again. And you’ve earned this: if forgetting is charged for, the toll
follows, and if forgetting is charged per halving, the size of the toll follows too; each
of those derivations hands back a system with the five parts and the toll, so Section 3’s
floor applies to it as it stands. That’s the rule from Section 3, now derived, with every
premise named, for any finite machine with a flag that stays up. In that section I only
declared it.

Here’s what you haven’t earned. I’m listing it so you don’t assume it. You haven’t
earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that’s Landauer, it’s measured for
beads and argued over for the general case, and in the checked work it’s an assumption
with a name. And even granting it, Landauer charges a run that knows where it is
nothing at all (the lifted cup), so what the physics forces is a floor on a device that
has to work whatever it’s holding. Any one run can come in under it. You haven’t
earned that any machine you’d actually want to build is of this kind, either, and there
are two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its running total inside its own
state, as a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many states, so the finite premise
fails for it as a whole. And you can’t patch that by giving the total a ceiling. A total
that only climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either stops at its top, and then
two different histories leave the same top value, which is a merge, or rolls back over
to zero, and then it doesn’t only climb. So any running total a finite machine keeps
for itself has a horizon: it’s honest up to its width and no further. And a machine
whose price list charges the step that raises the flag, but lets some other step merge
two states for nothing, raises the flag honestly and still doesn’t charge for forgetting
in general, so the merge-pricing premise fails for it. Either one puts a machine outside
these theorems as stated, though a finite piece of it can still sit inside. The machine
I build later (Section 16) misses in both ways. It keeps counters with no ceiling, so
it’s infinite outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a counter down among
them, can land two different states on one for free. So for it the toll is a rule I chose;
the chairs force it only on finite machines that price every merge, and it isn’t one.

A finite piece can still sit inside, and here’s the smallest one I could build where every
premise is a theorem. None of them is left as a hypothesis. Four slots times a flag,
eight states. Three moves: stamp (set the flag, go to the next slot, cost one), jump to
slot a (cost two), next slot (cost zero). It’s finite (fin_finite) and permanent (fin
_permanent); the next-slot move forgets nothing (fnext_injective); the stamp
and the jump merge (fcertify_merges, fjump_merges); merges are priced (fi
n_merging_priced), and priced per halving (fin_compression_priced). So
this section’s two conclusions hold on it outright (fin_a2_from_merging_price,
fin_a2_from_compression_price, FiniteCertMachine.v). The counting lemma
underneath, that a duplicate-free list with at most K preimages per image has at most
K times as many members as images, is proved generically (fiber_bound_compre



                                           115
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


ssion). Merge pricing alone would take any price of at least one for the jump. The
jump’s price of two is what the halving price asks, since the jump squeezes four states
into one. One more fact about it, also checked: each move’s price is exactly the number
of halvings in its largest squeeze. For a move that costs c, no state is landed on by more
than 2c states, and some state is landed on by exactly that many (stamp squeezes at
most two states into one, jump to a slot squeezes four, and next-slot squeezes nothing).

The machine Part IV builds runs this eight-state machine. Seen through a window that
shows only a line number, read modulo four as the slot, and a flag, a short program of
that machine, once a two-instruction setup has run, does what the eight-state machine
does, one move at a time, and pays exactly what the eight-state machine charges
(Section 16.17 has the construction and the exact statements). The machine as a whole
is still not merge-priced: some of its free steps merge states, so the finite piece is a
piece, and the machine around it keeps the choice the chairs don’t force.

And you haven’t earned anything about what the flag means. Four chairs don’t know
what they’re certifying. The bill is for raising a flag that stays up. Whether raising
that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural fact, the “vouching” I keep
promising and keep not delivering, is a question for the machine of Part IV, and here
it has moved exactly this far: on a finite machine that charges for every merge, if that
flag stays up, it was paid for.

One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the premises, but the
premises were chosen, and “permanent” in particular was chosen by me. Why should
a certificate stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest about it?
That’s a fair question, and merge or revoke is the start of an answer (the three-card
machine only showed that the converse of Corollary 4.5 fails): on a finite machine
that charges for every merge, a flag that goes up for free is a flag the same move takes
back somewhere, and a record that can be silently taken back is the thing the bulla
and the hash chain and the write-once disk were all built against. “Permanent” here is
exactly that: the flag can’t be lowered. The toy in Section 3 didn’t have it; the lineage
in Section 3 was built around it; I chose it. Whether that was the right job to pick out
of the five is something you can argue with me about, and I’d want you to.

And “permanent” is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No
physical record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some
rate, however slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo’s
point from the chairs. The theorems in this section need permanence on every state,
including states the machine never visits, forever. Weaken that to “the flag stays up on
the states that actually turn up, for as long as anyone cares,” and merge-or-revoke tells
you what goes wrong: the move could take the flag down somewhere nobody ever
looks, and then it isn’t forced to merge at all. A version of the toll stated in chances
and time spans would be a different theorem, and I don’t have it.

One piece of it I can hand you, and it’s checked. Take one move and repeat it from


                                           116
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


one start, forever. On a finite machine the states that run passes through are finitely
many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot nothing on those states, it would be
a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every one of them back around, the start
included, where the flag was down. So if the flag goes up along that run and stays up
from some point on, the move merges two states the run itself visits. The shared chair is
one the machine actually sits in. And it doesn’t touch the known-state point above: a
merge among states the run visits still costs Landauer nothing if the run knew where it
was and something outside timed the step. Checked as nec_f_orbit_merges_vis
ited and nec_f_repeat_merges_visited (NecFRepeat.v), for any map iterated
from a start whose flag is down, with the flag up at every step from some point on; no
permanence premise is used.

Runs that mix different moves split two ways, and the answer is short enough to give
here, checked like the last one. If the moves are picked from outside, in any order at
all, the answer is no. Take two states, one reading no and one reading yes. Move a
swaps them; move b does nothing. Run a once and then b forever: the flag goes up
at the first step and stays up for good, and neither move merges anything anywhere.
The swap would take the flag down from the yes-state if it ever ran there; on this run
it never does, and that’s exactly the weakened permanence this paragraph is about.
But if the machine is closed, picking its next move from its own state, the run is the
orbit of one map, the step with whatever move the state picks, and the single-move
argument applies to that map as it stands. Now say the moves come in a pattern that
eventually repeats, one word w of moves over and over. Suppose the flag is down at
some step after the repeating starts, and goes up and stays up after that. Count the
repetitions from a step where the flag was down (start w at that letter if you have to)
and run the same argument on the composite of w’s moves, at the states where such a
repetition begins. It merges two of those states, both visited; follow the two through
the letters of w, and the first letter where their paths meet merges two states the run
visits at that letter’s place in the pattern. So: moves picked from outside, no; a closed
machine or a repeating program, yes (nec_f_outside_moves_no_merge, nec_f
_closed_merges_visited and nec_f_word_merges_visited, NecFRepeat.v;
the last finds the letter and the two repetitions, from a flag down at the start and up at
every repetition from some point on).

And one limited piece of the chances-and-time-spans version, set in continuous time
and checked in all but one step, because it shows exactly where the known-state es-
cape stops. Take a device with no outside hand at all: a little random process hopping
among finitely many states at rates that never change, with the usual physical con-
ditions (every hop has a reverse hop, and the rates obey local detailed balance), able
to get from any state to any other. Left to run, it settles into a long-run spread π and
spends stretches with the flag up and stretches with it down; call their mean lengths
Tup and Tdown . Start it in a no-state you know. Then the entropy it produces from then
                                  
on is at least ln 1 + Tup /Tdown , in units of k B . The argument is three lines once the



                                           117
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


pieces have names. With fixed rates, the entropy produced is at least the drop in rela-
tive entropy between the device’s spread and π; that’s half of Massimiliano Esposito
and Christian Van den Broeck’s split of entropy production (2010). A start known to
be in state s has relative entropy − ln π (s), which is at least − ln π (no), where π (no)
is the long-run chance of the flag being down, and the relative entropy runs down
to zero as the device settles. And the long-run chances of up and down stand in the
ratio of the mean stretch lengths, because the crossings up and the crossings down
                                               
balance, so − ln π (no) = ln 1 + Tup /Tdown . Read it this way: each doubling of how
long the record stays up, against how long it sits down, costs about one more k B ln 2,
and a record that stays up forever on a fixed-rate device costs without bound. That’s
Murashita, Funo and Ueda’s absolute irreversibility landing on the flip at last, with
1 − λ the long-run chance of the starting state. It isn’t new physics: nothing in it
needs a record, since an autonomous reset to a fixed state obeys the same bound,
and the time-symmetric-control result above covers the same ground with an error
rate in place of the time ratio. And it isn’t the theorem I said I didn’t have. It’s a
first honest step toward it, and it pins down where “the premise sets no heat floor
for a known state” needs its outside clock. Hold that argument to what it says. The
entropy is added up from the moment the device sits in the known no-state s until it
has settled, over one whole relaxation. The starting spread is all on s, and π is the de-
vice’s long-run spread. The inequality rests on fixed rates, finitely many states, every
state reachable from every other, a reverse for every hop, and local detailed balance
to read the entropy as heat. It’s one bound on one relaxation, and it doesn’t charge
each certification again. It also isn’t the permanence of the finite-state theorems on a
noisy device: on this device the flag comes back down, and Tup and Tdown are average
stretches. The discrete-time core is checked, for a finite chain whose steady spread π is
positive and satisfies detailed balance (RelaxationEntropy.v): the entropy produced in
one step is exactly the drop in relative entropy to π, and never negative (re_sigma_i
s_drop and re_sigma_nonneg); from a known start s the entropy produced in the
first T steps is − ln π (s) minus the relative entropy left at step T, so it never exceeds
− ln π (s) and reaches it in the limit exactly when that remainder goes to zero (re_k
nown_start_total and re_known_start_bound); − ln π (s) ≥ − ln π (no) for a
start among the no-states (re_known_start_vs_set); the flow from the no-states to
the yes-states equals the flow back (re_flux_balance); and with each mean stretch
taken as its mass over that flow, − ln π (no) = ln(1 + Tup /Tdown ) (re_stretch_rat
io).

That’s the bound, and two things under it were still promises when I stated it: that
the device actually settles, and that “mean stretch length” means what it sounds like.
Both are checked now, and here’s what each one says in plain words.

Settling first. A chain doesn’t have to settle. It can get stuck in a corner, or cycle
round forever. What rules that out here is a condition named for Wolfgang Doeblin,
a German-born French mathematician, son of the novelist Alfred Döblin, who took



                                           118
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


his doctorate at the Sorbonne in 1938 for work on chains like this one and died in
June 1940, at twenty-five. In words: from wherever the device is, its next step lands
on each state with at least some fixed fraction δ of that state’s long-run chance. No
state is ever out of reach in one step, and none is favoured so heavily that the others
starve. Under that condition each step shrinks the distance between where the device
is and where it’s going by the factor 1 − δ, so the distance dies off geometrically
and the spread converges to π at every state (rc_contract and rc_converges,
RelaxationConvergence.v). Here’s the payoff for the bound. The entropy produced
from the known start stays under − ln π (s), and it also gets there: after T steps it falls
short by at most (4/m)(1 − δ)2T , where m is the smallest long-run chance of any state
(rc_known_start_gap and rc_known_start_limit). So − ln π (s) is the exact
price of the whole relaxation, and the bound is reached.

The same story holds when the device hops at random moments, at fixed rates, with
no clock ticking. At every instant the relative entropy to π falls at exactly the rate
entropy is being produced, and that rate is never negative (rcd_D_derivative, r
cd_sigma_nonneg and rcd_D_monotone, RelaxationContinuous.v); add the rate
up between two times and you get exactly the drop in relative entropy between them
(rcd_produced_window). For settling, Doeblin’s condition becomes a condition
on rates: the rate of hopping from any state x to any state y is at least c times π (y),
for some fixed c > 0. Then entropy is always being produced at least c times as fast
as the relative entropy still left, and that forces the relative entropy down at least as
fast as e−ct (rcl_sigma_ge and rcl_D_decay, RelaxationContinuousLimit.v). One
wrinkle needed its own proof. A known start puts all its weight on one state and none
anywhere else, and the logarithms in the relative entropy go bad at zero. The check
shows the relative entropy is still continuous at the starting instant, because u ln u
goes to zero as u does (rcl_D_at_zero). So adding up the production from the start
out to infinity gives exactly − ln π (s) (rcl_known_start_total).

I should say what Doeblin’s condition costs. It asks for every hop to be possible
directly, in one step or at a positive rate. A device whose states reach each other only
through other states can still settle, and the standard theory of these chains says the
conclusion holds for it too, but the proofs here don’t cover that case. For a chain that
ticks, the condition holding for some fixed number of steps would be enough for the
same argument; I’ve checked it for one step.

Then the stretches. The bound used the fact that the long-run chances of up and down
stand in the ratio of the mean stretch lengths, and I took the mean length of a stretch
with the flag up to be the long-run weight of the up-states divided by the flow into
them. That’s a theorem, and it’s checked in steps. Start each stretch the way the flow
starts them, count the steps until the chain leaves the up-states, and the average is
exactly π (up) over the flow, again under Doeblin’s condition (rs_mean_stretch,
RelaxationStretch.v). The proof is a telescoping sum: the long-run weight that has
stayed up for k steps splits into the stretches that started just now and the weight that


                                           119
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


stays up one step more.

With the stretches measured in seconds, when the device hops at random moments, it’s
checked too, and the route is different. Ask, for each up-state, how long on average the
device takes to leave the up-states from there. Call that its leaving time. The leaving
times obey one plain rule: from any up-state, the rate out of it times its leaving time,
minus the rates into the other up-states times their leaving times, comes to exactly one
second. Average the leaving times over the way the flow starts stretches, multiply by
the flow, and the rule plus the balance of the steady spread (as much weight flows into
each state as out of it) rearrange the sum into exactly π (up) (rsc_mass_over_flo
w, RelaxationStretchContinuous.v). That the rule has a solution at all needs proving,
since nothing promises it in advance, and Doeblin’s condition supplies it: run a clock
that ticks faster than any rate in the chain, and the leaving times are the limit of a
count that only grows and never passes one over c π (down) (rsc_leave_exists).
Last, the seconds themselves. Take the chance that a stretch started by the flow is still
running at time t, with the chain stopped the moment it leaves the up-states. That
chance starts at one and falls at least as fast as e−c π (down) t (rsc_S_decay). The time
spent up, which is that chance added up over time, comes out to the averaged leaving
time minus what’s still running, and as time runs on it closes in on π (up) over the
flow (rsc_mean_stretch_time and rsc_stretch_identity). Mass over flow,
in seconds. The bound’s two premises are both checked now, in steps and in seconds.

The next section is about a different door entirely. Forgetting has had its section; the
question now is whether finding out costs, because the demon’s whole trick was that it
knew which way the molecule was going, and I owe you a straight answer on whether
knowing is free.

5 Learning is free, committing is not
I ended the last section owing you an answer about knowing. The bill so far sits on
forgetting: on a finite machine, a flag that stays up was paid for because raising it
merged two states. But there’s a thing that looks like the opposite of forgetting and
feels like it ought to cost at least as much, probably more. Finding out. Every time a
machine rules out a possibility, it knows more than it did. If forgetting a bit costs, does
learning one cost too? I had a strong feeling about this, and you probably have it too,
so here it is first: learning is the expensive part. Most physicists had that feeling as
well, for a long time. It’s why the demon took a hundred and fifteen years to exorcise.
Or didn’t. “Exorcise” is the word the people who think it worked like to use. John
Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last section, called their two-part
paper on it “Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell’s Demon,” and I read that Roman
numeral as a joke about how many times the demon has been declared gone. So hold
the word loosely. This section is me finding out where the feeling goes wrong. I’m
going to tell you the version where the exorcism worked, because it’s the version that
says where the bill goes, and the door from the last section stays open behind it.


                                           120
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


5.1 A small being at a small door
You met Maxwell’s demon in Section 3, in one paragraph. It gets a whole section here,
because the step it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this
section is about.

In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for electric-
ity and magnetism two years before, in 1865, and to my mind had as good a claim as
anyone to being the most important physicist alive, wrote a letter to his friend Peter
Tait describing a problem he couldn’t get rid of. Take a box of gas at one temperature,
with a wall down the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine, he said, a
“very observant and neat-fingered being” sitting at the door, who can see individual
molecules coming. When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens the door and
lets it through. When a slow one approaches from the right, same. Otherwise it keeps
the door shut. It never pushes anything; it only opens and closes a frictionless door
at the right moments. After a while the right side is hot and the left side is cold, and
you’ve got a temperature difference you could run an engine off, made out of noth-
ing but looking. That’s supposed to be impossible. It’s the thing the second law of
thermodynamics says can’t happen, and the second law is the law physicists are least
willing to give up; Arthur Eddington, the English astronomer, wrote in a 1928 book of
popular lectures that a theory found to contradict it has nothing for it but to collapse
in deepest humiliation, and nobody has had to test that yet.

Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell’s demon, though
not by Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon in Nature in
1874, and Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed “Concerning Demons,” tried
to take the name back: “Call him no more a demon but a valve . . . ” Nobody listened,
which is probably for the best, because “Maxwell’s valve” would not have lasted a
century. But keep his correction, because it’s exactly right and it’s the whole problem:
the being does no work. It opens and shuts a door. So physicists spent the next century
trying to find where the being was cheating. I want you to feel the pull of the obvious
answer, because I felt it and so did most of them: the being has to see the molecules.
Seeing costs. Case closed. In 1929 Leo Szilard built a one-molecule version of the box
and did the arithmetic, and said the second law survives if finding out which side the
molecule is on costs at least as much entropy as the being gains. In 1951 the French
physicist Léon Brillouin made it concrete: to see a molecule you have to bounce light
off it, and the way the philosopher of physics Jeffrey Bub sums up the result, finding
out that way costs at least k ln 2 of entropy for every bit, which is kT ln 2 of heat,
Landauer’s number before Landauer, and there was your toll on looking. For thirty
years that was the answer. Information costs because getting it costs.

That’s a price on one way of looking, and it doesn’t show that every possible way of
making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.

Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the demon.


                                          121
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


Four years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own later telling,
he was waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having just read a
newspaper report in which Ernest Rutherford, the physicist who had announced the
atomic nucleus in 1911, called the hope of getting power out of atoms moonshine, and
as the light changed it occurred to him that an element which gave off two neutrons
when it swallowed one could keep a reaction going by itself. That’s the nuclear
chain reaction, thought up crossing a street. It’s his memory of himself, and Richard
Rhodes’s history of the bomb opens with it, in a first chapter called “Moonshine,”
which is where most people meet it, so hold it as the man’s own story. A timestamp
it isn’t. Does it change anything about the demon? No. What it adds is a picture of
the man: the same mind looked at one molecule in 1929 and one neutron in 1933, and
both times the question was what a single small step forces downstream.

5.2 Bennett moves the bill
In 1982 Charles Bennett, who’d already shown in 1973 that computation can be done
without forgetting, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a
molecule and writes down which side it’s on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture
the being’s notepad, which starts blank. After looking, the notepad says “left” or
“right.” Two possible worlds before (molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad
blank). Two possible worlds after (left, “left”; right, “right”). Nothing merged. Two
in, two out, and you can read the before off the after. Copying what you see onto a
blank page forgets nothing, and a step that forgets nothing is a step Landauer doesn’t
charge for. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing light) and
took it as the price of getting information at all. Bennett gave a way of looking that,
on his account, doesn’t pay it.

So where is the bill? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After the first
molecule the page is full. To do the next one it has to wipe the page. And wiping takes
two possible worlds (pad says “left”; pad says “right”) to one (pad blank). That’s the
merge. That’s the step with no way back. The demon pays every cycle, and what it
pays for is making room to see again, and the amount it pays is at least what it gained,
and the second law sleeps soundly. That’s the rule from his 2003 notes I quoted in
Section 3: erasing and merging cost, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn’t.

Section 3 separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see exactly which
step pays, and why the other one was tempting, because looking feels like the active
part. It’s the thing the being does. Wiping feels like housekeeping. The housekeeping
is where the money goes. If there’s a sentence in this section I’d want you to carry out
of it, that’s the one, and the idea in it is Bennett’s.

5.3 Two different things called “narrowing”
Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense, and
I’ll give it to you as a picture because that’s how I eventually got it.



                                          122
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Draw the machine’s possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row above it:
the dots that you, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two different
rows. The first is a fact about the machine. The second is a fact about you, about
what you’ve seen and what you’ve ruled out. Both rows can shrink. They shrink for
different reasons, and only one of them costs.

The machine’s row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state. That’s a
merge. That’s what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section 4, a run
can’t shrink the machine’s own row by more halvings than it paid for. That’s the
theorem just below, and it’s the Section 4 squeeze bound run forward along a whole
program. That section took it one step at a time. No new idea; the same chairs.

Exactly. Write ⌈log2 n⌉ for the index-bit count of n: the smallest whole number k with
2k ≥ n, the number of yes-or-no questions it takes to pick one of n things. It is 0 at
n = 1, and I set it to 0 at n = 0 too, a convention for empty lists, since the logarithm of
zero isn’t a number. Wherever I write an ordinary logarithm without the rounding, its
argument is positive. For a run t and a list D of starting states, let imgt ( D ) be the set
of states the run can end in, starting from somewhere in D, and write |imgt ( D )| for
how many there are (in Section 4 the symbol for one move already meant the count;
here I need the set and its size both). Let cost(t) be the run’s total cost.


Theorem 5.1 (The machine’s own narrowing is priced). If the cost satisfies the halving
price (Premise 4.4), then for every run t and every list D of starting states with no repeats,

                        ⌈log2 | D |⌉ ≤ cost(t) + ⌈log2 |imgt ( D )|⌉.

Proof. By induction on the run. A single move of cost c shrinks a list with no repeats
by at most a factor 2c (that’s the halving price), which costs at most c in rounded
logarithms; the states reachable after the rest of the run from the shrunk set are exactly
those reachable after the whole run from the original. Add the costs.

Checked as run_narrowing_priced_log (KnowledgeNarrowing.v). The run itself
is the witness; nothing else is handed in. That will matter in Section 8, and I’ll say why
at the end of this section.

Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn’t have
shown you. You cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine. It
didn’t merge anything; it didn’t know you were watching; it would have done the
same thing with nobody in the room. The physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name for
mixing these up, and I think it’s one of the most useful names in all of science: the
mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as if it were a property
of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head. The machine’s row is in the
machine. The halving price is about the machine’s row, and crossing a candidate off
yours doesn’t move it.


                                             123
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he’d argue with where I just took his
phrase. In a 1965 paper on Gibbs’s and Boltzmann’s entropies he wrote that entropy is
“an anthropomorphic concept” (a phrase he credited to the physicist Eugene Wigner),
and by that he meant a property of the particular experiments you or I choose to do
on a physical system. On his account the system alone doesn’t carry it. So for Jaynes
the second law is about what’s known too, and the line I’d have liked to draw, that
the second law has opinions about the machine and none about you, is exactly the
line he’d refuse. Who’s right is one of the oldest fights in statistical physics, Jaynes’s
reading against Boltzmann’s, and I can’t settle it. I don’t have to. The spreads in
Section 4’s entropy theorems are spreads over the states the device might be in when
the step runs, and every theorem there holds whether you read those chances as
ignorance or as physics; “the floor comes from what you didn’t know” is the same
sentence in either reading, with “you” being whoever built the spread. What I need
from the fallacy is only this: the two rows are different rows, and only one of them is
the machine’s.

5.4 The demon on a sheet of paper
Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it
merge or not merge with your own eyes.

The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule’s side) and a display (the
notepad). Four states: write them as pairs, hidden then display. 00, 01, 10, 11. Two
moves.

MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a light
switch adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it’s 0, leave it. Draw the arrows.
00 goes to 00. 01 goes to 01. 10 goes to 11. 11 goes to 10. Look at the arrowheads:
every state has exactly one arrow landing on it. Nothing merged. MEASURE forgets
nothing.

WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well. 10
goes to 10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10. That’s a
merge, twice over. Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one.
MEASURE is allowed to cost zero.

Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you’re
shown, the display here, is what I’ll call a window: the part of the state an outside
observer gets to see. Section 7 is about windows in general; here the window is
just the display. The display starts blank, so your list of candidates is {00, 10}: two
possibilities, one bit you don’t know. The machine runs MEASURE. You look at the
display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could have produced it is 10. If it shows
0, only 00. Your list went from two to one. You learned the hidden bit. The machine’s
price for that move: zero. Its own row of possible states went from {00, 10} to {00, 11},
still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything else. You narrowed.
It didn’t. That’s the measuring half of Bennett’s argument on four dots, and WIPE’s

                                            124
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one bit gained, nothing
charged. Here’s the thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly where the crack
runs: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and every actual start in the
list, the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates before minus log2 of the
candidates after, both rounded up) are at most what the run was charged. Four dots,
and that sentence is false.


Definition 5.1 (What an observer knows). Fix a window w from states to what can be
seen. Given a list Ω of candidate starting states, a run t, and the actual start s0 ∈ Ω,
the observer’s knowledge K (Ω, t, s0 ) is the list of candidates s ∈ Ω whose run shows
the same thing through the window at every step as the actual run does.


Defined as knowledge (KnowledgeNarrowing.v).

If that definition looks familiar, it should. It’s the standard way logicians of knowledge
set it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can’t tell apart from
the actual one, given everything you’ve seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi’s
Reasoning About Knowledge, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs and observations
included). And it’s the logically omniscient kind from the opening chapter, the kind
where knowing some facts means knowing everything that follows from them, for
free. I’m using it on purpose, flaw and all. This section is about learning, and learning
in that sense is exactly the thing that’s allowed to be free. Settling is the separate act
with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.


Theorem 5.2 (An observer can learn for free). There is a four-state machine (the demon),
a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost 0, and candidates with |Ω| = 2, for which
|K (Ω, t, s0 )| = 1. So the claim “for every Ω with no repeats, every t, and every s0 in Ω:
⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ − ⌈log2 |K (Ω, t, s0 )|⌉ ≤ cost(t)” is false for that machine and that cost. In the
same machine, every cost satisfying the halving price charges WIPE at least one.

Proof. The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost 0
satisfies the halving price; the observer’s two candidates show different displays after
MEASURE; WIPE sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price needs its
cost ≥ 1.

Checked as observer_narrowing_can_be_free, demon_observer_learns,
demon_machine_spread_kept, measure_forgets_nothing, wipe_merges,
and wipe_costs_at_least_one (KnowledgeNarrowing.v).

The demon is the picture. The smallest case is smaller. The claim as written already
fails on a machine with two states and every move free, because the observer’s very
first look tells the two apart, and it never fails on a machine with one state (nec_f_t
wo_state_observer_free, nec_f_one_state_observer_priced, NecFNar-


                                             125
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


rowing.v). That’s why the interesting version is learning after the first look, which is
where the three states of Theorem 5.3 come in. And WIPE’s price needs less than the
halving rule: merge pricing alone charges it at least one (nec_f_wipe_under_merg
e_pricing).

I have to be exact about one thing the file is exact about. The halving rule is a floor. It
says merges cost at least this much; it does not say anything costs zero. So what the
theorem exhibits is one price schedule that meets the halving rule and charges MEA-
SURE nothing. A different schedule could meet the rule and still charge MEASURE;
nothing in counting forbids overcharging. The claim is “learning is not forced to cost.”
It isn’t “learning is free on every machine,” and on a given machine a schedule may
still charge it. That’s weaker than the section title. The title is the short form you’d say
before checking the fine print, so the title stays and this paragraph stays next to it.

The physicists had this freedom on the books long before me. Paul Fahn (1996), doing
the entropy accounting of Szilard’s one-molecule engine step by step, argued for a
symmetry between the measuring step and the erasing step: on his account, which of
the two you hand the bill to is partly a choice of bookkeeping, and the total is what’s
fixed. Sagawa and Ueda (2009) derived a bound on that total, with the split depending
on the memory. So, on their accounts, “a schedule could charge MEASURE instead”
is a known freedom in how the books are kept. I didn’t find a loophole. And the other
reading is very much alive. Ruth Kastner (2025) argues that Brillouin was essentially
right after all: once the physics of a real measurement is put back in, it’s measurement
that pays and foils the demon, erasure drops out of the bill, and Bennett’s free copy
fails as physics. The theorem above is about price lists, so it stands either way. What
hangs on her is whether a real demon can look for nothing, which is the same door
the next paragraph’s doubter pushes on.

And the doubter from the last section cuts this side too, so I owe it to you, since I
leaned on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at the scale of
molecules, thermal jiggling keeps any process that’s supposed to be thermodynami-
cally reversible from ever actually finishing, and finishing it takes more entropy than
Landauer’s amount. If he’s right, Bennett’s free measurement isn’t free in practice
either, because it’s one of those processes. The theorem above survives that, because
it’s about price lists: a schedule that meets the halving rule isn’t forced to charge the
copy, whatever a real device spends. What wouldn’t survive is the physics I’ve been
hanging on it, that a real demon can look for nothing. If Norton is right, the line
between learning and committing keeps its counting and loses its physics. I can’t
referee that one either.

5.5 Who holds the pen changes the bill
Now the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here. You find it by playing with
the four dots. Thinking about them won’t get you there. Run MEASURE twice. The
first copies the hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again,


                                           126
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


and adding a bit twice with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the
display is blank again. Check the arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and
then blank, and nothing merged, and the price was zero both times. So a display that
was blank before the first MEASURE can be put back to blank for free, by a second
MEASURE. Just not by WIPE.

What’s the difference? MEASURE consults the hidden bit when it clears the display. It
knows what’s written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and
so it can undo the copy. Nothing gets erased. WIPE doesn’t look. It sets the display
to 0 regardless, and “regardless” is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general
form of this in the 2003 notes: he lists the “erasure of one of two copies of data known
to be identical” among the logically reversible operations, because you’re removing a
duplicate, and no information is destroyed. And it goes further than Bennett in work
that came after him: the quantum physicist Lídia del Rio and colleagues argued in
2011 that the cost of erasing a system depends on how much the eraser already knows
about it, down to zero and in the quantum case past zero. The bill for clearing a record
is sent to whoever clears it, and it’s smaller the more they know. Try it with a card
under a cup and a sticky note. Write the colour on the note, then erase the note without
lifting the cup: two possible notes become one blank, a merge. Now do it again, but
lift the cup, check the note matches, and then erase: nothing unknown was destroyed.
Same blank note. Different bill.

5.6 The smallest machine that teaches for free, and the one that can’t
Two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by
comparing the start to the end, but an observer’s very first look already rules things
out before any step runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a step teach
you more, for free? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine that
can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows “true” only at W. Start with candidates {U, V}; both show false. Take one step.
From U you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and a
ring forgets nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule, and the file takes it.

Two states can’t do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can’t tell them apart at the
first look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are all the
states there are, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you
never learn anything. Try to draw a counterexample. You’ll draw the same two dots a
few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest number
of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a later
look, and that’s what teaching is.


Theorem 5.3 (Three states are the minimum for free teaching). Call a machine a free
teacher when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of candidates with no repeats



                                            127
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the observer knows strictly more
than after the first look, |K (Ω, t, s0 )| < |K (Ω, [ ], s0 )|. There is a free teacher with exactly
three states, and there is none with two or fewer.

Proof. Three: the ring U → V → W → U with the window true only at W, candidates
{U, V }, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price). Two
or fewer: two candidates that agree at the first look are, on a two-state machine, all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.

Checked as free_incremental_narrowing_with_three and no_free_incr
emental_narrowing_below_three (KnowledgeNarrowingMinimal.v), and the
demon-against-the-first-look form as demon_refutes_incremental.

5.7 What the toll prices, said at last
Now I can say, more precisely than I could two sections ago, what the mark in Section 3
is a mark for. Not for learning. What you know can be narrowed at no cost, with
nothing merged, on some machines under some honest price lists, and the demon is
one. Not for looking, not for copying, not for finding out. The mark is for the one
thing in Section 4 that couldn’t be done without merging, on a machine with finitely
many states: raising a flag that stays up. Learning is the demon writing on a blank
pad, which merges nothing. What the demon pays for is the wipe, a step with a shared
chair. The mark in Section 3 is paid for the same reason, because raising a flag that
stays up also has a shared chair, but it’s a different step: the demon machine has no
flag, and its file prices merges; commitments never appear in it. Same chair. Different
room.

This is also where I settle up with Rovelli, my closest neighbour from the opening
chapter, because I put him and Bennett on opposite sides of one door, and I owe you
how much of that is mine. All of the reconciliation is mine. Rovelli’s paper doesn’t
make it, and in four places his own framing points somewhere else. He reserves
“choice” for an outcome that is stable and not predictable, and he rules out a thermostat
because it runs on a predictable mechanism; the commit in this book is a step a rule
fixes in advance, so by his own definition his result doesn’t cover it. His choice
is a branching, one possibility splitting into two, and he calls choosing in a sense
the inverse of erasing, because branching is the inverse of merging; the toll comes
from a merge, the opposite shape. His stability is for a while: he says stabilization
means something only on times that aren’t too long next to the time it takes things to
thermalize, and past that nothing stays chosen; my permanence is forever (and the
last section owned up that forever is an idealization). And he doesn’t stand beside
Bennett at all: he holds that any measurement is dissipative, credits the point to the
philosopher of science Hans Reichenbach, and doesn’t cite Bennett. So what Rovelli
and I share is a sentence, that a choice that sticks costs something like Landauer’s


                                                128
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


bill. There’s no shared mechanism. Push on it and his coin hitting the ground, a fact
gained from something nobody could predict, sits closer to what this section calls
learning than to committing. I still think it’s the same instinct. That’s my reading, and
he doesn’t make it; you now have everything you need to disagree with it.

And on one point Rovelli isn’t the nearest physics. The nearest I’ve found is in bi-
ology. Thomas Ouldridge and Pieter Rein ten Wolde (2017) derived what they call
the fundamental costs of making a persistent copy of a polymer, one whose sequence
stays correlated with its template after the two have physically come apart, and of
destroying one. On their account a copy like that is a state out of equilibrium, and
making it has a thermodynamic bill they measure efficiency against. A companion
paper the same year, with Christopher Govern, does the same kind of accounting for
the molecules a cell uses to read out the state of its receptors, which is a measurement
in all but name. The way I read them, the copy that has to stay is the one with the
bill, and that’s the closest thing in physics I’ve found to the line this section draws
between finding out and committing. The differences, so it doesn’t get borrowed for
more than it is: theirs is heat, in chemistry, for a correlation between two molecules,
and their title has the destruction of copies in it too, so their copies don’t last forever;
mine is a count in a model of computation, for a reading that never turns off, with no
temperature anywhere. Same instinct again, from a different direction.

The chemistry has the sharp form of it, too, and it came two years later. Jenny Poul-
ton, Pieter Rein ten Wolde and Thomas Ouldridge (2019) studied minimal models of
polymer copying, and in those models, when the copy grows at equilibrium, with the
weakest chemical driving, a persistent copy’s accuracy and the efficiency of making it
both vanish; only driving the growth out of equilibrium, paying, buys a copy that still
carries information about its template after the two let go. That’s finding out against
committing, in chemistry, with the bill attached, and I’d rather say plainly that biology
had the distinction before I did. What stays different is the kind of thing the record is:
theirs is a correlation in a chemical ensemble, mine is a reading enforced by a step in a
model of computation.

Two more neighbours have “learning” and “commit” in their titles, so the slogan
shouldn’t be read against them by accident. Sebastian Goldt and Udo Seifert (2017)
did the stochastic thermodynamics of a neural network learning a rule, and argued
from it that learning has a thermodynamic cost: on their account, the entropy the
network produces bounds how much it can learn. That doesn’t contradict this section,
and here’s why. Their learner isn’t copying onto a blank page. Its weights are a driven
thermal system, jostled by noise and dragged toward what the data push them to,
and what they price is that physical process. This section’s free learning is narrower:
one way of finding out, a copy onto a blank, is allowed to cost nothing. Nothing here
says every way of learning is cheap, and theirs isn’t. From statistics, Aurélien Garivier,
Tor Lattimore and Emilie Kaufmann (2016) gave a proof that in a two-armed bandit
with Gaussian rewards, a strategy that explores first and then commits for good ends


                                            129
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


up, as the horizon grows, with at least twice the regret of the best strategy that keeps
deciding as it goes. That’s the closest published sentence I’ve found to “committing
isn’t free” with a number on it. Their price is reward lost, which is a different unit
from a mark on a ledger, so it’s a cousin. A twin would have to count marks.

So here’s exactly what “No Free Insight,” the name I gave the toll before I understood
it, covers, because I don’t want the name doing work it hasn’t earned. Insight in the
sense of finding out can be free. The insight the toll prices is the kind you’ve committed
to, written into a record the machine can’t silently revise. Whether that narrower thing
deserves the name is a fair thing to argue about; I kept the name because it’s the
question I started with, and because the narrowing is the finding. I don’t count it as a
retreat.

It also tells you how to read a bound that’s coming. Section 8 counts what it takes to
narrow a list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no questions
as it takes to point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact that holds for
anything with a list in it. Turning that count into a bill, saying a run actually paid that
many marks, is a different claim, and when the book makes it, for any certification
system in Section 8, the payment goes in as a hypothesis: a decision tree (a branching
chart of yes-or-no questions, which Section 8 builds) no deeper than the number of
paid steps the run took is handed in, along with the lists themselves and the fact that
the tree’s leaves cover the narrowing. This section is the reason it has to go in that
way. The narrowing alone doesn’t force anyone to pay; the demon just showed you
a narrowing that cost nothing. So wherever narrowing gets a price in this book, the
payment is a premise, and I’ll keep calling it one.

And one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that’s finite and
deterministic and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There’s no quantum
anything in it. This narrowing has nothing to do with “observation collapses the
state”: the narrowing here is bookkeeping in the watcher’s list, the machine never
notices, and the result would be the same if the watcher were a filing cabinet. In 2010
a group in Tokyo (Toyabe, Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did run a real demon,
a tiny particle walked up a staircase of potential by feedback on what a camera saw,
and the energy it gained was paid for by the information the camera took, with no
violation of anything. The demon is real, it works, and it pays. Where it pays is the
part that took a century.

What I still owe: everything so far says “at least one mark” and I’ve been keeping
the marks on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. What happens
when the machine keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in
principle reach in and change it? That’s the counter, and it’s the next thing I have to
build.

Part III

The logic

6 The counter
Everything so far has kept the marks on the side of the page. You played the toy, you
made a tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand. The machine never saw it.
That’s fine for a toy. For anything that’s going to run on its own, with nobody tallying,
the total has to live somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can,
in principle, reach it. So this section is about what a counter has to be before you’re
allowed to call it a receipt. I mean the counter of any machine whose state carries
a running total that every step bumps by whatever a price list says that step costs.
Section 3’s five parts don’t need one (there the total was a sum you did on the side),
so this is one piece added to the five, and the facts below are about anything that has
it. I’ll give you the answer first, because it’s short, and then spend the section on why
each word is there: a receipt is a total that lives in the state, that only climbs, that
equals the sum of what was charged, and that nothing else could have been.

6.1 A stick, split down the middle
The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about
1100, under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was
owed on tally sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (the
treasury’s own handbook from around 1180, the Dialogue of the Exchequer, gives them:
a thumb’s width for a hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound, a bare cut
for a penny), then split lengthwise so that each half carried the same notches. The
payer kept one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the word stockholder
comes from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to settle, you laid the
two halves together, and only the two original halves fit, because wood splits along a
grain nobody can copy. Add a notch to your half and the other half shows a gap where
the partner should be. Try to remove a notch and you find that wood can’t be uncut.
When they finally stopped using them, the clerks burned centuries of old tallies in the
furnaces under the House of Lords, overheated the flue, and burned down the Palace
of Westminster, which I mention because it’s the best fact I picked up for this book
and because it tells you how many of them there were.

Do it: notch a strip of card once for every coin you hand a friend, split it, keep half
each. Try to cheat, either direction. The three things you’ll find are the three things I
want. The total is the notches, added up, and nothing else (I’ll call that conservation).
You can add a notch but you can’t take one away (it only climbs). And two halves
that were notched together must agree; a half that disagrees is a forgery, and the wood
says which one (there is only one honest count). The treasury didn’t have the words.
They had the stick.


                                          131
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Economists read the same stick another way, and they’re not wrong either. Alfred
Mitchell-Innes (1913) made the exchequer tally his star witness that money is credit:
the crown paid the people it owed by “raising a tally” on some branch of its revenue,
a wooden acknowledgment of debt. A receipt to me, money to him, and it’s the same
piece of wood. Narayana Kocherlakota (1998) later proved a version of his point: in a
wide class of economies where nobody can be held to a promise, anything money lets
people do, a memory of everyone’s past dealings lets them do too. His title says it in
three words: money is memory.

6.2 Why it has to climb
Start with the second property, because it’s the one that does the most work and the
one people fight hardest. Why can’t the counter ever go down?

Because of what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section 3, says a run from NO
to YES costs at least one. That sentence is a floor: it says the run paid at least this much.
If the counter could come back down, a run could pay the toll, get its flag, and then
take the payment back, and the floor would be a floor on nothing; “this run cost at
least one” would be true of a run that ended having cost nothing. So a counter that can
fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the books, and a floor stated in terms of
it isn’t a floor. The counter only climbing is not a flourish. It’s what makes “at least”
mean something. This ledger records cumulative charges, each a whole number of
marks and none negative, so it never decreases. A refundable balance, one that pays
money back, would be a different accounting object with a different invariant, and the
floor here says nothing about it. (In Section 3’s abstract theorem the total is a sum of
whole numbers and climbing comes for free; this paragraph is about why a total stored
in the state, where a step could in principle write it, has to be designed so that no step
ever lowers it.)

The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other, pointing
in opposite directions, and that’s a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie Lamport
