Proof. Theorem 16.22(2) gives a loaded state and two runs from it that end with the
same window, one with the record up and one with it down, and, from one clean
loaded state, two runs with the same window, one whose ledger rose by at least 3 and
one made of free base moves that leaves the ledger where it started (that theorem’s
proof builds it; complete_two_runs states it). Both end states explain the same bare
transcript. A verifier complete for the claim accepts that transcript, since a state where
the claim holds explains it; a verifier sound for the claim then makes the claim true of
every state that explains it, including the one where it’s false. That’s (1), and (2) is the
same with the ledger: the paid run’s end state satisfies the claim, and the free run’s
doesn’t. For (3) the two runs are written out in the statement: three moves land on line


                                               156
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


4 in both runs with both counters at 0, and the same two-state argument applies.

Checked as ver_complete_no_record_verifier, ver_complete_no_ledge
r_verifier and ver_small_no_ledger_verifier (VerifierSmall.v), the first
two from complete_hides_record and complete_two_runs of ThieleCom-
pleteWindow.v. Put with the three escapes, the whole picture is one statement for
every Thiele-complete machine, ver_corollary, and for the small machine ver_
small_corollary: the bare-transcript verifier doesn’t exist; the collision survives
into any richer transcript that keeps it, so no verifier that only reads its bare part works
either; a verifier on full states exists; one on the bare transcript with a committed bit
exists, sound and complete when the bit is honest, and the unchecked bit breaks the
contract; and one on a truthful response exists. The collision is a premise of the richer-
transcript half, and the contract is assumed; no fourth way is claimed to be impossible,
and no hardness is proved.

In the three escapes the collision is gone, and no trick did it: the extra information
pulls A and B apart. The full-state transcript shows the counter outright. The honest
commitment for A carries a true bit and the one for B a false bit. The honest responses
are 1 and 0. In none of the three is the verifier asked to tell identical inputs apart,
which was the impossible job.

Now the limit, and I’d rather say it before you find it. A list of states has no authen-
tication built into it, so nothing in it stops a liar from handing over whatever the
verifier wants to see. The commitment contract is assumed, and the unchecked bit
above is what happens when the assumption is dropped. The response relation only
allows a truthful counter value, so asking a question here does not buy resistance to a
cheating prover. And the cost 1 is an abstract price I wrote down. It doesn’t measure
what it takes to authenticate a state, check a cryptographic proof or send a response.
What these three show is which extra distinctions a verifier can use. They are not an
adversary model, a security parameter or a hardness reduction.

So what would it take to make that commitment bit binding for real, against somebody
who wants to cheat? Cryptographers had to face that one in the open, and the place
I’d point is a short paper the computer scientist Manuel Blum, whose Turing Award
was for complexity theory and its use in cryptography, presented at the CRYPTO
meeting in 1981, “Coin Flipping by Telephone.” His setup: Alice and Bob have just
divorced, they live in different cities, and they want to flip a coin over the phone for
who gets the car, with nobody they both trust to do the flipping. If Alice flips and
announces, Bob has to take her word. If Bob calls it first, Alice can lie about how it
landed. Blum’s way out is for one side to commit first: send something that fixes the
choice without showing it, and open it only after the other side has called. And what
keeps that commitment binding isn’t anybody’s promise. It’s a bet that a certain kind
of big number is hard to factor. Push on that and you’re standing on the honest edge of
this subsection. In Blum’s protocol, binding is earned, on the condition that factoring


                                            157
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


is hard. Here it’s written into the contract and assumed outright, and the unchecked
bit above shows what’s left without it. That’s why I won’t say these escapes beat a
cheater. Blum’s paper is the kind of thing it would take, and nothing like it is in this
chapter.

Now point the three escapes back at the record this book is about, because that’s
where they bite hardest. A record kept in a machine’s state is bits too. Hand someone
outside a copy of those bits with a note saying “the flag is up,” and they’re reading
a window: the run that really raised the flag and a box built to print that it did cast
the same shadow. So putting the record in the step answers “was this earned?” for
whoever can see the state and trusts the step that wrote it. For anybody else it moves
the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust the box that says it ran?” Crossing that
line takes one of the escapes: the whole state, from a box you already trust; a bound
bit, which in practice means a signature over the record or a quote from measured
hardware (and Section 14 shows a quote vouches only for what was measured); or
asking, against a box that might lie, which is the cryptographers’ business. One more
relative deserves its name here, verifiable computation: the box hands back its answer
with a short proof that the answer is right, which a checker can verify without redoing
the work (Pinocchio, built in 2013 by the computer scientists Bryan Parno, Jon Howell,
Craig Gentry and Mariana Raykova), and proof-carrying data passes proofs like that
along a whole chain of parties who don’t trust each other (the computer scientists
Alessandro Chiesa and Eran Tromer, 2010). That’s the strongest export there is, and
notice what it exports: the claim. The history stays behind. The proof shows the
answer is right for that input. It doesn’t show which machine did the work, or when,
and any box with the input can make one. Nothing in this book supplies any of
these escapes. The model’s record is local to the machine that keeps it, and the small
machine of Part IV keeps its record in its state with no signature on it at all.

7.7 What this isn’t
Three things this isn’t, and I’d rather take them off the table now.

It isn’t mysticism. Nothing here says the window is false or the state is unknowable.
The wall is a function, the objects are its inputs, and the only claim is that the function
isn’t one-to-one on the thing you asked about. A richer window recovers it. Plato’s
prisoners could have turned around.

Rice’s theorem is the neighbour this looks most like. It isn’t Rice’s theorem, though it
rhymes with it. The logician Henry Rice, in a paper of 1953, proved that no program
can decide any interesting property of what another program does from its code, and
a cousin of the fact here is that a run which hasn’t halted yet looks, so far, exactly like
one that never will. But Rice is about what’s computable. The cube is about what’s
there. The cube theorem holds for a toy with two states and nothing to compute;
the obstruction is missing information, and cleverness doesn’t come into it. I’d be
overclaiming if I let the famous theorem lend its weight to the small one.


                                           158
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


And it isn’t “with enough data you can recover anything.” Kalman’s unobservable
states stay unobservable for all time. The question is never how much of the window
you’ve got. It’s which window.

The counter lives in the state, and whether anyone outside can read it depends entirely
on what they’re shown, and a window with a pair like that in it can’t price the flag
exactly, with any rule, ever. Which raises the question I’ve been pushing in front of
me since the buckets. Fine, the flag went up and was paid for and I can see it in the
right window. What does that entitle me to? A paid flag is a paid flag. What’s the
claim behind it, and when am I allowed to lean on it?

8 Structural entitlement
I keep writing the word “vouch” and then taking it back. Let me stop doing that and
say what it would take. A reading went from NO to YES, the toll charged the move
that did it (Section 3), maybe the reading stays up (Section 4 says what it costs to make
it stay), and the right window shows it (Section 7). Now: what is a later step allowed
to do because of that? That’s a different question from “is the thing true,” and the gap
between those two is the subject of this section, and I’d argue it’s the subject of most
of the arguments people have about evidence, so give me the long way round.

8.1 The coin that moved
Here’s an experiment you can run on a friend, and I’d ask you to actually run it,
because the feeling of it is the point. Put a coin under one of three cups while they
watch. Say, cup one. Send them out of the room. Move the coin to cup three. Then,
and this is the trick, put a second coin under cup one. Bring them back and ask: “Is
there a coin under cup one?”

They say yes. They’re right; there is. And they have a reason: they watched you put
it there. True, and believed, and justified by what they saw. And it’s not knowledge,
and you can feel that it isn’t, because their reason points at a coin that left. The coin
that makes them right is not the coin they’re thinking of.

That’s the trap from the opening chapter, done with cups: Edmund Gettier’s three-
page paper from 1963, “Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?”, which broke a definition
of knowledge in about the time it takes to read it. The definition was that you know
something when it’s true, you believe it, and you’ve got good reasons. Gettier took
it from two philosophers of the 1950s, Roderick Chisholm and A. J. Ayer, and the
only place he mentions Plato is a footnote saying Plato “seems to be considering”
something like it in the Theaetetus. I’d assumed people had leaned on that definition
since Plato. As far as I can find, they hadn’t. The Stanford Encyclopedia’s entry
on the analysis of knowledge calls the idea that it was ever widely held “a bit of a
convenient fiction,” and Julien Dutant, a philosopher at King’s College London, wrote
a 2015 paper called “The Legend of the Justified True Belief Analysis” arguing that the
older tradition asked for something stronger: a mark on the belief that can’t be wrong.


                                          159
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


I’ve read only summaries of Dutant’s paper, so take that last part as his, secondhand.
Gettier’s two cases, and the cups, show a belief that passes all three tests and still isn’t
knowledge, because the reasons and the fact aren’t connected; they just happen to
agree. Bertrand Russell had a related case in 1948: somebody looks at a stopped clock
at the one moment it happens to be right, and they’re right about the time, and they
know nothing.

Is 1963 the bottom? Not even close, and 1948 isn’t either. The Stanford Encyclopedia’s
entry on the analysis of knowledge, which is where I’d send you to check me, gives a
case from the eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara: you’re looking for
water on a hot day, you see water ahead, it’s a mirage, and when you get there you
happen to find water under a rock. And one from Peter of Mantua, a logician of the
late fourteenth century who died in 1400 and whose Logica survives in manuscript:
Plato is running right next to you, you take him for Socrates, so you believe Socrates is
running, and Socrates is in fact running, in Rome, where you can’t see him. Older still?
Maybe. This is where the trail goes cold, which isn’t the same as where it ends. What
it changes is how much I trust the shape. People in different centuries, languages and
traditions kept building the same trap by hand: a reason that points at one thing, and
a truth that happens to be sitting on another.

What’s missing is a wire from the reason to the fact. Ask your friend what they’d need,
to be entitled to “there’s a coin under cup one,” and they’ll tell you: lift the cup. Not
“remember putting it there.” Lift it, now, and look. That lifting is an event, it happens
on the record, and after it the reason and the fact are the same object.

8.2 Plato nearly had it
Who was Theaetetus, though? The dialogue is named for a real person, and I wanted
to know who. He was a mathematician. In the dialogue he’s a teenager, and he tells
Socrates that his teacher Theodorus had been showing them, one case at a time, that
the side of a square of area three, or five, and so on up to seventeen, can’t be named
by any fraction: the Pythagoreans’ diagonal from Section 2, done again case by case.
The young man’s idea was to stop going one case at a time and find one word for all
of them. Euclid’s tenth book, on lengths that share no common measure, is thought
to be largely his work, and he’s credited with being the first to study the eight-faced
and twenty-faced solids, the two Plato assigned to air and water in the Timaeus. The
dialogue opens with him being carried home to Athens from the army at Corinth,
badly wounded and sick with the dysentery going round the camp, barely alive; the
usual date is 369 BC. And the conversation itself has come down as a record. Euclid
of Megara (not the geometer) says he took notes as soon as he got home, filled them
out later, and had Socrates correct them whenever he came to Athens, and he has
the result read aloud. So the dialogue about what turns a true belief into knowledge
survives as a checked record of what was said. That changes nothing in the argument.
I just like that the book about knowledge is named for the man who took the diagonal
and made it general.

                                            160
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


I want to be fair to the Theaetetus here, because it’s easy to be quick with the ancients
and they deserve better. Socrates, in that dialogue, doesn’t just say “true belief plus
reasons.” He tries three different senses of what the “account” behind a true belief
could be: a statement you can say aloud; a list of the thing’s parts; and, third, the
mark that sets this thing apart from everything else it could be confused with. He tries
each, and each fails, and the dialogue ends with nobody knowing what knowledge
is, which is one of the more honest endings in philosophy. But the third sense is the
one I’d underline. An account as the thing that distinguishes: the test that gives the real
case a value no rival gives. He couldn’t make it work because he had no way to say
what the account had to be attached to. Two and a half thousand years later, here’s
this book’s guess: the thing it has to be attached to is a state, and the account is an
object sitting in it. I’m not claiming that settles Plato. I’m claiming he was pointing at
the right thing, and that’s my reading of the dialogue, which you can check against it
in an afternoon.

Push on that once more, because Socrates gives his own reason for dropping the third
account, and it isn’t the one I just gave. If the account means knowing the mark that
sets the thing apart, then knowledge has been defined as true belief plus knowledge
of something, and the word you were trying to define is back inside its own definition.
A circle. Does a check get out of it? It gets the word out: a test that ran and found the
mark isn’t defined in terms of knowing. Whether the test was any good is still a real
question, and it’s the question the rest of this section puts a price on. So I’d say the
circle moves. It doesn’t vanish. It moves somewhere you can look at it, which is the
most I’d claim.

8.3 The shape, said once
So here’s what I mean by entitlement, and it has three parts, and I’ll try to earn each.

A run is entitled to a claim when three things are present. First, an object, carried in the
state: a grouping, a relation between groups, a counter, a package of constraints. That’s
a thing you could print. A belief doesn’t count. Second, a checked relation between
that object and the claim: a test that was actually run, with its result on hand. “A test
exists” doesn’t count. Third, an event on the record that says this object was put there
and paid for, so that anyone auditing the run can point back at the moment the claim
was marked.

Said as a definition, so the rest of the section has something to point at:


Definition 8.1 (Entitlement). A run is entitled to a claim when three things are on hand:
an object carried in the run’s states; a checked relation between that object and the claim,
meaning a test that was run and whose result is on the record; and a paid event, a move
of the run at which the object was put in place and which the price list charged at least
one. In a certification system (Definition 3.1) a move that takes the reading from no to
yes is such a move, because the toll charges it. This is the book’s word; there’s no Coq


                                            161
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


definition of it.


Without the third part, the object may be sitting right there and the claim may be true,
and the run still hasn’t earned it. That’s the cups: the coin is under cup one; the reason
is disconnected from it; nobody lifted the cup. Put it on Section 3’s sheet of paper,
the one with the NO box, the YES box and the tally line, and grow the toy by one
thing: the state is now the box you’re in plus whatever is written on the sheet beside it.
Next to the boxes, write a note: “coin under cup one, checked.” Writing the note is a
WORK move, and WORK costs nothing. The note is an object, it’s on the paper, and it
might even be true. What it doesn’t have is a crossing on the record: no move took the
reading from NO to YES when the note went down, and there’s no mark under the
line for it. The note is raw data, forged in one write, and the five parts allow a system
that lets you write one, because nothing in them says what an ordinary move may put
in the state. A note put down by the move that crosses has a receipt, and the receipt is
the event. One limit on that word “receipt”: the crossing records that something was
paid for at that moment. What the crossing move actually looked at before it crossed
is up to whatever the move does, and the five parts don’t say.

And here’s the part to hold on to. Nothing in the five parts makes a later move read the
reading. The step function is handed the state and a move name, and it’s allowed to
ignore the YES box completely; plenty of systems will. So when I say a run is entitled, I
mean what someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and the receipt.
The system doesn’t have to enforce it, and unless somebody builds it to, it won’t.

This is a good place to line up the three things the word established has had to mean so
far, because they blur easily, and a blur here would make the book look like it proves
more than it does. The yardstick is the opening chapter’s four conditions for a check
being about this very claim: the same property, the same thing, the same edition, and
an honest check.
