After the column of questions, the first column is Section 3’s bare toll: a paid crossing,
and nothing says a check happened at all (Section 9 has a remark saying exactly
that). The second is this section’s entitlement. The third is the small machine of
Part IV, whose step won’t let a commit through without a passing check of the same
property, on the same thing, at the same edition, for every program from a clean start
(Theorem 16.8, and Theorem 16.9 for a run that ends certified), whose checker comes
with a proof that it says what it means (Lemma 16.1, Theorem 16.11), and whose
certified runs from a clean start cost at least three (Theorem 16.16). Even there two
things are missing, and the first is in the table, where you’ll see it. The step doesn’t
police whether a check could have failed: a property every value has is a perfectly
legal check, sound and useless. And in all three columns the status belongs to whoever
reads the record. The machine doesn’t know anything. What its flag means is assigned
from outside, by whoever says what each property means.

Why does the honest check carry so much? The philosopher Linda Zagzebski, who
works on knowledge and the virtues of a careful mind, argued in 1994 that any ac-
count of knowledge whose justification leaves even a small gap between having good
reasons and being right lets a Gettier case through: take a case where bad luck makes
the reasons point the wrong way, then add a stroke of good luck that makes the belief
true anyway. The first three conditions plus an honest check close that gap by con-
struction, and only one half of honesty is needed for it, the half that says no when the
property is false. Saying yes whenever it’s true is extra. A check that can be wrong, a
test suite that sometimes passes broken code, puts you straight back in her gap, and
then the record certifies something smaller and still true: this procedure said yes.

And who certifies that the check is honest? Not the record. Honesty is a fact about
what the check does on every input, and the opening chapter already said a finished
state can’t hold that kind of fact. It has to be carried by a proof about the checker, done
once, outside every run, and nothing on the record pays for it. So an established claim
is two things stuck together: a run property the record carries and a program property
a proof carries, and the proof is entitlement for the auditor. The machine gets none
from it. Section 16 shows where that chain of reasons stops on a real machine.

The engineering version of this was already built, in 1996 and 1997. The computer
scientist George Necula, then at Carnegie Mellon, called it proof-carrying code: when
you ship a program to a host that doesn’t trust you, you ship a proof with it that the
program obeys the host’s safety rules, and the host checks the proof that arrived before
running anything. Not your reputation. Not “a proof exists somewhere.” The one
in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook’s certificates had the same bones,


                                           163
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


from Section 3: a claim comes with a witness that’s cheap to check, and the checker
checks that witness. And the Scottish philosopher David Hume, in 1748, arguing
about miracles in his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, laid out the thing the
receipt replaces. He weighed testimony against evidence, and wrote that “a wise man,
therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.” The way I read him, the whole of
his argument is a method for how much to trust a witness when you have no receipt.
The move in this book is to stop weighing. A claim on the record is either backed by
its object and its paid event, or it’s testimony from outside, and a run that leans on
testimony hasn’t earned it itself. It can inherit it, but only as far as the copy it leans on
is genuine, which is Section 7’s problem of a record shown from outside.

Robert Brandom, a philosopher at the University of Pittsburgh, built a whole account
of language on two words this book leans on, commitment and entitlement, and his
Making It Explicit (1994) is where I’d send anyone who suspects I invented the pair.
In his picture, as I read it and as his reviewers describe it, people talking keep score
on each other: what each speaker is committed to, what they’ve put themselves on
the hook for, and what each is entitled to, what they’re licensed to claim. You can be
committed without being entitled (a reckless assertion), many claims count as entitled
by default until someone challenges them, and entitlement can be borrowed: I can
claim a thing on your say-so and defer to you when I’m challenged. Lay mine beside
his and the differences are the content. His score is kept by the other people in the
room; here it’s a reading in the state. His entitlement often comes by default; here it’s
an event that has to happen and is charged. And his deferral is my testimony, which
I’ve just let back in on a leash: borrowed entitlement is only as good as the copy is
genuine. The leash has an older formal cousin, the jurisdiction rule of Burrows, Abadi
and Needham’s logic of authentication (Section 7), where you take a statement on
an authority’s word only if you already believe the authority has jurisdiction over
it. It came first, presented in 1989 and printed in 1990, years ahead of Brandom’s
book of 1994, and its words are believes and jurisdiction where his are commitment and
entitlement.

There’s a whole field that would want a word here too, the logic of belief revision,
which asks how a reasonable mind should change what it believes when something
new comes in. Its nearest neighbours are worth naming, and I couldn’t keep them
apart until I put them back on the table with the cups. Your friend believes the coin is
under cup one. They can learn something that doesn’t clash with that, say cup two is
empty, and just add it. They can lift cup one, find nothing, and have to change their
mind about a table nobody touched. Or you can tell them you moved the coin. The
last two felt alike to me at first. They aren’t. In one the friend was wrong. In the other
the friend was right, and then the table changed.

Krister Segerberg, a Swedish logician at Uppsala, built a logic of irrevocable revision
in 1998: accepting something so that it can’t be given up. That’s the firmness question
taken to its end. Isaac Levi, a philosopher at Columbia who spent a career on how


                                            164
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


beliefs get fixed and unfixed, split adding a belief into a deliberate kind and a routine
kind (I cite his 1991 book; the split goes back to his 1980 one). Deliberate is reasoning
your way there. Routine is where you take on whatever a procedure you committed
to in advance hands you, the way you’d accept a reading off a thermometer you’ve
already decided to trust, or what’s under a cup when you lift it. What I think the split
rests on is when the trust goes in: once, before the data comes. A passing CHECK is
routine in exactly that sense, with a checker proved honest once, outside every run.

Neil Tennant, a logician at Ohio State, and Gösta Grahne, a computer scientist at
Helsinki, I first filed as two separate complaints. They’re one move made from op-
posite sides. The target is the best-known impossibility in that field, the Swedish
philosopher Peter Gärdenfors’s 1986 theorem that a natural rule for conditionals, the
one his paper calls the Ramsey test, can’t live with rational revision. Tennant argued
in 2008 that it goes through only by treating some additions as revisions: the friend
who learned cup two was empty gets counted as having changed their mind. Grahne,
working on updates and counterfactuals, argued in 1998 that Gärdenfors’s theorem
bites only revising, so the friend whose coin was moved is out of its reach. Side by
side, they squeeze the theorem from both ends into one case: being wrong about a
table nobody touched.

The line this book leans on hardest is between two kinds of change. Revising is
changing what you believe about a world that stayed put. Updating is changing it
because the world moved. Two computer scientists, Hirofumi Katsuno and Alberto
Mendelzon, drew that line for knowledge bases in a 1991 paper on the difference
between updating a knowledge base and revising it; database researchers had been
working on updates with incomplete information since the mid-1980s, Arthur Keller
and Marianne Winslett among them. Grahne’s result stands on it. And look at what
the friend sees: an empty cup one is the same empty cup whether they misremembered
or you moved the coin. The evidence alone can’t tell revising from updating; that’s
a fibre. What tells them apart is a count of how often the cups were touched. The
machine in Part IV keeps that count as an edition number for each thing, and its
version rule treats every write as an update: a write moves the edition number, so
every fact about the old edition stops counting for the new one.

And Alexandru Baltag, Bryan Renne and Sonja Smets, three logicians at Amsterdam,
gave a logic in 2014 that keeps apart three things Gettier’s cases blur: justified belief,
explicit knowledge and conclusive evidence. The friend who watched has justified
belief; the friend who lifted the cup has conclusive evidence. Explicit knowledge I
read as knowing with the justification written out beside it, the way the record keeps
its check, and I’m less sure of that one. Put them together and they say something
exact about this book’s record. A record that’s never wrong and never corrected would
be a dogmatist’s dream if its sentences were about the present. They aren’t. Each says
a property held of a thing at one edition, and that sentence stays true after the edition
number moves on. The record can be infallible and never corrected only because its


                                           165
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


sentences are edition-stamped. Strip the stamps, and the first write would turn it into
a liar that can’t take anything back.

Push on that and it gives twice. The record is Segerberg’s irrevocable acceptance every
time, with no revising in it. If a check was dishonest, the only fix that fits a record like
this is a second record on top saying “withdrawn,” the way a revocation list works,
so the infallibility leans on the checker, proved once, outside. And the record is never
wrong partly because it only talks about past editions. Whoever reads it wants now,
and getting from “held at that edition” to “holds now” crosses every update since.
The record doesn’t make that step for you.

And the logicians the opening chapter named in passing, the ones who taught the
logic of knowing to count. Here they are properly, and this time I want to see what
each price rests on. Ho Ngoc Duc, in 1997, gave the logic of knowing an operator
for “true after some train of thought”: an agent doesn’t know every consequence of
what it knows now. It can come to know any of them by taking steps of reasoning.
Steps. I took that at first for the thing I was after, until I saw which way it points.
His operator points forward, at what the agent could come to know. A record points
back, at what was checked. One arrow, read from opposite ends. And Sergei Artemov
and Roman Kuznets, in 2014, turned logical omniscience into a question of cost: a
logic escapes it when every valid claim that something is known comes with a proof
whose size is bounded by a polynomial in the size of the claim. The usual modal
logics of knowledge can’t pass that test unless NP equals coNP, which most people
would bet against, and justification logic passes it for knowledge stated together with
its justification, because the size of the justification pays for the search. That last
clause took me a few reads. What I think it means is Cook’s certificate from the proof-
carrying-code paragraph above: put the justification inside the claim, and the hard
part, finding it, was paid before the claim was written. Their price rests on an open
bet, and it’s a price on looking. A price, of a sort. Steps and a price are both there,
then, in their own form. What I still don’t find in them is the one I care about: a single
act that closes a question for good and is charged as that act. Their steps are steps of
reasoning, and their price is on finding a proof. Neither is on settling. I couldn’t get
past the journal’s paywall to Artemov and Kuznets’s paper, so my account of it comes
from how other people describe it.

Push on mine the same way and it gives. A check is one of Duc’s trains of thought,
so my act is the last step of his train, where the walking stops. What I’ve added is a
direction and a charge on stopping. And the charge rests on a choice. I put it inside
the step, and nothing forced me to.

Three things entitlement is not. It isn’t permission: an access control system says who
may write to what, and that’s granted from outside and says nothing about truth;
a process with permission to write the note still has no entitlement. It isn’t “true,
therefore usable”: that’s the cups. And it isn’t “sound by luck”: a shortcut that gives


                                            166
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate is the stopped clock. The
count below has one condition aimed at it, and I’ll tell you what the condition says
and how much it actually catches.

8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals
Now the number, because a book about a bill has to say how much. Here’s the idea in
a form you can do with three playing cards. Shuffle cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down.
Sort them using only questions of the form “is this one bigger than that one?”, and
count the questions. There are six orders the cards could be in. Each question has two
answers, so after one question you’ve split the six into at most two piles, after two
questions at most four, and you need to get down to one. Four is less than six, so two
questions can’t always do it, and three can, and you can draw the tree of questions
on paper and see it: six leaves, three deep. The number of questions you need is at
least the base-two logarithm of the number of possibilities you started with, rounded
up: that’s log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded to 3. Donald Knuth, a computer
scientist at Stanford, gives this, in the volume on sorting of his The Art of Computer
Programming, as the lower bound for all comparison sorting, and the shape of the
argument is just: a tree f questions deep has at most 2 f leaves, so it can’t tell apart
more than 2 f cases.

And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards.
There are 120 orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven questions,
and seven is enough, though not by the obvious method. Finding the way is a good
evening with a deck of cards (Knuth has it, under the name merge insertion, from the
mathematicians Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now twelve cards. They
can be in 479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the count says at least 29.
Ford and Johnson’s method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells, a mathematician at
Los Alamos who built a programming language for exactly this kind of combinatorial
search, showed by a computer search that nothing does better: twelve cards need 30.
The floor was 29. The price is 30. So the count is a floor and only a floor; it never
promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this section has to be read
exactly the same way.

Ralph Hartley, an electronics researcher at the lab that became Bell Labs, writing in the
Bell System Technical Journal in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly
this way: the logarithm of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count.
That’s the measure here, and I’ll say plainly it’s Hartley’s. Shannon’s would need a
distribution over the list, and there isn’t one. There’s just the list’s length.

Here’s the same count with something you can hold. Put three coins under three cups.
Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible rows under the cups. Someone
hands you two answers: heads under the first cup, tails under the second. Lift the
first cup and compare. A matching answer leaves four possible rows. Lift the second
and compare. A match leaves two. The last coin can still be either way. The list really


                                          167
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a claim about which way the
last coin faces.

This is a parlour game, and an old one. In A Christmas Carol, in 1843, Scrooge’s nephew
Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks of something,
and everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no. He’s thinking of
an animal, a disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and lives in London,
and the answer is Uncle Scrooge. Most people know the game as twenty questions,
and twenty is a good number for it: each yes-or-no answer can at best cut the field in
half, and twenty halvings take a million or so possibilities, 220 = 1,048,576, down to
one. Push on that, though. The halving only happens because Fred answers truthfully
about what’s actually in his head. Lie once and the count still shrinks; it shrinks
around the wrong animal. That’s the cups again: the four and the two are real because
you lifted the cup and compared. Being told what was under it wouldn’t have made
them real.

Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are “still on the table,”
the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior and
the second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as a list you could print. They
aren’t “the space of possible worlds.” Picture the ruling-out as observations, each
observation that ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the card
tree. And here’s the claim: if that tree is no deeper than the number of paid steps the
run took, and the tree has enough leaves to cover the narrowing in a way I’ll spell out
in a moment, then the counter rose by at least log2 of the prior’s length, rounded up,
minus log2 of the posterior’s length, rounded up. At least as many marks as index bits
the list lost, where the index bits of a list are the yes/no questions it takes to point at
one entry of it, the card count again. That’s the bound.

“Paid step” needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least one for.
In a certification system the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is one; a
price list is free to put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check), and
the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches and leaves
with nothing written on them, and “no deeper than the number of paid steps” is a
count along the run that happened. It isn’t a walk down the tree. A paid step doesn’t
have to have asked any question at all.

Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn’t say about the run. It takes the two lists,
the tree and the covering as given. It doesn’t say the run produced the posterior from
the prior; nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given lists, a tree
and a covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover the rounded
drop in list length. That’s Section 5’s warning come due: watching can narrow for free,
so the payment can’t be dug out of the narrowing. It goes in as a premise, the tree’s
depth against the paid steps, and I’ll keep calling it one.




                                             168
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


8.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test
Before the count, one link that’s pure logic, and Plato’s third account is the whole
of it. Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each
candidate looks like from outside. The list’s membership test accepts an observation
when some candidate on the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get
pickier: anything the short list’s test accepts, the long list’s accepts too. The word for
that, and it runs backward from English, is stronger: the stronger test is the one that
lets fewer things through.

Pickier, though, isn’t the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take
all six orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card
2: 1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: “is 1 left of 2?” Every survivor says yes,
and the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior’s test accepts yes and no, the posterior’s
only yes. Strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: “is the first card a
3?” Now 3-1-2 says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among the removed
orders 3-2-1 says yes and 2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no. Same strength,
even though three orders are gone. What made the difference is a removed candidate
whose observation no survivor shares. That’s Plato’s mark, the thing that sets this case
apart from everything it could be confused with, turned into a function. Narrow the
list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and the test is strictly stronger;
narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.

8.6 The count, exactly
Here are the words and the count, for any system with Section 6’s counter. A list is
a finite list of candidates, repeats allowed, and |Ω| is the length of the list Ω, repeats
counted. ⌈log2 x ⌉ is the base-two logarithm of x rounded up: the smallest k ∈ N with
2k ≥ x. At x = 0 it is 0, the convention for empty lists set in Section 5. And a −̇ b is
subtraction on whole numbers that stops at zero, so 3 −̇ 5 = 0.


Definition 8.2 (Decision tree). A decision tree is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees.
Its depth is 0 for a leaf and one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf count
L( T ) is 1 for a leaf and the sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is written on
a tree: no question, no answer, no candidate.


Lemma 8.1 (A tree is no wider than two to its depth). For every decision tree T, L( T ) ≤
2depth(T ) , and so ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ).

Proof. Induction on the tree. A leaf has one leaf and depth 0, and 1 ≤ 20 . A branch
with subtrees of depths d1 , d2 has at most 2d1 + 2d2 ≤ 2 · 2max(d1 ,d2 ) leaves, which is 2 to
its own depth. The second half: L( T ) ≤ 2depth(T ) means depth( T ) is one of the k with
2k ≥ L( T ), and the rounded-up logarithm is the smallest of them.

Checked as decision_tree_leaves_le_pow2_depth and decision_tree_lo


                                             169
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


g2_up_leaf_bound (DecisionTreeBound.v). Both are stated over the tree type alone,
a leaf or a branch, with nothing about any machine in them.


Theorem 8.2 (Paid narrowing, counted). Take a system with a counter µ and a price list
c that obey conservation (Theorem 6.1): each step raises µ by exactly its charge. Let Ω and
Ω′ be lists with |Ω′ | > 0, let T be a decision tree with |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ | (the tree covers the
narrowing), and let t be a run from s ending at s′ in which at least depth( T ) steps are charged
at least one each. Then

                          ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

Proof. The rounded-up logarithm respects order, so the covering gives ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ ≤
⌈log2 ( L( T ) · |Ω′ |)⌉. It is also subadditive on products of positive numbers, ⌈log2 ab⌉ ≤
⌈log2 a⌉ + ⌈log2 b⌉, because 2⌈log2 a⌉ · 2⌈log2 b⌉ ≥ ab. So

                  ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ),

the last step by Lemma 8.1. By hypothesis at least depth( T ) steps of the run were
charged at least one, and no step is charged less than zero, so the sum of the charges
is at least depth( T ). By conservation that sum is µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

For any system with a counter that obeys conservation it is two checked theorems, put
together by hand; nothing in Coq joins them. nec_e_cs_count_any (NecEEnt.v)
proves it over any certification system with the sum of the charges of a run in place
of the counter’s rise, and without needing |Ω′ | > 0; and nec_f_conservation
(NecFCounter.v), stated over any counter machine kept by a price list, says that sum is
the counter’s rise. A system that is both gets the theorem. The bill form is also part of
Theorem 8.3 below. The tree half is the checked lemma above; the rest is arithmetic on
three whole numbers, the two lengths and the leaf count, and on the counter. Notice
what’s missing from the hypotheses: anything tying the lists to the run. That’s the
honest shape of the bound.

Three honest small prints, all of them visible in the statement. Both logarithms round
up separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the prior and the posterior
round up to the same number of index bits (four candidates narrowed to three, say)
the bound says nothing. The lists are plain lists, repeats allowed, so “index bits” is
a difference of rounded list lengths with repeats counted; a list can get shorter by
dropping a duplicate without losing a single candidate, and “a candidate was ruled
out” and “the list got shorter” are two different claims. And the difference isn’t the
number of questions anyone asked.

The covering condition, |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, is the nearest thing the count has to an anti-
stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each survivor
standing for a little crowd of the prior’s candidates, itself included, a crowd no bigger


                                               170
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


than the tree has leaves. Then the condition says every candidate in the prior fits in
some survivor’s crowd. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It
doesn’t say why anything was deleted. So the condition rules out deleting too much
for the tree you’ve paid for. It doesn’t rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy
every hypothesis of the count and have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices
the size of the drop. It says nothing about the honesty of it. And the covering can’t
just be dropped. On the small machine one yes-or-no question with a big constant in
it narrows 2n candidates to one, n index bits, for a ledger of three, so for any n ≥ 4 the
bound is false without it (Section 16.17).

Here’s a side trip worth taking, because it looks like it breaks the count and doesn’t.
Two information theorists, Rudolf Ahlswede and Gunter Dueck (1989), noticed that
asking “is it this one?” is a different job from asking “which one is it?” If each receiver
only wants to know whether the message is theirs, a noisy channel used n times
can serve a number of receivers that grows like two raised to two to the nC, with
C the channel’s capacity, where naming the message only gets you two to the nC.
That’s identification, and on its face it says checking can be exponentially cheaper than
naming. But their tests are allowed to say yes wrongly once in a while. Make the yes
sound, a test that never says yes to the wrong message, which is the only kind of check
this book lets raise a record, and the double exponential collapses. The argument is
two lines of pigeonhole. I argue it here, and nothing checks it. Each receiver’s test, to
be any use, says yes on some output its own message can produce, and soundness
means no other message can produce that output; so those outputs are all different,
one per receiver, and there can’t be more receivers than outputs, |Y |n for an output
alphabet Y. Single exponential, the same order as naming. So for a check that never
lies, the card count is the right scale after all, and the cheap trick needs a check that
can be fooled.

8.7 What you’ve got
A paid flag is not a true claim; Section 7 left it at “a paid flag is a paid flag,” and
Section 9 will say it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation
behind it gives you is entitlement: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as
established, and can point at the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing in the
five parts makes the system itself read the flag; I said that above and I’m saying it
again because it’s the sentence most likely to get lost.) Entitlement costs at least the
index bits of narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree and a covering somebody
supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree’s depth. The cups say why entitlement
and truth are different. Plato says what the checked relation has to do: distinguish.
Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.

Put the three pieces on one hypothesis list (narrow the list with a test that separates,
find the paid event, count the bill against a tree the run paid for) and you get a
single statement, structural entitlement, once over any certification system and once,
under the longer name structural entitlement represented, for every Thiele-complete

                                           171
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


machine, the small machine included (Section 16.17). The first one reads as follows.


Theorem 8.3 (Structural entitlement, over any certification system). Take a certification
system (Definition 3.1), a state s that reads no, and a run t from s that ends in a state that
reads yes. Take a type of candidates, a type of observations with an exact equality test, an
observation obs of each candidate, and a decoder d that turns a run into an observation (what
its record shows). Take lists Ω and Ω′ of candidates and a decision tree T such that: (H1) Ω′
strictly narrows Ω: every member of Ω′ is in Ω, and some member of Ω isn’t in Ω′ ; (H2) some
dropped candidate w, in Ω and not in Ω′ , shows an observation different from every survivor’s;
(H3) the decoded run d(t) is shown by some survivor; (H4) |Ω′ | > 0 and |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |;
(H5) at least depth( T ) steps of the run are charged at least one each. Then (1) the membership
test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than the membership test of Ω; (2) some step of the run took the
reading from no to yes, and that step was charged at least one; and (3) the sum of the charges
of the run’s steps is at least ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉.

Proof. (1) is the cards’ argument: the dropped w shows something no survivor shows,
so the posterior test says no where the prior test says yes, and every survivor was in
the prior, so nothing the posterior accepts is refused by the prior. (2) The run starts
at no and ends at yes, so at some step the reading goes from no to yes, and the toll
charges that step at least one. (3) is the proof of Theorem 8.2 with the sum of the
charges in place of the counter’s rise: the covering and Lemma 8.1 bound the index
bits by depth( T ), and the sum of the charges is at least the number of steps charged at
least one. On a system that obeys conservation the sum of the charges is the counter’s
rise.

Checked as ent_narrowing_strengthens, ent_cs_count and ent_cs_entit
lement (EntitlementSmall.v); the tree lemma underneath is also there, as ent_lea
ves_le_pow2 and ent_log2_leaves_le_depth. Theorem 8.2 is the same count
with the counter’s rise, so for a system that obeys conservation it’s the special case.
Three things in the hypotheses feed nothing, and I’m naming them here so you don’t
have to find them: (H3) isn’t used by any of the three conclusions; from (H1) only
the inclusion is used, and the gap goes unused; and in (H2) the words “not in Ω′ ” go
unused, since a candidate whose observation differs from every survivor’s can’t be a
survivor itself. And (H4)’s |Ω′ | > 0 is used in that proof but can be dropped too: the
covering forces it once the prior has a member (nec_e_cs_entitlement_strong
er, NecEEnt.v).

A statement like that is true by packaging: it takes the hypotheses in and hands the
conclusions back, and the right word for it is a checklist. A checklist for leaning on a
claim. It discovers nothing about leaning.

And a checklist isn’t nothing. On 30 October 1935, at Wright Field, northeast of
Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing’s new four-engine bomber, the Model



                                              172
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


299. Shortly after take-off it plunged back onto the field and caught fire; that’s how
the wire report of that day has it, and the later histories add that it pitched up and
stalled first, which is what elevators locked in a raised position would do. Two men
died of their injuries, the Army’s pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing’s chief test pilot,
Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks on, a locking
mechanism worked from inside the cockpit that holds the control surfaces still while
the plane sits on the ground. There’s a famous line that a newspaper called it too much
airplane for one man to fly. I couldn’t find that line in any paper from 1935; the earliest
place I could find it is a New Yorker article from December 2007 by Atul Gawande,
a surgeon who writes about how people get complicated work right, and he names
no newspaper, so take it as a lead. What I can find is what came after. The answer
was a card: a list of things to check, in order, every time, and the crews of the airplane
worked through written checklists for each phase of flight. The most careful history
of it I found is by Walter Boyne, a retired Air Force colonel and a former director of
the National Air and Space Museum. By his account it wasn’t the first written routine
for a pilot; those go back before the First World War. And it’s this crash, he says, that
made the checklist the way a crew flew. The airplane went on to be the B-17. Nothing
on that card was a discovery. Every item on it was something the pilots already knew.
What the card did was make sure none of it got left out when it mattered. That’s what
putting entitlement’s hypotheses on one list does: it finds nothing new about leaning
on a claim, and it makes the hypotheses impossible to drop quietly.

Before any machine, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the “insight” in “No
Free Insight” (Section 5), because I’ve been using it as if it meant one thing.

9 What insight is
I named the rule in this book “No Free Insight,” and the name ran ahead of any careful
account of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not learning
(Section 5), not looking, not copying. It’s time to say what’s left, and to say it in a way
that someone who studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn’t laugh at. So who
are those people, and what did they find? Here’s what I ran into, pushed on as I go.
Where a story reached me secondhand, I treat it as a lead to check.

9.1 Sultan and the sticks
In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station
with a colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until 1920,
five years longer than planned, with the chimpanzees to watch. The famous one is
Sultan. Food is outside the cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each too short, but
one fits into the end of the other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks, plays with the
sticks, and then, by Köhler’s account, at a moment you can see, joins them and reaches
the food. Köhler’s words were Einsicht and einsichtig, which came into English as
“insight,” and the whole school of psychology he belonged to, the Gestalt school, said
that’s what thinking is: a restructuring, the moment two sticks stop being two sticks


                                           173
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and become one tool. Stacking up tries until one works was, for them, something else.
Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935 and in English in 1945, five
years after he died at thirty-seven; he’d spent his last years working with Köhler at
Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a box of tacks, matches, and the task
of fixing the candle to the wall. Almost nobody sees that the box is a shelf, until they
do. And then he found that if you hand people the box empty, with the tacks poured
out beside it, they solve it far more readily. Same objects. What changed was which
relation among them was on the table.

I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn’t add an object. Sultan had
both sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived was a
relation, which is to say a piece of structure in Section 2’s sense, and the arrival was
sudden. Hold that, because the thing the toll prices also arrives in one step, and at its
best it’s also a relation.

9.2 It isn’t a feeling
But here’s the finding I’d hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes
from someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked
people to solve problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how “warm” they felt,
how close to the answer. On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth
climbs steadily and peaks at the answer, which is what you’d expect. On insight
problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then the
answer arrives, and if anything the people who felt warmest beforehand were more
likely to be wrong. She put that last finding in the title of a 1986 paper: premonitions
of insight predict impending error. The feeling of being close is not a gauge of being
close. Try it yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds while
doing a long sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.

And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well.
Archimedes, a mathematician who died in 212 BC, asked by Hiero, the king of Syra-
cuse, whether a goldsmith had cheated him on a crown, gets into a bath, sees the
water rise, and runs home naked shouting “eureka,” I’ve found it. That comes from
Vitruvius, a Roman writer on architecture, writing about two centuries later. Is it
true? Galileo Galilei, then a young Italian mathematician, at twenty-two, in 1586,
took it as known that Archimedes caught the goldsmith. What he didn’t buy was the
method. Water spilling over the side, as Vitruvius tells it, was to him “a crude thing,
far from scientific precision,” and he guessed some writer had set down a rumour. So
he wrote a little tract, La Bilancetta, proposing a balance weighed in air and in water
instead, which he thought was probably what Archimedes actually did, since it rests
on Archimedes’s own results. Whether there was ever a bath, or a shout, nobody can
check now. What survives is a story two centuries late, wrapped around a real man
and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept: the bath, the shout, the run-
ning home naked. The feeling. What it left shaky is the part that would count as the
check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The bit everybody remembers is

                                          174
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


the bit that tells you least.

So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the “aha,” is keyed to something
that the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn’t the feeling of having it.
That’s a relief, because a system of states and moves doesn’t have feelings, and a word
that only meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The version this book
can price has to be keyed to an event, and the question is which.

9.3 What happens when a computation learns
Here’s the split, and I’ll say what the toll does with each part, and then I’ll say who
decided the split. Keep Section 3’s sheet of paper in front of you: the NO box, the YES
box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and VOUCH.

The first thing: raw observation. Something comes in and gets written down. A counter
ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting on it,
and the reading doesn’t move because of it. Later moves can read what it wrote,
but that reading is a move of its own. This is the demon’s pad in Section 5, and it’s
what the statistician Dennis Lindley measured in 1956 as the information provided
by an experiment, the words of his title, and defined as the expected drop in your
uncertainty: a real quantity, and a quantity about what was seen. It can be free. The
toll says nothing at all about a move that doesn’t cross from NO to YES, so a price
list may charge it zero: on the paper, STAY and WORK cost nothing, and Section 5’s
watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates without paying a mark. “Can be” is
the honest word. A price list is allowed to charge for looking anyway, and whether
looking costs anything in the physical world is a different question that this sheet of
paper doesn’t touch.

Lindley’s measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good,
who was Alan Turing’s main statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in
1979 that Turing had worked out the expected weight of evidence an experiment
would give, to judge one of the codebreaking procedures before running it, and so
partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work that stayed secret. Turing
measured evidence in bans, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth of one called a deciban,
and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of the sheets
used in that procedure were printed. It’s the same base-ten unit other people call the
hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that Turing didn’t
know the logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a paper by Charles
Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from the opening chapter, who’d called it the weight
of evidence. Peirce is as far back as Good takes it. What it changes: nothing in the
argument, but it shows how well trodden this first kind of thing is. For a century and
a half careful people have measured what an observation tells you, and every one of
those measures is about what was seen. That’s the side of the line the toll leaves alone.

The second thing: certified insight. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES.
Here is where the toll lives. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that

                                          175
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


move costs at least one mark, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays at
least one somewhere along the way, which is Section 3’s universal floor. What’s being
charged for, at its best, is exactly the Gestalt thing: a relation, committed to. One tool,
claimed, out of two sticks. “At its best,” because Section 3 was careful about what YES
means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A crossing that writes down which relation
it’s committing to carries Sultan’s tool with it. A bare crossing, VOUCH on the paper,
commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the same.

The third thing isn’t a kind of event. It’s an observation about the price: it’s flat,
whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep relation,
a result nobody could have guessed, Sultan’s two sticks become one tool. The toll
charges the crossing at least one. It doesn’t charge the striking crossing more, because
the floor’s proof never looks at anything but the reading before and after. On the
paper: VOUCH from NO makes one mark whether you were thinking of Duncker’s
box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost. The depth of what’s certified adds meaning. It
doesn’t add a mark.

The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In 1962
the psychologist Sam Glucksberg ran Duncker’s problem with money on it: some
people were told they could win five or twenty dollars depending on how fast they
solved it. With the tacks in the box, the people chasing the money did worse than
the people who weren’t. With the box empty the problem was easier for everybody,
and the accounts I’ve read don’t agree on what the money did there, so I’ll leave that
half alone. Paying more didn’t buy the insight, and on the hard version it got in the
way. That’s a fact about heads. It says nothing about records, and I won’t push it
further than that. But it’s a nice mirror for the paper. On the paper a deeper crossing
isn’t charged more, and in Glucksberg’s room a bigger prize didn’t bring the crossing
sooner. In neither place does the price measure the depth.

Here they are, exactly, for any certification system (Definition 3.1). Runs are written
as lists, the way Section 3’s proof wrote them: [ ] is the empty run, and i :: t is the run
that starts with move i and carries on with the run t.


Definition 9.1 (Certified insight event, raw observation). In a certification system, a
step from state s by move i is a certified insight event when it turns the reading on:
cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is raw observation when no step by it,
from any state, is a certified insight event.


Remark 9.1 (What the toll prices, and what it doesn’t). Read off Definition 3.1 and
Theorem 3.1, and checked on the board as a certification system (nec_f_board_raw
_free, nec_f_board_floor and nec_f_board_floor_flat, NecFPaperToys.v).
(1) The toll puts no bound on the cost of a raw-observation move; on Section 3’s board
STAY and WORK are raw observation and cost 0. (2) Every certified insight event is



                                           176
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


charged at least 1, by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to one reading
yes has total cost at least 1, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat: the floor’s proof
uses nothing about the end state but its reading, so adding any hypothesis about what
else the end state shows leaves the bound at 1 and cannot raise it. A system that wants
to charge more for a deeper certification has to write that into its price list, move by
move; the toll doesn’t do it for anyone.


So the account comes down to two facts and a warning. Looking can be free. Turning
the reading on can’t. And putting something remarkable behind the reading doesn’t
make it cost any more.

Who decided the split? Not the costs alone. The toll prices exactly one thing, the
crossing. A price list is free to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a send,
a check) and free to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into raw observation and
certified insight is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book’s. The
part that’s forced is the floor under the crossing, and Section 4 is the argument for it;
anything a price list charges beyond that is a choice, and any concrete machine owes
you its whole table so you can see which choices it made.

9.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first
The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being exposed: you
make a conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for
something, where “real” means the test could have failed. His word for that earned
credit is corroboration. I’ve leaned on that idea through this whole book, and here’s
where a certification system has a version of it, and here’s where the version is weaker
than Popper and I have to say so.

Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin under a
cup, a formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail, and it doesn’t
move the box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt, pass or fail,
fits Popper, because what made his test count was that it was really run and could
have failed. That’s the test. It’s raw observation in the sense above, because it never
turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol is two moves:
test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking work and one for
the crossing.

But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step is
handed the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the reading
crossed. Play VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you land in
YES and make one mark, the same box and the same mark as the player who checked
first. The two tally lines differ by exactly what the CHECK was charged, and if you
charged it nothing they don’t differ at all. The mark for the crossing is the same mark
either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid for. It does not say it was earned.
Popper’s corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn’t.


                                             177
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in the
state when it passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark is
there. That’s a design, written into the step function, and it’s a perfectly good one.
Nothing in the five parts or the toll asks for it. That’s a real gap between the word
and the bare system, and the only honest thing is to leave it visible: the toll prices the
commit, and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or
about a design somebody chose. The five parts don’t guarantee it.


Remark 9.2 (Nothing makes the crossing wait). Read off Definition 3.1, and checked
on the board as nec_f_board_no_wait (NecFPaperToys.v). The toll constrains
cost(i ) for moves that cross, and nothing else; the step function is any function of the
current state and the move. So a certification system may have a move that crosses
from a state no check has touched, and the toll still holds. On Section 3’s board
extended with CHECK, the run [VOUCH] from NO crosses with one mark, and so
does [CHECK, VOUCH]. Making a crossing depend on an earlier check is a condition
on the step function, which a particular system can impose and the definition does
not.


9.5 What the word means
Insight, in the sense this book prices, is a relation committed to, in a move that flips
a reading from off to on, and that move costs at least one mark, in any system with
the toll, for any relation, whatever its depth. (And one edge from the paper: a bare
crossing that commits to nothing pays the same mark, so “a relation committed to”
is what the crossing is at its best. The toll doesn’t guarantee it.) Three boundaries,
each from a different place. From Metcalfe: it isn’t a feeling, and a system’s version
has to be an event. From the proof: the price is flat; a shallow commit and a deep
one both cost at least one, and cost is not depth. A system can pay heavily to check a
trivial claim, and Duncker’s box, a real insight, is still one small commit. And from
the two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its own. Price and correctness
are separate books.

Which leaves a suspicion I’d have in your place. Everything so far has been one
reading on one sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the shape
of that record something I picked, or is it what any honest record has to look like, on
any machine at all? That’s the next section: take any machine that steps, bolt a record
onto it, and see what shape it’s forced into. How a concrete machine hangs actual
claims on its parts, a checked property of one counter at one edition, and where those
sit in the state, comes in Part IV.

10 Records over any base: the latch
For the whole book so far I’ve been building up a thing with a flag and a counter,
and a fair reader is entitled to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for


                                           178
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


one machine, the one I keep promising to build. So here’s the section that answers
the suspicion with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what’s left. Take any
machine that steps deterministically: a Turing machine, a register machine (a few
numbered boxes that each hold a whole number, and a program that adds, subtracts
and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church’s way of computing by nothing but
plugging expressions into expressions; Section 13 builds one), anything. Call it the
base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I’ll state, and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I’ll show you the shape first because it’s a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

10.1 A cup and a die
Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule: the first time a coin lands in front of it,
turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and put
a coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. The cup turns over on the first six and
stays turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number, the roll that turned the
cup, is where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record.

That’s a latch. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when two British
physicists teaching engineering in London, William Eccles, a radio pioneer, and Frank
Jordan, applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds whichever state
you last put it in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches in the device
you’re reading this on descend from it. Cut its reset wire and what’s left has one input,
“set,” and the rule new state = old state or set: once set, it stays set. The cup is that circuit:
a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn’t call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a trigger relay.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can’t source, so I’ll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that’s very close to this book’s. In the mid-
1950s Wen Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma
Corporation in Garden City, New York, was asked by the United States Air Force,
in the accounts of his career I could find, for a more flexible and secure way to hold
the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside the guidance computer of the Atlas
missile. What he and his Arma colleague William Henrich patented (filed in 1957,
granted in 1962, under the plain title “Storage matrix”) was a grid with a connection
at every crossing, where you set the numbers by taking out the connections you didn’t
want, physically or by burning them out with too much current. The word burn is
right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a chip. The descendants are
called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in one stays
blown: there’s no current you can send to grow it back. A whole memory built out of
cups with no reset wire, because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly
change later. Does that prove anything here? No. The theorem below doesn’t care
what a cup is made of. But it’s good to know the shape wasn’t invented for a sheet of

                                               179
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: every honest record over any base is a cup
with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.

10.2 What “honest” has to mean
Here’s where the content is, and I’ll give you the five rules, because the theorem is
only as strong as they are.

A machine extends a base when there’s a map from the bigger machine’s states down
to the base’s, and that map starts in the base’s start states, reaches every one of them,
moves in step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the
map), and agrees about halting. The bigger machine may carry as much hidden state
as it likes beyond the base. That’s the “any base” part: the base doesn’t get to see the
extension, and the extension doesn’t get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a record, a yes/no reading, and a ledger, a counter. It’s an honest
extension when five things hold. One: the record’s next value depends only on the
base’s current state and the record’s current value. (I’ll call this driven by the computation.
It says the record answers to what the machine is doing. A clock on the wall or
someone’s hand doesn’t get a say.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section 6).
Three: the step that turns the record on costs at least one; that’s the toll (Section 3).
Four: once on, the record stays on; that’s permanence (Section 4). Five: some run from
a start state actually reaches a step that turns the record on; otherwise the record is
decoration.

Here are the words exactly. On/off is true/false, ∨ is “or” (on when either side is on),
and nextk is k steps.


Definition 10.1 (Base, record-carrying machine, cover). A base B is a set of states with
a step function nextB , a set of starting states, and a halting predicate. A record-carrying
machine M is a set of states with a step function next M , a set of starting states, a record
rec from states to Booleans, a ledger µ from states to whole numbers, and a halting
predicate. The cost of a step is cost(m) = µ(next M (m)) −̇ µ(m). A cover of B by M is a
map π from states of M to states of B that sends starting states to starting states, has
every starting state of B as the image of some starting state of M, commutes with the
steps, π (next M (m)) = nextB (π (m)), and agrees about halting: m halts exactly when
π (m) does.


Definition 10.2 (Honest extension, latch). M with cover π is an honest extension of
B when (R1, driven by the computation) there is one function f such that, for every
state m, rec(next M (m)) = f (π (m), rec(m)); for every state m, (R2, ledger) µ(m) ≤
µ(next M (m)); (R3, toll) if rec(m) is off and rec(next M (m)) is on, then cost(m) ≥ 1; (R4,
permanence) if rec(m) is on, so is rec(next M (m)); and (R5, a reachable write) some


                                             180
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


starting state m0 and some k have rec(nextkM (m0 )) off and rec(nextkM+1 (m0 )) on. An
event is a function h from base states to Booleans, and its latch is the step (b, r ) 7→
(nextB (b), r ∨ h(b)). M factors as the latch of h when, for every state m (reachable or
not),

        (π (next M (m)), rec(next M (m))) = (nextB (π (m)), rec(m) ∨ h(π (m))).


Now the theorem. Under those rules, the base state and the record move exactly as a
latch: the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, and never
off, and the event is read off the extension’s own rule by asking it what it does when
the record is off (stated exactly below). That’s a statement about what the base and
the record do together. The hidden state the extension carries can’t push the record
anywhere (R1) doesn’t allow, since the record’s next value is a function of the base
state and the record’s own value. The theorem doesn’t say the whole extension is a
bare latch machine, and it doesn’t make hidden state show up anywhere in particular:
an extension can carry a field that touches neither the record nor the ledger. And the
event is pinned down only on base states that some state with the record off covers;
on a base state with no such state above it, f (b, off) is whatever (R1)’s function says,
and nothing in a run ever consults it.

I promised the content was in the definition, and here’s what that means: the proof is
a short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only two of the five
rules, “driven by the computation” and “permanent.” The ledger, the toll, and the
reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A latch is what you get from “answers only
to the base” plus “never comes back down,” full stop. The other three rules matter
for the converse: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event,
priced at one unit per write, is an honest extension. Put the two together and you’ve
got: honest records are exactly latches. One shape, no others, over any base.


Theorem 10.1 (The record is a latch). Let B be any base and M an honest extension of
it through π, with f the function of (R1). Then M factors as the latch of the event h(b) =
 f (b, off).

Proof. The base half of the equation is the cover’s step clause. For the record, split on
rec(m). If it is on, permanence (R4) makes the next value on, and on ∨ h(π (m)) is on.
If it is off, (R1) makes the next value f (π (m), off) = h(π (m)) = off ∨ h(π (m)). Only
(R1), (R4) and the cover are used; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are discarded.

Checked as record_axis_is_latch_holds (StructuralRecordAxis.v), with the
definitions BaseMachine, BaseCover, computation_driven, HonestBaseExt
ension and latch_factorization (StructuralCoreAnyBase.v), and the clauses
(R2) to (R5) as ledger_carried, rc_a2 (StructuralCore.v), record_permanent
and reachable_record_write (StructuralCoreCover.v).


                                           181
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways. It never
asks what the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down is base,
and the record’s rule is allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is extension,
and (R1) keeps the record’s rule from reading it. Draw the line low, so the base is only
the computation’s own working state, and (R1) is a real demand. Draw it high, put
every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1) is easy to meet, and the latch
shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds wherever you draw the line,
and that’s exactly why it can’t tell you where a record’s meaning lives. The meaning
lives in what the event h reads, and that’s in the base by construction. The pieces
above the line, the record and the ledger, are the ones that never steer anything; the
pieces that make a flag mean something sit below it, where this theorem doesn’t look.
So when the machine in Part IV arrives, ask it first which parts it puts above the line.


Theorem 10.2 (Every reachable latch is an honest record). Let B be any base and h any
event. Let Latchh have states (b, r, x ), starting states (b, off, 0) with b starting in B, step
(b, r, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), x + δ) with δ = 1 when r is off and h(b) is on and δ = 0
otherwise, record r, ledger x, halting as b halts, and cover (b, r, x ) 7→ b. Suppose some starting
b0 and some k bring Latchh from (b0 , off, 0), in k steps, to a state whose record is still off and
whose base state satisfies h. Then Latchh is an honest extension of B.

Proof. (R1) holds with f (b, r ) = r ∨ h(b). (R2): each step adds 0 or 1. (R3): a step that
turns the record on has r off and h(b) on, so it adds 1. (R4): on ∨ h(b) is on. (R5) is
the supposition. The supposition asks for the first time h holds on some run; any run
from a start that reaches an h-state has such a first time, though the checked statement
uses only the first-time form.

Checked as latch_core_honest (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v).

A reversible base needs one more thing to carry a record, and the next theorem says
exactly what. If the base never merges two states, keep every earlier record value in a
growing history beside the latch, and the whole step merges nothing either; but on a
finite state space a permanent record can’t be written by a step that merges nothing
at all. A step that merges nothing is called injective: no two states go to the same next
state. And r :: H is the history H with r put on the front, as in Section 9.


Theorem 10.3 (Records on reversible machines). (1) Let B be a base whose step is injective.
The machine with states (b, r, H, x ), step (b, r, H, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), r :: H, x + δ)
(δ as in Theorem 10.2), starting states with r off, H empty and x = 0, has an injective step,
and under the supposition of Theorem 10.2 it is an honest extension of B. (2) On a finite state
space, a single injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.

Proof. (1) Equal images have equal base parts, so equal base states by injectivity; equal
histories r :: H, so equal records and histories; and equal ledgers once the equal δ is

subtracted. Honesty is the proof of Theorem 10.2 with the history carried along. (2) is
Theorem 4.1 of Section 4 with a single move.

Checked as history_latch_injective, history_latch_honest and finite
_reversible_cannot_write (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v), the last from perma
nent_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentCertification.v).

So a base that never merges can still carry a record, if it’s allowed to grow a history
that never ends. A machine with finitely many states can’t carry one without merging:
on a finite machine the record’s first write is a merge, and Section 4 already put the
price on that.

Process-calculus people ran into the same thing from the other side. Vincent Danos
and Jean Krivine, two theoretical computer scientists in Paris, wanted to pin down
what a transaction is. They took in 2005 a reversible version of CCS, Robin Milner’s
calculus of processes that talk to each other, where every step can be rolled back, and
modelled a transaction as a process that wanders freely through everything that can
be undone until it performs an action declared irreversible, which is the commit. The
way I read it, they start from steps that all come undone and ask what has to be added
before anything sticks, and the theorem above starts from a record and asks what
the step under it must be. In their calculus, as in the theorem, a permanent effect
needs a step with no way back, and the calculus has to say which steps those are. The
word I tripped on was declared. Theirs are labelled. Mine, I thought, are picked out
by counting, since on a finite machine the first write merges whatever anyone calls it.
Push on that and it gives. I choose the event h, and on a base that grows its history
forever the write merges nothing (Theorem 10.3), so there my permanence is declared
too.

There’s an arrow of time in that theorem, and I should say where it came from, because
I put it there by hand. Every starting state has the record off. That’s the only reason a
raised record means the event happened: it was down at the start, and only h lifts it.
Turn the cup up before the first roll and it tells you nothing about the die. So the clean
start is an assumed ready state, a past hypothesis in miniature. The past hypothesis
is the physicists’ name for an assumed low-entropy beginning of the universe, which
several of the accounts below lean records on. Whether every trusted record leans on
it is their argument, and I’m not settling it. Nothing in this book derives one; every
theorem here about records assumes its small version and starts from there.

When I went looking for who else had found the arrow hiding in the start, I got five
papers that read like five unrelated answers. They lined up once I asked each one the
same thing: what does the cup being down at the start rest on? There are two places
to put it. You can put it at the beginning, as a fact about how things started. Or you
can put it in the structure of what causes what. David Wolpert, then a physicist at Los
Alamos and the same Wolpert as the free-lunch theorem, sorted memory systems in



                                           183
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


1992, and one of his kinds works only because it begins in a prepared state set up by
a process that runs one way, which is how it leans on the second law. That’s the cup
put down by somebody before the game, at the first place. Wolpert and Jens Kipper,
a philosopher at Rochester, put in 2024 that sorting on a formal footing, and they say
plainly that they have no formal proof this kind can only remember the past. I trust
them more for that sentence. What I think they’re saying is that a prepared start buys
you a memory, and getting its direction too takes something they can’t yet prove.

Aram Ebtekar, an independent researcher in Vancouver, and Marcus Hutter, who
works on the theory of general artificial intelligence at Google DeepMind and the
Australian National University, built in 2024 a reversible toy world, imposed a past
hypothesis on it, coarse-grained it, and got records of the past and none of the future.
As I read their route, the clean start doesn’t go straight to the records. It goes through
a causal structure first, and the arrows come out of that. Thomas Blanchard, a philoso-
pher of science at Cologne, got in 2024 the same lopsidedness of knowledge out of
the causal Markov condition, a condition on causal structure. So Blanchard starts at
the second place, which is the middle of Ebtekar and Hutter’s road. That took me a
while to see, because one is a toy world and the other is philosophy of causation. They
go from the start to causes to records; he goes from causes to records. The fit is my
reading, and it’s mine to defend. And Carlo Rovelli, two years before his paper on the
cost of choosing from the opening chapter, studied traces in “Memory and entropy”
(2022) and concluded that a memory turns low entropy into available information.
He’s at the first place, and he says what the beginning gets spent on. Read against the
latch, that’s the blank the record uses up: the flag can say yes once because it started
at no.

So does the latch explain why records point backwards? No. I’ll say that plainly, so
it doesn’t look like it does. The step runs forwards and the runs start clean, and a
theorem built on those two can only hand the arrow back. Push further and it gives in
a second place. The history that grows forever looked like a way around the clean start.
It starts empty, so it leans on the same blank. Under a step that forgets nothing, on a
finite set, no permanent record can ever be written, past or future, which is Zermelo
again. On the map the book sits at the first place, with Wolpert and Rovelli, and it sits
there by assumption. Ebtekar and Hutter at least imposed their start on a world with
its own dynamics and watched what came out. I wrote mine into the definition.

Constructor theory, which Section 4 brings in as a neighbour of the chairs, has a paper
on time (Deutsch and Marletto, 2025) saying that laws stated as which transformations
a device can and can’t bring about can’t mention time at all, so duration has to come
from relations between physical systems, clocks, that have their own dynamics. What
I think they’re saying is that whenever you want a duration you point at a second
system and count what it did. That’s the position this book is in by construction. The
step count is the only time in it, and it comes from the machine’s own steps. The next
subsection has a record turned at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, and (R1) throws it out,


                                           184
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


which read beside them is a rule about which system may be the clock: the one being
recorded. Push on it, though. Their laws have no step in them, and the paper’s work
is getting duration and dynamics out of clocks and timers. I put a step, nextB , into
the definition of a base. So I’m in their position only at the far end of their argument,
where a clock already exists. The base is my clock, and I assumed it.

Physicists have built this latch on paper too, in quantum mechanics, and it behaves
the way the last theorem says. The question that sorted them for me is where the
cup puts what it forgets, since a closed quantum system with separate energy levels
comes back (Bocchieri and Loinger, earlier) and the theorem left only two ways out:
a history that never ends, or a merge. Klaus Hepp, a mathematical physicist at ETH
Zurich, wanted a measuring device inside quantum mechanics itself, and studied in
1972 a particle that flips spins in a long chain as it passes, now called the Coleman-
Hepp model (I know Hepp’s paper only from accounts of it), and John Bell (1975)
took it apart: the record is exactly definite only for an infinitely long chain, which is
the reversible escape above, a history that never ends, in quantum clothes. Jonathan
Halliwell, a theoretical physicist at Imperial College London, used in 1999 a two-state
detector that flips once when a particle crosses a point and is kept from flipping back
by a large environment, which is a latch with the environment holding the history. His
abstract calls it effectively irreversible, and I like that he puts the word effectively right
there where you can see it. And Murray Gell-Mann, the physicist who named the
quark, and James Hartle, of the University of California at Santa Barbara, gave in 1995
the property a name inside their framework of decoherent histories: the permanence
of the past, past alternatives that stay settled as the story is extended into the future.
They name (R4) for whole histories and leave the cup to others. So Hepp’s chain, as
Bell read it, is exact and infinite, and Halliwell’s detector is finite and only effectively
permanent. Mine is finite, exact and permanent at once, and it gets there by letting the
first write merge. Push on that and it gives: I never say where the merged state goes.
Hepp’s chain had to be infinite. Halliwell had to put his in an environment. Mine just
goes, and the toll writes a unit in a counter. That’s fine in a model of computation, and
it’s exactly where this stops being physics.

10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the clock
A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each
hypothesis dropped, and it does, and they’re the two ways a record goes wrong in the
world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step:
on, off, on, off. It’s driven by the computation; it’s not permanent; and it’s not a latch
of any event. This is a toggle, a piece of working state. A record you can revoke is
working state wearing a record’s clothes, and if a revocation has to stick, that’s a second
latch (“revoked”), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work: you add
an entry; you never delete the certificate. Alin Tomescu, a computer scientist then at
MIT, and his coauthors (2019) built append-only authenticated sets and dictionaries

                                             185
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


for transparency logs, and revocation fits that shape exactly: a revocation goes in once
and stays. The pair theorem (stated below) covers two latches that can each read the
other; do it with two cups where the second only turns over on an even roll if the first
is already up, and you’ll see the second can never turn before the first.

Dialogue theorists built a version of that two-latch rule for arguments. Give each
speaker a row of cups, one for every claim they’ve made. Everybody I read in this
field is answering two questions about those cups: whose hand turns them, and can
they come back down. C. L. Hamblin, an Australian philosopher and logician who
also came up with reverse Polish notation for early computers, wrote Fallacies (1970),
and it has a chapter on formal dialectic where each speaker has a commitment store,
a list of what they’re on the hook for, and the rules of the dialogue update it. The
speaker doesn’t. I know that chapter from other people’s accounts of it. That’s an
answer to the first question, and it’s (R1) for arguments: the cup answers to what
happened in the dialogue, and the speaker’s hand is kept off it. Henry Prakken, who
works on AI and law at Utrecht, built in 2005 dialogue games for argumentation on
stores like that and made commitments sticky: a claim can be retracted only when
it has been challenged, and claims and backtracking carry a price. He also floats a
convention that once a player has retracted a proposition, that player can’t take it on
again, which is a revocation that stays revoked, the way an entry on a revocation list
does. That’s an answer to the second question, and it took me a second pass to see
that it’s two answers. A cup can come down, and coming down costs. And once it has,
the taking-back is itself a cup that stays up. Erik Krabbe, an argumentation theorist at
Groningen, names in 2001 the awkward part of that: retraction is frowned on, and yet
resolving a dispute takes somebody retracting a doubt or a point of view, so the rules
have to say when taking a commitment back is allowed. As I read him, he’s standing
between the two ends of the second question. A store that never gives can’t settle a
dispute. A store that gives freely isn’t a store. The part of all that I’d keep is Hamblin’s,
that the store belongs to the rules. It doesn’t belong to the speaker. Take the pen away
from the program. And this book answers Krabbe with a price: a take-back is a second
cup, “revoked,” and turning it costs at least one like any other write, so a retraction is
allowed, permanent and paid for. That’s Prakken’s convention with the toll attached.
Where mine gives is his first condition. He lets a claim come down only when it’s
been challenged, and nothing in my latch asks why the second cup turned. The pair
theorem lets the second cup’s event read the base and the first cup, and nothing in it
requires a challenge to be there.

The same field has a notion that looks a lot like earning. In the abstract argumentation
of Phan Minh Dung, a computer scientist at the Asian Institute of Technology in
Bangkok (1995), arguments attack one another, and the grounded semantics starts from
the arguments nobody attacks and keeps adding the ones they defend. Look at how
it’s built: things go in and never come out, which is a row of cups turned one at a
time. Pietro Baroni and Massimiliano Giacomin, at Brescia, introduced in 2007, and



                                            186
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Martin Caminada, then at Aberdeen, revisited in 2014, strong admissibility: a set is
strongly admissible when every argument in it is defended by others in the set that
don’t lean back on it, so the support bottoms out. That’s the argumentation form of
an earned claim. Above the bottom, nothing in it is in by default, which puts it at the
far end from Burge’s default on the testimony map in Section 7. Caminada argues it
plays a vital part in the dialogue games that decide grounded acceptance. I’ve read
Caminada’s paper; Dung’s and Baroni and Giacomin’s I know through what later
papers say about them. Notice the bottom, though. An argument nobody attacks
gets in on a check that can’t fail, and this book says a check that can’t fail establishes
nothing. Now turn that on my own cups, because it lands. My first write needs only
that h holds, and what h reads sits in the base, where the latch theorem doesn’t look. I
