charge a unit for it. A unit is a price. It isn’t a check. So my earned records bottom out
the way Dung’s do, in something let in without an argument, and the one difference
is that mine pays to get in. Whether a machine’s earned record certifies exactly the
strongly admissible sets is the kind of statement I’d have to prove before I said it, and
I haven’t.

A record that’s allowed to change its mind isn’t lawless, though. It’s somebody else’s
subject. Count how many times the cup may be turned. Once, from down to up, is the
latch. More than once and you’re somewhere else, and the people who went there sort
it two ways: by how many turns are allowed, and by how long the game runs. The
philosopher Hilary Putnam, then at MIT, and E. Mark Gold, a computer scientist at
a research lab in Santa Monica, in back-to-back papers in 1965, looked at questions a
machine answers by guessing and revising, where the answer is whatever the guesses
finally settle on. Putnam’s paper says outright that you’re never sure you have the
correct answer. That stopped me the first time. What kind of answer can’t you ever
be sure you have? The way I came to read it: the cup’s position at any moment is the
current guess, the answer is where it ends up, and nobody watching can tell when
it’s done moving. Yuri Ershov, a logician in Novosibirsk, sorted those in 1968 by how
many revisions they’re allowed (that’s how his hierarchy is described; I haven’t read
his paper). Allow one, from no to yes, and you get exactly the sets a program can list.
That level I did check, in a modern account of the hierarchy by Rod Downey, Carl
Jockusch, Timothy McNicholl and Paul Schupp, four computability theorists, and it’s
a short exercise once you see it. That’s what a permanent record raised by a search
catches. Allow two, three, and so on, and every extra change buys new sets: the rungs
of the ladder are all different. A record that can come back down lives on that ladder.
Now put Putnam’s worry on my cup, because it lands. On the bottom rung a yes is
final the moment it appears, and a no never is. Down means not yet. A single cup of
mine can certify that something happened and can never certify that it didn’t; a final
no would take a second cup, turned by finding a reason, and that’s the pair of latches
again. That’s what the bottom rung costs, and I’d rather name it. This book stays on
the bottom rung. I’m pointing at the ladder. I’m not climbing it.



                                           187
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The ladder doesn’t stop at finite time, and the people who followed it past infinity
have names for the two kinds of record I just described. A definition that only ever
adds, stage after stage, and keeps everything it has at each limit, is an inductive def-
inition (the long treatment is a 1974 chapter by Wayne Richter and Peter Aczel, two
recursion theorists). That’s the latch run through the infinite, a cup that goes up at
some stage and is still up at every stage after. Let it take things back, and keep what
stays put from some stage on, and you have what John Burgess, a philosopher and
logician at Princeton, called in 1986 quasi-inductive definitions, which he met in the
revision theories of truth that grew up beside the logician Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory
of truth, which builds up the true sentences in stages. Burgess’s paper measures how
complicated the truths of those theories get. I’ve read its abstract. The place where
he names them I haven’t. What took me a few reads is that Burgess’s rule at a limit
is Putnam and Gold’s rule, keep whatever the guesses settled on, applied at every
limit stage along the way. That’s my reading of how the two fit. If it’s right, the split
between a cup that only goes up and a cup that settles is the same split at finite time
and past it. A permanent record is the first kind. A toggle that’s allowed to settle is
the second. Joel Hamkins and Andy Lewis, two set theorists, let a Turing machine
keep running through the ordinals in 2000. At a limit a cell keeps its value if it settled,
and reads 1 if it kept flipping back and forth forever, and the trick they use again and
again is the toggle: flash a flag on and off every time a guess changes, and at the limit
the flag is on exactly when the guess changed infinitely often. A flag that can come
back down is how that machine learns what no finite run could tell it. A permanent
one can’t do that trick, because at a limit a cell that only ever goes up just stays up. So
past infinity the toggle is the clever one. A latch tells you a thing happened at least
once. Their flashing flag tells you it happened infinitely often. I threw the toggle out a
few paragraphs back anyway, and I’d do it again, because before the limit its reading
can’t be relied on, and nobody using a machine of mine gets to wait for a limit. One
finite-time fact belongs beside it, so nobody concludes too much from permanence.
Hao Wang, a logician then at Oxford, described in 1957 a machine whose only write is
to mark a square and which can never erase one, and it computes everything a Turing
machine does. Permanence of a machine’s own memory costs it no computing power.
What the book prices is a permanent reading raised by a step that has to work whether
or not the reading is already up, which is a different thing. So the cost I named a
paragraph ago is a cost in what a reading can claim. Computing power doesn’t pay it.

Drop “driven by the computation.” Take a base that counts, and a record that switches
on at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, whatever the base is doing. It’s permanent. The
computation doesn’t drive it. This is a timestamp. A timestamp is not evidence. It says
when. It doesn’t say what happened, and a record switched by an outside party or a
clock records that party or that clock and leaves the computation out. Try it with the
die: play twenty rolls with the rule “turn the cup after roll seven no matter what,” and
notice you’ve recorded nothing about the dice.



                                           188
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


StructuralRecordAxis.v proves exactly the facts I named for each: the toggle is driven,
isn’t permanent and isn’t a latch; the clock is permanent and isn’t driven. That each
also keeps the other rules (the ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a
run reaches it) is true by inspection, and isn’t a separate theorem.

Permanent but undriven is a clock, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a record is
the thing that’s both. That’s the whole discrimination, and I think it’s the most useful
single sentence in this book for looking at systems other than the one I build, which is
why it’s here.

The pair theorem and the two counterexamples, exactly. The base for both counterex-
amples is the counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a
starting state, and nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: ¬r is r flipped, and a
statement in square brackets, like [k = 5], reads on when it’s true and off when it isn’t.


Lemma 10.4 (Two records are two latches). Let c1 , c2 be two records on M, with cover
π onto a base B, such that: there is one function F with (c1 (next M (m)), c2 (next M (m))) =
F (π (m), c1 (m), c2 (m)); the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs
at least one; and each record is permanent. Then there are h1 , h2 with c1 (next M (m)) =
c1 (m) ∨ h1 (π (m), c2 (m)) and c2 (next M (m)) = c2 (m) ∨ h2 (π (m), c1 (m)) for every m.

Proof. Take h1 (b, r2 ) to be the first part of F (b, off, r2 ) and h2 (b, r1 ) the second part of
F (b, r1 , off), then split on each record as in Theorem 10.1.

Checked as record_pair_is_two_latches_holds (StructuralRecordAxis.v).


Lemma 10.5 (The toggle). Let the toggle have states (n, r ), step (n, r ) 7→ (n + 1, ¬r ),
every state starting, record r, ledger n, cover (n, r ) 7→ n onto the counter. It is driven by the
computation, with f (b, r ) = ¬r; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of no event.

Proof. At (0, on) the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
on ∨ h(0) = on there.

Checked as toggle_computation_driven, toggle_not_permanent and togg
le_not_latch (StructuralRecordAxis.v).


Lemma 10.6 (The clock). Let the clock have states (b, k, r ), step (b, k, r ) 7→ (b + 1, k +
1, r ∨ [k = 5]), every state starting, record r, ledger b, cover (b, k, r ) 7→ b onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.

Proof. Permanence: on ∨ x is on. Not driven: the states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) have
the same base state and the same record, and their next records are on and off, so no f
of the base state and the record can give both.


                                                189
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Checked as clock_record_permanent and clock_record_not_driven (Struc-
turalRecordAxis.v). “Driven” is a condition on every state. The clock makes every
state a starting state, so the two states the proof compares are both ones a run can
begin at, even though a clock started at (0, 0, off) would never reach (0, 5, off).

10.4 Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.
Here’s a sentence I have to take apart: “there’s only one honest way to carry a record.”
Three different things get squeezed into that breath.

First claim: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books,
starting at zero and adding each move’s price? Yes, on every state reachable from the
start; that’s Section 6’s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

Second claim: is every honest extension of a base the same machine, charges and all? No,
and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any honest extension
and add one more coin to the bill on every step, whatever the step is. Now walk the
five rules. The record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the bill
never touches it. The ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything.
The step that turns the record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a floor
and a surcharge only raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same
run still reaches the write (R5). So the billed machine is honest, and it isn’t the machine
you started with: wherever the original sat still for free, the billed one pays a coin a
tick for sitting still. Do it with the cup and the die. Charge a coin for every roll, six
or not. The cup turns over on the same roll as before. You’ve changed the bill and
nothing about the record. A machine that charges for CPU time is honest and isn’t the
one that doesn’t.

But the billed machine isn’t a different structure. It’s the same record, steps and halting
with a different price list. So the claim worth keeping is sameness up to the price
schedule: compare two machines by their record, their halting and their steps, through
their maps down to the base, and don’t compare charges. Fix which event the record
is, and the bill stops mattering; a flat surcharge, or any surcharge that depends on the
current state, sits on the same structure. That’s the first free choice. The walk above
is the whole argument, and it’s checked over an arbitrary base, with any surcharge
that depends on the current state: the billed machine is honest (nec_w_billed_h
onest), has the same latch event (nec_w_billed_same_latch), steps along with
the original on record, halting and base (nec_w_billed_same_up_to_schedul
e), and pays each step’s cost plus the surcharge (nec_w_billed_step_cost), all in
NecWArgued.v.

And then the second free choice, and this one still surprises me. Which event is the
record? Nothing in the five rules picks it. The converse above already says so, if
you read it twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at
one unit per write, is an honest record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on
the first six. Another turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire;

                                            190
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


both are honest. Roll a one first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about
whether anything has been recorded. So which permanent reading counts as the record is
a second thing nobody forces on you. The price list is one free choice. The event is the
other. That second choice is the question Section 15 is about: what, if anything, makes
certification the event worth recording. “The ledger passed one” is an event too, and
so is anything else the base can reach.


Corollary 10.7 (The event is a free choice). Let B be any base and h1 , h2 two events, each
meeting the supposition of Theorem 10.2. Then Latchh1 and Latchh2 are both honest extensions
of B. If some base state b has h1 (b) on and h2 (b) off, then one step from (b, off, 0) leaves the
first record on and the second off.

Proof. Honesty is Theorem 10.2 applied twice. The step is the latch’s own rule: off ∨
h1 (b) is on and off ∨ h2 (b) is off.

Checked as nec_w_event_free_choice (NecWLatch.v), whose proof is latch_c
ore_honest (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v) applied to each event.

Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes
doesn’t, with odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds?
No, and the counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently
loaded coins. Here’s the setup, said carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at
random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive, never
empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least
one. Call such a record an honest probabilistic record. Call two such records the same
schedule when the same moves are possible and every move is charged the same, and
the same in probability when the weighted lists are equal.


Theorem 10.8 (The schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities). (1) There are two honest
probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in probability. (2) There is
an honest probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its current value describes.

Proof. (1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights 1 and 1, the other with
weights 1 and 2; from on, both stay on with weight 1; both charge 1 for the write. Same
possible moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off
both to off and to on, while a latch r ∨ h(r ) gives one value.

Checked as schedule_determines_probabilities_refuted and determin
istic_latch_handles_branching_refuted (ProbabilisticRecord.v), with the
definitions in ProbabilisticRecordCore.v. These are finite-weight models on one bit
with no base underneath; they say nothing about any particular machine.




                                               191
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Third claim: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every honest record-carrier
has to have? I don’t claim it. Nothing needs it.

10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about
The theorem is stated for any base, and the checked work instantiates it on three mod-
els of computation that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program); a
register machine of the kind the computer scientists Stephen Cook (of the certificates)
and Robert Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost indirect addressing (any pro-
gram); and a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an argument is worked out
before it’s plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a term with no step left to
take step to itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one generic theorem applied
to that base (the checked names are listed with the formal statement below). So a reg-
ister machine with an honest record is a register machine plus a cup. So is a lambda
calculus. (There’s one more instance, the machine I build later, where a particular flag
is shown to be an honest record and the same theorem makes it a latch, in Section 16.)

Here are the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function, a set of
starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing else about
its instruction vocabulary.


Definition 10.3 (Three concrete bases). The tape base has a finite Boolean list t, a head
index h, a program counter q and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond the list
returns false. Writing at h extends the list with false cells if needed, then changes that
cell. Moving right increments h and extends the list through the new head position.
Moving left decrements a positive h; at h = 0, it prepends a false cell and keeps the
head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

Instruction                                   Next state
Write a bit                                   Perform the write and advance q by one.
Move left or right                            Perform the move and advance q by one.
Branch to j                                   Set q := j if the current cell is true; otherwise
                                              advance q by one.
Halt                                          Leave the entire state unchanged.
ClaimTapeIsZero with parameter δ              Advance q by one and do nothing else.



An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state, and
halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by every
instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction neither erases
the tape nor charges the cost field; the name supplies no extra semantics.

The random-access base has a register function X : N → N and a program counter q.
For a fixed finite program its instructions are:




                                           192
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele



Instruction                                   Next state
Constant (i, c)                               Set X (i ) := c.
Add (i, j, k )                                Set X (i ) := X ( j) + X (k ).
Subtract (i, j, k )                           Set X (i ) := max(0, X ( j) − X (k)).
Indirect load (i, j)                          Set X (i ) := X ( X ( j)).
Indirect store (i, j)                         Set X ( X (i )) := X ( j).
Positive branch ( j, a)                       Set q := a if X ( j) > 0; otherwise advance q
                                              by one.
Jump to a                                     Set q := a.
Halt                                          Leave the entire state unchanged.



Each register-writing instruction advances q by one; its operands are evaluated in the
old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program also leaves
the state unchanged. Starting states have q = 0 and arbitrary register contents. A
state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program. Unit cost here counts
instructions. It has nothing to do with the certification ledger.

The lambda base uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in Definition 13.3.
To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function part of an application. If that
part cannot step and is an abstraction, either substitute an argument that is already
an abstraction or take a step in the argument. If neither applies, the term cannot
step. Variables and abstractions cannot step by themselves, and there is no reduction
under an abstraction. The base leaves a term unchanged when it cannot step and calls
precisely those terms halted. Every term is allowed as a starting state, including open
terms.


These definitions make the three examples bases in the sense of Definition 10.1. Apply-
ing the latch theorem to them does not assert universality, an execution-time bound,
or a simulation between the three bases.

There’s also a relation defined between bases, weak base equivalence: two bases are
equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related
states agree on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched by
some number of steps, possibly zero, on the other. That “some number of steps” is the
stuttering idea Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section 6’s message counters) put
forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn’t count as different
because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one. The relation carries no
cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step and a Turing machine differ
in price. The relation never looks at price, so on what it does look at they can match.
It’s proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch form is preserved across it.

There is a limit to that statement. The “preserved across it” proof throws away its
equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds on every base regardless, so the preservation
is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in the checked work are two of the bases

                                           193
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


actually related by this relation. The relation is defined, it’s an equivalence, and it is
not used to connect the Turing machine to the register machine to the lambda calculus,
or any of them to the machine in Part IV. It would be easy to read that list as if it did.
What’s proved is that each base, separately, carries a latch. That’s the honest sentence.


Definition 10.4 (Weak base equivalence). Bases B1 and B2 , with observations o1 and
o2 into one common set, are weakly equivalent when some relation R relates every
starting state of each to some starting state of the other, and any related x, y have
o1 ( x ) = o2 (y), the same halting, some n ≥ 0 with R(nextB1 ( x ), nextnB2 (y)), and some
n ≥ 0 with R(nextnB1 ( x ), nextB2 (y)).


Theorem 10.9 (Outside bases, and the relation). (1) Weak base equivalence is reflexive,
symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly equivalent, Theorem 10.1 holds over one
exactly when it holds over the other. (3) Theorem 10.1 holds over each of the three bases in
Definition 10.3, for every fixed program where the base has one.

Proof. (1) Reflexive with equality as R and one step against one. Symmetric by revers-
ing R. Transitive by composing the two relations; a step on the first base is matched by
n steps on the second, and those n steps by some number on the third, by induction
on n. (2) and (3) apply Theorem 10.1 directly. In (2) the equivalence hypothesis is
discarded.

Checked as weak_base_equiv_refl_holds, weak_base_equiv_sym_holds, w
eak_base_equiv_trans_holds (through weak_match_left_runs and weak_
match_right_runs), weak_equiv_preserves_record_latch_holds and re
cord_axis_is_latch_on_tm_holds (CrossBaseGranularity.v), record_axis_i
s_latch_on_ram_holds (CrossBaseGranularityRAM.v) and record_axis_is_l
atch_on_l_holds (CrossBaseGranularityL.v), with weak base equivalence and the
tape base defined in CrossBaseGranularityCore.v, transitivity stated in CrossBaseG-
ranularityTransCore.v, and the random-access and lambda bases defined in their own
files.

10.6 Records with more than two values
A cup has two positions. Some records have more: a counter of how many checks
passed, a level that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a
time. For each value a, “the record has reached a” is a yes/no reading, and each of
those readings is a latch. What doesn’t go through is squeezing the whole record into
one cup. “Rises” needs one word: the values come with an order ≤, “is at or below,”
which needn’t compare every pair (that’s what makes it a partial order), and [ a ≤ x ] is
the yes/no reading “x has reached a.”


Definition 10.5 (A growing record). Let the record take values in a set A with a


                                            194
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


partial order ≤ decided by a Boolean test. A record ρ on M, with cover π onto a
base B, is an honest growing record when: there is one function f with ρ(next M (m)) =
f (π (m), ρ(m)); it grows, ρ(m) ≤ ρ(next M (m)); the ledger never goes down and every
step that changes ρ costs at least one; and some run from a starting state reaches a step
that changes it.


Theorem 10.10 (Growing records are families of latches). (1) For every honest growing
record there is an h with

                     [ a ≤ ρ(next M (m))] = [ a ≤ ρ(m)] ∨ h( a, π (m), ρ(m))

for every value a and state m: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read the current value.
(2) The thresholds determine the value: if [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y] for every a, then x = y. (3) For a
growing record, charging every change is the same as charging every threshold that switches
on. (4) One latch is not enough: a three-valued record that climbs 0 → 1 → 2 over a one-state
base, each climb charged one, is honest, and no single Boolean latch with a decoding from the
base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct k-bit words, each word’s set bits
contained in the next one’s, has at most k + 1 members.

Proof. (1) Take h( a, b, x ) = [ a ̸≤ x ] ∧ [ a ≤ f (b, x )]. If a ≤ ρ(m) already, growth and
transitivity give a ≤ ρ(next M (m)); otherwise the equation is the definition of h. (2)
Antisymmetry, with a = x and a = y. (3) Growth plus antisymmetry turn “the value
changed” into “some threshold switched on,” and back. (4) Over one base state, a
latch and a decoding can produce at most two values, and the record takes three. (5)
Each strict step up the chain adds at least one set bit, and there are only k bits.

Two cautions about that. In (1) each threshold’s event may read the record’s current
value, so the events aren’t all functions of the base alone. And (3) charges a step when
it switches some threshold on: a step that switches on three thresholds at once owes
at least one, and nothing here makes the charges add up per threshold.

Checked as growing_record_decomposes_holds, thresholds_determine_
record_holds, record_price_iff_threshold_price_holds, one_latch_
refuted and chain_needs_bits_holds (GrowingRecord.v), with the definitions
in GrowingRecordCore.v. The order need not be finite; (5) is the finite-memory bound.

10.7 What the base being free buys you
The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record isn’t
special pleading for one machine. Over any base, under rules you can read, a record
that answers to the computation and never comes down is a latch on an event, and the
proof doesn’t care what the base is. What a particular machine adds on top of the latch
is a choice of price list and a choice of event, and both are choices. The surcharged cup
shows the first: the bill can change and the record not notice. The two cups on one die
show the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine I build will have

                                               195
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


to make both choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is a question I’ll
get to (Section 15), and won’t claim to have settled. Before that, the opening chapter
promised more than two positions. Earlier in this section a record that rises got cut
into one cup per threshold; the next section asks how much of the rest of the book
survives once a record has more places to be than up and down.

11 The whole direction
Back in the opening chapter I said something I couldn’t yet back up. I said established
didn’t feel like a switch to me. It felt like a direction with lines drawn across it, and the
switch was just the first line. Then I said the one piece of that I could settle was that a
single switch isn’t enough once there are three or more stages, and I pointed here. So
here’s where I pay that off, and where I find out how much of the rest survives being
pushed on.

The cup of Section 10 has two positions. Everything the book has proved about the
toll so far (the floor, the merges, the squeeze, the windows) was proved for a cup. The
question for this section is blunt: if the record has more places to be than up and down,
how many of those results come along, and which ones break?

11.1 A row of cups
Get four cups and a pencil. Write five stages of a sentence on a strip of paper, left to
right: guessed, announced, refereed, printed, machine-checked. Those are close to the stages
the Kepler story moved through in the opening chapter. Hales’s referees ran seminars
on his proof for years and ran out of energy before they could certify it, so here refereed
stands for that long reading, which is part of why the last stage exists. You don’t have
to believe my version of that story to use them. Now put a cup between each pair
of neighbours, upside down. The first cup means “at least announced,” the second
“at least refereed,” the third “at least printed,” the fourth “at least machine-checked.”
When the sentence reaches a stage, turn over every cup up to that stage. Cups only
ever get turned right side up. None of them has a reset wire.

Two things to notice with the cups in front of you. Each cup by itself is exactly the cup
of Section 10: it reads yes or no, and once yes it stays yes. And four cups were enough
for five stages. Try it with three. You can’t: three cups that only ever turn up, in order,
give you at most four different arrangements along the way. I’ll prove both of those in
a minute, and the proof is about as short as the experiment.

Now a harder strip. Some checks don’t line up. A referee can read a proof, and a
machine can check it, and neither of those is above the other: a refereed proof hasn’t
been machine-checked, and a machine-checked proof hasn’t been refereed. Draw it as
a diamond. Nothing at the bottom, refereed on the left, machine-checked on the right, both
at the top. Moving up the diamond is still only ever moving up, but now there are
two ways up from the bottom, and the two middle points don’t compare. That’s what
a partial order allows: some pairs simply aren’t comparable. Put a cup on each point


                                            196
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


that isn’t the bottom, one for “at least refereed,” one for “at least machine-checked,”
one for “both.” Each cup is still a latch. The record is now a place on the diamond,
and the three cups together tell you which place.

Whatever the shape of the strip, a straight line of stages or a diamond or something
with a hundred points, I’ll call the set of places the record can be the direction, and each
question “has the record reached at least this place?” a line across it. One line is one
cup.

11.2 The order, said exactly
The strip and the diamond each come with an order you can see by looking: whether
one place is at or below another. Said exactly, the order is a test. For any two places x
and y it answers “is x at or below y?” with yes or no, and I write a yes as x ≤ y. The
test has to obey two rules: every place is at or below itself, and if x ≤ y and y ≤ z
then x ≤ z. An order that obeys just those two is called a preorder. If it also obeys a
third rule, that x ≤ y and y ≤ x together force x = y, it’s a partial order, and that third
rule is called antisymmetry. The two-point order, no below yes, is the cup. The whole
numbers in their usual order are a straight strip that never ends.

The cups say the same thing in their own terms. For a place a, the cup for a asks “has
the record reached at least a?”, so with the record at x it’s up exactly when a ≤ x, and
I write its answer as [ a ≤ x ]. In the row of cups I said the cups together tell you which
place the record is at. On the strip and the diamond you can check that with your eyes,
and part (2) of Theorem 10.10 already proved it whenever the order is partial, though
I hadn’t asked what in that proof was doing the work. My first guess was that it held
for every order.

Why bother with the bare preorder at all, when every strip on the table is a partial
order? Because I wanted to see what the third rule was doing, and the way to see what
a rule does is to take it away. Take a preorder with two places, call them left and right,
where each is at or below the other. There are two cups, one asking “at least left?” and
one asking “at least right?”, and both are up at left and both are up at right. Look at the
table and you can’t say where the record is. Now build a record that swaps between
left and right on every single step and charges nothing. Every rule I’m about to state
is satisfied. The record never drops below anywhere it was, because each place is at
or below the other. No cup ever moves, so the toll in the next subsection has nothing
to charge. The record moved on every step and nothing on the table noticed.


Theorem 11.1 (The cups fix the place, and only with antisymmetry). (1) In a partial
order, if two places x and y leave the same cups up, [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y] for every a, then
x = y. (2) In a preorder that isn’t a partial order this can fail: there’s a preorder with two
different places that leave the same cups up, and a record over it, driven by the computation
and growing in that preorder, that changes on every step while no cup moves.



                                             197
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Proof. (1) Look at the cup for x. It’s up when the record is at x, since x is at or below
itself, so it’s up at y too, and that says x ≤ y. The cup for y gives y ≤ x the same way.
Antisymmetry gives x = y. (2) Left and right above, with the record swapping every
step.

Checked as bp_thresholds_determine and thresholds_fail_on_preorder
(AxCore.v), and indiscrete_loses_record (AxLatch.v).

So in a partial order the cups are the place, and in the preorder I built they aren’t.
That second half holds in every preorder that isn’t partial, by one line: if x ≤ y and
y ≤ x with x ̸= y, then a cup that’s up at either one is up at the other, by transitivity.
So the cups fix the place if and only if the order is partial (nec_f_same_rung_s
ame_cups, nec_f_non_partial_cups_fail and nec_f_cups_iff_partial,
NecFCups.v). My first guess was right on every strip I could draw, and it was right
because of a rule I hadn’t noticed I was leaning on. On a bare preorder, putting two
places on the same rung tells the toll not to care about moves between them, and it
doesn’t. I don’t think that’s a defect. It’s the order telling you what you agreed to
count.

11.3 The toll, over the whole direction
One cup had one rule: the step that turns it right side up pays. Now there’s a row of
cups, or a diamond of them, and a single step can turn over several at once. Here’s
the rule I’d guess first, and it turns out to be the right one: a step that turns over any cup
pays at least one. A step that turns over three cups at once still only has to pay one. The
rule asks whether a step turned something over. It doesn’t ask how many.

What does that rule buy? The same thing one cup bought. Take any run, and suppose
some cup is up at the end that was down at the start. Somewhere along the run a step
turned that cup over, and that step paid. So the run paid at least one. Count the same
way and you get more: the run paid at least once for every step that turned anything
over.

Now look at what that argument didn’t use. It didn’t care whether the cups sat in a
row or a diamond or something with a hundred points. It didn’t care how many there
were. It didn’t even use the fact that cups never get turned back down. If something
could knock a cup back over, the argument still works, because all it needs is the one
step where that cup went up.

To say it exactly I want to put it in terms of places, so here’s the translation. The cup
at a place a is up exactly when the record is at or above a. Say a step takes the record
from x to y. The cup at y is up afterwards, since y is at or above itself, and it was down
before exactly when y isn’t at or below x. And if y is at or below x, any cup that’s up at
y was already up at x. So a step turns over some cup exactly when it lands somewhere
that isn’t at or below where it started. The same reasoning says a run ends with some



                                             198
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


cup up that was down at the start exactly when it ends somewhere that isn’t at or
below where it started.


Theorem 11.2 (The toll over any direction). Take a machine whose record is a place in any
preorder, and say a step turns a cup over when it takes the record from x to a place that isn’t
at or below x. (1) Every step that turns a cup over costs at least one exactly when, from every
start, every run that ends somewhere not at or below its start costs at least one. (2) When that
holds, a run costs at least the number of its steps that turn a cup over. (3) It holds exactly when
every cup, on its own, pays the toll of Section 10: for every place a, a step that turns the cup at
a from down to up costs at least one. The floor of Section 3 is (1) with one cup.

Proof. (1) and (2) are the walk above. For the other half of (1), a run of one step
that turns a cup over ends somewhere not at or below its start. (3) is the translation
above.

Checked as ax_floor_iff_a2, ax_cost_ge_exits, ax_view_a2 and ax_a2_i
ff_views (AxCore.v, AxLatch.v), with the one-cup floor as two_point_nfi. When
the cups only ever go up, as on the strip and the diamond, a step that turns a cup over
is just a step up (ax_exit_is_strict_rise).

That surprised me a little. I’d filed the floor away as a fact about one bit. Nothing in it
was about one bit. It was about one cup going up, and anything you build out of cups
has that.

11.4 One line isn’t enough
Now the payoff I owe the opening chapter. Could a cleverer single cup do the job
of all four? One latch, and some decoding that reads the record’s place off the latch
and whatever the machine shows? Section 10 already shut that door in the smallest
case: over a machine with one visible state, a record that climbs through three places
can’t be produced by one latch and a decoding, because one latch and one visible state
make two outcomes and the record has three.

So try a second guess, closer to the cup’s own rule. The cup’s rule was “new value is
old value or the event.” The obvious rule for a whole row is “new place is old place
joined with the event’s place,” where joining two places means going to the lowest
place at or above both. On the row: the event names a place, and you turn up every
cup as far as that place. Here’s where it breaks. Take the strip 0 < 1 < 2, a cup at 1
and a cup at 2, over a machine with one visible state, so the event has to be one fixed
place. Let the record jump from 0 straight to 2, turning up both cups in one step, and
stay put at 1 and at 2. From 0 the event has to turn up both cups, so the fixed place is
2. From 1 the same event would turn up the second cup as well, and the record stays
at 1.

What works is giving every cup its own event, and letting the event for a cup look at


                                               199
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


where the record already is. That’s exactly what Theorem 10.10 said, and this is why
it had to say it. That leaves how many cups. In the row of cups I asked you to try five
stages with three and said you couldn’t. Theorem 10.10 (5) already bounded the chain
from above. Here’s the count behind that again, with the matching example added,
and with an arrangement of k cups read as a k-bit word, a one for every cup that’s up.


Theorem 11.3 (Lines a direction needs). (1) A list of different arrangements of k cups, each
keeping up every cup the one before had up (a chain of different k-bit words in which each
word’s set bits are among the next word’s), has at most k + 1 members, and for every k there’s
such a chain with exactly k + 1. So a straight strip of n + 1 stages needs exactly n cups. (2)
Over a machine with one visible state, take the record on the strip 0 < 1 < 2 that jumps from
0 to 2 and stays put at 1 and at 2. It grows and is driven by the computation, and no rule of
the form “join the record with a fixed place” reproduces its steps.

Proof. (1) Going from one arrangement to the next, which is a different one, turns up
at least one more cup, and there are k cups, so there are at most k steps and k + 1
arrangements. For the matching chain, take no cups up, then the first, then the first
two, and so on, packed to the left: that’s the row of cups. (2) Joining 0 with a fixed
place g gives g, and from 0 the step has to give 2, so g is 2. Joining 1 with 2 gives 2,
and from 1 the step has to stay at 1.

Checked as chain_bits_exact (AxLatch2.v) and chain3_not_join_latch
(AxLatch.v).

So five stages need four cups. One won’t do it, and three won’t either. Cups that
only turn up, that is: n write-once threshold bits. An ordinary binary counter holds
n + 1 stages in about log2 (n + 1) bits, because its bits go down as well as up, and the
theorem says nothing against that. The switch isn’t wrong. It’s the first line, and a
straight strip with more than two places needs more of them, exactly one fewer than
it has stages. A direction that branches needs at least as many cups as the steps in its
longest strict climb, and it can need more. Put three places above a bottom, none of
them above another. The longest climb is one step, and one cup can’t tell four places
apart.

People got here before me, and from a direction I didn’t expect, which was program-
ming for many processors at once. Lindsey Kuper and Ryan Newton’s LVars (2013),
“lattice-based data structures for deterministic parallelism” in their own title, are mem-
ory cells whose value only climbs in an order, where a read can’t ask for the value
and can only ask whether it has climbed past a threshold. That’s a cup. What the
cup buys them took me a couple of reads. As I understand it, writers running side by
side can push the value up in a different order on every run, and a cup that’s up stays
up whatever the order was, so a program that only ever looks at cups can’t see the
others’ timing. Amin Timany and Lars Birkedal (2021), coming at it from proofs about



                                             200
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


programs, show in Coq, as I read their paper, that any preorder at all can be carried
as monotone ghost state in a program logic. That’s the closest thing I’ve found to the
decomposition into lines being checked by somebody else. The match is my reading,
and if it’s off, that’s on me.

The two rest on the same thing, a value that only climbs and a question that only asks
whether it’s past a point, and they use it for opposite jobs. In an LVar the threshold
read steers the program. Ghost state, as far as I understand the term, lives in the proof,
and the running program never reads it. Here the record is never allowed to steer
anything, so I sit with the ghost state. Push on that and it gives a little: Section 2’s
glance, the whole reason to keep a record, is a read. What keeps me on that side is
that a glance worth trusting gives the answer the long way would have given. Their
purposes aren’t mine. But the shape is theirs first. What I can’t find in either is a price
on crossing a line.

11.5 Why crossing a line has to cost
Part II showed that the cup’s toll isn’t an arbitrary rule. It’s forced by three premises,
and the argument that ties them together was the chairs: on a machine with finitely
many states, a record that goes up and stays up has to seat two states in one chair at
the step that raises it (Theorem 4.1), and a step that seats two in one chair is a step that
forgets which one it came from. Does that survive the whole row of cups? Mostly, and
the parts that don’t survive are the interesting ones.

The room needs a flag, and now there are many cups, so the first job is to pick one.
My first guess was the cup for the place where the record starts. That goes nowhere:
the starting state already has that cup up, so it’s already inside the room, and there’s
nobody at the door. The cup that works is the one the step turns over, the cup for the
place a where the record lands. It’s up after the step, since a is at or above itself, and it
was down before, which is what turning a cup over means. So the room is every state
with the cup at a up, and the state the step starts from is the one at the door. If the
move keeps everybody in the room inside it and seats nobody twice, the insiders fill
the inside chairs between them and there’s no chair left for the newcomer. So one of
two things happened. Either two states shared a chair, or somebody who was in the
room got moved out, which means their cup at a went back down. I’ll call that second
thing a revocation.


Theorem 11.4 (Turning a cup over merges). On a machine with finitely many states and
a record in any preorder: (1) if a move turns a cup over at some state and lands the record at a
place a, then either the move merges two states, or there’s a state with the cup at a up that the
same move takes to a state with the cup at a down, which is a revocation; (2) if the record only
grows, so that no cup ever goes back down, the move merges; (3) if the record only grows, the
toll holds exactly when every move that turns a cup over at some state, and merges, costs at
least one, so merge pricing gives the toll.



                                              201
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Proof. (1) Gather every state with the cup at a up. There are finitely many. If the move
keeps each of them there and is injective, it maps that collection into itself without
two landing on one, so it hits all of them, including the state it sends the starting state
to; injectivity then says the starting state was in the collection already, and it wasn’t,
because its cup at a was down. So either some state in the collection has its cup at a
knocked down, or the move isn’t injective. (2) Growth rules out the knocking down.
(3) If the toll holds, every move that turns a cup over somewhere pays, merging or not.
The other way, a move that turns a cup over merges by (2), so the hypothesis charges
it.

Checked as ax_exit_merges_or_revokes, ax_growth_exit_merges and ax_
a2_iff_flipping_merges_priced (AxMerge.v), with ax_a2_from_merge_pr
ice for the derivation. It’s the room again, once for every cup.

Each premise there can be knocked out, and I wanted to see each one go, because a
premise you’ve never seen fail is one you don’t understand yet.

Knock out finiteness. Take the whole numbers as the states, which gives a row of cups
that never ends, and let the record be the state itself, one more on every step, at no
charge. Every step turns up one more cup. The step never merges anything: different
numbers go to different numbers. Merge pricing holds, because there are no merges to
price, and the toll fails on every single step. The room broke at the one place it needed
to be finite. Everybody moved one chair along, and there was always another chair.
That’s Charles Bennett’s 1973 escape in miniature, the way I read it: a machine that
keeps its whole history never has to forget, so it never has to pay, for as long as it has
room for the history. With infinitely many states it always has room.

Knock out growth. Take a two-state machine whose record flips back and forth be-
tween two places, so a cup goes up on one step and gets knocked back down on the
next. The two states just trade chairs, so nothing merges, and the price list is honest
about merges. The step that turns the cup up pays nothing. It takes the other branch
of (1): the state that had the cup up gets moved to where it’s down. It revokes.

Knock out the price on merges. A two-state machine that stamps every state with yes
turns the cup up wherever it was down, merges at the stamp, and charges nothing. Of
course the toll fails; nobody asked the merge to pay.


Theorem 11.5 (Three ways out). (1) There’s a machine with infinitely many states, a
growing record and an honest merge price on which every step turns a cup over and the toll
fails. (2) There’s a two-state machine with an honest merge price whose record doesn’t grow,
which turns a cup over and fails the toll. (3) There’s a two-state machine with a growing record
whose merges aren’t priced, which fails the toll.


Checked as history_escape, toggle_escape and free_merge_escape


                                              202
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


(AxMerge.v). So the toll over a whole direction rests on exactly the three things
the cup’s toll rested on: finitely many states, a record that doesn’t come down, and
merges that pay. Nothing extra got smuggled in when one cup became a row, and
nothing the one cup needed got left behind.

I’d half expected the diamond to need something new, some extra rule for the two
middle cups that don’t compare. It didn’t. Every cup gets its own room, and every
room is the old one.

12 The shadow, exactly
Section 7 put the machine behind a window and asked what an outsider could tell.
It found that two states can look the same through the window and differ in what
matters, and that a price computed from the window can’t be exact if the window has
a collision (Theorem 7.2). That was for one cup. With a whole row of cups in hand I
can ask the sharper version of the same question, which is also the one I actually care
about. Take the ordinary machine, the one with no cups and no ledger, and let it look
at itself. What’s the shape of everything it can’t see, and what does the toll cost in
terms of that shape?

12.1 The ordinary machine is a shadow
Take any machine with a record and a ledger, and sweep both off the table, the cups
and the counter. What’s left is a machine that steps the same way and knows nothing
about either, provided the step’s effect on everything else never depends on the cups
or the counter: sweeping them off has to commute with the step. A system whose
control reads its record or its ledger has no shadow in this sense. Where the premise
holds, call what’s left the shadow. Over any one state of the shadow there’s a pile of
full states, one for each place the record could be, with its own cups up, and each
value the ledger could hold, all of them casting that same shadow. Section 7 already
called the pile over a point the fibre over it. The shadow is one particular window, the
one that shows everything except the cups and the ledger.

The shadow has its own fibres, and every move has piles of its own too: the states
a move sends to one landing spot. I’ll call those the move’s landing piles. A fibre is
everything that looks the same before anybody moves. A landing pile is everything
that ends up in the same spot after one move. Keep the two kinds apart, because the
whole section turns on how they meet.

12.2 Pricing from the shadow
First the window question, over a whole row. A window price charges each step from
what the window shows before and after it. It meets the floor if it charges at least one
for every step that turns a cup over, and it’s exact if it also charges nothing for any step
that turns no cup over. A collision is two steps that look the same through the window,
where one turns a cup over and the other doesn’t.



                                            203
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


With one cup, the fix in Section 7 was to put the cup in the window. So my first guess
for a row was that the window has to show some of the cups. Try the smallest version:
a record in the whole numbers, and a window that shows only the first cup, the one
that asks “at least one?” Let the record rise on some steps and hold still on others.
Once it’s past one, that cup is up before and after both kinds of step, so a step that
turned over a cup further along looks exactly like a step that turned over nothing.
That’s a collision. So then, I thought, the window has to show every cup. That’s
wrong too, from the other side. Take a record in the whole numbers that rises on every
step, and a window that shows only whether the record is even, which on the row is
whether an even number of cups are up. You can’t read the record off that window.
Every step changes the evenness, though, and every step turns a cup over, so charging
one for every step is exact.


Theorem 12.1 (Window prices over a direction). (1) If the window has a collision, every
window price that meets the floor charges at least one for some step that turns no cup over,
so no window price is exact. (2) On a machine with finitely many states and moves, whose
views can be told apart by a yes-or-no test, an exact window price exists exactly when the
window has no collision. (3) Along any run, a window price that meets the floor charges at
least the number of steps that turn no cup over but look, through the window, like a step that
does. When it can be decided, for each pair of views, whether some step showing them turns
a cup over, some window price meets the floor and, among the steps that turn no cup over,
charges one on exactly those, so that number is the least overcharge. (4) A window can price
exactly without showing where the record is: there’s a record in the whole numbers, rising on
every step, and a window that shows only whether the record is even, which prices every step
exactly although no rule reads the record off it. (5) There’s a record in the whole numbers and
a window that shows only the one cup “at least one,” and that window has a collision.

Proof. (1) The two colliding steps get the same bill. The floor makes it at least one
because of the step that turns a cup over, and the other step pays it too. (2) Without
a collision, “does some step that looks like this turn a cup over?” is a question about
what the window shows, and on a finite machine you can answer it for every pair of
views; charge one exactly when the answer is yes. (3) A step that turns no cup over
but looks like one that does gets that step’s bill, which is at least one by (1)’s argument;
add along the run. For the other half, charge one exactly when the answer to (2)’s
question is yes, which needs that question to be decidable, and count the overcharge.
(4) Every step changes the evenness, so the window sees every step as a move, and
every step turns a cup over. (5) The first cup, as above.

Checked as ax_window_collision_overcharges, ax_window_no_exact_pr
ice, ax_window_exact_iff_no_collision, ax_overcharge_lower, ax_ov
ercharge_tight, ax_exact_without_position and ax_threshold_window
_blind (AxWindow.v).



                                             204
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Item (4) changed how I think about this. I’d assumed a window had to see the cups to
price them. It doesn’t. It has to see them move. A window that knows nothing about
where you are, and knows exactly when you’ve gone somewhere, can send the right
bill every time.

12.3 What a priced move destroys
Now the fibres. Part II showed that the step raising a permanent flag on a finite
machine seats two states in one chair, and Theorem 11.4 showed the same for a step
that turns any cup over, once the cups only go up. Which two? It matters a great deal.
If they’re in different shadow fibres, then the ordinary machine lost something and
the record didn’t. If they’re in the same fibre, the ordinary machine lost nothing, and
what got destroyed was only ever off the table: two states that cast one shadow, told
apart by their cups or their ledger, crushed into one.

My first guess was that it’s always the second kind, because the cups are where
everything happens. It isn’t always. It depends on whether the ordinary machine
forgets anything on its own.


Theorem 12.2 (The toll prices a collapse inside a fibre). On a machine with finitely many
states and a growing record: (1) a move that turns a cup over somewhere sends two different
states to one landing spot; (2) if the shadow’s step for that move forgets nothing, sending
different shadow states to different shadow states, then those two states are in the same shadow
fibre, and every landing pile of the move lies inside one fibre; (3) without that premise it can
fail: there’s a two-state machine whose two states sit in different fibres and whose shadow step
forgets, so the merge at the step that turns the cup over lands two states from different fibres
and no fibre loses a point. (4) The halving price, which says a move of cost c shrinks any
collection of states by at most a factor of 2c , holds exactly when every landing pile has at most
2c states, on a machine of any size.

Proof. (1) is the room of Theorem 11.4, with growth. (2) If two states land on one spot,
their shadows land on one shadow spot, and the shadow’s step tells shadows apart,
so the two states cast the same shadow to begin with. (3) The stamp from the three
ways out, with each state as its own shadow: both states land on yes, and so do their
shadows. (4) is the worst pile-up of Premise 4.4: one landing pile is a collection that
lands on a single spot, and any collection is at most the number of spots it lands on
times the biggest pile. Neither half needs the machine to be finite.

Checked as ax_exit_collision, ax_fibre_collapse_exit, ax_step_fibre
_in_fibre, shadow_merge_escape, ax_compression_iff_fibres, ax_pric
ed_spots and ax_spots_priced (AxShadow.v, AxInfinite.v).

So on a machine with finitely many states and a record that only grows, when the
ordinary machine forgets nothing, the toll is a price on crushing a fibre: on taking two



                                               205
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


states that cast one shadow, which only what’s off the table told apart, and making
them one. The last of those premises is the one I just showed you failing.

12.4 How much gets destroyed, on average
The halving price is a worst case. It prices the largest landing pile a move can have.
The next question is the average one: if I don’t know which state the machine was
in, cups and all, but I have some spread of chances over the states, how much do I
lose, on average, about which state it was, once I know where it landed? That’s what
Shannon’s conditional entropy measures (Section 4 built the entropy from scratch, so
I won’t do it again here). Write it in bits.


Theorem 12.3 (The halving price in bits bounds the average loss). Take any spread of
non-negative weights over the states, uniform or not. (1) If every landing pile has at most N
states, the conditional entropy of the state given its landing spot is at most the total weight
times log2 N bits. (2) So on a machine with finitely many states and the halving price, the
average information a move destroys is at most its cost in bits, times the weight. (3) The bound
is reached: the even spread on a pile of 2c states loses exactly c bits. (4) On a machine of any
size and for any spread, even one whose entropy is infinite, the same bound holds for every
finite family of landing piles of a priced move.

Proof. Inside one pile, Gibbs’s inequality: the entropy of a spread over n states is at
most log2 n, with equality for the even spread. Add over the piles, weighting each by
its share. The halving price makes n at most 2cost , and log2 2c = c.

Checked as ax_fibre_gibbs, ax_loss_le, ax_priced_loss_bits, ax_pri
ced_loss_tight (AxProb.v) and ax_inf_loss_bits (AxInfinite.v). These use
Coq’s real numbers, and they lean on four standard-library assumptions, all named
in Section 22: the two decidability principles that come with the reals, functional
extensionality, and excluded middle.

Where does it stop? My first guess was one place, a landing pile with infinitely many
states, and that the average would blow up there right along with the worst case.
That’s half right, and the half that’s wrong surprised me. No finite toll can price a
move that sends infinitely many states to one spot, and that’s a theorem. But the
average depends on the spread. Put weight 12 on the first state, 14 on the next, 18 on
the next, and so on, and the information lost by crushing the pile never reaches 2 bits,
however many of its states you count. Under that spread, two bits of toll would cover
the average, though nothing covers the worst case. So I went looking for a spread
                                                                                  k
that does blow up, and it took a nastier one: blocks of states, block k holding 22 states
and a share (k+1)(1 k+2) of the weight, which adds up to one. Under that spread the loss
grows past every bound. No toll covers it, on average or otherwise.


Theorem 12.4 (An infinite pile). (1) A move that sends infinitely many states to one spot


                                              206
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


isn’t priced by the halving price at any finite cost. (2) Under the halving spread 2−( j+1) , the
information lost by crushing the pile, counted over its first n states, is less than 2 bits for every
n. (3) Under the block spread, the information lost grows past every bound, so no cost covers
it.


Checked as ax_collapse_unpriceable, ax_geometric_loss, ax_block_mas
s_n, ax_block_loss_unbounded and ax_block_no_toll (AxInfinite.v).

And heat? Part II already said where the line is, and it’s the same line here. Landauer’s
principle, that crushing c bits’ worth of possibilities costs at least c kT ln 2 of heat on
average, is a premise from physics, and a contested one (Section 4). Nothing in this
section proves anything about heat. What the counting does give is this: under that
premise, on a machine with the halving price, a move’s cost priced at kT ln 2 per unit,
times the weight of the piles, is always enough to cover the minimum the premise
would demand, for every spread and every finite family of landing piles. Checked
as ax_toll_covers_landauer_minimum (AxInfinite.v). If the premise falls, that
sentence falls with it, and every theorem above it stands, because none of them used
it.

12.5 What the shadow is
Put the two sections together and here’s the shape I’ve been circling since the Flatland
night. The ordinary machine is the shadow of a machine with a row of cups beside it.
Over every shadow state there’s a whole fibre, a pile of states that differ only in their
cups and their ledger, and the ordinary machine can’t tell them apart, on a machine
whose step never looks at the cups. On a machine that pays the toll, a step that turns a
cup over costs, whichever cup it is and however many it turns, and on a machine with
finitely many states whose record only grows, when the ordinary machine forgets
nothing, what that cost pays for is exactly crushing two states of one fibre into one. A
window can send the right bill without seeing the cups, if it sees them move. And on
a machine with the halving price, where each unit of cost pays for at most one halving,
the bill in bits, times the weight of the spread, is never less than what got crushed on
average.

What I haven’t shown is that any of this is out there in the world, that nature keeps
a direction like this over its own shadows. That’s a belief of mine, and nothing in
this book proves it. What I’ve shown, and you can check, comes with its premises
showing. A machine whose record is driven by the computation and climbs a partial
order is a row of cups, one latch for every line. If it also has finitely many states, never
lets the record come down, and prices its merges, it has to pay this way. And when
its ordinary machine forgets nothing, what it pays for is exactly this. It’s less than the
Flatland night promised me. It’s also the part of it that held when I pushed.




                                                207
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


12.6 Shortcuts
Here’s the question every machine with a record has to face, and no amount of good
design makes it go away. A cup is worth turning over because something later glances
at it and doesn’t have to work the thing out again: that’s Section 2’s glance, reading a
block’s bucket off the table without applying the rule from scratch. Call any move like
that a shortcut, and call it sound when it gives the answer the long way would have
given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning on what was done so nothing is redone, and
the wall I’m about to show you doesn’t look at cost at all; the next section says exactly
what it does look at.) So: can a machine decide, from inside, whether its own shortcuts
are sound? That’s a wall, and it’s the same wall the logician Kurt Gödel and Turing
hit, and I have to show you that it’s there before I show you anything that pretends to
be on the other side of it.

13 The diagonal
In Section 2 I said you’d watch the same move get made again and again as the book
went on: somebody says “everything is X,” it’s true enough to do real work with,
and then somebody draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now, because
Sections 10 to 12 just handed a record, and a whole direction of them, to any system
that steps, and the next thing anyone wants from a system with a record is for it to tell
sound shortcuts from unsound ones by itself. Before I let anything claim that, I have
to show you the wall every such claim runs into, and then show you exactly where a
system with a record stands relative to the wall. Not on the far side. Nobody’s on the
far side.

13.1 Five names and a table
Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick
and you should own it. Write five friends’ names down the left of a page. Next to
each name, write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now build a
new string: its first digit is the opposite of the first digit of the first row; its second digit
is the opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down the diagonal.
Look at what you’ve made. It differs from row one in position one, from row two in
position two, from every row at that row’s own position. So it’s nobody’s string. Your
table of five missed something.

With five rows and five digits that’s a cute fact. Georg Cantor, a mathematician
working out how to compare infinite sets, made the point in 1891 that it works for
any list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all infinite strings of
two symbols, I’ll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I’ll hand you back a string
that’s on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such strings than there
are places on any list, and that’s where “some infinities are bigger than others” comes
from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, where I’d write 0 and 1, and that paper
wasn’t even his first proof of the fact. The first was in 1874, by a harder road through
the real numbers, and in 1891 he called the new one much simpler. The diagonal was

                                              208
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


him finding the easy way.)

Now look at what the argument did, because it’s going to do the same thing again
and again, in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not every name
below is a flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene’s theorem is the tool that makes
the diagonal buildable, Rice’s is the general form, the one from Ken Thompson, who
built the original Unix operating system at Bell Labs, is an attack that uses the same
trick, and the last, Lawvere’s, is the theorem that makes them all one.) There was a
table: rows are the things being listed, columns are questions, each cell says “does
row i do column j.” There was the diagonal: the cells where a thing is asked about
itself. There was a flip: something with no fixed point, like turning yes into no, applied
along the diagonal. And the thing that got refuted was the assumed object, the complete
list. Nothing outside the assumption was touched. Table, diagonal, flip, and the
assumption eats itself. Hold those four.

13.2 The same move, again and again
Russell, 1902, from Section 2: the collection of all collections that don’t contain them-
selves. That’s Cantor’s flipped diagonal with “contains” as the table, and Russell said
as much, in The Principles of Mathematics in 1903. He got there, he wrote, by running
Cantor’s argument on a supposed collection of everything, which ought to be the
biggest collection there is. What got refuted was the assumed object, the collection of
everything, and Zermelo’s fix was to stop assuming it.

Jules Richard, a French mathematician who taught at the lycées of Tours, Dijon and
Châteauroux, took his doctorate in Paris in 1901 and wrote mostly on geometry, in
1905, in a short note, a letter to the editor of a French science review: some phrases
(his were in French) define real numbers (“the ratio of a circle’s circumference to its
diameter”); there are only countably many phrases, so list the numbers they define
in order; run Cantor’s diagonal down their decimal expansions and you get a real
number no phrase defines, except that you just defined it, in the phrase that describes
the diagonal. The lesson I take from that one is the lesson this whole section turns
on: keep apart the language a system talks in and the language you use to talk about it.
Mix them and the diagonal bites you.

Richard’s paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes with a
footnote I can’t resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited it to G. G.
Berry, a junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. A paradox that has outlived
empires, and it came from the library desk. In the version in Principia Mathematica it’s
about syllables. Take the phrase “the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen
syllables.” There are only so many phrases shorter than nineteen syllables, so they
name only so many numbers, so some least number is left over, and the phrase picks
it out. Now count the phrase: the, least, in-te-ger, not, name-a-ble, in, few-er, than,
nine-teen, syl-la-bles. Eighteen. In eighteen syllables it has named the number that
can’t be named in fewer than nineteen. Same lesson as Richard’s, in a smaller coat:


                                            209
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


“nameable” is a word about the language, used inside the language, and that’s where
the bite is.

Kurt Gödel, 1931, with an improvement in 1936 by Barkley Rosser, a logician who
had studied under Alonzo Church at Princeton and whose trick lets the theorem
assume only that the system is consistent: the big one, and I’ll say exactly what it says,
because every word of it is carrying weight. Take any consistent formal system with a
mechanically checkable list of axioms that can do a bit of arithmetic. Then there are
sentences it can neither prove nor refute. The engine is a lemma that lets you build,
for any property you can write down, a sentence that the system proves equivalent to
that property holding of the sentence’s own code number. Apply it to “not provable”
and you get a sentence equivalent, inside the system, to its own unprovability. Table:
sentences by code. Diagonal: a sentence about its own code. Flip: provable to not-
provable. Two cautions the Stanford Encyclopedia stresses, and I’ll repeat them. The
sentence doesn’t literally “say” anything about itself. It’s provably equivalent to a claim
about its code, which is less mystical and more exact. And the theorem doesn’t say
the sentence is unknowable. It says this one system can’t settle it.

And how did the world take it? Mostly, at first, it didn’t. Gödel, twenty-four years
old, announced the first theorem during a round-table discussion on the last day
of a conference in Königsberg in September 1930, and by the account of Solomon
Feferman, one of the editors of Gödel’s collected works, the room met it with general
incomprehension. Except for one man. John von Neumann pulled Gödel aside to talk
about it, kept thinking about it, and a couple of months later saw that the argument
gave something more: a consistent system of this kind can’t prove its own consistency.
He wrote to Gödel with it in a letter dated 20 November 1930. Gödel had already got
there. His paper had reached the journal three days earlier, with that second theorem
announced in it, and von Neumann left the credit with Gödel. It’s the “somebody got
there first” shape from the opening chapter, with one difference: here the man who
got there second was von Neumann.

Alan Turing, 1936. I’d always taken it that Turing proved the halting problem un-
decidable, and here I had to go and look. The set theorist Joel David Hamkins and
his coauthor Theodor Nenu went back to the 1936 paper and report that the word
“halting,” the modern statement, and the self-referential proof everyone teaches are
all, strictly speaking, absent from it. What Turing proved undecidable were two
other questions about his machines (whether a machine prints infinitely many digits;
whether it ever prints a given symbol). The second is equivalent to halting and the
first is strictly harder. So their answer cuts both ways, and they say so: Turing never
stated the halting problem, and he essentially proved it, because his second question
is a short translation away from it. The name came later. Martin Davis seems to have
been the first to write “halting problem,” in a book of 1958, and Stephen Kleene had
already stated the problem, without that name, in his 1952 textbook Introduction to
Metamathematics. The textbook version is still right as mathematics, and here it is, on


                                           210
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


two index cards. Card A is the Checker: hand it any program card and it announces
“halts” or “runs forever.” Card B is the Contrarian: “Hand me to the Checker. If it says
I halt, run forever. If it says I run forever, stop.” Hand B to A. Either answer is wrong.
There’s no Checker. Table: programs by programs. Diagonal: a program run on itself.
Flip: halt to loop.

Stephen Kleene, 1938, the logician whose textbook I just mentioned, and this is the
one that turns the paradox into a tool, so slow down. Everything above needs the
self-referring object to exist: Gödel’s sentence has to be buildable, the Contrarian has
to be able to “hand me to the Checker.” Kleene’s second recursion theorem says: for
any transformation of programs you can compute, there’s a program that behaves
exactly as if it had been handed its own source code. Any program may be written
as though it already had a copy of itself in hand. He stated it almost in passing, in
a paper on something else, and proved it in the last two lines of one of its sections.
I have that count from Yiannis Moschovakis, a logician at UCLA and Athens who
wrote a 2009 paper on it called “Kleene’s Amazing Second Recursion Theorem,” and
he calls it a little gem. It’s the reason “programs that print their own source” exist
in every programming language that can compute whatever a Turing machine can
(they’re called quines, after a philosopher I’ll come to in a moment; try “Print the
following twice, the second time in quotes: ‘Print the following twice, the second
time in quotes:’ ” and obey it). Self-reference in computation isn’t a paradox. It’s a
construction. The paradoxes happened only when someone assumed an unrestricted
collection or language; the theorem happens when you build the self-referrer honestly.

And where does the word quine come from? Not from the philosopher himself. Dou-
glas Hofstadter coined it in 1979, in Gödel, Escher, Bach, in honour of Willard Van
Orman Quine, who had made a long study of self-reference that works indirectly.
Quine left a sentence you can take apart at the table, from a 1962 essay on paradox.
Here it is, all of it: “yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation” yields falsehood
when preceded by its quotation. Do what it says. Take the part in quotation marks,
put a quoted copy of it in front of itself, and look at what you’ve built: it’s the whole
sentence, word for word. So the sentence says that it itself is false. That’s the liar para-
dox, but look at how it got there: no “this sentence” anywhere, no pointing at itself,
just an instruction to quote and copy, the same move as the print-twice instruction
above. That’s Kleene’s trick in plain English, and it’s why the paradox and the tool
look so alike. The paradox is what you get when the copy asserts something about its
own truth. The tool is what you get when the copy just does something.

Henry Rice, 1953, whom you met briefly in Section 7: the general form. Any property
that depends only on what a program does, whatever its text, and that’s true of some
programs and false of others, has no algorithm that decides it for all programs. “Does
this program halt” is one such property. “Does this program ever output 7” is another.
“Does this program contain an if-statement” isn’t, because that’s about the text. One
standard proof goes straight through Kleene.


                                            211
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


And the one that’s actually an attack: Ken Thompson, in his Turing Award lecture,
published in 1984. Build a compiler that, when it compiles the login program, plants a
back door, and when it compiles a compiler, plants both habits into that one too. Then
delete the trick from the source. The compiled compiler still carries it, and recompiling
a clean source with the poisoned binary re-plants it, forever. Reading the source never
reveals it. A locksmith teaches an apprentice to cut a spare for every town-hall key
and to teach that to every apprentice they train, and never to write it in the manual;
years later the manual is spotless and every locksmith in town cuts the spare. That’s
the recursion theorem with a knife in it, and his moral was that you can’t trust code
you didn’t write entirely yourself, which is a sentence I’ll come back to in Section 22
when I tell you what the trusted base of this book is.

And Thompson wasn’t first either, and he said so. Pull on the lecture’s acknowledg-
ment the way the opening chapter pulled on Bitcoin’s footnotes: he writes that he first
read of the possibility in an Air Force critique of the security of an early implementa-
tion of Multics, a time-sharing system from the 1960s, and that he couldn’t find a more
specific reference to it, and he asks anyone who can to send him one. The critique
is Paul Karger and Roger Schell’s 1974 security evaluation of Multics, which already
