described a trap door planted in a compiler that, because the compiler is written in
its own language, keeps itself alive. So the knife was in the drawer ten years before
the lecture was printed. Then the obvious next question: is there any way out, or is
“trust no binary you didn’t build” the bottom? There’s a partial answer, and it took
a while. David A. Wheeler, in a 2005 paper and a 2009 dissertation at George Mason
University, worked out diverse double-compiling: compile the suspect compiler’s source
with a second, independently made compiler, use the result to compile that source
again, and compare the output bit for bit with the suspect binary. If they match, the
binary really is what its source says, unless both compilers were poisoned in the same
way. The trust doesn’t vanish. It moves, from one compiler to the claim that two
unrelated ones weren’t rigged together. That’s the shape of every stopping point in
this book. You don’t reach the bottom. You reach a place where you can say exactly
what you’re trusting.

Bill Lawvere, in 1969, proved a fixed-point theorem that, as I read it, makes all of
these one theorem in disguise: if a set can be mapped onto all the functions from itself
to some target, then every function on the target has a fixed point; so if the target
has a function with no fixed point (a flip), no such covering exists. Cantor, Russell,
Gödel, halting, as instances of one shape. Noson Yanofsky retold it in 2003 without
the category theory. I mention it because “it’s the same wall” is a claim I make below,
and I want you to know it’s fair at the level of proof shape, and that every instance has
its own boundary of who counts as a decider, and that boundary is exactly where most
overclaims live.




                                          212
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


13.3 Four things it doesn’t give you
Before I point this at a system with a record, here are four conclusions the theorem
doesn’t reach. Each one looks as if it follows, and I wanted to see exactly where each
one stops.

“Gödel shows minds aren’t machines.” John Lucas, a philosopher who spent thirty-
six years as a fellow of Merton College, Oxford, argued it in 1961, in a paper called
“Minds, Machines and Gödel.” Roger Penrose, the Oxford mathematical physicist who
later shared a Nobel prize for his work on how black holes form, revived it twice, in
two books, The Emperor’s New Mind in 1989 and Shadows of the Mind in 1994. I’m sure
of who argued it and when. Whether they’re right is the question, and the standard
replies, as far as I can tell, have held up: the Gödel sentence is true only if the system
is consistent, so a human who “sees” its truth has to know the system is consistent,
which is the hard part; and nobody can build the Gödel sentence of a system they can’t
specify, so humans might be machines too complicated to diagonalise. The theorem
has a conditional in it and the argument drops the conditional.

And here’s the part that’s easy to miss: Gödel himself didn’t go as far as Lucas. In a
lecture on the day after Christmas in 1951, at a meeting of the American Mathematical
Society at Brown University, he drew from his own theorems only an either-or. Either
the human mind, even inside pure mathematics, infinitely surpasses the powers of
any finite machine, or there are problems about whole numbers, of a certain simple
kind, that no proof the human mind can conceive will ever settle. Feferman, writing
about that lecture, says Gödel privately believed the first half and still stated only the
disjunction, because he didn’t have a knock-down argument against the machine side.
Gödel wrote soon afterward that he meant to publish the lecture, and never did; the
text sat among his papers until after his death. So the man whose theorem gets quoted
for “minds aren’t machines” stated an either-or and left the deciding to whoever came
next. That’s the conditional again, kept, by the person with the most right to drop it.

“Undecidable means unknowable.” Two senses share the word: a problem with no
single algorithm correct on every instance, and a sentence independent of one partic-
ular system. Neither means nobody can know a given answer. Any single instance
is decidable, trivially: for any one program, one of “say yes” and “say no” is right.
What’s ruled out is one inside procedure that’s right on every case.

“Everything interesting is undecidable.” Rice is about behavioural properties over
all programs. It says nothing against checking the text, nothing against deciding for
specific programs, nothing against analyses allowed to say “I don’t know,” nothing
against finite-state model checking or type checking. Real compilers are limited by
cost and by choosing to be sound-but-incomplete. The diagonal isn’t what stops them.

“Self-reference is a paradox.” It’s a theorem with a construction. Kleene, quines,
Thompson.



                                           213
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


13.4 Now point it at the record
Here’s the question Section 12 left open, with nothing in it but what Parts I to III have
built. A system steps; a record rides along and latches on an event (Section 10); when
the event is a certification, Section 8 said the reading, with its object and its paid event
behind it, is what lets an auditor treat a claim as established, and for a claim that a
shortcut is sound, that’s what makes the shortcut admissible. So: can a system like
that have, as one of its own programs, a procedure that correctly decides, for every
program, “does this program admit a sound shortcut”? That would be autopilot.
Hand it any program and it says yes or no, and it’s always right.

That’s the question in plain words, and the checked statement is narrower, so here it is
before the proof. In the theorem, “admits a shortcut” is any property of programs with
two features: two programs that behave alike agree on it, and there’s one program
that has it and one that doesn’t. That’s all the argument gets to look at. The diagonal
doesn’t see soundness. Each system that wants the wall picks its own property, and
whether that property lines up with being entitled to soundness in Section 8’s sense
is a separate fact about that system, checked one system at a time if it’s checked at all.
A procedure that returns soundness records for some programs, or only for restricted
inputs, or with outside evidence, is not what the wall rules out.

So in the theorem “shortcut” is a label. The plain-words gloss at the end of Section 12,
leaning on a record so the thing isn’t worked out again, is about how a program gets its
answer, and how is exactly what extensionality throws away: the theorem only gets
to see what programs do, and it treats any two that do the same as one. A question
like “is there a cheaper program that gives the same answers?” isn’t the theorem’s
question, and a wall for it would need a different theorem. The nearest thing I know
of is Manuel Blum’s speedup theorem, from 1967, and it goes somewhere stranger:
there are computable functions with no fastest program at all, where every program
for the function has another that’s faster on all but finitely many inputs. That’s a fact
about cost. It isn’t a wall about deciding, and nothing in this book proves anything in
that territory. Each use of the wall also names its sameness. In the substrate theorem
it’s the substrate’s own ≃; on L it’s what a term computes; on the small machine’s
host, in Section 16.18, it’s everything a program ends with, the record included. A
particular notion of shortcut gets the wall only after someone proves it behaves alike
on programs that are the same in the sense in use, and holds of one program and fails
of another.

The answer is no, under premises. The proof is the two index cards, and I’ll give you
the premises because they’re the whole content. Suppose there were such a decider,
one that says yes exactly when a program admits a shortcut. Build the flip: “if the
decider says yes about me, behave like a program that admits no shortcut; if it says
no, behave like one that does.” If the system has a recursion theorem (a program
can be handed its own code), and if that flip is one of the transformations the system
can carry out, and if “admits a shortcut” depends only on behaviour (two programs

                                            214
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


that behave the same agree on it), and if there’s at least one program each way, then
there’s a program that behaves exactly like its own flip, and whatever the decider
says about it is wrong. Both cases close in a line each. That’s structural_shortc
ut_undecidable, which rules out a decider that says yes if and only if a program
admits a shortcut, stated for any substrate with those fields. (A substrate here is the
bare shape the class asks for: programs, a run that may fail to give back a state, a
counter with a step relation it never goes down along, an encoding of programs as
data, a notion of “representable” transformation, and the recursion theorem for those.
Nothing about what the states are made of. The smallest checked instance is the nat
family below.) It’s Rice’s trick one floor over, and I should be careful with that. Rice’s
theorem is stated for the functions Turing machines compute. This wall is the same
diagonal with different premises: it carries its own recursion theorem and its own list
of representable transformations, and it picks the property. So it isn’t a corollary of
Rice as Rice stated it, and it doesn’t show that any property is harder or easier to decide
than classical halting. And here’s something about its proof that I want you to have: it
never touches the counter, the toll, or the step relation. It uses the recursion theorem,
representability of the flip, the two witnesses, and extensionality, and nothing else.
(The file’s header calls the substrates it covers ones that respect the toll. The proof uses
neither the toll nor the counter’s climbing. It’s the diagonal, clean.)

Here’s the setting and the wall, with every word pinned down so you can poke at it.


Definition 13.1 (Substrate). A substrate has a type of states, a type Prog of programs,
and a run map that takes a program and a state and either gives back a state or gives
nothing. It has a counter µ on states and a step relation along which µ never decreases;
an encoding enc of programs as states with a decoder dec such that dec(enc( p)) = p;
and a predicate Rep on maps f : Prog → Prog, the transformations the substrate
counts as its own. Two programs are equivalent, p ≃ q, when run( p, s) = run(q, s) for
every state s. The last field is the recursion theorem: for every f with Rep( f ) there is a
program p with p ≃ f ( p).


Definition 13.2 (Shortcut predicate). A shortcut predicate on a substrate is a property
A of programs with two programs y and n such that A(y) holds, A(n) fails, and A is
extensional: p ≃ q implies A( p) ⇐⇒ A(q). For a Boolean function d on programs,
its flip is f d ( p) = n if d( p) is true and f d ( p) = y if d( p) is false.


Theorem 13.1 (No inside decider). Let a substrate carry a shortcut predicate A with wit-
nesses y and n. Then there is no Boolean function d on programs such that Rep( f d ) holds and,
for every program p, d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p).

Proof. Suppose d is such a function. Since Rep( f d ), the recursion theorem gives a
program p with p ≃ f d ( p). Split on d( p). If d( p) is true, then A( p) holds by correctness,



                                             215
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


and f d ( p) = n, so p ≃ n, and extensionality turns A( p) into A(n), which fails. If d( p)
is false, then A( p) fails by correctness, and f d ( p) = y, so p ≃ y, and extensionality
turns A(y) into A( p). Both cases are contradictions. The argument uses the recursion
theorem once, the two witnesses, extensionality, and nothing about µ, the step relation,
or the encoding.

Checked as structural_shortcut_undecidable (StructuralUndecidability.v;
the correctness it rules out is d( p) true exactly when A( p)), stated over the class S
ubstrate (Substrate.v) and its extension WithShortcutPredicate. Every field
named above is a premise; the theorem is about every substrate that supplies them.

So the wall is there. Now the honest part: who counts as a decider. The theorem rules out
a decider whose flip the substrate can itself represent. It says nothing about a decider
standing outside, and an outside decider can exist for the very same property, correct
on every program. That’s the boundary of the sentence, and the boundary is Richard’s
lesson: the language you talk about a system in is a different language from the one it
talks in. You’ll see it in miniature in a minute, on the nat family, with a pencil.

Two forms of the wall live in this section, and they’re honest in different ways.

The nat family (nat_self_undecidable): a tiny substrate built so that program two
is the Contrarian for a given candidate decider d, and for every d, d is wrong about
program two. It’s a family, one instance per d, and its recursion theorem holds by
construction. It’s the index cards made formal and nothing more.


Theorem 13.2 (The nat family). Fix any Boolean function d on N. Let the substrate
Nd have programs and states N; program 0 returns 1, program 1 returns 0, program 2
returns 0 if d(2) is true and 1 if it is false, and every other program gives nothing; µ is
constantly 0; Rep( f ) holds when f ( p) = 1 for every p with d( p) true and f ( p) = 0 for
every other p; and A( p) holds when program p returns 1 on input 0. Then it is not the case
that d( p) = true ⇐⇒ A( p) for every p.

Proof. The recursion theorem of Nd holds with the fixed witness 2: for a representable
f , f (2) is 1 or 0 according to d(2), and program 2 returns exactly what that program
returns. The witnesses for A are 0 and 1. The flip of d is representable by the definition
of Rep, so Theorem 13.1 applies to d itself. Directly: A(2) holds exactly when d(2) is
false.

Checked as nat_self_undecidable (NatSubstrateInstance.v), with the built-in
recursion theorem nat_recursion_theorem; the general form, no decider whose
flip is representable in Nd , is nat_structural_shortcut_undecidable in the
same file.

Now push on it once more, because the nat family shows the outside decider in three


                                           216
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


lines, and you can do them yourself. Stand outside Nd , knowing d. Write down a
new decider e: say yes on program 0, say “not d(2)” on program 2, and say no on
everything else. Check it against A. Program 0 returns 1, so A(0) holds and e says yes.
Program 1 returns 0, so A(1) fails and e says no. Program 2 returns 1 exactly when
d(2) is false, and that’s what e says. Every other program gives nothing, so A fails and
e says no. So e is right about every program. Does that break the wall? No, and here’s
the bit that matters: in Nd a flip is representable only if it says 1 exactly where d says
yes, so the flip of e is representable only if e and d agree everywhere, and they disagree
at program 2. The correct decider exists; its flip just isn’t one of the substrate’s own
moves. (That one isn’t a separate theorem in the Coq. It’s three lines and a pencil,
and you just did it.) Undecidable from inside and decided cleanly from outside, at the
same time, about the same property. That’s not a paradox. It’s two different people
asking.

And the one where the recursion theorem is proved from the rules, closed under the
global context, which is why it exists: L, the weak call-by-value lambda calculus that
Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka presented in 2017 as a model of computation in
Coq, and which a group at Saarland has since used as the seed of a whole library
of undecidable problems. The development here builds its own copy of L from the
reduction rules, so the L results below assume nothing from that library. There, L
_recursion_theorem is a theorem with a proof, Rice’s theorem follows (L_ric
e), halting follows (L_halting_undecidable), and the diagonal is reproved in
the shape of the substrate theorem (L_structural_shortcut_undecidable), for
any property of programs that depends only on what they compute and that holds
of one program and fails of another. The statement mentions no shortcut. That’s
the diagonal for a fixed model, closed under the global context, with its hypotheses
in its statement. It isn’t an instance of the generic class (the class wants a run map
that always answers, with a state or with nothing, and L’s evaluation can run forever
without ever answering), so it’s the argument reproved. The generic theorem isn’t
applied here. Both are true; they’re different sentences.

Here’s what that string of words means, because L is the strangest thing in this book
that computes, and the smallest. The lambda calculus is Alonzo Church’s, from the
1930s, and it’s a programming language with one idea in it: functions. A term is one of
three things. A variable. A function, written λ followed by its body, the body saying
what to do with whatever you hand it. Or one term applied to another, written side
by side. Running a program is one move, over and over: when a function meets an
argument, put the argument into the body where the variable was. No numbers, no
memory, no instructions, and in 1937 Turing published a proof that it computes exactly
what his machines compute. “Weak call-by-value” is two house rules about the order
of moves: an argument is run down to a finished function (a value) before it’s put in,
and nothing runs inside a function that hasn’t been handed anything yet. Variables are
written as numbers counting how many λs back they were bound (a trick of Nicolaas



                                           217
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


de Bruijn, who ran the Automath proof-checking project at Eindhoven from 1967 and
comes back in Section 22; it means two variables can never get mixed up by sharing a
name), and a term is closed when every variable in it is bound inside it, so it leans on
nothing outside. Last piece: to hand a program to a program, L needs a way to write
any term as data, the way a program’s source is a string you can pass around. The one
used here is the Scott encoding, named for Dana Scott, a student of Church’s who went
on to build mathematical models of the lambda calculus itself. As far as I can trace it,
the encoding first appeared in lecture notes of his from Berkeley in 1962 that he never
published. All you need about it is that every term t gets one code, written ⌜t⌝, and the
code is itself a closed value. Two tools get built on top of that in the proof: a quoting
term Q that takes the code of a term to the code of that code (a program that prints
its own source needs exactly this move), and a fixed-point combinator, a term that lets a
function call itself, which is how Q works its way through a code of any size.


Definition 13.3 (L, as built here). A term of L is a variable (a de Bruijn number), an
application s t, or an abstraction λs; the values are the abstractions. One step is weak
call-by-value, left to right: (λb) v steps to b with v substituted when v is a value, a
step inside the left part of an application is a step of the application, and so is a step
inside the right part once the left part is a value. A term s evaluates to v when s reaches
v in some number of steps and v is a value; p ≡ q when p and q evaluate to the same
values. Every term t has a code ⌜t⌝, its Scott encoding, which is a closed value. A map
f on terms is L-computable when some closed value s has s ⌜ p⌝ ≡ f ( p) for every p. A
term D decides a property P of terms when, for every p, D ⌜ p⌝ reaches λλ.1 (true) if
P( p) holds and λλ.0 (false) if it fails. P is extensional when p ≡ q and P( p) give P(q).


Theorem 13.3 (Recursion, Rice and halting for L). (1) For every closed value s there is a
closed term t that reaches s ⌜t⌝; hence every L-computable f has a term p with p ≡ f ( p). (2)
Let P be extensional, with P(y) and not P(n) for closed terms y and n. Then no closed term
decides P. (3) No closed term decides halting, the property of evaluating to some value.

Proof. (1) A closed quoting term Q takes ⌜t⌝ to the code of ⌜t⌝; its constructors, re-
cursive program and terminating induction are given in Appendix G. A closed term
mkapp takes two codes to the code of their application. Let A = λx. s (mkapp x ( Q x ))
and t = A ⌜ A⌝. One step gives s (mkapp ⌜ A⌝ ( Q ⌜ A⌝)), and the argument reduces
to ⌜ A ⌜ A⌝⌝ = ⌜t⌝. For the second half, take s computing f ; then t ≡ s ⌜t⌝ ≡ f (t). (2)
Given a closed decider D, the flip λx. D x (λ_. n) (λ_. y) (λz.z) is a closed value; on the
code of p it reaches n when D answers true and y when D answers false. Take its t
from (1). If P(t), then t ≡ n and P(n); if not, t ≡ y and P(t). Both are contradictions.
(3) Halting is extensional; apply (2) with y = λz.z and n = (λx. x x )(λx. x x ), which
steps only to itself and so never reaches a value.

Checked as second_recursion, L_recursion_theorem, L_rice, and L_halti


                                             218
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


ng_undecidable (LRecursion.v), with the quoting term’s specification Q_spec and
the substrate-shaped form L_structural_shortcut_undecidable (no decider
whose flip L can compute says true exactly when the property holds) in the same file.
The file uses only Coq’s standard library.

That’s the wall on paper, on a family built to fit it, and on one outside model, closed
under the global context. The machine built in Part IV fills in this same shape, closed
the same way: on its host machine, the one the universal program runs on, which has
a counter for every whole number, programs are numbers, Kleene’s recursion theorem
is a theorem, and so is Rice’s, and the fixed point can be taken to agree on what the
program computes and also on the ledger and the flag (Section 16.18).

Here’s the picture all of that fills in, lined up against Turing’s, one column per axis.

asks: does it halt?                             asks: does it admit the shortcut?
the wall: no Turing machine decides halting     the wall: no decider whose flip is

Read the table as two uses of one diagonal, each under its own premises. That’s all
it says. The structural wall never uses µ; the µ entry only says what that axis counts.
The nat result is a family indexed by the candidate decider, and L’s results are about
one fixed model and properties that mention no shortcut. Neither hands you a second
fixed undecidable problem, and neither separates Turing degrees: a property can
sit behind the wall from inside and be decided cleanly from outside, as the pencil
argument on Nd showed. And “admits the shortcut” in the right-hand column is the
theorem’s sense, any behavioural property with a yes and a no. “Has a cheaper way
to the same answer” is a second question, and the column has no wall for it.

13.5 How to kill it
Three ways, and I mean them as instructions.

One: produce, for some substrate with a shortcut predicate, a decider whose flip the
substrate can represent and that’s correct on every program. That breaks the generic
proof at a named step, and I’ve named the steps.

Two: for the nat family, produce a d that correctly decides the predicate of the substrate
built from d.

Three: for L, produce a closed term that decides some extensional property holding
of one closed term and failing of another. That breaks L_rice, which rests on the
reduction rules and Coq’s standard library and nothing else.

An outside decider alone doesn’t count against any of the three; the pencil argument
on Nd is why.

                                              219
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


13.6 What this does to the book
It does two things. It keeps me honest: nothing in what follows claims that a system
with a record can check its own shortcuts on autopilot, because that’s a wall, the same
wall, and I showed you the bricks. And it tells you what a record can do, which
is the thing Part III has been about since the counter: it can carry a shortcut with
its receipt, so that the question “was this earned” is answered by an event you can
point at. No decider has to exist for that, which is lucky, because on a system with a
recursion theorem no inside one can. The diagonal says such a system can’t automate
the judgement from inside, for any behavioural property with a yes and a no. The
latch says you can record the commitment. Those are different jobs, and a record does
the second.

The diagonal has a famous cousin that seems like it ought to bite a record too, so let me
walk right up to it. Gödel’s second theorem says a consistent system strong enough
for arithmetic can’t prove its own consistency, and Martin Löb, a logician answering
another logician’s question, sharpened that in 1955: if such a system proves “if this is
provable, it’s true,” it already proves the thing itself. So can a record vouch for itself,
and does Löb stop it? My first guess was that Löb stops it, since a record looked like
a system talking about itself. Here’s where I landed instead, and mostly it’s a relief.
Hold two things side by side: “there’s a receipt for this somewhere,” and the receipt in
your hand. Löb’s theorem is about provability, the bare claim that some proof exists, the
receipt somewhere. A record of the kind this book keeps is a different animal: an event,
a check of some claim that passed, a commitment to it, and a certificate, at a definite
step of the run. The receipt in your hand. It doesn’t say which claim or which step,
as the two runs in Section 16.18 show; it says the event happened. Sergei Artemov,
the logician from the opening chapter, drew exactly that line in 2001, between implicit
provability (“there is a proof”) and explicit evidence (“this is a proof”). As I read him,
for explicit evidence the reflection step “if this is a proof of F, then F” is harmless,
while for the bare “there is a proof” it’s what Gödel and Löb forbid. Why, in my
words: a receipt in your hand you can look at, and a receipt somewhere you take on
the system’s own word. A record sits on the explicit side.

Push on that and it gives, because a receipt is only as good as whoever wrote it. Its
trust rests on the checker meaning what it says, and that gets settled once, from outside
the machine. I don’t think it can be moved inside, and Gödel’s second theorem is my
reason. The theorem says a consistent system strong enough for arithmetic can’t prove
its own consistency, and a checker vouching for itself would be doing something close
to that. That last step is my reading. The theorem itself stops at consistency. So I
didn’t get rid of the receipt somewhere. I moved it out of the machine and handed it
to whoever reads the record. Try to move that proof inside the system, so it can certify
its own checker or a successor’s, and you hit exactly the wall Eliezer Yudkowsky and
Marcello Herreshoff named the Löbian obstacle in 2013, writing about agents that
want to trust their own rewrites. As I understand their draft report, they came at it


                                           220
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


from the far side, an agent wanting to trust a successor’s proofs the way it trusts its
own. Same arrow, pointed forward, same wall.

One more thing falls out of the same picture, and it’s a short argument with no checked
theorem behind it, so take it at that weight. Can a record rest on itself, the way the
sentence “this sentence is certified” would like to? Not if it’s earned and permanent.
The check that a certificate stands on happened while the record was still down,
because the record goes up only after that check passes, and once up it never comes
back down. So no claim whose truth needs the record already up can be the claim a
certificate stands on. Saul Kripke’s 1975 theory of truth calls a sentence like that, one
that only ever leans on itself, ungrounded, and earned records are grounded in his
sense: every one bottoms out in a check that didn’t lean on it. Caspar Oesterheld’s
2019 work on programs that cooperate by simulating each other needed a grounding
step of the same kind to stop an infinite regress. I haven’t checked this in Coq, and
I’m not claiming more than the paragraph says.

One last distinction, because the two are easy to conflate and conflating them is the
easiest way to misread this book. There’s a second wall, nothing to do with the diagonal.
It’s Section 7’s kind of wall, a window with a colliding pair in it. Two states that differ
in their certification reading can look identical through a window that doesn’t show
that reading, the stamp inside the closed drawer and the drawer opened and shut,
and then no function of the window recovers the reading (Theorem 7.1: a decoder
has to give one answer on everything the window lumps together). That’s missing
information. Nothing about it is undecidable; it holds for finite things with nothing
to compute; and it sits beside Rice. None of Rice is underneath it. The property the
diagonal uses (any behavioural property of programs with a yes and a no) is a different
kind of thing from the reading the window hides, and nothing here says the two are
the same. Two walls, two axes. The diagonal is about what no inside procedure can
decide. The window is about what no outside observer can see. I’ll need both, and I’ll
try not to call one by the other’s name again. The machine I build later has a colliding
pair of exactly that kind (Theorem 16.14).

14 Five small models
A toll, a counter, two kinds of wall and a latch, and every one of them shown on paper,
on cups and cards and dice I made up. I’ve been building a toy and claiming it’s the
smallest version of something people actually do. Time to go and look at what people
actually do. I picked five systems that keep records other people rely on, with real
money or real security behind them, and asked each the one question this book is
about: is there a price on the moment the record is written? Not on the work around it. On
the write. I’ll tell you the answer first, because it’s a single sentence and it surprised
me: of the five specifications, read through the transcriptions I made of them, only one
prices the write, and that one has a leak at exactly the place Section 6 said a counter
leaks, where it goes down.


                                           221
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Three things are easy to blur in a section like this, so I’ll name them now and keep
them apart all the way through. There’s the real specification: the document real money
and real security run on. There’s my transcription: one mechanism copied out of that
document into Coq, small enough to check. And for some of the five there’s a wrapper:
a tiny abstract model that takes one premise as given and says what follows from it.
A claim proved at one level isn’t a claim at the level above it. Near the end I’ll walk
one system, gas, through all three, so you can see exactly where each claim stops.

What I built for each is a fragment: a small Coq model of the one mechanism I’m
asking about, transcribed from the system’s own specification where there was one,
and nothing more. Not the system. I’ll say for each one what the fragment is and what
it isn’t, because “Ethereum has been formalised” is the kind of sentence that gets a
book thrown across a room, and rightly.

14.1 Proof-of-stake finality: the price is on going back
Ethereum and chains like it decide which blocks are final by having validators, people
who’ve locked up money (their stake), vote on checkpoints: blocks picked out at
regular numbered rounds called epochs. A vote isn’t for one checkpoint. It’s a link from
a checkpoint the validator already trusts, the source, to a later one, the target, and
every chain starts from one first block, its genesis, which counts as trusted from the
start. In the design Vitalik Buterin and Virgil Griffith published in 2017, called Casper,
a checkpoint is justified when validators holding two thirds of the stake vote a link to
it from a justified source, and finalized when it is justified and a two-thirds link runs
from it to its direct child. The record is “this checkpoint is final.”

What’s priced? Two rules: don’t vote for two different targets in the same epoch, and
don’t cast a vote whose span, source to target, surrounds the span of another of your
votes. Break either and your deposit can be destroyed, which is called slashing. The
theorem they prove, called accountable safety, says that if two conflicting checkpoints
are ever both finalized, at least a third of the stake broke a rule and can be slashed.
So the price is on reversal, on making the record contradict itself. The write itself,
finalizing, is free: honest validators finalize all day and nobody loses anything.

Do it with three validators. Let A and B vote one branch, B and C vote a competing
branch. Each pair is two of three. Both branches finalize. Now read the rule: B cast
two different votes with the same target epoch. B is the third that gets slashed; A
and C are clean. That’s what a fork costs and who pays, and the checked work has
exactly this instance (casper_fork_exists, casper_fork_slashable), so the
theorem’s premise isn’t vacuous: forks of that kind can be built, and the theorem fires
on them.

The fragment: a transcription of a published Coq proof of Casper’s accountable safety
(the casper-proofs development from Runtime Verification and the University of Texas
at Austin, itself based on Yoichi Hirai’s proof in Isabelle, another proof checker; proofs
redone on the standard library), with validator sets as predicates and quorum inter-

                                           222
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


section as a premise. A quorum is a set of validators big enough to act, here two thirds
of the stake, and quorum intersection is the arithmetic of the three-validator example:
two thirds plus two thirds is four thirds, so any two quorums share at least a third.
The fragment takes the overlap as given. It doesn’t do that arithmetic. No deposits,
no rewards, no fork choice (the rule for picking a branch to build on), no connection
to anything else in this book. accountable_safety: a finalization fork implies that
a set of validators the size of that overlap, at least a third of the stake, is slashed. And
finalization_without_slashing: a one-validator chain finalizes and nobody’s
slashed, which is the “write is free” sentence in a degenerate setting, and only there.

Here’s the fragment, small enough to read in one sitting. Every name below is from
the transcription.


Definition 14.1 (Casper setting and votes). A setting has a type of validators, a type
of block hashes with a parent relation and a genesis hash, and two classes of validator
sets, the “two-thirds” sets Q1 and the “one-third” sets Q2 . It carries two premises:
quorum intersection, for any two sets in Q1 some set in Q2 lies inside both; and at most
one parent per hash. A state says, for each validator, target hash h, target epoch t and
source epoch u, whether that validator voted the link (h, t, u). A link from p at epoch
u to h at epoch t is justified by q when q ∈ Q1 , every member of q voted (h, t, u), h is
the (t − u)-th descendant of p, and t > u. Genesis is justified at epoch 0, and a block
reached from a justified block by a justified link is justified. Block h is finalized at epoch
v with child c when c is a child of h, h is justified at v, and the link from h at v to c at
v + 1 is justified. A finalization fork is two finalized blocks h1 ̸= h2 , neither an ancestor
of the other. A validator is slashed when it voted two different targets with the same
target epoch (a double vote), or voted links (h1 , t1 , u1 ) and (h2 , t2 , u2 ) with t1 > t2 and
u2 > u1 (a surround vote). The state is quorum-slashed when some set in Q2 consists of
slashed validators.


Theorem 14.1 (Accountable safety). In every setting (so under quorum intersection and at
most one parent), every state with a finalization fork is quorum-slashed.

Proof. Let the fork be h1 finalized at v1 and h2 at v2 . If v1 = v2 , the two links into epoch
v1 + 1 are each voted by a set in Q1 ; quorum intersection gives a set in Q2 that voted
both; their targets differ, since equal children would give h1 and h2 the same child and
so, by at most one parent, h1 = h2 . That set double-voted. If v1 ̸= v2 , say v1 < v2 , walk
down the chain of justified links that justifies h2 , by strong induction on the epoch
gap. Every block on that chain is an ancestor of h2 , so none descends from h1 . Some
link in the chain starts at or below v1 and lands above v1 . If it lands at v1 + 1, it and
the finalization link of h1 have distinct targets at that epoch, and the intersection set
double-voted. If it starts at v1 , its source is a justified block at v1 other than h1 , and
the links that justified those two blocks give a double vote the same way. Otherwise it
starts below v1 and lands above v1 + 1, so it surrounds the finalization link of h1 , and

                                              223
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


the intersection set made a surround vote.

Checked as accountable_safety (CasperFFG.v), a transcription of the casper-
proofs Core/AccountableSafety file at a pinned commit with proofs redone on the
standard library; validator sets are predicates, and both premises are fields of the
setting record, so they are hypotheses of every theorem. The record reading is confl
icting_records_are_priced (CasperRecordReading.v).


Theorem 14.2 (The premise can hold, and the write is free). (1) In the three-validator
setting where each validator has stake 1, Q1 is the sets of stake at least two thirds and Q2 the
sets of at least one third, the state where A and B vote one branch and B and C the other has
a finalization fork; B is slashed, A and C are not, and { B} is in Q2 . (2) In the one-validator
chain setting, one vote finalizes genesis and no validator is slashed.

Proof. Both are computations on fixed finite data. In (1) B voted two different targets at
epoch 1, which is the double vote; A’s and C’s votes are one link at epoch 1 from source
0 and one at epoch 2 from source 1, which neither double-vote nor surround.

Checked as casper_fork_exists and casper_fork_slashable (CasperFork-
Witness.v), and finalization_without_slashing (CasperRecordReading.v).

One thing that means for the record itself: finality is revocable at a price, the price is
named, and a final block can hold a false statement.

And the obvious next question: is the 2017 design what Ethereum actually runs? Partly,
and the paper’s own title is the clue. It’s called Casper the Friendly Finality Gadget, and
its first sentence says it’s a finality system that overlays a chain still choosing its blocks
by proof of work. A gadget, bolted on top. In 2020 a larger group, Buterin among
them, wrote up Gasper, which joins Casper’s finality to a fork-choice rule called LMD
GHOST, and on 15 September 2022, in the switch people called the Merge, Ethereum
stopped choosing blocks by proof of work at all and went over to proof of stake. So
the checkpoints and the two slashing rules above are one part of a system that holds
real money today, and the transcription is of that part’s safety proof as the 2017 design
states it. Everything between the two, the fork choice and the rest of the running
protocol, is the gap between my transcription and the running system, which I walk
through near the end of this section with a photocopied recipe and a kitchen. Does
any of that move the price? No. Finalizing is still free for an honest validator. What
costs is contradicting yourself.

14.2 Gas: the one that prices the write
Every operation on Ethereum costs gas, paid in ether by whoever sent the transaction.
The yellow paper, Ethereum’s formal specification, gives the reason in one line: every
computation is fee-bearing so the network can’t be abused and halting questions are
sidestepped. The record I care about is a nonzero slot in the shared storage, which

                                              224
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


every full node in the world (every computer keeping its own complete copy of the
chain) has to keep forever.

And here it is: writing a fresh storage slot from zero to nonzero costs twenty thousand
gas, by the table in the paper’s appendix, plus twenty-one hundred for touching a cold
slot, one the transaction hasn’t touched yet (after the first touch it’s warm). As I read it,
the point is to discourage storage growth, since storage grows every node’s database.
That’s a price on the write, at the moment of the write, and it’s the only one in the five.

Where does a number like twenty-one hundred come from? Somebody picked it,
so the obvious next question is who, and why, and the answer has a date on it. In
September 2016, just as Ethereum’s developers were gathering in Shanghai for Dev-
con 2, their developer conference (the third one, since they started counting at zero),
attackers started filling blocks with an operation that was cheap in gas and expensive
in fact: it sent every node off to read data from its disk, and nodes fell behind the chain.
The first repair, a fork that October called Tangerine Whistle, raised the prices of the
operations the attack had leaned on. The cold-slot charge came later, in a proposal by
Vitalik Buterin and Martin Swende called EIP-2929, switched on in the Berlin upgrade
of April 2021, and the motivation it gives is still those 2016 attacks. So twenty-one hun-
dred isn’t a law of nature or a measurement of anything deep. It’s a scar: a price set
after somebody found the place where the old price was wrong. That doesn’t change
the argument; the write is still priced at the moment of the write. It does change how
I read the rest of that table: some of its numbers, at least, are somebody’s answer to
“what did this cost last time,” which is a record of a different kind.

Now the leak, and it’s Section 6’s leak. Set a slot and then clear it in the same transaction
and you get a refund. Count it through: first write twenty-two thousand one hundred;
clearing it costs a hundred and credits a refund of nineteen thousand nine hundred;
net, twenty-three hundred. That’s revoked_write_nearly_free, and persiste
nt_write_priced is the other half: leave it set and you pay at least twenty thousand.
The write is priced. The revoked write nearly isn’t. But I have to add what the fragment
leaves out, because twenty-three hundred on its own misleads: the realized refund
is capped at one fifth of the gas the whole transaction used (that’s the 2021 change
from Section 6, the one that ended the refund-hoarding token’s advantage). So a real
set-then-clear pays a lot more than twenty-three hundred. How much more? The
cap is a fifth of everything the transaction used, and that includes the twenty-one
thousand every transaction pays just for existing. Take a transaction that does nothing
but set and clear the slot: it uses 43,200 gas, so the cap is 8,640, so it pays 34,560, which
is 13,560 on top of the base. (Look at the slot alone and forget the base, which the rule
doesn’t do, and you’d get 17,760.) Either way it’s far above twenty-three hundred.
The counter-level net is twenty-three hundred. The bill is not.

Here’s the arithmetic the way the specification has it, so you can redo it with a pencil.




                                            225
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


Definition 14.2 (One slot in one transaction). A slot run records the slot’s value at
the start of the transaction (original), its current value, whether it has been touched
(warm), the gas charged so far, and the refund counter. A store of a new value charges
2100 if the slot is cold, plus 20000 if the slot still holds its original value, the new value
differs, and the original is 0 (2900 if the original is nonzero), and otherwise 100. It
adjusts the refund counter by the specification’s rules; in particular, when the new
value equals the original value 0, the refund grows by 20000 − 100 = 19900. The run
starts fresh: original and current 0, cold, gas and refund 0. The net charge is gas minus
refund.


Theorem 14.3 (Pricing the persistent write and the revoked one). (1) For every list of
stores from a fresh slot, if the slot ends nonzero then the net charge is at least 20000. (2) Storing
1 then 0 leaves the slot at 0 with net charge 2300; storing 1 alone has net charge 22100.

Proof. (1) By induction on the list, with the invariant: while the original value is 0, the
net charge is at least 0 when the current value is 0 and at least 20000 when it is not.
Each store keeps it, which is a finite case split on whether the slot is warm and which
of the original, current and new values are equal. A fresh slot satisfies it. (2) Direct
computation: 2100 + 20000 = 22100 for the first store, 100 for the second, refund 19900,
and 22200 − 19900 = 2300.

Checked as persistent_write_priced and revoked_write_nearly_free
(EVMStorageGas.v), transcribed from the execution specification’s storage instruction
and gas table at a pinned commit. The end-of-transaction refund cap of one fifth is not
in the fragment.

The fragment: one slot, one transaction, the gas and refund arithmetic transcribed
from the Ethereum execution specification at a named commit. No stack, no call
context, no other slots, and no refund cap; the file says so.

Then the wrapper, which is a different kind of object, and the walk near the end is
about exactly that difference. It’s a gas schedule in the abstract: any states, any steps, a
cost per step, a yes/no commitment flag, and a charge predicate saying which steps
get billed. It formalises no EVM (the Ethereum virtual machine) at all. It is Section 7’s
result with the whole-run ceiling, the one that pins the amount as well as which
steps pay, under a new name, and the file says that too. Its two halves are worth
reading separately. Leave one committing step unbilled, and a one-step run commits
for nothing (undercharged_opcode_admits_free_commitment), so the floor
fails outright; one missed commit is enough. Bill one step that doesn’t commit, and
the schedule charges more than the number of commits on that one-step run (overc
harge_breaks_exactness), so the ceiling fails. And the class isn’t empty: in any
system, the bill that charges one exactly on a step that raises the flag and nothing on
any other meets both halves (Section 7’s step price).



                                                226
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


And the wrapper itself, which is the cleanest thing in this section and has the least
Ethereum in it.


Definition 14.3 (A gas schedule). A gas schedule has states, instructions, a step, a cost
c(s, i ) ∈ N that may depend on the state, a Boolean commitment flag on states, and
a Boolean charge predicate χ(s, i ), with two premises: a charged step costs at least 1,
and an uncharged step costs 0. A step commits when it takes the flag from false to true.
For a run t from s, let c(t) be its total cost and n(t) its number of committing steps.
The schedule has the floor when c(t) ≥ n(t) for every run, and no overcharge when
c(t) ≤ n(t) for every run. It has unit pricing when c(s, i ) = 1 if χ(s, i ) and 0 otherwise.


Theorem 14.4 (Gas schedule exactness). For every gas schedule: it has the floor and no
overcharge if and only if χ(s, i ) holds exactly when the step from s by i commits, and it has
unit pricing. Moreover, (1) if some committing step from an uncommitted state is uncharged,
that one-step run costs 0 and the schedule fails the floor; (2) if some charged step does not
commit, the schedule overcharges.

Proof. The equivalence is Section 7’s characterization with the whole-run ceiling, un-
der another name. From right to left, each step’s cost is 1 on a committing step and 0
otherwise, so a run’s cost counts its commitments. From left to right, apply the floor
and no overcharge to one-step runs: a committing step must cost at least 1, so it is
charged; a charged step costs at least 1 and may not exceed its commitment count, so
it commits and costs exactly 1. Parts (1) and (2) are those one-step runs read the other
way.

Checked as gas_schedule_exactness, which proves both directions, undercha
rged_opcode_admits_free_commitment, undercharged_opcode_breaks_
certification_floor and overcharge_breaks_exactness (GasMetering.v);
gas_schedule_exactness is exact_commitment_pricing_characterizat
ion (CommitmentPredicateAdequacy.v) carried over unchanged.

Gas prices storage growth and computation. It says nothing about whether what’s
stored is true.

14.3 Attestation: hash chains, and a quote about the past
A trusted platform module, the small chip on most laptop motherboards, keeps a
handful of registers that can only be extended: the new value is a hash of the old value
together with a digest (a short hash) of whatever software just loaded. You can’t set
them; you can only fold more in. A quote is the chip signing those register values
together with a number the asker chose, a nonce, so the asker knows the quote is fresh.
Intel’s SGX does the equivalent for an enclave, a walled-off region a program runs in.
The record is the extended register.



                                             227
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


What’s priced? Nothing in the specification. Reversal isn’t expensive. It’s infeasible:
you’d have to invert a hash or steal a key. That’s the difference between a price and
a wall, and it’s easy to blur. A price can come in three kinds. It can be economic, a
fee or a deposit the protocol takes (Casper and gas are here). It can be cryptographic,
a reversal made infeasible by a hardness assumption, which makes it a wall with no
exact price on it (attestation and transparency are here). Or it can be physical, energy
spent, which none of these five specifications touches. And the record’s permanence
is only as long as the register lives: a platform’s registers are cleared when it resets, so
the permanence is per boot.

Why the registers, then, when something that lasts would make a better record? Be-
cause the quote is what a remote asker reads, and the registers are what it signs. The
same chip has longer-lived records, and they’re closer to the cup than anything else
in this section. Version 2.0 of its specification has storage slots of a kind it calls a bit
field, changed only by a command that ORs new bits into the old value: a bit can be
set and never cleared, which is r ∨ h from Section 10, on a laptop motherboard. It has
counters that can only be incremented, and a counter’s first increment starts it at the
largest value any counter on that chip has ever held, so deleting one and making a new
one can’t wind it back. And those slots are rationed. Bryan Parno and his coauthors,
building a system called Memoir in 2011, noted that the specification of the day only
required a counter to be able to tick once every five seconds, and that the chip’s storage
was expected to survive about a hundred thousand writes in its whole life, so writing
once a second would wear it out in under twenty-eight hours. Memoir writes to it
twice per boot. Permanent, finite and rationed: the honest record has a budget, the
way Theorem 10.10’s chain of k-bit words can only climb k times. Phones and small
controllers go one floor further down, to fuses like the PROMs in Section 10: a version
number kept as a row of fuses, one more blown at each security update, and boot code
that refuses anything older. An industry guide on it, Rob Smart’s 2021 explainer for
PSA Certified, a security certification scheme for chips and devices, tells designers to
make sure there are enough fuse bits to last the number of updates expected over the
device’s lifetime, which is part (5) of that same theorem, written as a design rule.

What all of this is for is rollback. Memoir’s example is a password checker restored
to an old saved state to undo a user’s password change, and in 2017 a system called
ROTE did the same job for Intel’s enclaves by having several machines vouch for each
other’s counters, with the stated result that the only way left to break it is to reset
every one of them to its start. In 2016 Raoul Strackx and Frank Piessens’s Ariadne
got the cost of that job down to flipping a single bit of non-volatile memory per state
update, which they call the theoretical lower limit. Notice who the attacker is in every
one of these: whoever gets to put an old state back. A bad program doesn’t come into
it. A record kept by the step can’t see that attacker, which is why every guarantee in
Part IV about a record’s earned history is stated from a clean start, and a restored start
is outside all of them. The per-step toll still holds after a restore. It just can’t tell you



                                            228
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


what happened before it.

Replicated services put the same kind of record somewhere else: inside each replica,
where a replica that’s been taken over still can’t make it say two different things.
Byung-Gon Chun and coauthors’ attested append-only memory (A2M, 2007) is a log
a replica can only add to; Dave Levin and coauthors’ TrInc (2009) shrinks that to
a trusted counter; MinBFT (Giuliana Veronese and coauthors, 2013) uses a trusted
counter to reach agreement with 2 f + 1 replicas when f of them can lie, where the
usual count is 3 f + 1; and Damysus (Jérémie Decouchant, David Kozhaya, Vincent
Rahli and Jiangshan Yu, 2022) has a small trusted service, the Checker, that keeps a
monotonic counter of where the protocol is. Allen Clement, Flavio Junqueira, Aniket
Kate and Rodrigo Rodrigues (2012) worked out, with proofs, what such a record buys,
and as I read their result it’s a good warning for this book. On its own, stopping a
replica from saying two different things doesn’t lower the 3 f + 1 bound in an asyn-
chronous network at all. Add signatures that a third party can check, and it turns
any protocol that survives crashes into one that survives liars, with no extra replicas.
The way I read it, a record helps the others only as far as they can check what it says,
which is Section 7’s point from the other side.

There’s a fourth kind under those three, and it’s the one that always pays. It’s the
logical kind: Section 4’s room of chairs applies to any of these records. On a finite state
space, a step that switches a record on somewhere, and never switches it off anywhere,
forgets something. That needs no premise about money, keys or heat. The economic,
cryptographic and physical payments each need a premise of their own about their
kind (a fee rule, a hardness assumption, Landauer’s principle), and they hold exactly
where that premise holds.


Theorem 14.5 (The logical level always pays). For any states S, instructions I, step and
Boolean reading: if a duplicate-free list names every state, the instruction i never turns the
reading from on to off, and i turns it on at some state s, then the step by i is not injective.


Checked as permanent_write_has_logical_payment (PricingPhysicsAudit.v),
from permanent_at_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentRecordPricing.v); the
proof is Theorem 4.1 with permanence required only of the one instruction i.

What the quote can do is say what was measured. It can’t say the measured code is
correct, and it can’t say anything about runtime state that was never folded in. A
correctly measured buggy program attests beautifully. The fragment proves that exact
limit: one register, a hash about which nothing is assumed, a quote as a pair, and no
function of the quote decides a runtime flag the quote ignores (quote_cannot_atte
st_unmeasured_state), which is Section 7’s cube again. And a companion shows
that a sign-and-verify interface alone gives no authenticity (a scheme where verify
always says yes passes the interface), so a cryptographic premise has to be added; the



                                             229
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


fragment doesn’t model signatures, formats, or a freshness check (the nonce is just a
field the verifier fixes).

The same limit, turned outward, is the honest edge of the opening chapter’s four
conditions. Every one of them is about a thing the machine holds: same property,
same thing, same edition, honest check. For a claim about the world (the oven is hot,
the parcel arrived) there’s no edition the machine controls. Whatever reads the world
is a window onto it, and “nothing changed between the check and the commit” stops
being something a step can enforce and becomes a premise about the sensor. So a
record can establish claims about the machine’s own state, and claims about the world
only through named premises about whatever measured them. A correctly recorded
sensor reading certifies the sensor.


Definition 14.4 (Platform and quote). Fix any functions H : N × N → N (the extend
hash) and δ : N → N (the digest); nothing is assumed about either. A platform is a
measurement log (a list of numbers) and a Boolean runtime flag. Its register is the log
folded from 0 by H. The quote with nonce n is the pair (δ(register), n).


Theorem 14.6 (The quote cannot attest unmeasured state). For every nonce n there is no
function D from quotes to Booleans with D (quoten ( P)) = flag( P) for every platform P.

Proof. Take two platforms with the empty log, one flagged true and one false. Their
quotes are equal, since the quote never reads the flag, so D would have to return both
values on one input.

Checked as quote_cannot_attest_unmeasured_state (TPMQuoteGap.v). In
the same file, quote_decides_measured_claims says any Boolean claim about
the retained digest can be read off the quote. The companion is tpm_interface_a
uthenticity_refuted (TPMQuoteAuthenticity.v): a scheme whose verify always
says yes satisfies the sign-and-verify interface while accepting a signature no key
produced.

14.4 Certificate transparency: visible, unpriced
The certificates that make your browser show a padlock are issued by hundreds of
authorities, and a bad or compromised one can issue a certificate for a domain it
shouldn’t. Certificate Transparency makes authorities submit every certificate to pub-
lic append-only logs built as Merkle trees, so that anyone can check that a certificate
was logged and that the log never rewrote its past. It was specified in RFC 6962 in
2013 and revised as RFC 9162 in 2021. I went looking for which one the running
logs follow, and it’s still 6962: Mozilla’s reference for web developers says browser
implementations are based on 6962, and as late as November 2025 Chrome’s team was
only proposing to drop its rule that every certificate carry a timestamp from at least
one 6962 log. The fragment I transcribe is 9162’s. A Merkle tree is Section 3’s hash


                                          230
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


chain folded into a tree: hash each certificate (those are the leaves), hash the leaf hashes
in pairs, hash those in pairs, and so on up to one root hash. To prove one leaf is in, the
log hands you only the few hashes sitting beside the climb from that leaf to the root,
the path, and you redo the climb yourself. A second check, consistency, shows that a
bigger tree is a smaller one with leaves added on the end and nothing rewritten. The
record is a leaf in the tree.

Priced? Nothing. The RFC says it in its first section: logs let interested parties detect
misissuance afterward. They don’t prevent it. And a log that shows different views to
different people (a split view) can defeat the auditing, so logs are still trusted parties.
What it buys is visibility.

Which raises the obvious question: if nothing’s priced, why does any authority bother
logging? Nothing in the RFC makes it. The answer is a browser. Chrome’s team set
the rule, enforced from Chrome 68 in July 2018, that every certificate issued after 30
April 2018 had to meet its transparency policy, and a publicly trusted certificate that
doesn’t is simply not trusted by Chrome: the visitor gets a full-page warning in front
of the site. So there is a price after all. It isn’t anywhere in the specification. It lives
in one vendor’s browser, and it’s the price of being shown to that browser’s users at
all. Is that the bottom? Not quite, because it means the strongest lever on this record
is a policy one company can change, which is a fact about who holds the stamp. The
tree has nothing to do with it. That policy changes nothing in the table at the end of
this section, which asks what each specification prices. But it’s worth keeping two
sentences apart: “the specification prices nothing” and “nothing is priced.”

Do the inclusion proof by hand, because it’s the most satisfying ten minutes in this
section. Take the RFC’s own seven-leaf example tree and verify that leaf d3 is in it
from the path the log hands you: three hashes and a rule about which side to hash
on, depending on whether your position is odd. Three hashing steps and you land
on the root. The checked work runs the RFC’s own examples (rfc9162_example
_inclusion_d3 and its siblings, including the awkward lone-leaf case) through a
transcription of the RFC’s verifier control flow with a symbolic hash. Verifier logic
only: no signatures, no gossip (auditors comparing the views they were shown), no
misbehaving log.


Definition 14.5 (Inclusion check, RFC 9162 section 2.1.3.2). Given a leaf index m, a tree
size N, a leaf hash, a root hash and a path, the check rejects unless m < N. Otherwise
it walks the path from the leaf with two counters starting at m and N − 1, hashing each
path element on the left or the right according to the counters as the RFC specifies and
halving the counters, and accepts when the second counter ends at 0 and the result
equals the root. A symbolic hash makes a leaf hash ℓ( x ) and a node hash ν( a, b) free
constructors, so two hashes are equal only when they are built the same way.




                                            231
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


Theorem 14.7 (The RFC’s own examples pass). With the symbolic hash, in the RFC’s
seven-leaf tree with leaves d0 , . . . , d6 (writing dk also for its leaf hash ℓ(dk )), the inclusion
check accepts leaf 3 with path [d2 , ν(d0 , d1 ), ν(ν(d4 , d5 ), d6 )], and likewise leaves 0, 4 and 6
with their paths; the consistency check from size 4 to size 7 accepts. For every input with
m = N, the inclusion check rejects.

Proof. The examples are evaluation of the transcribed functions on constructor terms.
The boundary case is the first test, m < N, failing.

Checked as rfc9162_example_inclusion_d3, its siblings rfc9162_example_
inclusion_d0, rfc9162_example_inclusion_d4 and rfc9162_example_in
clusion_d6, rfc9162_example_consistency_4_7, and rfc9162_inclusio
n_boundary_safe (RFC9162Merkle.v). The append-only history is list append, and
ct_extension_preserves_entries says appending keeps every old entry.

14.5 Proof-carrying code: no price, no permanence
Necula’s idea from Section 8: ship untrusted code with a proof that it obeys the host’s
policy; the host computes what would need to be true and checks the proof with a
small checker. The record is the checked proof, and it’s held only for the moment of
loading. Priced? No. Checking is cheap by design, which is the whole point, and
the producer paid to build the proof off the host. Permanent? No; nothing’s written.
The fragment is a three-instruction memory-bounds language with the policy “every
address is below the limit”: the checker accepts exactly when the condition holds, and
a certificate implies the condition. One example is checked on top of that: a program
that reads address two under a limit of two is rejected. Not the paper’s real case study,
and no bridge to anything else in this book. And its limit: a program that writes
garbage to address zero passes if zero is below the limit. The proof is of the stated
policy and nothing else.

And what was the paper’s real case study, the one my fragment isn’t? Network packet
filters: the little programs an operating system runs on incoming network traffic to
decide which program gets to see which packet. They run inside the kernel, the most
trusted part of the system, and they have to be fast, so they’re exactly the code you’d
most like to take from a stranger and least like to trust. In the 1996 paper that first
set out the idea, Necula and Peter Lee wrote several filters by hand in the assembly
language of a DEC Alpha, shipped each with its proof, and reported a one-time cost
of 1 to 3 milliseconds to check the proof, after which the filter ran with no checks at
all. That’s “checking is cheap by design” with a number on it. It changes nothing
about my fragment, which still isn’t that case study, and it doesn’t add a price: the
milliseconds are the checker’s work, and nothing is being written down for them to
be a toll on.


Definition 14.6 (The bounds fragment). Instructions are READ a, WRITE a v, and


                                                 232
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


HALT. For a memory limit L, the policy allows READ a and WRITE a v when a < L,
and always allows HALT. The verification condition of a program is that the policy
allows every instruction in it. A certificate is a list of per-instruction policy facts, one
for each instruction in order. The checker tests the policy on each instruction and
returns the conjunction.


Theorem 14.8 (The checker is the verification condition). For every limit L and program
P: the checker accepts P exactly when the verification condition holds; any certificate for P
gives the verification condition; and with L = 2 the checker rejects READ 2 followed by HALT.

Proof. The first two are induction on the program and on the certificate, one instruction
at a time. The third is a computation: 2 < 2 fails.

Checked as pcc_checker_accepts_iff_vc, pcc_certificate_implies_vc,
and pcc_unsafe_program_rejected (NeculaPCC.v, definitions in NeculaPCC-
Target.v).

14.6 One example, three levels
Before I lay all five side by side, let me walk one of them up and down the three levels
from the start of the section, because every claim in here lives at exactly one level and
it’s easy to let a claim slide up a floor without noticing. Gas, since it’s the one place all
three line up. Think of a restaurant’s real recipe, my photocopy of one page of it, and
a cookbook chapter on what any recipe has to contain. I can check my photocopy line
by line. That tells you nothing about what the kitchen cooks tonight.

The real specification. Ethereum’s execution specification says, in a document that
runs real money, what a storage write costs, what clearing it refunds, and how the
refund is capped at the end of the transaction. None of what I checked is at this
level. What the network actually charges is whatever the clients people run actually
compute, and the evidence for that is the clients and the chain. This book has none of
it.

The transcription. I copied one mechanism out of that document, one slot in one
transaction, gas and refund arithmetic only, at a named commit (Definition 14.2, Theo-
rem 14.3). What the result tells you: if the storage rule is what I copied, then leaving
a fresh slot set costs at least twenty thousand, and set-then-clear nets twenty-three
hundred at the counter. What it can’t tell you: anything about the refund cap (not
copied, which is why the bill came out so different from the counter earlier), the stack,
calls, other slots, or whether any client implements the rule as written. The boundary
of the claim is the edge of the copy.

The wrapper. The gas schedule of Definition 14.3 isn’t Ethereum. It’s any system
with steps, a cost per step and a yes/no commitment flag, plus one thing stipulated:
a charge predicate, with the premise that a charged step costs at least one and an


                                            233
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


uncharged one costs nothing. That premise is the whole of what the wrapper adds,
and it’s added by hand; no specification supplies it. Given it, the theorem says the bill
is exact, never letting a commit go free and never billing a non-commit, exactly when
the charge predicate is the commit predicate at unit price. What that tells you is what
exact pricing would have to look like, in any system. It doesn’t say Ethereum meets
it, and Ethereum doesn’t: real gas bills computation that commits nothing, which the
transcription shows in numbers. So the wrapper prices a definition, the transcription
prices a copied rule, and neither prices the chain.

The other four sit on the same three levels, and only one more wrapper is spelled
out in this section. Casper’s transcription is the accountable-safety proof above; its
wrapper is a small gadget with the stake at risk handed in. A finalize step that risks
nothing turns the record on for free, which breaks Section 3’s toll (the file calls that
free forgery), and one that risks at least one unit has a floor (nothing_at_stake_is
_free_forgery, slashing_finality_floor, PoSFinality.v). It records exposure
to loss (no collateral is destroyed in it), has no Casper checkpoints in it at all, and is
priced by stipulation, the same way the gas wrapper is. Attestation, transparency and
proof-carrying code have transcriptions that prove what their verifiers do and no price
theorem, because their specifications carry no price. Their wrappers, which I don’t
spell out here, are Section 7’s verifier argument told in each system’s vocabulary, with
a colliding pair behind each one, and that argument is all they carry here.

How to knock down the four claims with the most weight on them, since the book’s
rule is that every claim gets a way to break it. For the gas transcription: a list of stores
from a fresh slot that ends nonzero with net charge under twenty thousand. For the
gas wrapper: a schedule that never lets a commit go free and never bills a non-commit,
whose charge predicate still differs from the commit predicate at some step. For the
finality gadget: a finalizing trace from unfinalized to finalized whose charged stake is
zero while the gadget claims a floor. For the attestation fragment: a verifier reading
only the quote’s fields that decides a runtime flag the quote ignores.

Each row proves what its own transcription says. Reading a row as a claim about a
