The first three are Minsky’s machine, plus a HALT so a program can say it’s done.
The last three are the record’s. Read them as a chain: you can only certify with a
commitment in the channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only
way into the table is a check that passed. Three links, and each one costs.

One of what? One unit of µ, the same unit as Section 3’s toll. Why one? Why would
ten be worse? Because one is the smallest positive whole number, which is honestly
the whole defence, and Section 4 is the section where I tried to do better than that for
the flag. That argument doesn’t reach this machine, though (the end of the chapter
says why), so here the one is a choice, full stop.

Where does that one come from, though? It’s older than Coq by about a century. In
1888 the German mathematician Richard Dedekind published a little book whose title
asks what numbers are and what they’re for, and in 1889 the Italian mathematician
Giuseppe Peano published a booklet, written in Latin, that set out the axioms for the
whole numbers in the form people still teach: there’s a first number, and every number
has a next one, and a few rules about how “next” behaves. I had the two of them
down as working independently. I went looking, and the Stanford Encyclopedia’s

                                              251
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


entry on Dedekind says Peano acknowledged Dedekind’s priority, which is why the
axioms often go by both names. (Peano’s booklet is also where the sign ∈ that you
met in Section 2 comes from: he wrote it as a Greek epsilon, for the Latin est, “is.”)
Coq builds its whole numbers exactly that way, out of zero and “the next one” and
nothing else, so inside Coq the number three really is S (S (S O)), the next of the next of
the next of zero. What that changes here is small and I like it: the one a CHECK costs
isn’t a number pulled from a hat. It’s one application of the smallest step the number
system has. You can’t charge less than one S and still charge something.

The zeros matter just as much: computing is free on this ledger. Plus one, minus one
and jumping around cost nothing at all. Only the three acts that make a claim cost,
and each of them costs whether it passes or traps. Failing is not a discount.

The version rule. Here’s why versions exist, with numbers. Start with A = 4, version
0. CHECK is even A passes, and the table gets the fact (even, A, 0). Now INC A: A
becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT is even A. The machine looks
for (even, A, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (even, A, 0).
No match. Trap. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true about edition 0, and
completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1. A fact is about one
edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because versions only go
up and never wrap. That’s the whole trick against stale evidence: you can’t check a
number, change it, and then commit to the check.

That’s the opening chapter’s time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug, the file checked and
then swapped, and the database answer to it is Kung and Robinson’s: at commit time,
check that nothing you read was written in the meantime, and back out if something
was. The version rule is that check, done by the step, on one counter. It also shows
where the guarantee ends. It works because one step does every write and every
write bumps a version. A second writer that changed a counter without bumping its
version, a second processor or a device writing memory on its own, would walk right
around it, and none of the theorems below are about a machine with one of those.

Processor designers put a cousin of this check in silicon. Jensen, Hagensen and
Broughton, at Lawrence Livermore in 1987, described a pair of instructions now called
load-linked and store-conditional: the load reads a word and the processor starts
watching it, and the store goes through only if nothing has written that word since;
otherwise it fails and the program tries again. It’s tempting to say CHECK is the load
and COMMIT is the conditional store, and it’s wrong in two places. COMMIT doesn’t
write the counter it checked, and the thing doing the watching, the fact, sits in a table
the step keeps. No single processor holds it. The hardware version does cover the
second writer, because the watching happens on the memory everyone shares, which
is exactly the case the version rule leaves out.

The real kinship is older, and it’s somewhere else. Picture the table and the counters
shared by many processors, with CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY each done as one


                                           252
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


indivisible step. Maurice Herlihy (1991), a computer scientist who has spent his career
on how many processors can share memory safely, ranked shared objects by how
many processors each one can bring to agree on a single value with nobody ever
waiting on anybody. Test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what
was there, brings exactly two. A sticky bit, the idea of Serge Plotkin (1989), a Stanford
computer scientist working on distributed algorithms, is a cell the first writer jams for
good, with the first writer’s value, and everyone after can read it; it brings any number.
I guessed that the shared object would sit at the top with the sticky bit, because a write
that kills every fact about a counter, together with a commitment other processors can
see, looks like a way to build one. Ranking the object takes its operations, what each
one returns, which steps are indivisible, how it starts and which processes run it, and
then a proof that every processor decides, they all decide the same value, the value
is one somebody proposed, and nobody waits. Here it is, with every instruction one
indivisible step and the whole state readable, and the object is at the top. The reason is
the order of the fact table. Each processor CHECKs a property that holds of a counter
at zero, PZero to propose 0 and PEven to propose 1, then reads the table and decides
the bit of its oldest fact. The table only gains entries at the front, and a CHECK that
finds it full trips the trap, after which nothing moves, so the first CHECK of the run
fixes the oldest fact for good. Every processor that decides decides that bit, the bit
is somebody’s proposal, and each one decides after two of its own steps whatever
the others do (sc_agreement, sc_validity, sc_wait_free, SmallConsensus.v).
The version rule and the commitment play no part. The trap alone doesn’t do it: it
records that something trapped, and it doesn’t hand everyone the first writer’s value.

Now take the version rule away, let failures change nothing, keep only the properties
“at least n” so that a checked property only ever turns true, drop the decrement, and
make the fact table, the commitments and the flag sets and latches that only grow. I
guessed that then the object drops to the bottom rung, the level of plain memory, which
is the shared-memory face of what the database researchers Joseph Hellerstein and
Peter Alvaro (2020), at Berkeley and Santa Cruz, call CALM, where monotone means
nobody has to coordinate. That’s proved too, by Herlihy’s own kind of argument. Let
the updates return nothing and let the whole state be readable. If at every state, of any
two updates, one leaves the state alone, or the two commute, or one overwrites the
other, then no protocol brings two processors to agreement with nobody waiting (m
c_no_consensus). The monotone object has that property, with registers beside it,
because an instruction that would succeed still succeeds after anything else has run (m
c_mono_interfere, mc_mono_no_consensus, MonotoneConsensus.v). The toll
changes neither result. Neither idea is mine: the top is Plotkin’s and the bottom is the
monotone fact that field already knows.

Process-calculus people have a statement of the same split. Johannes Åman Pohjola
and Joachim Parrow, computer scientists at Uppsala University (Parrow is one of
the inventors of the pi-calculus, a mathematical model of processes that talk over



                                           253
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


channels), in 2016 proved, with the proof checked in the Isabelle proof assistant, that
no model whose parallel composition is monotonic, where a neighbouring process
can never stop a step, has a consensus process. One of their examples of a model
that does is test-and-set, an instruction that writes a cell and reports what was there.
Test-and-set isn’t a sticky bit: in Herlihy’s ranking it brings two processors to agree,
and a sticky bit brings any number.

Their setting is small enough to check here whole. A model is any set of processes with
a step relation and a way to compose two processes that doesn’t care about order or
grouping. Composition is monotonic when whatever a process can reach alone, it can
still reach with anything set beside it. A consensus process is one where any number
of copies, run together, can end up agreeing on either of two outcomes, and once a
run has one outcome it can never show the other. Their theorem goes through in a few
lines: run half the copies to one outcome and the other half to the other, and if neither
half can block the other, the two outcomes meet on the same state (cs_no_consens
us_monotonic, ConsensusSeparation.v). Then the machine goes into it. A process is
a shared machine state with a crowd of threads, each proposing a bit, and composing
two processes pools their threads on one state. One thread proposing each bit is a
consensus process in exactly their sense, for the outcomes “some thread decided 0”
and “some thread decided 1” (cs_machine_consensus), so by their theorem that
composition isn’t monotonic (cs_machine_not_monotonic). The small machine
sits on their non-monotonic side, checked. What puts it there in the run is the order
of the fact table, the same as above; a store that refuses a stale commit for good, as
the version rule does, refuses in the same spirit. The shared-memory version of their
split is the pair of results above: the small machine’s object reaches agreement for any
number of processors, and the monotone variant reaches it for none (sc_agreement,
mc_mono_no_consensus).

Security people know the pattern by a third name. A check that blesses a value, and
a write that takes the blessing away, is close kin to dynamic taint tracking, where a
label rides along with the data and a sanitizing step changes it; the labels go back
to the computer-security researcher Dorothy Denning’s 1976 lattice model of how
information is allowed to flow. How much a monitor like that has to remember is a
studied question too: Chamseddine Talhi, Nadia Tawbi and Mourad Debbabi (2008),
three security researchers at universities in Quebec, worked out which rules a monitor
can still enforce when its memory is bounded. The version rule is one small, specific
member of that family, done by the step.

Notice what isn’t a write. DEC on a counter that’s already 0 doesn’t change the counter,
so it doesn’t change the version. It’s a test that happens to move the line number.

The fact table. Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK traps. It doesn’t push
an old fact out to make room. That’s a choice with a bill attached, and I’ll put the bill


                                          254
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


in the section on what this machine doesn’t do.

Traps. Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else in the core; the ledger
still takes the instruction’s cost. Once it’s up, every instruction leaves the core alone.
A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove things about any list of instructions,
programs or otherwise, because an adversary doesn’t have to run my programs; they
can feed the machine whatever they want. For those lists, an instruction after a trap is
still charged its cost, and still changes nothing.

Now the exact version.


Definition 16.1 (Properties, checker, meaning). A property is one of: Zero, Even, or
Ge(n) for a whole number n. The checker eval( p, v) computes yes or no: v = 0 by equal-
ity, evenness by the parity function, n ≤ v by comparison. The meaning holds( p, v) is
the arithmetic statement: v = 0; there is an m with v = 2m; n ≤ v.


Lemma 16.1 (The checker says what it means). For every property p and every whole
number v, eval( p, v) = yes if and only if holds( p, v).

Proof. Split on the three properties. Equality with zero returns yes exactly at zero;
comparison with n returns yes exactly when n ≤ v. For evenness, the parity checker
returns yes at 0, no at 1, and the same answer at v + 2 as at v. Induction in steps
of two gives yes exactly at 0, 2, 4, . . ., the numbers 2m. Those are precisely the three
meanings.

Checked as eval_iff (EarnedCore.v).


Definition 16.2 (Core, state, claim, start). A core k holds two counters A, B and their
versions (whole numbers), a line number, a fact table (a list of facts, a fact being a
triple of a property, a counter and a version), a channel (empty or one fact), and a
trap bit. Write val(k, c) and ver(k, c) for counter c’s value and version. A state s is a
core, written core(s), with a ledger µ(s) and a flag cert(s). The claim p of c in k is the
fact ( p, c, ver(k, c)). The table’s room is 16. The start start( a, b) has counters a and b,
versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an empty channel, the trap down, µ = 0 and the flag
down. A state is clean when its table and channel are empty and its flag is down.


Definition 16.3 (Instructions, costs, the step). The instructions are INC c, DEC c j,
HALT, CHECK p c, COMMIT p c and CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap
down as in the table above. Passing any check, commitment or certification requires
the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK passes when eval( p, val(k, c)) = yes
and the table holds fewer than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim p of c is in
the table, and CERTIFY passes when the channel holds a fact; a failing one sets the
trap and changes nothing else. On a core with the trap up, every instruction changes


                                            255
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost 1, the rest 0. One step on a state
is
                                                                                     
      exec(s, i ) = cexec(core(s), i ), µ(s) + cost(i ), cert(s) ∨ fires(core(s), i ) ,

where cexec is the core’s step and fires(k, i ) is yes exactly when i is CERTIFY and
passes at k. For any list t of instructions (a trace), run(t, s) applies them in order and
cost(t) adds their costs. A program is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a program
run fetches the instruction at the line number and executes it, and stops when the trap
is up, the line holds HALT, or the line holds nothing.


Defined as cexec, exec, run, total_cost, run_prog, start and Minimal.Ear
nedCore.clean_start (EarnedCore.v).

Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The core
moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag becomes
“it was up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.” The core’s move doesn’t mention µ or
the flag anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.

A worked run, the shortest one there is. The program: CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is
zero A; CERTIFY. Start at start(0, b), for any b. Line 1: A is 0, the checker says yes, the
table is empty so there’s room, and the fact (zero, A, 0) goes in. µ = 1. Line 2: the claim
about A’s current edition is (zero, A, 0), and it’s right there. Into the channel. µ = 2.
Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. µ = 3. Line 4 has no instruction, so
the program stops. Three paid acts, in order, a flag that’s up, and a channel that names
the last earned commitment, which here is (zero, A, 0).

Now start the same program at start(5, b). Line 1: A is 5, the checker says no, the trap
goes up, µ = 1, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and you can run
it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the first. The same
three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others, because the check
could have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that has a no pile, which
is the only kind the opening chapter counts as establishing anything.

Could I have picked an even dumber claim? Sure, and the machine would have let me.
CHECK at least 0 A passes on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY
on it raises the flag for 3 from every start (stop the presses: a number is at least zero).
The step doesn’t police that. It checks order, aboutness and that the checker tells the
truth; whether the question was worth asking isn’t something it looks at. A check that
can’t fail establishes nothing, and this machine will charge you three and raise the flag
for it anyway. Spotting that is the reader’s job, with the property in hand, and it’s on
the list at the end of the chapter.

Others walked into the same line from communication. Three theoretical computer
scientists, Oded Goldreich, Brendan Juba and Madhu Sudan (2012), built a theory of


                                            256
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


communication with a partner you may not understand, in which getting a message
across counts only as a way to reach a goal, and the central notion is sensing: being
able to tell, from what you see, whether you’re making progress. The sensing they
ask for is safe: when there’s no progress it says so, and so it never reports a success
that didn’t happen. Their main result, as I read it, is that safe sensing, with a partner
who could help if you spoke its language, is enough for one strategy that reaches the
goal with every such partner. A check that can fail and never lies, standing in front of
a verdict you can’t take back. That’s their theorem, in their setting, and it’s the same
shape.

16.4 It computes everything two counters can
First the base, because if the base can’t compute, nothing else here matters.


Definition 16.4 (Two-counter program, compile, window). A two-counter program M
is a list of instructions, each either MINC c or MDEC c j. A configuration is a triple
(line, a, b). One step of M: if the line holds no instruction, M has stopped; MINC adds
one to c and goes to the next line; MDEC subtracts one from c and goes to line j if c is
above 0, and goes to the next line if c is 0. mrun(n, M, x ) is n steps from x, staying put
once stopped. The compile of M replaces each MINC c by INC c and each MDEC c j by
DEC c j. The window of a core k is the triple (line number, val(k, A), val(k, B)).


Theorem 16.2 (Step for step). For every two-counter program M and every core k with the
trap down: M has stopped at window(k ) if and only if the program compile( M ) has halted
at k; and if M steps from window(k ) to y, then one program step of compile( M ) from k
lands on a core with window y and the trap still down. So for every n, n program steps of
compile( M ) from k land on a core whose window is mrun(n, M, window(k )), with the trap
down.

Proof. Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If it’s
MINC c, the compiled INC c adds one to c and goes to the next line, which is exactly
the window’s move (the version also moves, but the window doesn’t show versions).
If it’s MDEC c j, split on whether c is 0, and both sides do the same thing in each
case. Neither instruction can trap. The run statement is induction on n, one step at a
time.

Checked as simulation_step and simulation_run (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 16.3 (Halting matches). For every two-counter program M and whole numbers a,
b: M stops after some number of steps from (1, a, b) if and only if the program compile( M)
halts after some number of program steps from start( a, b).

Proof. The start has window (1, a, b) and its trap is down. Apply Theorem 16.2 after



                                           257
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


any number n of steps: the two configurations still have the same window, the trap is
still down, and one is stopped exactly when the other is halted. The same n witnesses
termination in either direction.

Checked as halting_correspondence (EarnedCore.v).

Now the part that isn’t mine. Proving that halting is undecidable for two-counter
machines is real work, and it’s already done, checked, in a shared Coq project called
the Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs (presented by Yannick Forster, Dominique
Larchey-Wendling and coauthors at CoqPL 2020). The two-counter result in it is
Larchey-Wendling’s, reached from his and Forster’s work on Minsky machines (CPP
2019) by way of FRACTRAN, a model of computation invented by John Conway, the
English mathematician best known for the Game of Life, which the library uses as a
stepping stone. Their two-counter machine has the same two instructions as Minsky’s,
with the same rule for zero. Andrej Dudenhefner, one of the library’s authors, writes
that rule out in his 2022 paper on deciding questions about two-counter machines:
DEC on a counter at zero goes on to the next instruction, and otherwise it takes one
off the counter and jumps. So the only thing I have to prove is that their machine and
my INC/DEC fragment are the same machine, step for step, and then borrow their
theorem.

One honest wrinkle about what “undecidable” means in that library, because it isn’t
the textbook sentence. Every function you can write in Coq is a program, so in that
library “decidable” means “some Coq function answers it.” Coq by itself can’t prove
that no Coq function answers a question without an extra assumption about what
programs are. So the library says the strongest thing it can without one: if anything
decided this, then the questions on which a single-tape Turing machine doesn’t halt
could be listed by a program, which is the classic thing that can’t be done. That’s their
convention, and the theorem below inherits it exactly.


Theorem 16.4 (Halting is undecidable for this machine). The library’s two-counter ma-
chine agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop, and its termination match those of
the compiled program, so a library problem ( P, a, b) halts if and only if the compiled program
halts from start( a, b). Consequently, the question “does program P halt from start( a, b)?” is
undecidable in the library’s sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape
binary Turing machine halting enumerable.

Proof. The agreement is a case split on the library’s instruction at the current line,
and then induction along the run, ending in Theorem 16.3. The compile map is
then a reduction from the library’s two-counter halting problem, which the library
proves undecidable, and the library’s own lemma carries undecidability across a
reduction.




                                             258
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Checked as mm2_step_iff, mm2_stop_iff, mm2_terminates_iff, mm2_halti
ng_iff and earned_core_halting_undecidable (EarnedCoreLinks.v), the last
applying the library’s MM2_HALTING_undec.

What that buys, and what it doesn’t. It buys: the base of this machine is a universal
machine in Minsky’s sense, and nobody (in the library’s sense) can predict in general
what it’ll do. What it doesn’t buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives
conveniently. The counters start holding a and b, given directly; there’s no encoding
layer in my files. Minsky’s prime-power packing is how you’d get from “any Turing
machine” to “two counters,” and that construction is his and the library’s, and I use it
as it stands.

Is “given directly” just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody found
exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, then at the MIT AI Lab, wrote a ten-page
memo titled “A Two Counter Machine Cannot Calculate 2 N .” He spells out the con-
vention first: a counter machine computing a function starts with n in one counter
and zero in the others. Then he gives a proof that a two-counter machine started that
way can’t compute 2n . His theorem is checked here, for every program of the small
machine (tc2_no_pow, Tc2Pow.v) and for every machine with a finite control whose
counters are read only through zero and parity above a threshold (am_no_power_o
f_two), by the same chain of stages that proves the theorem about multiplying near
the end of the chapter (Theorem 16.54): along an arithmetic progression of inputs the
outputs grow by a fixed amount, and powers of two don’t. So the packing Minsky
needs is precisely the thing two plain counters can’t do for themselves. Hand the small
machine its inputs straight and there are functions of them it can’t compute; hand it
the inputs already packed and it computes anything a Turing machine can. That’s no
contradiction with the undecidability above, which ranges over every program and
every starting pair, packed ones included. The base hides nothing. It just needs its
input pre-chewed, and the chewing is somebody else’s.

16.5 It’s a certification system, and the flag is a latch
Now the record. Three facts first, all of them read straight off the step line.


Theorem 16.5 (Ledger, toll, permanence). For every state s and instruction i,
µ(exec(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ), and for every trace t, µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t). If
cert(s) is down and cert(exec(s, i )) is up, then i is CERTIFY, it passes at core(s), and
cost(i ) ≥ 1. If cert(s) is up, so is cert(exec(s, i )).

Proof. Read the ledger component of Definition 16.3: it adds exactly cost(i ). Repeated
substitution along a trace gives the sum of its costs, or, equivalently, induction on the
length of the trace does. The flag’s new value is its old value or fires(core(s), i ). A
false-to-true change therefore requires that event, whose definition requires a passing
CERTIFY. CERTIFY costs 1. An already true flag stays true under the same disjunction.



                                           259
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Checked as mu_conservation, mu_conservation_trace, only_certify_cer
tifies, a2 and cert_permanent (EarnedCore.v).

That third clause in the middle is Section 3’s toll, for this machine. Which means this
machine is one of the things Section 3 was about, and Section 3’s theorem applies to it
without my lifting a finger.


Theorem 16.6 (An instance of the certification system). The states, the instructions, the
step exec, the cost and the flag, with the toll of Theorem 16.5, form a certification system
(Definition 3.1). So the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) holds here: if cert(s0 ) is down and
cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions 16.2 and 16.3, their step and
cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the five data fields of Definition 3.1.
Theorem 16.5 supplies its one required rule. Applying Theorem 3.1 gives the claimed
bound.

Checked as earned_cs and earned_core_floor (EarnedCoreLinks.v); earned_
core_floor is universal_nfi_any_substrate, the checked name of Section 3’s
theorem, applied to earned_cs. The same floor is proved directly, without the link,
as nfi_floor (EarnedCore.v).

Then Section 10. Section 10 said: take any base, and any record that answers only
to the base and never comes back down, and the record is a latch. This machine has
a base: a program together with a core, stepping by the program step. And it has a
record, the flag, with the ledger riding along. So the question is whether it’s an honest
extension in Section 10’s five-rule sense (Definition 10.2), and if it is, Section 10 does
the rest.


Theorem 16.7 (The flag is a latch of the base). Let the base have states (program, core),
stepping by the program step, starting at start( a, b)’s core for any a, b, and halting when the
program has halted. Map each (program, state) to (program, core). Then the machine, run as a
closed machine on (program, state), is an honest extension of that base, and so its flag factors
as the latch (Theorem 10.1) of the event “the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.”

Proof. The rules of Definition 10.2 one at a time. Driven by the computation: the next
flag is the old flag or “the next instruction is a passing CERTIFY,” which is a function
of the base state and the old flag (that’s the step line). Ledger: µ only adds. Toll:
Theorem 16.5. Permanence: Theorem 16.5. A reachable write: the three-line program
of the worked run raises the flag from a start. Section 10’s theorem then gives the
factorization.

Checked as earned_core_honest and earned_core_is_latch (EarnedCore-


                                              260
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Links.v), the latter by record_axis_is_latch_holds; the step-level facts are cer
t_latch and base_blind (EarnedCore.v).

So far, nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Parts II and III already
promised about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part neither of
them could give.

16.6 Commitments are earned
Here’s the shape before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of instruc-
tions at all, chosen by somebody who’d love to cheat. Look at the moment a COMMIT
would pass. Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there’s a CHECK of exactly the
same claim that passed and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and between
that CHECK and now, nothing touched the counter. Not “probably.” Not “on the
programs I wrote.” On every list of instructions anybody can write.

To say “nothing touched it” exactly, one word.


Definition 16.5 (Untouched). A list of instructions mid, run from a state s, leaves
counter c untouched when, for every way of splitting mid as t1 , then i, then t2 , executing
i at the core reached by running t1 from s leaves both ver(·, c) and val(·, c) as they
were.


Defined as untouched (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 16.8 (A commitment was checked first). Let s0 be clean and pre any trace after
which COMMIT p c would pass. Then pre splits as pre1 , then CHECK p c, then mid, where:
the CHECK passes at the core reached by pre1 ; CHECK p c and COMMIT p c each cost at
least 1; c’s version after pre1 equals its version after pre; and mid, run from just after the
CHECK, leaves c untouched.

Proof. COMMIT passes, so the claim ( p, c, ver(c)) for the current version is in the table.
By the no-forging invariant (Theorem 16.12 below), that fact was written by a passing
CHECK p c at some point pre1 , with the version c had then; since it’s the current
version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go down, and any instruction
that changes a counter’s value also raises its version, so an instruction in mid that
touched c would have left c’s version higher at the end than at the CHECK. It isn’t. So
nothing in mid touched c.

Checked as earned_commitment_provenance (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 16.9 (A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified). Let s0 be




                                             261
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


clean and t any trace with cert(run(t, s0 )) up. Then for some p and c, t is

            pre1 , CHECK p c, mid1 , COMMIT p c, mid2 , CERTIFY, post,

where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY passes
at its state, c has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and mid1 leaves c
untouched.

Proof. The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by Theorem 16.5
it’s a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the channel, the channel
starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some earlier COMMIT
p c passed. Theorem 16.8 at that COMMIT gives the CHECK, the equal version, and
the untouched stretch.

Checked as earned_certification_provenance (EarnedCore.v).

And the failure side, so you can see the refusals are clean, with nothing left half-done:


Theorem 16.10 (Unearned steps trap and change no claim). If COMMIT p c would not
pass at a core k, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the channel and the table as they were.
If CERTIFY would not pass at a state s, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the flag as it
was.

Proof. If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up. Oth-
erwise, the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set the
trap, leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch, and
its fires value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false, which leaves it
unchanged. The instruction’s charge still applies to the ledger.

Checked as unearned_commit_traps and uncommitted_certify_traps
(EarnedCore.v).

If that rings a bell, it should. It’s Milner’s move from the opening chapter: in LCF
a theorem is a value that only the rules of the logic can build, so nobody can just
print one (Milner and two colleagues on his Edinburgh project, Michael Gordon and
Christopher Wadsworth, wrote the system up in 1979, and Gordon, who went on to
build the HOL prover at Cambridge, told its history in 2000). Here the thing nobody
can print is one bit, and what guards it is one step rule. Milner’s guard was a type
checker. Same architecture, much lower down.

A provenance theorem is also an itemised receipt, and the itemised receipt has a
history that’s exactly this gap. James Ritty ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and believed
some of his staff were pocketing money. On a steamboat trip to Europe in 1878 he
watched a mechanism that counted the turns of the ship’s propeller, and wondered


                                               262
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


whether something like it could count the money instead. In 1879 he and his brother
John patented a “Cash Register and Indicator,” and they sold a version under the
wonderful name Ritty’s Incorruptible Cashier. The first model was this book’s counter
(Section 6) with brass on it: press a key, the amount goes onto a dial showing the day’s
running total. No drawer, no paper. At closing time you hold the dial up against the
cash. And that’s all a total can do. It tells you that the money is short. It can’t tell
you which sale went missing or who rang it up. The paper came later. The patents
passed to other owners, first a Cincinnati salesman named Jacob Eckert, and in 1884
to John H. Patterson, who renamed the business the National Cash Register Company,
and the story told about that company is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept
for the shop’s own books, one handed to the customer. That last part I only have
from histories of the company and of the machine, so hold it the way you’d hold
any company’s story about itself. The order is right either way: first a total that can
tell you something’s wrong, then a list that tells you where. The ledger µ is the dial.
Theorem 16.9 is the list: which CHECK, of which claim, about which edition, before
which COMMIT. The theorem supplies that list about the run. The machine doesn’t
keep it as data anyone can read back from the end state, and nothing in the theorem
gives a procedure for rebuilding it from there. A fact in the table holds a property, a
counter and a version number. That’s neither the counter’s value back then nor a log
of what happened in between.

Read Theorem 16.9 once more for what it doesn’t say. Between the CHECK and the
COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, it isn’t
promised anything. You can check A is even, commit to it, add one to A, and then
certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about the edition that
was current when you committed. The certificate is historical: it says “this was checked
and committed about this edition,” and it says nothing about whether that’s still true.
I think that’s the right meaning for a certificate (a birth certificate doesn’t expire when
the baby grows), but it’s a meaning, and you should know which one you’re getting.
So a certificate doesn’t say the claim holds at the CERTIFY, and it doesn’t say the
claim holds at the end of the run. A CERTIFY that rechecked the version would give
a different guarantee. That’s a possible extension, and the historical theorem doesn’t
need it.

16.7 What a passing check means
Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn’t yet say the CHECK was right, and
that’s a separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly
ordered chain of check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to
everything. So: what does a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?


Theorem 16.11 (Checker soundness). Let s0 be clean and t any trace, and let k be the core
of run(t, s0 ). For every fact ( p, c, v) in k’s table with v = ver(k, c), the property holds of the
counter’s current value: holds( p, val(k, c)). In particular, if COMMIT p c would pass at k,


                                                263
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


then holds( p, val(k, c)).

Proof. Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a
version no higher than its counter’s, and if its version equals its counter’s, its property
holds of its counter’s value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds
there. A passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said yes, so
by Lemma 16.1 the property holds. A write raises one counter’s version, so every old
fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer applies to it.
Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after every instruction,
so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where the claim is in the
table at the current version.

Checked as checker_soundness and committed_claim_holds (EarnedCore.v),
through the invariant sound and its one-step form sound_step.

So, on a run from a clean start, a live fact means exactly this: one of three arithmetic
properties holds of one counter’s current value. Not “the program is correct.” Not
“the number is interesting.” The property, of the value, now. That’s all “checked”
means on this machine, and it’s enough to be true. Three events stay separate here.
The property holding of the value is one. A CHECK passing is another: a CHECK of a
property that holds still doesn’t pass when the table is full or the trap is already up. A
certification is a third, and it needs a COMMIT and a CERTIFY after the CHECK. So a
CHECK that didn’t pass says nothing about whether its property is false.

So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. From a clean start, the record
carries the run’s half of the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim about
the same edition, then a CERTIFY. The other half, that the checker says yes exactly
when the property holds, isn’t in any run. It’s Lemma 16.1, a proof about the little
program the step calls, checked once by Coq and priced by nothing on the ledger. So a
claim established here stands on two legs: a fact about this run, carried by the record,
and a fact about the checker, carried by a proof that whoever reads the record has to
accept. That’s the Münchhausen trilemma from the opening chapter taking its third
horn on purpose: the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page, where
you can decide whether you’d have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is
the reader’s. The machine doesn’t know anything. It keeps the order.

The question in that paragraph is older than any checker, and its most famous wording
isn’t about what you’d guess. “Who will guard the guardians?” gets quoted about
governments and police and, lately, proof assistants. Where’s it from? Plato’s Republic
has the worry, sort of: in Book III (at 403e), Glaucon, Plato’s older brother and one of
the people Socrates is talking with, says it would be absurd for a guardian to need a
guardian, which is close in words and opposite in mood, a man calling the question
silly. The Latin, quis custodiet ipsos custodes, is from the Roman satirist Juvenal’s sixth
satire, and it’s a joke about a husband. His friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set


                                           264
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


guards on her; the line asks who’ll watch the guards, since she’ll start with them. And
it gets better. In 1899 an Oxford undergraduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of
that satire in a medieval manuscript in the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies
lack, partly overlapping the familiar ones, and the famous question sits in that tangle.
Scholars have argued ever since about whether those lines are Juvenal’s at all. So the
most quoted sentence about trusting the checker comes with a doubtful source of its
own. Does that change anything here? No. The only answer I know that works is
de Bruijn’s (Section 22 has it): you never get rid of the last guard, you make the last
guard small enough to watch yourself. Lemma 16.1 is one line per property. Euclid
had the instinct: five postulates you can hold in your head, and everything else meant
to follow from them.

That split, a fixed checker proved sound from outside and a process that only gets to
act when the checker says yes, has a name in the writing on self-improving programs.
The AI researcher Jürgen Schmidhuber, at the IDSIA lab in Lugano, described a Gödel
machine (2003) that rewrites its own code only after its built-in proof searcher has
proved the rewrite useful, and Benja Fallenstein and Nate Soares (2015), researchers
at the Machine Intelligence Research Institute in Berkeley, survey agents that reason
about their successors through formal proofs a fixed checker accepts. Same architec-
ture, aimed at a different question: they want to know when a machine may trust a
smarter version of itself, and this machine only wants to know whether a flag was
earned. Keeping the checker’s proof outside the machine is my design choice. The
nearest theorem, in Section 13, is narrower: no procedure the substrate can represent
decides, for every program, a property that depends only on behaviour and holds of
one program and fails of another. It doesn’t say a machine can’t check a proof about a
checker, or verify a restricted part of itself.

Soundness rules out a lying checker. It doesn’t rule out a pointless question: at least 0
has a perfectly sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run showed.

16.8 Nothing gets forged
The proof of Theorem 16.8 leaned on an invariant I promised to show you. Here it
is. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions get a fact into the
table without a CHECK writing it? A DEC with a funny jump target, a COMMIT after
a trap, something I didn’t think of? The answer is checked one instruction at a time,
which is the only way I trust myself to answer it.


Definition 16.6 (Earned fact; no forgery). After a trace t from s0 , a fact f = ( p, c, v) is
earned when t is pre, then CHECK p c, then mid, where the CHECK passes at the core
reached by pre, f is exactly the claim p of c at that core, and, if f is live at the end (v
equals c’s version after t), mid leaves c untouched. The trace has no forgery when every
fact in the table after it is earned.




                                            265
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.12 (No forging). For every core k, instruction i and fact f in the table after
executing i at k: either f was already in k’s table, or i is CHECK of f ’s property and counter,
it passes at k, and f is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has no forgery, so does that
trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean start, every trace has no forgery.

Proof. The first part is a case for each of the six instruction kinds: only a passing
CHECK adds anything, and it adds exactly its claim. For the second, a new fact is
earned by the CHECK that just wrote it; an old fact stays earned, and if it’s still live
after the new instruction, its counter’s version didn’t move, so the new instruction
didn’t touch the counter and the untouched stretch grows by one. A clean start has an
empty table, which has no forgery, and the step carries it along any trace.

Checked as facts_step, no_forging_step and no_forging (EarnedCore.v).

16.9 A full table traps
Sixteen facts of room, and no eviction. Two halves to prove: nothing ever leaves, and
nothing ever overflows.


Theorem 16.13 (Bounded table, no eviction). Every instruction keeps every fact already
in the table. If the table holds 16 or more facts, CHECK p c puts the trap up and leaves the
table as it was. If the table holds at most 16 facts, it still holds at most 16 after any instruction.

Proof. With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only
CHECK can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an
entry. Success requires a previous length strictly below 16, so the new length is at
most 16. At length 16 or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.

Checked as facts_keep, full_table_traps and facts_bounded_step
(EarnedCore.v).

Why trap? Why not make room? Because “making room” means deciding which fact
dies, and a fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later. A table
that only grows is a history you can read back, and the provenance proofs above lean
on exactly that. The bill for it is real, though, and it’s in the subsection near the end of
this chapter on what the machine doesn’t do.

16.10 The window can’t see the record
Section 7 was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the theorem
that a window which can’t tell two states apart can’t price the step between them
exactly (Theorem 7.2). Here’s the smallest pair I could build where the window is
Minsky’s view of the machine (line number and the two counters) and the record is
everything else.



                                                 266
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Run two traces from start(0, 0). The earned run is CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY. The idle run is DEC A 0, three times. In the idle run, A is 0 every time,
so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs end on line 4,
with A = 0 and B = 0, both versions 0. Through the window, identical. One of them
has paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag up. The other has paid
nothing, holds nothing, can’t commit, and its flag is down. Two photographs, same
picture, different people.


Theorem 16.14 (Same window, different record). The earned run and the idle run from
start(0, 0) end at cores with the same window and the same versions of A and B, and with
different ledgers, different flags, different tables, and different answers to “would COMMIT is
zero A pass.”

Proof. In the earned run, CHECK adds (Zero, A, 0), COMMIT puts that fact in the
channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. No counter is
written. In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without writing a
counter or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or commitment.
Thus both final windows are (4, 0, 0) with versions (0, 0). The earned table contains the
current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated difference in whether
another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and flag.

Checked as receipt_separation (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 16.15 (No window oracle). There is no function g from windows to whole num-
bers with g(window) = µ at the end of every trace from start(0, 0). Likewise there is no
function from windows to yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every such trace, and none
that gives whether COMMIT is zero A would pass.

Proof. Such a g would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs of
Theorem 16.14 share. The same for the flag and the commit right.

Checked as no_mu_oracle, no_cert_oracle and no_commit_oracle (Earned-
Core.v).

This is Section 7’s shape, made of pebbles: the record lives off the window. Anybody
who only watches the counters and the line number, which is everything Minsky’s
machine is, can’t tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether the flag is
up. Not because they looked carelessly. Because it isn’t there to see.

Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy has
an old fight about exactly that, and it’s worth a detour, because it tells you which
side of the fight these theorems stand on. Leibniz said that for real things it can’t
happen. There are no two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote in 1716


                                             267
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


to Samuel Clarke, the English philosopher and theologian who was taking Newton’s
side against him in an exchange of letters, and he told a story to go with it. A clever
gentleman of his acquaintance, talking with him in front of the Electress Sophia of
Hanover, Leibniz’s friend and patron, in the garden at Herrenhausen she had helped
lay out, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared him to. He “ran
all over the Garden a long time” looking, and it was “to no purpose.” You can run his
search tonight with a handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains of rice: look hard
enough and every pair differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max Black, a Russian-born
philosopher teaching at Cornell, pushed back with a universe you can’t build at the
table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the same colour, the same
everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between them. There isn’t one,
and there are still two of them. People have argued about Black’s spheres ever since,
and I’m not going to settle it.

Here’s why I don’t have to. Leibniz’s claim is about every property a thing has. The
theorems above are about three: the line and the two counters. The two runs aren’t
indiscernible in his sense at all: one has a fact in its table and its flag up, and the other
doesn’t, and Coq tells them apart in a line. They’re indiscernible to a window, which
is a much cheaper thing, and it’s the thing that matters for a machine, because an
observer of a machine only ever gets a window. Leibniz’s gentleman would always
find his difference if he could look at everything. It doesn’t help him if all he’s allowed
to look at is three things about each leaf.

There’s a horse in this, too, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a mathematics
teacher named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever Hans, who an-
swered arithmetic questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in front of crowds.
Same answers out as a horse that could count: that’s the idle run’s matching win-
dow. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped looking at the answers and started
changing the conditions, and published what he found in 1907. Put blinders on Hans,
or have him asked by someone who didn’t know the answer, and the arithmetic fell
apart. Hans was reading the questioner: tiny, unintended movements of the head and
body as the hoof reached the right number. That’s the probe. Pfungst didn’t argue
with the answers. He asked a question the answers couldn’t fake, one that needed
the real thing to be there, the way a COMMIT needs a checked fact to be in the table:
run COMMIT is zero A after each of the two runs, and one passes and the other traps
(Theorem 16.14). And the part of the story I like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten
was never persuaded by Pfungst and kept showing his horse. A matching window
doesn’t need a cheat behind it, which is why you want a probe. An accusation is the
wrong tool for it.

16.11 The exact price is three
Section 3 said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that’s true and too
modest. A raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT
needs a CHECK, and each of those is its own instruction costing one. So at least three.

                                            268
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


One of what: three units of µ, one per paid act, each one the “one” I picked back in
the table. And three is the number of links in the chain. It isn’t a guess that happens
to hold.


Theorem 16.16 (The minimum price of a certificate). If s0 is clean and cert(run(t, s0 ))
is up, then cost(t) ≥ 3 and µ(run(t, s0 )) ≥ µ(s0 ) + 3. For programs: if the flag is up after n
program steps from start( a, b), then µ ≥ 3 there.

Proof. Theorem 16.9 finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
places in t, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
statement is Theorem 16.5. A program run is the run of the instructions it actually
executes, so the program form follows.

Checked as certified_run_min_cost and program_certified_min_cost
(EarnedCore.v).

The three is three independent units, one for each part of a clean start. A flag that is
down buys the first: a run that raises it costs at least one (nfi_floor). An empty
channel buys the second: with the flag down and the channel empty, a run that raises
the flag costs at least two (nec_s_floor_two). An empty table buys the third, and
that is the theorem above. Leave out any one part and its floor fails, and a cheaper
certificate is there: with the flag already up it costs 0, with a commitment already in
the channel 1, and with a live fact already in the table 2 (nec_s_clean_conjunct
s_each_buy_one, nec_s_min_cost_needs_flag_down, nec_s_min_cost_n
eeds_empty_channel and nec_s_min_cost_needs_empty_table). The exact
condition is nec_s_floor3_iff: every run from a state that raises the flag costs
at least three exactly when the flag is down and one of two things holds: the trap is
up, or the channel is empty and every fact in the table is about an older version of its
counter. And three is paid exactly from every clean start whose trap is down (nec_s_
witness_from_every_clean_start). All of these are in NecSClean.v, except nf
i_floor, which is in EarnedCore.v.


Theorem 16.17 (Three is tight). For all whole numbers a and b, run the program CHECK
is zero A; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from start( a, b). If a = 0, it
ends with the flag up and µ = 3 exactly. If a ̸= 0, it ends with the flag down and the trap up,
and for every n, n program steps from start( a, b) leave the flag down.

Proof. If a = 0, the checker for Zero says yes at 0, so the first instruction adds
(Zero, A, 0) to the empty table and charges 1. No counter changes, so the second
instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges 1. The third finds
the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges 1. The line is now 4, beyond the
three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The final
ledger is exactly 3. If a ̸= 0, the checker says no, so the first instruction sets the trap


                                              269
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up, so every
later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.

Checked as earned_run_check_can_fail and earned_run_refused_forev
er (EarnedCore.v), with the program named earned_run, and the lemma run_p
rog_trapped for a trapped run standing still. The version whose check can’t fail,
CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A; CERTIFY, certifies from every start for
exactly 3 (min_cost_tight, with that program named witness). So the floor of
three is reachable from any start at all, and that’s the machine declining to police trivial
checks. On that program the check distinguishes no inputs.

That’s the worked run from the start of the chapter, now as a theorem. The floor is 3,
and a run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the price. The bound
has no slack in it.

Don’t mistake that 3 for a measure of how hard a claim is to certify. It’s the same 3
for every claim, easy or hard, because only the three acts that make a claim are priced
and the counters work out whatever the check needs for free. A cost of certifying that
grows with the claim would have to price the checking itself, and that’s a different
question with its own literature. Four theoretical computer scientists, Guy Blanc,
Caleb Koch, Jane Lange and Li-Yang Tan (2022), studied one version of it under the
name the query complexity of certification: how many questions an algorithm has to
ask a black-box function to hand back a small certificate for its answer. Their count
moves with the function. Mine doesn’t move at all.

And that’s every piece of the model, standing on six instruction kinds: a base that
computes everything two counters can, a ledger that’s exact, a toll the universal floor
applies to, a flag that’s a latch of the base, a window that can’t see the record, and,
from a clean start, a commitment that can’t happen unless a check of the same claim,
on the same edition, came first and was right. Every result above is closed: Coq
reports no assumptions for any of them. That isn’t my say-so. EarnedCore.v and its
link file, EarnedCoreLinks.v, each end by asking Coq to print the assumptions of each
headline theorem, and the build of Section 22 compiles them and fails unless every
one comes back closed. The project-wide audit of Section 22 lists these files too, and
every theorem in them comes back closed there as well. The base file uses nothing
but Coq’s standard library, so you can check it with nothing else installed; the link file
adds only the book’s own abstract records and the library of undecidability proofs.

16.12 What it takes to be Thiele-complete
The front matter promised a definition of Thiele-complete with teeth, so here it is.
First, why it needs teeth. The easy definition goes: a Thiele machine is Thiele-complete
when its base can compute anything a Turing machine can. It looks fine, and it’s nearly
empty. Take Minsky’s two-counter machine, charge one mark for every move, and
pick any yes-or-no question about its configuration as the record. Every move costs


                                            270
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


one, so every move that raises the record costs one, so it obeys the toll. That’s a Thiele
machine with a universal base: a clock bolted to a computer. A machine whose record
never goes up passes too, since a toll on a raise that never happens is never broken.
Neither one earns anything, and a name both of them get for free isn’t saying much.

So the definition below asks for what the small machine actually does, written so that
any machine at all can be held up against it. You hand over a reading of the machine,
a list of things, and then the reading has to pass four clauses.


Definition 16.7 (Thiele-complete). A machine has states, moves, a step, a cost for each
move and a yes/no reading of each state, the record. An interface for it hands over: a
universal base, meaning a two-counter configuration shown by each state (its window),
a class of live states, a move for each two-counter instruction, and a loaded state for
each start (1, a, b); a type of claims, each with a meaning, a statement about a state; a
checker that says yes or no to a claim at a state; for each claim, a relation “the thing
this claim is about is unchanged” between two states; a set of clean states; a ledger, a
whole number for each state; and a kind for each move: a base move, CHECK of a
claim, COMMIT of a claim, or CERTIFY. The machine is Thiele-complete when some
interface meets four clauses. (a) Universal base. Each two-counter instruction’s move
is a base move; from every live state it acts on the window exactly as the instruction
acts on a configuration, and the state stays live; each loaded state shows (1, a, b), is
live and is clean; no base move changes the record; and a record that’s up stays up
under every move. (b) Earned record. Clean states have the record down. Every run
from a clean state that ends with the record up contains a CHECK of some claim c
that passes, then a COMMIT of c with the thing c is about unchanged at every state
in between, then a CERTIFY, with the record down just before that CERTIFY and up
just after it. A passing check means its claim’s meaning holds of the state it checked,
and a meaning that holds keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. (c)
Exact toll. Base moves cost 0, each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY costs exactly 1,
and each move adds its cost to the ledger. (d) Non-vacuity. Some claim c has a CHECK,
a COMMIT and a CERTIFY such that those three moves alone, from a loaded state,
raise the record exactly when c’s meaning holds there; and c holds at some loaded
state and fails at another. A Thiele machine whose base is universal, with no more
asked, is weakly Thiele-complete.


Defined as thiele_interface, thiele_complete_with and thiele_comple
te (ThieleComplete.v), with the four clauses as universal_base_clause, earn
ed_record_clause, exact_toll_clause and non_vacuity_clause, and the
easy notion as weakly_thiele_complete.

Read the four clauses as four plain sentences. (a) It computes anything a Turing
machine can, and the computing can’t reach the record: the base moves are the two-
counter machine, they leave the record exactly where it was, and a record that goes up


                                           271
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


stays up. (b) From a clean start, the record goes up only on top of the small machine’s
chain: a check that passed, a commitment to the same claim with nothing changed
underneath, then a certificate. (c) Computing is free and each of the three acts costs
one, so the ledger counts the acts. The steps in between go free. (d) Somewhere there’s
a claim whose check could have said no. A machine whose every claim is “at least 0”
doesn’t qualify, and neither does one with nothing to certify.

And look where the checker’s honesty sits. In (b), “a passing check means its claim
holds” is a field of the interface, proved once, outside every run, exactly where it sat
for the small machine (Lemma 16.1). The definition doesn’t ask the machine to vouch
for its own checker. The nearest reasons not to ask are Gödel’s second theorem, about
a system proving its own consistency, and the diagonal of Section 13, about deciding
a property of every program. Neither forbids a machine checking a proof about a
checker, so keeping that proof outside is a choice. Nor does it ask the checker to be
something a machine could run. Clause (b) wants a yes or no for every claim at every
state, sound for the claim’s meaning, and nothing in it says that answer has to be
computable. Every instance in this book has a checker that’s an actual program, so
anything those machines certify could be listed by a program that runs them. Inside
Coq with no extra assumptions that’s all there can be, since every checker you can
write there is a program, the same point I made about what “undecidable” means
in the library. An oracle gets in two other ways: read the definition as ordinary
mathematics, where any function counts, or add an axiom that hands Coq a function
knowing which programs run forever. Hand the definition a checker like that and it’s
still met, and the machine certifies claims no program could ever confirm. Nothing
in this book builds one. So “a Thiele-complete machine certifies exactly the claims a
program could list” is true only with “and its checker is computable” added, and the
definition doesn’t require that.

One word needs pinning before the theorems, using the three names set at the front of
the book. In clause (c), the exact toll is instruction-exact pricing: each of the three acts,
CHECK and COMMIT included, costs exactly one, so the ledger counts the acts that
make a claim. Back in Section 6, one of the cited results (a2_and_aara_iff_exac
t) is about rise-only pricing in its tightest bill, the exact schedule: one mark on the step
that raises the flag and nothing on any other step. Measured against the flag alone,
the small machine isn’t rise-only, since CHECK and COMMIT raise no flag and cost
one each; measured the way (c) asks, it is instruction-exact. Neither is wrong. They
answer different questions: does the ledger count the acts, or does it charge the flag
and only the flag? Simulation-exact accounting, the third name, comes up with the
universal program U below.


Theorem 16.18 (What every Thiele-complete machine has). Let a machine be Thiele-
complete through an interface. (1) It obeys the toll and has a universal base, so it’s weakly
Thiele-complete; its base runs every two-counter program step for step from every live state,


                                            272
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


and halting from a loaded state matches halting from the configuration it shows. (2) Along
any run, the ledger rises by exactly the number of CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY moves
in it. (3) A run from a clean state that ends with the record up contains at least three of those
moves and raises the ledger by at least 3. (4) Some CHECK fails at some loaded state, on a
claim that is false there, and some run from some loaded state raises the record. (5) On a run
from a clean state, the move that raises the record is a CERTIFY. (6) Every move costs 0 or 1,
and some move costs 0.

Proof. (1) A raise of the record isn’t made by a base move, by (a), so it’s a record move,
which costs one by (c). Running a program on the base is induction on its steps, each
matched by (a). (2) is (c), added up along the run. (3) Clause (b) finds a CHECK, a
COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different places, and (2) counts them. (4) is (d): the
three moves certify exactly where the claim holds, the claim fails at some loaded state,
and the check can’t pass there because (b) says a passing check means the claim holds;
at the loaded state where it holds, the three moves raise the record. (5) Clause (b) puts
the record down right before a CERTIFY and up right after it, and the record never
comes down, so that CERTIFY is the first and only move where it rises. (6) Every
move is a base move or a record move, and (a) supplies base moves.

Checked as thiele_complete_is_weak, base_runs_every_program, base_
halting_correspondence, ledger_counts_record_moves, certificate_
costs_three, check_can_fail, some_run_certifies, only_certify_rai
ses, complete_costs_at_most_one and complete_has_free_move (Thiele-
Complete.v).

Each item in the proof names the clause it comes from, and that’s all the definition
gives. A Thiele-complete machine needn’t have a fact table, a CHECK that traps
when it fails, a COMMIT that looks anything up, or claims about counters. The
definition asks for an earned chain on the runs that raise the record and leaves the rest
to the machine. So the small machine’s table provenance, its trap, and its channel are
facts about that machine, and they don’t carry over to every machine that meets the
definition. Its claims can be any labels its interface names, and its checker can be an
oracle, as the paragraph above says.

The second half of (6), that some move costs 0, is the one that kills the clock.


Theorem 16.19 (A clock is a Thiele machine and isn’t Thiele-complete). Take the two-
counter machine, let every move cost 1, and take as the record any yes/no question about its
configuration whatsoever; or take a flag that switches on, and stays on, the first time any
chosen test of the configuration says yes. Either way the machine obeys the toll and has a
universal base, so it’s weakly Thiele-complete, and it is not Thiele-complete. More generally,
no machine whose every move costs at least 1 is Thiele-complete.




                                              273
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Proof. Every move costs one, so any raise costs at least one: the toll holds for any
record. The machine’s own moves are the two-counter instructions, which gives the
universal base. But a Thiele-complete machine has a free move, by Theorem 16.18(6),
and this one has none.

Checked as clock_weakly_thiele_complete, clock_not_thiele_complet
e, latch_clock_weakly_thiele_complete and latch_clock_not_thiele_
complete (ThieleComplete.v).

That’s short, and it’s short because clause (c) does exactly the job it was written for:
it says computing is free, and a clock charges for computing. The other clauses earn
their keep too, and that’s worth checking, because a definition with a clause nothing
needs is a definition hiding something.


Theorem 16.20 (Each clause does work). (1) Take a free two-counter base with a ledger
beside it, and one extra move TICK that costs 1 and raises a flag. It obeys the toll, and read
with TICK as CERTIFY it meets the universal base clause and the exact toll clause; it is not
Thiele-complete, and more generally no machine with a move that raises the record from every
state is. (2) Take a free two-counter base and a record that never rises. It obeys the toll and
meets clauses (a), (b) and (c); it is not Thiele-complete, and more generally no machine whose
record never rises is.

Proof. (1) From a clean state, TICK alone raises the record. Clause (b) would need a
CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY inside that one-move run, and one move can’t
be three. (2) Clause (d) needs a run from some loaded state that raises the record, and
none does.

Checked as paid_latch_weakly_thiele_complete, paid_latch_meets_b
ase_and_toll, paid_latch_not_thiele_complete, one_move_record_e
xcluded, silent_weakly_thiele_complete, silent_meets_base_recor
d_toll, silent_not_thiele_complete and never_certifies_excluded
(ThieleComplete.v).

The paid latch is the receipt for nothing from the opening chapter, wearing a universal
base: honest about the price, silent about what was bought. The definition throws it
out.

Now the other direction. A definition nobody meets is as useless as one everybody
meets.


Theorem 16.21 (The small machine, the generic one and the sorted one are Thiele-com-
plete). (1) This chapter’s machine is Thiele-complete, read with INC and DEC as base moves,
CHECK p c and COMMIT p c as record moves on the claim “p holds of c,” CERTIFY as

The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


clean states as clean starts and the ledger as µ. (2) So is the same machine over any property
language with an exact equality test and a checker proved to mean what it says, as long as
some property is true of one number and false of another. (3) In particular the machine whose
property is “this counter, read as a list, is sorted” is Thiele-complete. (4) Every Thiele-complete

ter’s machine, that system agrees step for step and cost for cost with the one of Theorem 16.6,

Proof. (1) Clause (a) is Theorem 16.2 together with the step line: INC and DEC never
touch the flag, and the flag never comes down. Clause (b) is Theorem 16.9 with checker

Checked as earned_core_thiele_complete, earned_generic_thiele_com
