ees (EarnedGenericLinks.v).

And here’s the thing every machine that meets the definition can’t help doing. It’s
Section 7’s shape again, only this time it isn’t about one machine. It’s about all of them.


Theorem 16.22 (Every Thiele-complete machine hides its record and its ledger from its
window). Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an interface, and let its window be the
two-counter configuration its universal base shows. (1) For every state s there’s a loaded state
and one free base move from it that lands on a state with s’s window, with the record down and
the ledger unchanged. (2) There’s a loaded state and two runs from it that end with the same
window, one with the record up and one with it down; and likewise two runs from one loaded
state that end with the same window and ledgers at least 3 apart. (3) So no function of the
window gives the record at the end of every run from every loaded state, and no function of the
window gives the ledger. (4) The same holds of the certification system built from the machine.

Proof. Theorem 16.18(4) gives a loaded state and a run from it that raises the record,
and (3) says that run paid at least 3. Say it ends with window (line ℓ, x, y). Two-counter
instructions can steer any configuration to any other: empty A, fill it to x + 1, empty
B, fill it to y, then one DEC of A that jumps to line ℓ. Those are base moves, so from
the same loaded state they reach the same window, cost nothing, and leave the record
down, by (a) and (c). That’s two runs, one window, two records and two ledgers,
which is (2). A function of the window would have to give both answers on that one



                                               275
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


window, which is (3). For (1), load ( x + 1, y) and take just the last DEC. (4) is (3) read
through the certification system, whose runs are the machine’s.

Checked as complete_every_window_printed, complete_hides_record, co
mplete_hides_ledger, complete_no_record_oracle, complete_no_ledg
er_oracle and thiele_complete_hides (ThieleCompleteWindow.v), and comp
lete_cs_window_blind (EarnedGenericLinks.v).

The observer in that theorem sees one thing, the final window. An observer who
sees the window before and after each step, or the whole trace of windows, or who
is also handed the program and the start, is a different observer, and the collision
says nothing about them; given the program and the start, the run is fixed and so is
its record. The theorem’s two runs also start from the same loaded state, so they’re
reachable witnesses, which is stronger than two arbitrary states that happen to look
alike. And “no function of the window gives the record” is all it says. It doesn’t say
the window tells you nothing about it.

Notice how little that took, and say it out loud so nobody mistakes it for more. It’s the
fibre fact from Section 7 plus one observation: a universal base can print any window
for free. Which is the point. The window here is everything a Turing machine would
call the machine, the line and the counters. On a Thiele-complete machine, that’s
never enough to tell you what was established or what it cost, and it can’t be, because
computing is free and can’t touch the record. A richer window, one that shows the
flag, is a different window, and nothing above says it fails.

16.13 One machine that runs them all
The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it
pays for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for all of them,
the way Turing’s universal machine stands in for every Turing machine. Here’s what
I mean by that. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine running one fixed
program that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s record
kept and the guest’s toll collected by the host’s own steps. No program running on
the host has to keep a convention for it.

And I want it the hard way. The easy way is to give the host a move that means “take
one step of the guest,” and then “it runs any guest” is true because I wrote it that way.
There’s a host like that two subsections on, after the two programs, and it’s useful
as a picture. It isn’t Turing’s kind of universal. Turing’s universal machine has no
instruction for “do what the machine on the tape would do.” It has the same kind of
instructions every other Turing machine has, and one fixed table, and the table does
the reading and the deciding and the carrying out. That’s the bar here: one fixed
program, written in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction, with no step of
the guest built into anything.

Turing’s own explanation is worth having in your head, because the program below

                                           276
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


copies its shape. In the 1936 paper the universal machine’s tape starts with the machine
to imitate, written out as a string of letters, its standard description, and after it the
imitated machine’s complete configurations, one after another: where its head is, what
state it’s in, what’s on its tape. To take one step, the universal machine finds the last
configuration, looks through the description line by line, comparing, until it finds the
line for that state and that symbol, and then writes out the next configuration the way
that line says. Then it goes back and does it again. It leaves marks on squares so it
doesn’t lose its place. Every bit of that is ordinary instructions on an ordinary tape,
and nothing in its table knows any particular machine.

Turing’s universal program came first on paper, and one that people actually came
to use arrived through the side door. John McCarthy, who had started the artificial
intelligence project at MIT with Minsky, was writing up his new language Lisp around
1960 and wanted to show it was neater than Turing machines, so he wrote a universal
function for it, eval, the language describing how to evaluate itself, and argued it
was shorter and easier to follow than a universal Turing machine. In his own history
of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing to read; the notation for writing programs
as data was made up for the paper with no thought of using it in practice. Then
Steve Russell (S. R. Russell in McCarthy’s account), a programmer on that MIT project,
noticed that eval could serve as an interpreter and coded it by hand, and there was a
running language with an interpreter that nobody had planned. McCarthy adds that
the surprise froze some decisions he’d made “rather lightheartedly” for the paper. So
the trick has a habit: written to be read, it ends up being run. The program below goes
the other way round, on purpose. It’s written to run, and the proofs check that what
runs is what the page says.

The host. The program runs on a machine with the small machine’s instructions
and the small machine’s prices: INC, DEC, HALT for free, and CHECK, COMMIT,
CERTIFY for one each, with the same table of sixteen facts, the same channel, trap,
ledger and flag. One change: it has a counter for every whole number, each with its
own version, where the small machine had two. No new kind of instruction, no new
price.


Definition 16.8 (The host machine). The host machine is the machine of Definition 16.3
with one change: it has a counter, with its version, for every whole number r (a
register), and INC r, DEC r j, CHECK p r and COMMIT p r name one register each. Its
property language has one property, Slot. Write ⟨m, n⟩ for the number (2n + 1) · 2m ;
every positive number is ⟨m, n⟩ for exactly one pair, and 0 is no pair. Number the
small machine’s properties Zero 7→ 0, Even 7→ 1, Ge(n) 7→ n + 2. The checker of Slot
says yes at a value x exactly when x = ⟨m, v⟩ and the small machine’s checker says
yes to the property numbered m at v; its meaning is the same with holds in place of
the checker.




                                           277
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Defined as the machine of EarnedMulti.v, with pair, unpair, pcode, heval and hh
olds (UniversalCodes.v).

There’s one place the guest’s machine shows up in the host. The host’s single property
knows how to read the small machine’s three-word property language: “this number
is the pair (property, value) and the property holds of the value.” It doesn’t know
the small machine’s step. That’s the counter version of Turing’s universal machine
knowing the alphabet its guests write in.

Two facts that force the design. Why more counters? Because of two facts, and the
program looks the way it does because of them.

The first is about reading. On this machine a program that wants a counter’s value
in its own control flow has to take pebbles out (DEC) and put them back (INC), and
every INC, and every DEC on a counter above 0, is a write, so the counter’s version
goes up. A fact is about one version, so a read done that way kills every live fact about
the counter. Not every look is a write: CHECK reads a value without writing it, a
DEC on 0 changes no version, and a fresh CHECK after such a read can make a new
live fact. But the guest’s counters are exactly the ones the host has to read by taking
pebbles out, again and again, to decide which way a DEC jumps and to work out a
property’s answer, and each of those reads kills whatever fact was kept there. So the
host can’t keep the guest’s facts on its copies of the guest’s counters.

The second says that even if reading were free, a fixed program couldn’t. It’s the
pigeonhole.


Theorem 16.23 (No host fact on an exact copy of the guest’s counter). Take any host
property language with an exact equality test and any checker, a finite list Q of host properties,
and any translation of the small machine’s properties into members of Q whose host check
passes whenever the guest’s check passes on the same number. Then there are n ̸= m, with
Ge(n) and Ge(m) translated to the same host property, such that the guest program CHECK
Ge(n) A; COMMIT Ge(m) A traps within two steps from every start, while on every host
state with the trap down and room in its table, and some register holding a number at least n,
the translated CHECK and COMMIT on that register both pass and put the committed claim
in the channel.

Proof. A fixed program mentions finitely many properties, so Q is finite, and the
translation sends the infinitely many Ge(0), Ge(1), . . . into it: two of them land on
the same member. The guest’s COMMIT asks for Ge(m), and its table can only hold
Ge(n), so it traps (or its CHECK already trapped). The host sees one property twice:
its CHECK passes, since the guest’s would, and its COMMIT finds exactly what that
CHECK wrote.

Checked as pigeonhole_collision and no_exact_copy_host (UniversalNo-


                                               278
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Copy.v), with the same statement on the host’s certification system as multi_cs_no
_exact_copy (UniversalInterpreterLinks.v).

So the host keeps the guest’s facts somewhere else: in slots, extra registers used for
nothing but holding facts, one per checked fact, each holding the pair (property num-
ber, value) that the guest checked. The pigeonhole doesn’t bite a slot, because the
property lives in the slot’s number. The instruction doesn’t have to carry it: CHECK
Slot on a slot asks about whatever pair is sitting there, and there are infinitely many
pairs. A slot is written only when the program is moving a fact into it. And when
the guest writes the counter a fact was about, the program gives every slot about that
counter a nudge, one INC and one DEC, which leaves the number alone and pushes
the version up, so the host’s facts go stale at exactly the moment the guest’s do.

The program. Here’s U the way Turing would describe it, one register at a time and
then one job at a time. Registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and B. Register 2 holds
the guest’s whole program as one number: each instruction gets a number (an opcode
paired with its operands, INC as 0, DEC as 1, HALT as 2, CHECK as 3, COMMIT as 4,
CERTIFY as 5), and the list of them is packed with ⟨·, ·⟩, the empty list as 0. Register 3
is the guest’s line. Registers 4 to 13 are scratch. Registers 14 and 15 count how many
CHECKs on A and on B have passed. Registers 16 to 47 are mirrors, sixteen for each
guest counter, and registers 48 to 79 are the slots, sixteen for each guest counter. The
guest’s table holds sixteen facts in total, across both counters, and all sixteen can be
about one counter, so the host gives each counter room for all of them. That’s a host
reservation, and the guest’s own capacity stays sixteen in all. Register 80 is a dead end
that’s never written.

Each guest step goes like this. At line 1 the program copies the program number and
the guest’s line into scratch, putting the originals back as it goes, because copying
a counter on this machine means emptying it into two others and refilling it. If the
guest’s line is 0, or past the end of the program, it stops. Otherwise it peels instructions
off the front of the copy, one per line, until it holds the one at the guest’s line, and
splits that into opcode and operands. Then a chain of DECs on the opcode sends it to
one of six handlers.

   • INC c: INC the guest’s counter c, nudge every slot about c and zero its mirrors,
     add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.
   • DEC c j: DEC the guest’s counter c. If it was 0, add one to the guest’s line. If it
     wasn’t, nudge every slot about c, zero its mirrors, and set the guest’s line to j.
     Back to line 1.
   • HALT: stop.
   • CHECK p c: let k be the count of passed CHECKs on c. If k is below 16, build
     ⟨number of p, value of c⟩ in slot k of c, run CHECK Slot on that slot, set its mirror
     to the number of p plus one, add one to the count and to the guest’s line, and go


                                            279
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


      back to line 1. If k is 16, run CHECK Slot on the dead end, which holds 0, which
      is no pair, so it traps, just as the guest’s seventeenth CHECK does.
   • COMMIT p c: look through the sixteen mirrors of c for one equal to the number
     of p plus one. At the first match, run COMMIT Slot on that slot. With no match,
     run COMMIT Slot on the dead end, which traps.
   • CERTIFY: run CERTIFY, add one to the guest’s line, back to line 1.

Why the mirrors? COMMIT has to find the slot holding the claim, and it can’t read
the slot to find out, because reading would make the fact stale. So beside every slot
sits a mirror the program is allowed to read: the property’s number plus one while
the slot’s fact is live, 0 once the guest has written the counter. If a guest CHECK fails,
the host’s CHECK on the slot fails too, since the slot holds exactly the pair the guest
checked, and both machines trap.

Count what costs anything. Fetching, unpacking, copying, nudging, branching: all
INC and DEC, all free, the way computing is free on the small machine. The only paid
instructions are the CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY sites, and each guest CHECK,
COMMIT or CERTIFY makes the program run exactly one of them. So the host’s
ledger lands on the guest’s, mark for mark. And when the guest’s flag goes up, the
host’s goes up by the host’s own CERTIFY, standing on the host’s own COMMIT and
CHECK on a slot. It isn’t copying a bit. It runs the same chain on its own registers.


Definition 16.9 (The program U, and loading a guest). U is the fixed list of 3728
host instructions described above, starting at line 1 and mentioning registers 0 to 80;
exactly 69 of them cost anything. For a guest program P and a start ( x, y), the loaded
host hload( P, x, y) has register 0 at x, register 1 at y, register 2 at the number of P,
register 3 at 1 and every other register at 0, every version 0, line 1, an empty table and
channel, the trap down, ledger 0 and flag down. Write grun(m) for m program steps
of P from start( x, y), and hrun(n) for n program steps of U from hload( P, x, y).


Defined as U, hload, prog_code, grun and hrun (UniversalLayout.v, Universal-
Sim.v, UniversalRun.v, and UniversalCodes.v for prog_code), with the 69 paid sites
listed exactly by U_paid_sites (UniversalLayout.v).


Theorem 16.24 (U keeps pace with its guest). For every guest program P, start ( x, y) and
number of guest steps m, there’s a number of host steps n such that one of two things holds.
Either the host is back at line 1 with m ≤ n and related to the guest: registers 0 and 1 hold
the guest’s A and B, register 3 holds the guest’s line, the guest’s trap is down, the two ledgers
are equal, the two flags are equal, and the host’s table and channel hold, fact for fact, slot facts
matching the guest’s facts and channel. Or both have stopped, with the same counters, the
same trap, the same ledger, the same flag, and matching tables and channels. And from any
related pair where the guest hasn’t stopped, one guest step is matched by at least one host step


                                                280
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


that lands related again, or with both stopped.

Proof. The one-step part is a case for each thing the guest can do at its line: stop; INC;
DEC, taken or not; CHECK, passing, failing, or with a full table; COMMIT, found or
not; CERTIFY, passing or not. For each, the matching stretch of U is proved to land
where the case says. The relation carries the bookkeeping that makes the next case go
through: each count register equals the number of slots in use for its counter, each slot
in use holds (property number, checked value), a slot’s fact is current exactly when
the matching guest fact is, a live slot’s mirror is the property’s number plus one and a
stale one’s is 0, and unused slots, unused mirrors and the dead end are 0. A freshly
loaded host is related to the guest’s start. The run statement is induction on m.

Checked as hload_rel and U_step (UniversalSim.v), and U_simulation (Univer-
salRun.v).


Theorem 16.25 (Halting and answers match). For every P, x and y, the guest’s run of
P from start( x, y) halts if and only if U’s run from hload( P, x, y) halts. And whenever the
guest has halted at step m and U at step n, the host’s registers 0 and 1 hold the guest’s A and
B, and the two traps, the two ledgers and the two flags are equal.

Proof. Theorem 16.24: a halted guest is matched by a stopped host, and a host that has
stopped can’t be back at line 1 with the guest still running, because line 1 isn’t a stop.
A halted machine stays halted, so the two halting points carry the same values.

Checked as universal_halting and universal_output (UniversalRun.v).


Theorem 16.26 (The host’s flag is the guest’s, and its ledger is exact). (1) The guest’s
flag is up at some step of its run if and only if the host’s flag is up at some step of
U’s run. (2) For every m there’s an n at which the two are related, with m ≤ n, or
both stopped, with µ(hrun(n)) = µ(grun(m)). And for every n there’s an m with
µ(grun(m)) ≤ µ(hrun(n)) ≤ µ(grun(m + 1)): in between matching points, the host’s
ledger never gets ahead of the guest’s next step.

Proof. (1) Flags are equal at matching points and never come down. (2) Ledgers are
equal at matching points; inside the stretch of U that runs one guest instruction, at
most the one paid site of that instruction runs, so the host’s ledger sits between the
guest’s before and after it.

Checked as universal_flag_iff and universal_ledger_exact (Universal-
Run.v).

That’s a third sense of “exact,” and it’s the plainest of the three: two ledgers, one
number.

Theorem 16.27 (The host earns its own flag). If the host’s flag is up after n steps of U from
hload( P, x, y), then the instructions U executed contain, in order, a passing CHECK Slot on
a slot, then a passing COMMIT Slot on the same slot, with the slot untouched and its version
unchanged in between, then a passing CERTIFY; the slot held ⟨number of p, v⟩ at the CHECK,
with holds( p, v). And the guest’s own run from start( x, y) contains a passing CHECK p c,
then, with c untouched and its version unchanged, a passing COMMIT p c, then a passing
CERTIFY, with c holding v at its CHECK.

Proof. By Theorem 16.26 the guest’s flag rises too; find the guest step where it rises, a
passing CERTIFY, and the related host point just before it. The guest’s channel there
names a fact, and the relation says the host’s channel names the matching slot fact. The
host’s own flag rises at its own first passing CERTIFY, and nothing paid runs between
the related point and that CERTIFY, so the host’s channel hasn’t moved: it names that
slot fact. The host machine’s version of Theorem 16.9 gives the host’s CHECK and
COMMIT on that slot. The record kept with the slot says what pair it held and when,
and the checker’s meaning gives holds( p, v). The same theorem on the guest’s run,
up to the step where its flag rose, gives the guest’s chain on the same p and c, and the
record says c held v at its CHECK.

Checked as universal_earned (UniversalRun.v).


Theorem 16.28 (The host is Thiele-complete, and U’s halting is undecidable). (1) The
host machine, with Slot as its property and one move per instruction, is Thiele-complete
(Definition 16.7), and U’s run from hload( P, x, y) is a run of it. (2) Read as a certification
system it obeys the universal floor; a run of U that raises the host’s flag costs at least 3 there.
The system built from its Thiele-completeness agrees with it step for step and cost for cost, so
the same run costs at least 3 on that one too, and the universal floor of 1 holds there directly.
(3) U halts from hload( P, x, y) exactly when P halts from start( x, y), so the question “does
U halt from this loaded host?” is undecidable in the library’s sense of Theorem 16.4.

Proof. (1) The base is registers 0 and 1, run by INC and DEC; the claims are “Slot
holds of register r”; the rest is the host machine’s own versions of the small machine’s
theorems, and for non-vacuity, register 0 loaded with 1, which is ⟨0, 0⟩, the pair of Zero
and 0, against register 0 loaded with 0, which is no pair. (2) is Theorem 16.21(4) and
Theorem 16.27. (3) is Theorem 16.25, and the identity map reduces the small machine’s
halting question, undecidable by Theorem 16.4, to this one.

Checked as universal_thiele_complete and U_run_on_host_machine (Uni-
versalRun.v), and multi_cs_floor, interp_U_certified_floor, interp_U_
complete_floor, interp_complete_agrees, interp_halting_iff and int
erp_halting_undecidable (UniversalInterpreterLinks.v).

Put it together, plainly. One fixed program, 3728 instructions of the small machine’s six
kinds, with no guest step built into anything, runs every program of the small machine
from every clean start start( x, y). It halts exactly when its guest halts, with the guest’s
answer in its first two registers. Its flag goes up at some step of its run exactly when
the guest’s goes up at some step of the guest’s run, by its own check, its own commit
and its own certificate. Its ledger is the guest’s, mark for mark, wherever the two line
up. And the machine it runs on is Thiele-complete. Since the small machine runs
every two-counter program, U runs every computation. That’s the universal Thiele
machine of this book, for the small machine’s programs; the next subsection carries it
to every computably presented Thiele machine.

The fine print, before you take that anywhere. The guests start clean, from start( x, y);
the whole-run theorems are about loaded hosts, and only the one-step theorem is about
any related pair. The host’s property reads the small machine’s three-word language,
so a guest with a different property language needs a different host property; the host
of the next subsection has one, a single property that reads a universal claim language.
Sixteen slots per counter is the guest’s whole table size, reserved for each counter in
case every fact is about that one. And it’s slow: every guest step unpacks the program
number from the front, on a machine where copying a number means moving it a
pebble at a time.

Enforcement in the step is the reference monitor’s move from the opening chapter,
Anderson’s 1972 move: one mechanism everything has to pass through. What’s put
together here is a priced, earned record under that move, carried to every guest by
one fixed program. The move itself is Anderson’s. Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and
Fred Schneider (2006) worked out, in their model, which policies mechanisms like
that can enforce at all, and their paper is where I’d go to see why enforcing a property
of every run escapes the Rice-style walls that deciding one runs into.

Why make such a fuss about proofs that walk every case? Because the first universal
machine had bugs. It’s the machine in Turing’s 1936 paper, and nobody gets to call
Turing careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a problem of Thue,
pointed out that the construction leaned on a convention it hadn’t earned, and he
patched a small defect in how the universal machine writes out each complete con-
figuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined the National Physical
Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer, worked through the
universal machine’s tables and found more mistakes, much to Turing’s annoyance, as
the accounts of Davies’s life have it. (It’s the same Davies who later named the packet
in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed in a collection edited by Jack
Copeland, a philosopher and historian of computing who runs an archive of Turing’s
papers, The Essential Turing, in 2004. They may be some of the first bugs ever written,
in a program for a computer that didn’t exist yet. That’s a lovely claim and a hard one
to check, so take it as a lead. I can’t give it to you as a fact. What it changes here: a
universal machine is exactly the kind of construction where a careful person leaves a


                                            283
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


hole, U has 3728 lines for a hole to hide in, and its theorems are checked by Coq one
case at a time, which is the kind of check that catches Davies’s kind of slip. It doesn’t
catch a definition that says the wrong thing. That’s why the definitions are on the
page, for you.

16.14 Every computably presented Thiele machine, on one host
U runs the small machine’s programs, and through them every computation. But
a Thiele machine from somewhere else has its own states, its own moves, its own
prices and its own reading, and running it through the two-counter encoding keeps
its computation and nothing else. So the question Turing’s machine raises for this
book is the bigger one. Take any Thiele machine whose workings can be computed. Is
there one fixed program that runs every such machine as a guest, keeping its halting,
raising its own flag exactly when the guest’s reading would rise, on an earned chain
of its own, and keeping a ledger equal to the guest’s own prices, with the host’s flat
ones nowhere in it? There is, within limits I’ll list, and here it is.

First the class, said plainly. A computably presented Thiele machine is a certification
system in Section 3’s sense (states, moves, a step, a price for each move, a yes/no
reading) together with a driver that picks the next move from the current state or says
stop, and a way of writing states and moves as whole numbers. “Computably” means
four little programs, written in the plainest language of computable functions there
is, the one built from zero, plus one, picking an argument, composing, recursion and
search: one computes the driver, one the step, one the price, and one the reading, and
the reading’s program answers yes or no on every state there is. Run from a start s0 ,
the driver’s moves give one run. Its ledger after n moves is the sum of their prices, and
its latch after n moves says whether the reading has been yes at any state so far.

The host gets one thing the small machine doesn’t have: a paid move that certifies
nothing. On the small machine every charge comes from a CHECK, a COMMIT or
a CERTIFY, and those can bill seven: one passing CHECK and six COMMITs of the
same claim cost seven and raise no flag. But every passing CHECK takes one of the
table’s sixteen entries for good, every COMMIT rewrites the channel, and a failing
CHECK traps. So the host machine gets a seventh instruction kind, PAY: it costs one,
goes to the next line, and changes nothing else; it never raises the flag, takes no table
entry and leaves the channel alone. That’s why the compiler uses it.

How far the small machine gets without it is proved, and the count is short. Take
a run that never traps and ends with the flag down. No CERTIFY ran in it, since a
passing one raises the flag and a failing one traps. Every CHECK in it passed, since
a failing one traps, and each passing CHECK filled one of the table’s sixteen entries,
so there were at most sixteen. Every COMMIT in it committed a claim the table holds,
and the table holds at most sixteen, so at most sixteen COMMITs can be of claims the
run hadn’t committed before. That’s 32, and the only way past it is a COMMIT of a
claim already committed earlier in the run (pf_bound_start, PayFree.v). A claim


                                          284
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


names its counter’s version, and the version changes at every write, so a repeat needs
its counter left alone since the earlier COMMIT. A guest whose every move writes its
counters can’t do that, so it runs out of ways to pay after 32 (pf_no_repeat_boun
d). A simulated program that runs longer than that has to bill somewhere, and PAY
is where. Whether some other host without PAY could do the same job is a question I
haven’t settled, and I don’t claim it.

The definition of Thiele-complete sorts every paid move into CHECK, COMMIT or
CERTIFY, so PAY has to be filed under one of them, and it’s filed as a CHECK of the
empty claim, a claim that never holds. That’s a filing for the interface. It isn’t what
PAY does on the machine: a CHECK that fails on this machine traps, and PAY goes on
to the next line. With PAY filed that way the host stays Thiele-complete (pu_unive
rsal_thiele_complete, UniversalPRun.v), and its floor of three for a flag raised
from a clean start still holds with PAY present (pu_multi_certified_run_min_c
ost, EarnedMultiPriced.v).

The program is U with one more handler: a seventh branch on the guest’s opcode, for
PAY, that runs the host’s own PAY once. Call it UP ; it’s 3735 instructions, with 70 paid
sites, the 69 of U plus the PAY. The guest it runs is a program of the small machine with
PAY added, and that guest is where the presented machine goes. Its four programs
are compiled into two counters, by the packing Minsky used, with the undecidability
library’s compiler from computable functions to counter machines doing the hard
part; the guest keeps the presented machine’s state coded in its counter B, takes one
of its moves by running the compiled step, pays the move’s price in PAYs, and, when
the compiled reading says yes, checks, commits and certifies. The host’s one property
is fixed too: a claim is either one of the small machine’s three words about a number,
or “run reading program r on the coded state v,” and the host’s checker evaluates that
with one fixed routine for every presented machine there is. So nothing in UP knows
any particular presented machine. The machine arrives as data, the way Turing’s
guests arrived on the tape.

A fixed checker that runs whatever program it’s handed and always answers needs
saying how, so here is the routine. A claim of the second kind carries a number r. The
checker decodes r as a counter-machine routine: its instructions, where they sit, which
register holds the answer, which register holds the fuel, and how many registers to
load. If r doesn’t decode to a routine, the answer is no. Otherwise the checker loads
the routine’s registers from v, reads a fuel number f out of v too (the fuel register’s
entry in v’s prime factorisation), runs the routine for at most f steps, and says yes
exactly when by then the routine has left its code with 1 in its answer register. Every
input gets an answer within f steps, so the checker is total, and what it means is that
bounded run: yes if and only if the routine halts within the fuel the value carries, with
answer 1 (cg_ueval_total and cg_ueval_iff, CompilerChecker.v, through the
host’s one property pu_heval, UniversalPCodes.v). That’s how it stays clear of the
diagonal. A total evaluator E that agreed with every total yes-or-no program on that


                                          285
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


program’s code alone would let g(n) = ¬ E(n, n) contradict itself at its own code. This
checker never evaluates a program on its code alone: the fuel comes with the claim’s
value. The guest compiled from M runs M’s reading routine itself and puts at least
the step count it took into the fuel register, and at such a value the checker says yes if
and only if the reading says yes (cg_checker_exact).


Theorem 16.29 (One host runs every computably presented Thiele machine). Let M be
a computably presented Thiele machine and s0 a start state. Load UP with the guest compiled
from M’s presentation and s0 coded in. Then: (1) UP halts exactly when M’s run stops. (2)
For every n such that M hasn’t stopped before move n, there’s a host time t at which the host’s
register for the guest’s counter B decodes to M’s state after n moves, the host’s ledger is M’s
ledger after n moves plus a surcharge, and the host’s flag is M’s latch after n moves; and if
M stops at n, such a t has UP halted as well. (3) The host’s flag is up at some time exactly
when M’s reading is yes at some state of its run. (4) If the host’s flag is up at time t, the host’s
own instructions up to t contain a passing CHECK on a slot, then a passing COMMIT on the
same slot with the slot untouched in between, then a passing CERTIFY; and the slot held the
claim “reading program r says yes of v” for M’s own reading program r, that claim holds, and
v decodes to a state of M’s run where the reading is yes.

Proof. Two layers, each proved on its own. The bottom layer is the compiler: for every
presented machine, its guest program’s run passes through points that code M’s states
in order, with the guest’s ledger equal to M’s ledger plus the surcharge and the guest’s
flag equal to M’s latch, and the guest’s own flag stands on an earned chain whose
claim is M’s reading program applied to the coded state where the reading first said
yes. The top layer is UP , proved the way U was in the previous theorems, with the PAY
case added: it keeps pace with any guest of this kind, halting and flag matched, ledger
equal at matching points, and its flag earned on a slot. Compose the two. The earned
part takes one more step: the host’s chain gives a guest CHECK that passed, and a
guest run that ends with its flag up has exactly one passing CHECK, the compiler’s
CHECK of the reading on counter B. So the guest CHECK the host’s chain points to is
that one, and its claim is M’s reading at the first state where it said yes.

Checked as presented_universal (PresentedUniversal.v), whose five parts are
also stated separately as presented_universal_halting, presented_univer
sal_points, presented_universal_halt_point, presented_universal_
flag_iff and presented_universal_earned; the host layer is pu_universal
_halting, pu_universal_flag_iff, pu_universal_ledger_exact and pu_
universal_earned (UniversalPRun.v).

Two things the theorem doesn’t say. First, the host’s flag is M’s latch. If M’s reading
says yes at some state and no at a later one, the host’s flag stays up, so it says the
reading was yes somewhere in the run, and it doesn’t say the reading is yes now.
Second, what the host re-establishes is the reading: the claim it checked is “M’s reading


                                                286
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


program says yes of this coded state,” and that’s all. A bare certification system needn’t
tie its reading to anything true about sorting, proofs or the world outside. If M’s
reading is meant to say a list is sorted, that it does is a separate correctness theorem
about the reading, and the host doesn’t supply it. The two universal programs also
keep their own guests: U runs the small machine’s programs over its three words
about numbers, and UP runs computably presented machines over the universal
claim language.

Now the surcharge, because that’s where the ledger stops being exact, and it can’t be
helped. The host raises its flag the only way the host machine allows, by a CHECK, a
COMMIT and a CERTIFY, and those cost three. If M’s first move that turns its reading
to yes costs at least three, the host pays the difference in PAYs and nothing more is
owed. If it costs less, the host pays three there anyway, which is the larger of three
and the move’s price. The surcharge starts at that move: while M’s latch is down it’s
zero, so a run that never certifies is matched exactly. Whether anything could do better
depends on what M paid before. When M’s whole ledger at the raise is below three,
no program on the host machine can match it, since a raised host flag costs three from
a clean start. When M paid more than that earlier, nothing here says this compiler’s
surcharge is the least possible: part (1) of the theorem below bounds this compiler,
and part (3) is the only lower bound proved.


Theorem 16.30 (Exact, within two, and no better). Let M, s0 and the loaded host be as in
Theorem 16.29, and let M’s reading be no at s0 . (1) For every n before M stops there’s a host
time at which the host’s ledger lies between M’s ledger after n moves and that plus two, with
the state decoded and the flag matched as before. (2) If moreover every move that first turns
M’s reading to yes costs at least three, the surcharge is zero and the host’s ledger equals M’s
exactly at those times. (3) If M’s latch is up after n moves while its ledger is below three, then
no run of the host machine from a clean start, under any program at all, ends with its flag
equal to that latch and its ledger raised by exactly M’s ledger.

Proof. (1) and (2): the guest pays M’s prices in PAYs, a unit at a time, except at the
move where M’s reading first says yes. There it has to run its CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY, three units, and it makes up the rest of the move’s price in PAYs, so it pays
the larger of the price c and three. The price is at least one, because the move raised a
reading (the toll), so the excess is at most two, and none when c ≥ 3. (3): a raised flag
on the host machine costs at least three from a clean start, whatever the program, and
M’s ledger is less.

Checked as presented_universal_surcharge_le_two, presented_unive
rsal_exact and presented_universal_no_exact_below_three, with the
corollary for UP itself, presented_universal_U_no_exact_below_three (Pre-
sentedUniversal.v). If the reading is already yes at the start, the host has to raise its
flag at once, and that costs three on top of a ledger of nothing.


                                               287
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


And one machine carried all the way, by proof, so the class isn’t empty. Its states are
whole numbers, its one move adds one and costs three, its driver always picks that
move, and its reading is “at least three.” The four programs are written out from the
library’s building blocks and proved to compute those four things. Loaded into UP
from 0, the host never halts, its flag goes up, at the host time matching move n its
ledger is exactly 3n and its flag is up exactly when n ≥ 3, and the raised flag stands
on a host chain whose slot claims the machine’s own reading of a state at least three
(pu_demo_computably_presented, pu_demo_never_halts, pu_demo_flag_
rises, pu_demo_exact and pu_demo_earned, PresentedDemo.v). That’s proved.
Nothing executes UP on that guest.

Now the limits, each of which is in the statement, said plainly.

   • Readings that are decided. The reading’s program has to answer yes or no on
     every state. A reading a program could only confirm, waiting forever on the no
     cases, isn’t covered, and neither is a reading no program computes at all.
   • One run per start. The driver picks the move, so the guest is deterministic.
     A machine whose next move is somebody’s free choice gets in only with that
     choice written into its driver.
   • The record is the latch. The host’s flag is up once M’s reading has been yes at
     any state of the run, which is exactly the latch of Section 10. A reading that goes
     yes and then back to no is carried as “it was yes once.”
   • The ledger is exact up to the surcharge. When the reading starts at no, at most
     two, and zero when the first raising move costs three or more; when it starts at
     yes, three. And no program on this host, run from a clean start, can do better
     when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three.
   • Prices in whole units, paid one at a time. A move that costs a million is a million
     PAYs. Nothing here is fast, and the compiler’s packing is Minsky’s, so it’s slower
     still.
   • Proved; never run. The demonstration machine’s numbers come from theorems.
     Nobody has run UP on it: the files it lives in aren’t extracted, the compiled
     programs are far too big for any machine to step through, and some of the
     library’s pieces don’t compute inside the checker at all. Section 19 says what
     was run.

16.15 A simpler host, with the guest step built in
There’s a much simpler host than U, and I keep it in the book because it’s easy to read
and it shows the copy rule in one line. Its universality is by construction: it has a
move that runs one guest step by calling the small machine’s own step. So it isn’t the
universal Thiele machine of this book. U is. Read it as a picture of what U does the
long way, and as a host that starts from any guest state at all, clean or not.



                                          288
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest’s program as data, the guest’s counters,
its table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one guest step. In that
one move it looks at the guest’s flag, takes the step, looks again, and if the flag went
from down to up, the host’s own copy of that flag goes up in the same move, and the
host pays for it.


Definition 16.10 (The host). A guest is a program P of this chapter’s machine to-
gether with a state g of it (Definition 16.3). A host state h has six parts: its own
core core(h), its ledger µ(h), its own flag own(h), the guest program P(h) held as
a list of instructions, the guest state g(h), and the mirror m(h), a yes/no copy of
the guest’s flag. The host has two kinds of move. OWN i runs the instruction i
on the host’s own core, costs what this chapter’s machine charges for i, and raises
own exactly when that machine’s flag would rise. GSTEP b costs b. If the host’s
core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to its next line
and, if the guest’s next instruction costs at most b, runs that instruction on g(h);
in the same move the mirror becomes m(h) ∨ (¬cert( g(h)) ∧ cert( g′ )), where g′ is
the new guest state. The host’s reading is own(h) ∨ m(h). Its stored program is
U0 = [GSTEP 1; OWN (INC A); OWN (DEC A 1)]: one guest step, then two moves
that bring the host back to its first line. (The Coq file calls it U; I write U0 here so
nobody mixes it up with the universal program U.)


Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so GSTEP 1 runs every
guest instruction there is. Why charge the budget b? Why not the cost of whatever
instruction got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of the
move alone, which is what the certification system of Part II asks for: you read the
price of a host move off the move, the way you read the small machine’s prices off
its table, without peeking inside the guest. The bill for that is easy to see. A host that
steps a free guest instruction, an INC say, still pays one for the move.

So the host’s ledger is closer to a clock than to a receipt for its guests: one unit per
guest step, whatever the step was. It never falls behind the guest’s own bill (part (3)
of Theorem 16.33 below), and it matches that bill only when every guest step happens
to cost one. Could a cleverer host have simulation-exact accounting, a ledger equal
to its guest’s? Not with a price read off the move alone. GSTEP 1 is the same move
whether the guest’s next instruction is a free INC or a paid CHECK, so one price can’t
match both. A simulation-exact host has to be built the other way, with no guest step
to put a price on: that’s U, which pays only on the record moves it runs itself, so its
ledger equals its guest’s (Theorem 16.26).

And one thing about the definition before the theorems, so you know which of them
carry weight. GSTEP runs the guest’s instruction by calling the small machine’s own
step on the guest’s state: the guest’s step is a primitive of the host. So “the host runs
any guest” (Theorem 16.31) is true by construction. The host was built to do exactly


                                           289
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


that, and the proof is mostly unfolding. The theorems with something in them come
after it. From a loaded host, or any state where the two agree, the mirror always
equals the guest’s flag (Theorem 16.32). Nothing raises the mirror unless the guest
itself passes a CERTIFY inside a guest step the host paid for (Theorem 16.34). No
OWN move, in any host program at all, touches the guest’s state or the mirror (the
second sentence of that same theorem), and no host move of either kind rewrites the
guest’s program (hexec_gprog, UniversalThiele.v). And the mirror is tied to the
guest’s earned chain: after any host run from a loaded host, if the mirror is up, the
guest’s own run from its start contains a passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same
claim, then a CERTIFY (host_mirror_earned, UniversalThiele.v). So this host runs
any guest by construction and keeps the guest’s record by theorem, as a copy of the
guest’s flag. It never earns a flag of its own. U does both the long way: it runs the
guest with its own instructions, and it earns its own flag.


Theorem 16.31 (The host runs any guest). (1) If the host’s core is not trapped, then after
n moves GSTEP 1 the guest state is the guest program’s own run of n steps from g(h), the
guest program is unchanged, and the host is still not trapped. (2) If the host’s core is at line
1 and not trapped, then 3n steps of the program U0 leave the guest exactly where n steps of
its own program put it. (3) For every two-counter program M and inputs a, b: M halts from
(1, a, b) exactly when the host program made of OWN moves of the compiled M halts, from a
host whose core starts at ( a, b), whatever guest that host carries.

Proof. (1) Induction on n: a host that isn’t trapped stays untrapped through a guest
step, and with budget 1 the guest step is the guest’s own step. (2) One pass of U0
is a guest step, then INC A and DEC A back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3)
A host program made only of OWN moves is the small machine, core for core, and
Theorem 16.3 does the rest.

Checked as universal_simulation, universal_program_simulation and h
ost_thiele_complete (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 16.32 (The copy is the record). Say a host state h agrees when m(h) =
cert( g(h)). Every host move takes an agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host
trace and every stored host program does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In particular, if
h agrees and is not trapped, the mirror after n moves GSTEP 1 is the guest’s flag after n steps
of its own program.

Proof. One move at a time. An OWN move touches neither the mirror nor the guest. A
trapped GSTEP touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old mirror or
the crossing, and the guest’s flag is a latch (Theorem 16.5), so if the old mirror equalled
the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence is this together with
Theorem 16.31.



                                              290
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Checked as record_agreement_step, record_agreement, record_agreemen
t_program, hload_agrees and simulated_record (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 16.33 (The host’s step collects the guest’s toll). (1) If h agrees, is not trapped,
and the guest step that budget b allows takes the guest’s flag from down to up, then the mirror
is down before GSTEP b and up after it, the host’s ledger rose by exactly b, and b ≥ 1. (2) In
the run of (1) of Theorem 16.31, from a host that agrees, if the guest’s flag goes up between its
steps n and n + 1, the mirror goes up between the host’s moves n and n + 1, and that move
costs 1. (3) For every host trace t, µ( g(run(t, h))) + µ(h) ≤ µ(run(t, h)) + µ( g(h)): the
host’s ledger grows at least as fast as the guest’s.

Proof. (1) The guest’s flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem 16.5), which costs
1, and the budget let it run, so b ≥ 1; the mirror was the guest’s flag, so it was down,
and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3) Induction on
t: a guest step that runs costs the guest at most the budget the host paid, and every
other move leaves the guest’s ledger alone.

Checked as toll_enforced_by_host_step, every_guest_crossing_is_a_
host_crossing, host_pays_for_guest, host_cost_covers_guest and sim
ulated_cost (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 16.34 (No free host certification). If the mirror is down at h and up after a host
move i, then i is GSTEP b with b ≥ 1, the host was not trapped, the guest’s next instruction
was CERTIFY, and the guest’s flag went from down to up in that move. A trace made only
of OWN moves leaves the mirror and the guest state exactly where they were. And the host’s
own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY that passes on the host’s core.

Proof. An OWN move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped GSTEP does too,
so the rise is an untrapped GSTEP b whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by this chapter’s
step line.

Checked as no_free_host_certification_step, no_free_host_certific
ation, no_free_host_certification_program, guestless_runs_leave_
mirror and own_record_only_by_certify (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 16.35 (The host is a Thiele machine). For every host state and move, if the host’s
reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at least 1; the same holds for the mirror alone and
for the own flag alone. So the host read through own ∨ m, the host read through m alone, and
the guest class are certification systems (Definition 3.1), and any host trace that raises the
host’s reading costs at least 1.

The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Proof. The mirror’s half is Theorem 16.34; the own flag’s half is the small machine’s
toll on the host’s core. The trace form is Section 3’s universal floor.

Checked as host_toll, host_own_toll and host_mirror_toll (UniversalTh-

Remark 16.1 (Two guests, run). Load the guest CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY; HALT with both counters at 0. After two moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is
down; after three it is up, the guest’s flag is up, the host’s own flag is still down, and
the host has paid 3. Under the program U0 the mirror is down at host step 6 and up
at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five
moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for
nothing.


Checked as demo_certifies, demo_program_certifies and demo_forgery_
fails (UniversalThiele.v).

That copy can’t be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the copy only
rises in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A host program
that never touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was. From a loaded host
the copy always equals the guest’s flag, and the host’s ledger always grows at least
as fast as the guest’s, and a three-instruction loop runs any small-machine program
one guest step per pass. Here the mirror, the crossing test and the charge sit in the
host’s step rule, so Theorems 16.33 and 16.34 hold for every sequence of host moves,
including ones that never run a guest. That’s the simple version. Everything it gets
from its built-in move, U gets from ordinary instructions, plus an exact ledger and a
flag of its own.

16.16 The machine versus the program it runs
All three hosts in this chapter come down to one distinction, and it’s worth saying on
its own, because the two halves are easy to run together: the machine doing the stepping
(what the machine is) and the program it runs (what runs on it). The toll of Section 3 is
a property of the machine doing the stepping. A rule a program keeps holds as long
as the program keeps it.

Here’s the picture I keep for it. Play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The
game has a bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the
rules sheet: the Bank never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may
issue more by writing on any ordinary paper. Inside the game that’s fine; the players
agreed to it. The real bank’s teller, standing right there, has no opinion about any of it.
Push a thousand in Monopoly money across her counter and her ledger doesn’t move,
because her rules are about her own money. The game’s money is nothing to them.


                                           292
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


The real bank is the machine doing the stepping. The game is a program it happens to
be hosting. A rule that lives in the game holds as long as the players keep to it. A rule
that lives in the bank holds whatever the players do.

(And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that
an out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression.
The board is older. Elizabeth Magie, an American writer and game designer with
an economic argument about land to make, patented The Landlord’s Game in 1904,
with a square track, railroads and a square that sends you to jail, and in 1902, in The
Single Tax Review, described it as “a practical demonstration of the present system
of land-grabbing with all its usual outcomes and consequences.” Darrow sold his
version to Parker Brothers in 1935, and the company bought Magie’s patent for a few
hundred dollars, five hundred by the accounts I found. A story told by the company
selling the product is a lead to check, every time. It changes nothing about banks. It’s
a good reminder of who writes the story on the box.)

A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that includes
a Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and write a
table that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine obeys the
toll in its step relation. It’s an instance of the abstract certification system, so it can’t
be a counterexample to it. What it doesn’t do, built the ordinary way, is enforce the
toll on the programs it runs. A universal machine whose table was written only to
interpret carries the simulated certification bit as plain data on its tape. If the host is
programmable, so that other code shares that tape with the guest, any of that code
can flip the bit without paying, because the host’s step has no opinion about it. So an
ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t enforce the toll for its programs.
That’s how it’s built. It could. The simpler host above enforces it by having its own
step mirror the guest’s bit and charge for its crossing (Theorems 16.32 and 16.34), and
the universal programs U and UP are fixed tables that go one better: they earn their
own flag, by their own check, commit and certificate, exactly when the guest’s would
rise, and pay on their own ledger what the guest pays, U exactly and UP to within a
surcharge of at most two when the guest’s reading starts at no (Theorems 16.27, 16.26,
16.29 and 16.30). That’s a statement about which reading a step rule prices. It isn’t a
claim that Turing machines can’t price one.

Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the detour.
In 1974 two computer scientists, Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg, asked when
a machine can run guests, a whole operating system inside another, efficiently and
safely. Their answer is one sentence you could check against any instruction set. Call
an instruction sensitive if it reads or changes the machine’s own settings, the things
the host has to keep for itself, and privileged if running it outside the host’s own mode
makes the machine stop and hand control to the host, which is called a trap. For the
kind of machine they modelled: if every sensitive instruction is privileged, a host can
be built. The guest runs at full speed, and whenever it touches something that matters,


                                            293
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


the machine itself stops it and lets the host decide. That’s a host whose step has an
opinion.

Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass the
test? The most common one didn’t. In 2000 John Scott Robin, an Air Force officer, and
Cynthia Irvine, a computer-security researcher at the Naval Postgraduate School, went
through every instruction of Intel’s Pentium and found seventeen that are sensitive
and not privileged; POPF, which loads the processor’s flags, is the one usually pointed
at. A guest could run them and the host would never hear about it. The fixes came
two ways: VMware rewrote the guest’s code on the fly so the troublesome instructions
never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel and AMD added hardware
support so they’d trap. Does that change anything here? Not the theorems. Popek and
Goldberg were after speed and isolation. A record and a price weren’t their question,
so their result isn’t mine and mine isn’t theirs. It changes the picture, though. The
universal programs sit where they’d want a host to sit: the host’s own steps collect
each guest’s toll and earn each guest’s record again. And an industry learned the same
lesson the expensive way: a rule binds the guest only if it lives in the step underneath.

The smallest checked version of “a ledger beside an ordinary machine” is a Turing
machine configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one
more if it writes a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn’t disturb the machine.


Theorem 16.36 (A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing). Let a Turing
machine with transition table δ step a configuration c to tmn (δ, c) after at most n steps
(stopping when δ has no entry). Pair each configuration with a counter, and step the pair by
stepping the configuration and adding the step’s charge. Then for every n, δ and pair (c, m),
the configuration part after at most n steps of the pair is tmn (δ, c). In particular this holds
from (c, 0).

Proof. By induction on n. For n = 0 both sides are c. For n + 1, if δ has no entry at
c, both runs stop and both sides are c. Otherwise the pair steps to (c′ , m′ ) where c′ is
exactly the Turing machine’s next configuration, whatever m′ is, and the induction
hypothesis at (c′ , m′ ) finishes it.

Checked as thiele_simulates_turing_gen and thiele_simulates_turin
g (ProperSubsumption.v). The “Thiele” in those names is a local record, a Turing
configuration and a number. It isn’t a Thiele machine in this book’s sense, and the file
says not to cite it as one simulating Turing machines. A counter beside a machine is
the scorekeeper’s tally from Section 3: honest about the machine, and kept by whoever
holds the pencil.

One limit on all of this, so it isn’t read as more. Certification is one event. Other kinds
of observable a machine might carry would each need their own event, their own
evidence and their own cost law, and nothing here supplies those.


                                              294
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


16.17 Parts II and III, run on this machine
Parts II and III proved their counts and their collisions for any system with the named
pieces, and they left a promise: that the machine of this part would be put through
them. Here it is. The eight-state machine of Section 4 gets run by the small machine,
price for price. Structural entitlement, the count of what narrowing a list of rivals costs,
is proved for every Thiele-complete machine, with the small machine as a worked
member, a larger search on the host that has a counter for every number, and a run
that shows the count’s one awkward hypothesis, the covering, can’t be dropped. And
the time a check saves gets an exact exchange rate, for the part of the machine that
has no record. (The no-bare-verifier result is in Section 7, next to the collision it comes
from.)

The eight-state machine, run by the small machine. Look at the small machine
through a window that shows two things: its line number read modulo four, which
I’ll call its slot (the eight-state machine’s word from Section 4, unrelated to U’s slot
registers), and its flag. Call a state live when its trap latch is down, the fact “A ≥ 0”
about A’s current version is in its table, and its channel holds a commitment, which is
what CERTIFY needs in order to run.


Definition 16.11 (The eight-state machine, compiled). Stamp is the single instruction
CERTIFY. Next-slot is the single instruction INC B. Jump to slot a, for a one of 0, 1, 2, 3,
is the four instructions COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A; INC B; DEC B a.
The setup is the two instructions CHECK (A ≥ 0) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 0) A.


The two COMMITs in a jump change nothing but the line and the channel, and each
costs one, which is where the jump’s price of two comes from. The INC makes B
positive, so the DEC takes one off and jumps to line a for nothing, and B is back where
it was.


Theorem 16.37 (The small machine runs the eight-state machine). (1) For every live
state s and every move m of the eight-state machine, running m’s instructions from s ends in
a live state whose window is the eight-state machine’s step of s’s window by m, and the ledger
has risen by exactly m’s charge: one for stamp, two for jump, zero for next-slot. (2) The same
holds for any list of moves: the window after the compiled list is the eight-state machine’s run
of the list, the state is live, and the ledger has risen by the sum of the charges. (3) So a run of
compiled moves from a live state that takes the flag from down to up has raised the ledger by
at least one. (4) From any start ( a, b), the setup ends in a live state with window (slot 3, flag
down) and the ledger at 2; after it, any compiled list runs as on the eight-state machine from
(slot 3, flag down), with the ledger at 2 plus the sum of the charges; and if the flag is up at the
end, the whole run, setup included, contains the earned chain of Theorem 16.9.

Proof. (1) By cases on the move. On a live state CERTIFY runs, because a committed


                                               295
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


claim is on the channel; it raises the flag, moves the line on by one and charges one.
INC B moves the line on by one and charges nothing, and it touches only B and B’s
version, so the fact about A and the commitment stand and the state stays live. In a
jump, each COMMIT finds its fact in the table and succeeds, charging one, and the
INC and the DEC are free and end at line a, whose slot is a; the flag isn’t touched.
(2) is (1) over the list, by induction. (3) The eight-state machine’s own toll (Section 4)
says a run of its moves that takes the flag from down to up is charged at least one,
and (2) carries that charge across. (4) CHECK (A ≥ 0) passes at every value of A and
the COMMIT after it passes, which takes line 1 to line 3, slot 3, with two marks paid;
then (2) applies. A raised flag was raised by a CERTIFY, and Theorem 16.9 gives the
chain.

Checked as frag_runs_finite_machine, frag_pays_finite_price, frag_
runs_finite_trace, frag_certification_paid, frag_setup_live, frag
_program_runs and frag_program_earned (FragmentSmall.v), with the room
argument for the eight-state machine itself as frag_fin_toll and frag_cert_sy
stem in the same file. Three reservations, said now. The setup’s claim is true of every
value, so its CHECK can’t fail; it’s there because the small machine won’t CERTIFY
without a checked, committed claim. It isn’t there as a test. And the jump’s price of
two is two paid COMMITs, a choice a program makes that the machine allows and
doesn’t force. The window is a projection, too: the small machine’s full state keeps far
more than eight states’ worth.

And the whole small machine isn’t the eight-state piece it runs. It merges some states
for free.


Theorem 16.38 (The small machine’s merges). (1) A move of the small machine that takes
the flag from down to up is CERTIFY; CERTIFY merges two different full states into one (a
state with the flag down and the same state with the flag up land on the same state), and it
costs at least one. (2) DEC A 2 also merges two different full states, and it costs nothing. So it
is false of the small machine that every move that merges is priced.

Proof. (1) Only CERTIFY changes the flag, and it costs one. The two states with the
flag down and up, and a committed claim, are the same state after CERTIFY. (2) Take a
core at line 1 with A at 1 at version 0, and the same core with A at 0 at version 1. DEC
A 2 takes the first to A = 0 at version 1, line 2, a write; it takes the second to line 2
with A still 0 at version 1, because DEC on zero is no write. Same state, price zero.

Checked as frag_small_certify_merges, frag_small_certifying_step_
priced_merge, frag_small_dec_free_merge and frag_small_not_merge_

Structural entitlement, for every Thiele-complete machine. Theorem 8.3 was about
any certification system and handed the run’s payments in as a bill. For a Thiele-
complete machine (Definition 16.7) the bill is known. Call the CHECK, COMMIT and
CERTIFY moves of a run its record moves; each costs exactly one, so the ledger rises by
the number of record moves, and clause (b) says what a raised record must contain.


Theorem 16.39 (Structural entitlement represented). Let a machine be Thiele-complete
through an interface. Take a clean start s0 and a run t from it; a type of rivals and a type of
observations with an exact equality test; an observation obs and a representative observation
r of each rival; a decoder d from runs to observations; lists Ω, Ω′ of rivals and a decision tree
T. Suppose (M1) Ω′ strictly narrows Ω, as in Theorem 8.3, and (M2) some dropped rival
shows an observation different from every survivor’s; (M3) the run ends with the record up
and the decoded run d(t) is shown by some survivor; (M4) depth( T ) is at most the number
of record moves in t; (M5) |Ω′ | > 0; and (M6) the covering is by fibres: there is a map F
from rivals to lists of rivals such that every rival x of Ω lies in F (u) for some survivor u with
r ( x ) = r (u), the lengths of the lists F (u) over the survivors add up to at least |Ω|, and no
F (u) is longer than L( T ). Then (1) the membership test of Ω′ is strictly stronger than that
of Ω; (2) t contains the earned chain of clause (b), with the meaning of the claim true at the
CHECK and at the COMMIT; (3) ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ is at most the number of record
moves of t; (4) the number of record moves of t is exactly the ledger’s rise; and (5) the ledger
rose by at least 3.

Proof. (1) is Theorem 8.3(1). (2) Clause (b) applied to a run from a clean state that ends
with the record up gives the chain, and a passing check means the claim’s meaning
holds, which keeps holding while the thing it’s about is unchanged. (3) The fibres
cover: summing their lengths gives |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, and Theorem 8.3’s count finishes
it, with the record moves, which are the paid steps, in place of the charged steps. (4) is
clause (c) added up. (5) is Theorem 16.18(3).

Checked as ent_representation (EntitlementSmall.v), whose Coq statement is
printed in Section E. It’s a checklist, as I said in Section 8, and the small print is the
same kind. (M3)’s second half feeds no conclusion: only the record’s being up is used.
(M1) is used only for the inclusion. Its gap feeds nothing. And the first clause of (M6),
the representative observation, isn’t used by the count either. What the machine adds
to Theorem 8.3 is conclusions (2), (4) and (5): the payment is the machine’s own three
acts, each at exactly one, and a raised record carries the earned chain. The packaged
form, a record of the fifteen things a shortcut has to supply, with a theorem that every
inhabitant lands in the bound, is ent_shortcut and ent_every_shortcut_lan
ds_here. The count with the tree thrown away, in the form I use below, is ent_com
plete_tree_bound.

Two further statements, about the run’s own questions and about the record clause.


Theorem 16.40 (A floor with no supplied tree). Take a machine and an interface that
meets the exact-toll clause (c) of Definition 16.7, so each record act costs exactly one. Call the
questions of a run the claims of its CHECK moves, and say two rival states answer alike
when every one of those claims gets the same verdict at both (each verdict taken at the rival
itself, as it starts; the states the run passed through don’t enter). If, for a list Ω of rival states
and a number m > 0, the rivals of Ω that answer alike with any one rival, itself included, are
never more than m, then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 m⌉ is at most the number of CHECK moves of
the run, which is at most its number of record moves, which is the ledger’s rise.

Proof. A run’s questions give each rival an answer list, and answer lists are lists of
Booleans of length equal to the number of CHECK moves, so there are at most 2c
answer classes among the rivals, c the number of CHECK moves. The classes have at
most m members each, so |Ω| ≤ 2c · m, and the rounded logarithms follow. The rest is
clause (c).

Checked as ent_questions_floor (EntitlementSmall.v). The tree has gone: it is
the run’s own questions. There are limits, and they’re the ones in the statement. The
verdicts are taken at the rivals as they start. The states the run had reached when it
asked don’t come into it, and a free branch, DEC on zero, can still narrow a list for
nothing. So this prices a narrowing that the paid checks explain, and no more.


Theorem 16.41 (What the record adds). Let a machine be Thiele-complete through an
interface. (1) From a clean start, the record is up at the end of a run exactly when the run
contains the earned chain, and a run with the record up raised the ledger by at least 3. (2)
Conclusions (1), (3) and (4) of Theorem 16.39 hold without a clean start and without the record
being up, for a machine that only meets the exact-toll clause (c): the hypotheses (M1), (M2),
(M4), (M5) and (M6), and the decoded run being shown by some survivor, are all it needs.


Checked as ent2_record_adds, ent2_upgrade_iff and ent2_observed_re
presentation (EntitlementMore2.v). So the record doesn’t make narrowing cost
more. It adds the earned chain and a floor of 3, and that’s all it adds: a run that
narrows without ever raising the record is still bound to pay its index bits, and the
floor of 3 no longer applies to it.

Weights, and the partition form. Two more pieces of the same count, both checked.
First, suppose the rivals aren’t equally many: give each a whole-number weight, a
multiplicity, and call the sum of the weights of a list its mass. The count survives with
masses in place of lengths. If the prior’s mass is at most L( T ) times the posterior’s,
the rounded index bits of the two masses differ by at most depth( T ); so for any
certification system a run that paid at least that many charged steps has a bill at least



                                                 298
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


the drop, and for a Thiele-complete machine the representation theorem goes through
with masses and the same five conclusions. On such a machine the ledger rises by
the same number from every start, the number of record moves, so the expected rise
over a weighted prior is its mass times the record moves, and the drop in rounded bits
times the prior’s mass is at most that expected rise, with no averaging argument. The
weights are whole numbers, cross-multiplied, and no probability enters. Checked as e
nt2_weighted_bits, ent2_wreduction_covers, ent2_weighted_cs, ent2_
weighted_representation, ent2_rise_independent, ent2_expected_ri

the covering by fibres has a plainer form that doesn’t need the clause that the fibres
add up to the prior. Say the rivals are partitioned by the representative observation
when every rival looks like some survivor under it and no observation class, counted
inside the prior, has more than L( T ) members. The fibre lengths then add up to at
least the prior, because every rival is in the class of some survivor, so a partition gives
the covering, and the count holds under it. The converse is false: there are coverings
that aren’t partitions. Checked as ent2_cover_sum, ent2_partition_old_iff,
ent2_partition_to_reduction, ent2_partition_bits and ent2_reduct

A worked member on the small machine. Eight rivals: the starts ( a, b) with a ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}
and b ∈ {0, 1}, counter A at a and counter B at b. The run is CHECK (Even) A; CHECK
(A ≥ 2) A; COMMIT (A ≥ 2) A; CERTIFY, from (2, 0). The program raises the flag
from a rival exactly when a is even and at least 2, so exactly from (2, 0) and (2, 1),
and the posterior is those two. The decoder reads one “passed” for each CHECK in
the run’s receipts; the representative observation is “B is 0,” which isn’t constant; the
fibres are the four rivals that share B; the tree is the complete tree of depth 2.


Proposition 16.42 (The eight-start member). For every a and b, the run raises the flag
from ( a, b) exactly when a is even and at least 2. All hypotheses of Theorem 16.39 hold, with
eight rivals narrowed to two: the test of the posterior is strictly stronger; the index bits are
3 − 1 = 2; the run has 4 record moves and the ledger rises by exactly 4; and the earned chain
is in the run. The run’s own questions (Theorem 16.40) are its 2 CHECKs, so the floor is met
with equality. With the two CHECKs alone, the record stays down, the ledger rises by 2, and
the bound 2 ≤ 2 still holds.

A search through n bits. The same shape at a size you can’t enumerate, on the machine
of Definition 16.8, the one with a counter for every number, with the small machine’s
property language of Zero, Even and At-least-n, read at registers, in place of Slot. That
machine is Thiele-complete too (ent2_mmachine_complete, MultiThiele2.v). Hide
n = k + m bits, one in each of registers 0 to n − 1. The program asks k questions, one
per bit of the first k: CHECK “at least 1” of register i for a 1, CHECK “is 0” for a 0.
Then it COMMITs the first claim and CERTIFYs. The prior is every n-bit value; the
posterior is the 2m values that begin with the answers; the tree is the complete tree of
depth k.


Theorem 16.43 (A search through n bits). For 1 ≤ k ≤ 16 and any m: from a world
holding a value v of at least k bits, the program certifies exactly when v begins with its answers,
so the posterior is exactly the set of rivals it certifies from; the test of the posterior is strictly
stronger than the prior’s; the earned chain is in the run; the prior has 2k+m members and the
posterior 2m , so the index bits are exactly k; the run has exactly k + 2 record moves and the
ledger rises by exactly k + 2; and the run’s own questions are k CHECKs, so Theorem 16.40 is
met with equality. With the COMMIT and the CERTIFY left off, the questions alone narrow
2k+m values to 2m , the record stays down, and the ledger rises by exactly k. And no run from a
clean start that raises the record contains more than 16 CHECKs before its CERTIFY, so with
17 questions no start certifies.

Proof. Each question is a CHECK of whether one register holds a given bit, which
passes exactly when it does; a failing CHECK traps. So the program certifies exactly
when every answer is right, which is when v begins with the answers. The counting is
the count of bit strings, and the representation theorem applies with every hypothesis
a theorem. The cap is the fact table: it holds sixteen facts, never evicts, and a CHECK
on a full table traps (Theorem 16.13), so a seventeenth CHECK before the CERTIFY
ends the run in a trap.

Checked as ent2_search_certifies_iff, ent2_search_posterior_is_ce
rtified, ent2_bit_search, ent2_search_lands, ent2_search_question
s_floor, ent2_search_observed, ent2_questions_cap and ent2_no_sear
ch_past_16 (BitSearch2.v, BitSearchMember2.v, BitSearchObserved2.v). The sixteen
belongs to the machine. The program has no say in it: it’s the same ceiling as the item

Unasked bits can be any number. The lists, the tree and the fibres are supplied here, as
in the representation theorem, and tied to the run only for this member. The covering
still prices only the size of the drop. Its reason goes unpriced.

The covering can’t be dropped. It’s a hypothesis, and one might hope it’s a nuisance
one could remove. It isn’t, and the small machine shows it. Fix n ≥ 4, take the
2n starts with A below 2n as the rivals, and run the three-move chain on the claim
