The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


“A ≥ 2n − 1”: CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY. It certifies exactly from A = 2n − 1, so
the posterior is one start, n index bits are gone, and the ledger rose by 3. So for n ≥ 4
the claim “the index-bit drop is at most the ledger’s rise” is false for this run, and no
tree of depth at most 3 covers the narrowing, whatever the representative observation.
One property with a big constant in it carries n bits in a single yes-or-no question;
what the bound prices is a narrowing whose classes are balanced, a tree with enough
leaves. A narrowing of any other shape is outside it. Checked as ent2_uncovered
_posterior, ent2_uncovered_claim_false and ent2_no_cheap_covering
(CoveringNeeded2.v).

The time a check saves. The question is whether counter A is at least m. There are
two ways to find out. The free way uses base moves only, INC and DEC, which cost
nothing. But a base move reads A one unit at a time: a DEC takes a unit off A or finds
it empty. After n moves, a run that started with A at least n has never seen A empty,
so it can’t have behaved differently for different such A except by a constant shift in
A itself. The paid way is one CHECK (A ≥ m): one move, a ledger of one, and the
line it ends on says which way it went. Certifying the answer takes the whole chain,
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY.


Theorem 16.44 (The time tax). (1) No program of two-counter instructions that runs fewer
than m moves has its final line number and its final B determine whether A ≥ m at every
start; in particular none tells A = m − 1 from A = m. (2) A program of m DECs and INCs
(a ladder: DEC A and on success go on to the next pair, otherwise INC B) decides it in exactly
m moves, from the line number and B, and costs 0. (3) The paid chain of three instructions
raises the flag exactly when A ≥ m and has a ledger of exactly 3, whatever m is. (4) A single
CHECK (A ≥ m) decides it in one move from the line number, with a ledger of exactly 1,
whatever m is. (5) So if a ledger unit is worth λ moves, the paid route to deciding costs 1 + λ
and the free route costs at least m, and the paid route is cheaper exactly when 1 + λ < m; the
paid route to certifying costs 3 + 3λ.

Proof. (1) Take the starts (m − 1, b) and (m, b). When n < m both have A ≥ n, so in
the first n moves no DEC finds A empty in either run, and the two runs differ only by
the shift of one unit in A. They end at the same line with the same B, though A ≥ m
holds of one and not the other. (2) Run the ladder: each pair either takes a unit off A
and moves on, or finds A empty and falls through to the INC. The line after m moves
is 2m + 1 exactly when all m units were there. It’s all DEC and INC, so it costs 0. (3) is
the price table: CHECK (A ≥ m) passes exactly when A ≥ m, a failing CHECK traps
and the flag stays down, and the three moves cost three. (4) is the same price table
with one instruction: a passing CHECK goes on to the next line and a failing one traps.
(5) is arithmetic on (1) to (4).

Checked as ent2_free_run_shift, ent2_free_cannot_decide_fast, ent2_
ladder_decides, ent2_machine_free_cannot_decide, ent2_machine_la


                                             301
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


dder_decides, ent2_ladder_free, ent2_chain_decides and ent2_time_t
ax (TimeTax2.v), the first three for two-counter configurations and the next three for
the same programs compiled and run on the machine, with the certifying comparison
3 + 3λ < m inside ent2_time_tax, (4) as nec_e_time_tax_one_paid_move,
and the lower bound and the one-move decider together as nec_e_time_tax_fre
e_needed (NecESearch.v); the deciding comparison 1 + λ < m is arithmetic on those.
The exchange is sharper than a comparison of two particular programs: the free side
is a lower bound over every program of INC and DEC, so no choice of program is
involved, and the paid side is constant. The limits: the bound is for programs that
make no record move, INC and DEC with falling off the end as stopping. It doesn’t
cover every Thiele-complete machine, because the definition doesn’t forbid a base
move that changes a counter by more than one unit, and such a machine is a different
machine, one the bound doesn’t speak for. And the two routes put their answers
in different places, the free one in the line number and the paid one in the flag; this
compares two ways to answer one question. It doesn’t compare two certifications.

16.18 The diagonal, on this machine’s programs
Section 13 left the diagonal standing on any substrate and on a little family built to
fit it, reproved it on L, which isn’t a substrate because its evaluation can run forever,
and said what a machine has to supply to fill in the same shape, two things: programs
that can be handed to programs as numbers, and a recursion theorem for the trans-
formations it can carry out. This machine’s universal program reads a whole guest
program out of one register, with a numbering of programs that goes there and back
(Definition 16.9), and halting is undecidable here in the library’s sense (Theorem 16.4).
What’s left are the two classical results that turn a universal machine into a place
where the diagonal bites: Rice’s theorem and Kleene’s recursion theorem. They come
with a wrinkle I should put first, because it decides which machine they’re about.

The wrinkle is the one from earlier in this chapter, at the end of the subsection on what
two counters compute. The small machine takes its inputs straight into two counters,
and Schroeppel’s memo gives a proof that two plain counters can’t even compute 2n
from n. Rice’s reduction has to keep a program’s input safe while a copy of a halting
instance runs. Kleene’s construction has to run an evaluator while keeping its input.
Two counters have nowhere to keep it. So the two theorems land where they’re true
and where I could prove them. The host machine of Definition 16.8, the one with a
counter for every number that U runs on, is a fine programming system: its programs
are numbers, an input sits in register 1, and there’s room to spare. On it both theorems
hold in full. On the two-counter machine itself the story splits, and I’ll tell it at the
end of the subsection: Rice’s theorem holds on every input, by a trick for keeping the
input that I’ll show you; Kleene’s holds when inputs are written as powers of two, the
way Minsky packed them; and on plain inputs Kleene’s is false, and that’s a theorem
too.

The host machine’s programs are numbered the way U numbers a guest’s. Write

                                          302
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


⟨m, n⟩ for (2n + 1) · 2m . INC r is ⟨0, r ⟩, DEC r j is ⟨1, ⟨r, j⟩⟩, HALT is ⟨2, 0⟩, CHECK r is
⟨3, r ⟩, COMMIT r is ⟨4, r ⟩, CERTIFY is ⟨5, 0⟩, and a program is the list code: the empty
program is 0, and an instruction x followed by a program t is ⟨ x, code(t)⟩. Every
number decodes to some program, and decoding a program’s code gives the program
back. Say a host program outputs y on input x when, started with x in register 1 and
every other register 0, with a clean table, it halts with y in register 0.

Rice first, because it’s the shorter road. Henry Rice, whom you met in Section 7,
proved in his 1951 doctoral thesis, and published in 1953, that no program decides any
property of what programs do unless every program has it or none does. Properties
of how a program is written aren’t covered. The road from halting is a single detour.
Take a property of what programs do, a program y that has it, and a program n that
doesn’t. Given an instance of two-counter halting, a Minsky program H with starting
counters a and b, build a host program that first loads a and b into two fresh registers,
then runs a copy of H moved onto those registers, then empties both, then runs y.
If H halts on ( a, b) the built program behaves like y and has the property. If H runs
forever the built program never stops on any input, and it behaves like the program
that loops, which lacks the property (if the looping program has it instead, swap the
roles of y and n). Everything the built program does before y is INC and DEC, which
pay nothing and touch no fact, channel, trap latch or flag. So a decider for the property
would be a decider for halting, and the library already says what that would cost:
the complement of single-tape Turing-machine halting would become something a
program could list, the same synthetic sense of “undecidable” as Theorem 16.4. Two
words carry the weight, and they’re the ones to check in the statement: what “behaves
the same” sees, and where the program starts.


Definition 16.12 (Behaving the same, on the host). A host program ends in a state
when it halts there, from the start with x in register 1 and the rest clean; a trap counts
as stopping. Two host programs behave the same when for every input x, any state one
ends in has a state the other ends in that agrees with it on every register’s value, the
fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the flag, and the same the other
way round. The line number and the versions aren’t compared. A property of host
programs is extensional when behaving the same carries it from one program to the
other.


Theorem 16.45 (Rice’s theorem on the host machine). Let Π be an extensional property
of host programs that some program has and some program lacks. Then Π is undecidable in
the library’s sense.

Proof. The reduction above. The prefix before y leaves every register but the two fresh
ones as it found them, and empties those, so when H halts the built program ends in
whatever state y ends in from the same input, with the same ledger, table, channel, trap
and flag. When H doesn’t halt, the built program stops on no input. The reduction is

                                             303
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


from the complement of halting, so no excluded middle is needed; the proof splits on
the decider’s own answer for the looping program.

Checked as sm_host_rice, with the reduction’s two halves as sm_rice_prog_ha
lts and sm_rice_prog_diverges (SmHostRice.v). A property that depends only
on the partial function a program computes, whether it stops and what it leaves in
register 0, is extensional, so it’s covered; the files also derive that case again from the
recursion theorem below, as sm_host_rice_fun (SmKleene.v).

On the small machine itself the same road works from the clean start, and only from
there. Say two two-counter programs behave the same from the clean start when, what-
ever state one halts in from counters (0, 0), the other halts in a state with the same
counters, trap latch, ledger and flag, and the same the other way round. The fact table
isn’t compared, because the prefix moves the versions of A and B by fixed amounts
and the facts carry versions. There is no input to keep, since the program starts at
(0, 0), and H’s instance is loaded straight into A and B.


Theorem 16.46 (Rice’s theorem for the small machine, from the clean start). Let Π be a
property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a program to any program that behaves
the same from the clean start, held by some program and lacked by some other. Then Π is
undecidable in the library’s sense. In particular “halts from the clean start” is undecidable.


Checked as sm_guest_rice and sm_guest_halting_clean_undecidable
(SmGuestRice.v). That’s the clean start only. Every input is harder, because the stan-
dard reduction has to keep the input safe while the halting instance runs, and two
counters have nowhere obvious to keep it. The way through is at the end of the
subsection.

Kleene’s recursion theorem is the deeper one, and it’s a construction, which is Sec-
tion 13’s point about Kleene’s little gem (Moschovakis’s phrase): the content is the
building, and the contradiction in Section 13 was just the last line. It says: for every
transformation F of programs that some program can carry out on numbers, there’s a
program p that computes the same thing as F ( p). The shape of the building is the old
one. From the program that carries out F, build an evaluator that reads a number, treats
it as a program’s code, specialises that program to its own code, runs F’s program
on the result, and runs whatever program comes back. The specialising step is what
logicians call s-m-n: fix one input of a program and get a new program that needs one
input fewer. Then the witness is the evaluator specialised to its own code. Run on any
input, it builds its own code, hands it to F’s program, gets the code of F ( p), and runs
that.

Here’s each piece on the host machine, with its exact premise.




                                             304
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.47 (s-m-n, and a universal program for host programs). (1) For a number c
and a host program V, let spec(c, V ) be c copies of INC 2 followed by V with its jumps moved
to follow them. Then for all x, y, spec(c, V ) outputs y on input x if and only if V, started with
x in register 1 and c in register 2, halts with y in register 0. (2) There is a host program W
made only of INC, DEC and HALT such that, for all c, x, y, W started with x in register 1 and
c in register 2 halts with y in register 0 exactly when the host program numbered c outputs y
on input x.

Proof. (1) The prefix writes register 2 c times and nothing else, so it moves that regis-
ter’s version from 0 to c. A fact records a version, so after the prefix every later version
of register 2, and the version in every fact the run records about register 2, is c more
than in a clean run. A CHECK or a COMMIT reads versions only to ask whether two
versions of the same register are equal, and adding c to both keeps the answer, so the
two runs take the same steps. The run is V’s run from the stated start, moved down by
c lines. (2) is the evaluator. A finite algorithm decodes a number into a program, runs
it step by step on given registers, and, searching over the number of steps, returns the
output of the first halting run. I wrote that algorithm out in Coq, turned it into a term
of the lambda calculus L, and ran the library’s compiler from L to Minsky programs,
which gives a program of two-counter instructions that a host program can be read
off from, instruction for instruction. The tools supply the program that computes the
evaluator. The fixed-point argument below is not theirs.

Checked as sm2_smn_all (SmSmnAll.v), an if and only if statement that carries no
premise on register 2, and sm_host_universal (SmKleene.v); the narrower form
of (1), with the premise, is still there as sm_smn. The numbering is sm_hcode, sm_h
decode and sm_hdecode_hcode (SmCodes.v). Be exact about one thing: U is not
that universal program. U runs two-counter guests, and a two-counter guest given its
input plainly can’t run the evaluator. With inputs written as powers of two one can,
as Theorem 16.53 near the end of this subsection shows. W runs host programs, and it
can, because it’s a host program on a machine with registers.


Theorem 16.48 (Kleene’s recursion theorem on the host machine). (1) For every host
program T there is a host program e such that for all x, y: e outputs y on input x if and only if,
for some d, T outputs d on the number of e, and the program numbered d outputs y on x. (2)
So for every transformation F of host programs that some host program carries out on numbers
(on the number of p it outputs the number of F ( p), for every p), there is a host program e such
that for all x, y, e outputs y on x if and only if F (e) does. (3) The same on numbers: for every
function f on numbers that some host program computes, some number e has the program
numbered e and the program numbered f (e) output the same on every input.

Proof. (1) Let E be the following program of INC and DEC, built the same way as W
from one finite evaluator, with T’s number t written in. On inputs x and c it computes
the number of spec(c, Pc ), where Pc is the program numbered c, runs T on that number

                                               305
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


to get d, and then runs the program numbered d on x. Let c0 be the number of E, and
let e = spec(c0 , E). By (1) of Theorem 16.47, e on input x does what E does on x and
c0 . And E on c0 builds the number of spec(c0 , Pc0 ), which is the number of e, since Pc0
is E. So e hands its own number to T, gets d, and runs d on x. (2) and (3) are (1) with T
carrying out F or f .

Checked as sm_second_recursion, sm_kleene and sm_kleene_codes (SmK-
leene.v). That fixed point is of the function: e and F (e) stop on the same inputs and
leave the same number in register 0. Their ledgers, flags and fact tables can differ,
because the marks e pays are the evaluator’s. I’d like a fixed point that agrees on the
record too, and the next two theorems say how much of that can be had. The ledger
and the flag can be had. Every register can’t.


Theorem 16.49 (The recursion theorem, up to the record). Let F be a transformation of
host programs that some host program T carries out on numbers. Then there is a host program
e such that, for every input x, any state e ends in has a state F (e) ends in that agrees with it on
register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts in the table, and whether the
channel is empty, and the same the other way round. So e stops on x exactly when F (e) does,
and the ledgers are equal exactly, with no surcharge. T may itself check, commit and certify.

Proof. The construction is Theorem 16.48’s, with a different evaluator. The first step is
to see that a record is small. From a clean start, a host program that stops has a record
I can read off five numbers, in this order: what it left in register 0; how many facts the
table holds; what is left of the ledger once the facts, the trap and the flag are paid for,
which I’ll call the commits; 1 if the flag is up and 0 if not; and 1 if the trap latch is up
and 0 if not. The record obeys a short rulebook. The table holds at most sixteen facts.
The latch is a single bit. A commit needs a fact behind it, a certify needs a commit,
and the channel is empty exactly when no commit was paid. The ledger is the facts,
plus the commits, plus the flag, plus the trap, and that’s all of it. Those are the only
properties of a record the replay will use, and I proved them by following the plain
machine alongside the real one, one step at a time.

The second step is five blocks, one for each number. Each block reads the code of T,
runs T on the number of the specialised program, runs the program that comes out on
x, and returns its number. All of that happens on plain data: the blocks are programs
of INC and DEC, built the way W was, from an evaluator written out in Coq, turned
into a term of L and compiled to Minsky programs. So if T has marks of its own, they
are simulated and never paid.

The third step is the payment. The evaluator puts 1 in a fresh register, which satisfies
the host’s one property, and CHECKs it once for every fact. It COMMITs to that claim
once for every commit. It CERTIFYs once if the flag is up. It copies the first number
into register 0. And if the trap latch is up, it CHECKs a register that holds 0, which



                                                306
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


fails, and the host traps. Everything before the payments is INC and DEC and costs
nothing, and the payments cost what the record costs, so the ledger is exact. Specialise
the evaluator to its own number, as before.

Checked as sm2_kleene_obs (SmFixedPoint.v), with the five numbers as sm2_f
inal_numbers and the evaluator’s specification as sm2_ev_spec (SmTally.v) and
the replay program as sm2_VG_forward and sm2_VG_halt (SmFixed.v), where
the trap latch is up exactly when the fifth number is 1 and the flag exactly when
the fourth is positive; sm2_kleene_fun gives back the version that compares only
the function. Two limits, and the second one is a theorem. First, e pays after it has
computed everything. It is not the way U runs a guest, mirroring every move: e pays
the counts, CHECKs, then COMMITs, then the CERTIFY, whatever order F (e) used,
so the order of the record’s events isn’t preserved, and for a program F (e) that never
stops, e never stops and pays nothing, though F (e) may pay without bound. The
relation says nothing about states in the middle of a run. Second, no fixed point agrees
on every register, or on what the facts name.


Theorem 16.50 (No fixed point of full behaviour). There is a transformation F of host
programs, carried out by a host program, such that no host program e behaves the same as F (e)
in the sense of Definition 16.12.

Proof. Let F ( p) be the one-line program INC r, with r one above the number of p. A
host program carries this out on numbers; I got it from the same route through L. None
of it was written by hand. A program’s number is at least every register it names: the
number of an instruction is above its register, and the code of a list is above every
instruction in it. So e can’t name r, the register F (e) writes. On input 0 the run of F (e)
ends with 1 in register r, and if e stops at all, it ends with 0 there. If e doesn’t stop, then
it already differs from F (e), which does. Either way they don’t behave the same.

Checked as sm2_no_exact and sm2_reg_bound (SmNoExact.v). A variant of F that
also CHECKs register r and commits to it gives F (e) a fact and a commitment about
r that e can’t have, so no fixed point agrees on the fact table alone, or on the channel
alone, or on the versions of the registers (nec_e_no_fixed_point_facts, nec_e
_no_fixed_point_versions, NecEHost.v). What survives is what Theorem 16.49
states. Whether one more fixed register could be added to that list I haven’t settled
either way, and I don’t claim it.

And with the recursion theorem proved, the wall of Section 13 goes up on this machine
without a premise left over. Call a property of host programs functional when it
depends only on the partial function a program computes.


Theorem 16.51 (The diagonal on the host machine). Let Π be a functional property of
host programs that some program has and some program lacks. (1) Read “ f is representable”


                                             307
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


as “some host program carries f out on numbers.” Then no function d from programs to
Booleans whose flip is representable is right about Π on every program: this is the argument of
Theorem 13.1, reproved for host programs, with its recursion premise a theorem here. (2) No
host program decides Π outright: there is no program D that, on the number of every program,
halts with a number in register 0 that’s 1 exactly when the program has Π.

Proof. (1) The flip, send programs that d calls good to the program lacking Π and the
others to the one having it, is carried out by a host program by hypothesis. Theo-
rem 16.48(2) gives a program e that computes what its image computes; Π holds of
e exactly when it holds of the image, and the image lacks it exactly when d calls e
good, so d is wrong at e. (2) From a deciding program D build a host program that
computes D’s flip on numbers, by the same route through L and the Minsky compiler,
reading the Boolean off D’s runs with the standard library’s unbounded search; then
(1) applies. This one is an outright negation. The synthetic notion doesn’t come into
it.

Checked as sm_no_inside_decider and sm_no_host_decider (SmKleene.v,
SmDecider.v).

Rice and Kleene are the ingredients the diagonal of Section 13 asks a substrate for, and
the wall they put up doesn’t care about the record: the base does the computing and
the flag watches. A program’s ledger and flag are among what “behaves the same”
sees on the host, so a nontrivial property of those is undecidable too, in the library’s
sense of Theorem 16.45, and the fixed point is up to the record, as far as the theorems
above say and no further.

Now the two-counter machine itself, which I promised at the start of the subsection:
Minsky’s two bins of pebbles and nothing else. Rice, first. Say a two-counter program
behaves the same as another on a set X of inputs when, on every input n in X, started
with n pebbles in bin A and none in bin B, one stops exactly when the other does, and
then they agree on both bins, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, and on which property
and which counter each recorded fact and the channel are about. The versions are left
out: they say which write a fact is about, and the trick below moves them.

The trick is the whole problem. Rice’s reduction has to keep the program’s input safe
while a copy of a halting instance H runs, and there’s no third bin to keep it in. My first
guess was bin B, and that dies at once, because H needs both bins. The second guess is
Minsky’s own packing: keep several numbers in one bin as powers of different primes,
H’s two counters as the exponents of 2 and 3, and the input as the exponent of 5. That
dies more quietly. To put the input there, the program would have to turn n pebbles
into 5n , an exponential, and Schroeppel’s memo, from earlier in this chapter, gives a
proof that two plain counters can’t even build 2n from n. I had no way to build 5n .

What works is to stop keeping the input beside the work. Turn n pebbles into 6n + 5,



                                             308
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


which is only adding, and then multiply in H’s counters as powers of 2 and 3. H runs
by halving the pile and splitting it in thirds and building it back up, and the 6n + 5
rides along in the middle of every one of those piles. It’s odd, and counted off in threes
it leaves two over, so no halving or thirding ever reaches into it.


Theorem 16.52 (Rice’s theorem for the two-counter machine, on any inputs). For any
set X of inputs, a property of two-counter programs that’s carried from a program to any
program that behaves the same on X is undecidable in the library’s sense, unless every program
has it or none does, and then it’s decidable. X can be every input, the powers of two, or {0}.

Proof. For every input: given a two-counter instance H starting from counters a and b,
build a program that turns the input of n pebbles in bin A into (6n + 5) · 2a · 3b , runs H
inside the exponents of 2 and 3, divides out every 2 and every 3 when H stops, takes
away 5, divides by 6, and then runs the program that has the property. Because 6n + 5
shares no factor with 2 or 3, the coding never mistakes it for an exponent, and the
input comes back whole. If H halts, the built program behaves the same as the one
with the property on every input; if not, it never stops on any input. The reduction is
from the complement of halting.

Checked as tc_rice and tc_rice_dichotomy (TcRice.v).

So 6n + 5 is the place to keep the input that two counters seemed not to have. It isn’t
beside the work. It’s inside it, in a factor the work never touches. I like that one more
than I can justify: the input hides in the leftover that every halving and thirding walks
straight past.

Kleene needs more than keeping an input. It needs a program that runs a program.
So write a number x as 2x pebbles and read a result as the exponent of 2, the way
Minsky did. With inputs written that way, there’s one two-counter program, call it
U2 , that, started on 2x · 3e , stops with 2y exactly when the program numbered e gives
y on x; specialising a program to a number is exact; and the recursion theorem holds.
(U2 is a different program from the universal host program U, which runs on the
machine with a register for every number.) Checked as tc_universal and tc_smn
(TcPacked.v).


Theorem 16.53 (Kleene for the two-counter machine, inputs written as powers of two).
(1) For every transformation F of programs that some program carries out on program numbers,
there’s a program e that computes the same function as F (e), with inputs and outputs written
as powers of two. (2) The fixed point is of the function only: there’s such an F for which no e
behaves the same as F (e) once the properties and counters of the recorded facts count.


The counterexample in (2) is short. Let F ( p) check that bin A holds at least the number
of p plus one. A program can only record facts about properties it names, and every


                                             309
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


property it names is below its own number, so no e records what F (e) records.

Checked as tc_second_recursion, tc_kleene and tc_no_fine_kleene (Tc-
Packed.v, TcNoFine.v).

Even with Schroeppel in hand, my first guess about Kleene was that the powers of
two were a convenience, and that plain inputs would only take more work. They
don’t take more work. With plain inputs, Kleene’s theorem is false. A transformation
is carried out if some program, started on 2n where n is the number of a program p,
stops with 2m where m is the number of F ( p).


Theorem 16.54 (No plain recursion on two counters). (1) No program of n lines stops
with c · x pebbles in bin A, started on x pebbles in bin A and none in bin B, for every x, where
c = N! + 1 and N = 16(n + 1)(2n + 1)16 . (2) So there’s a carried-out transformation F
such that no program e computes the same plain function as F (e).

Proof. (2) from (1): let F ( p) multiply bin A by c for the length of p. A program carries
F out by the same route through L as before, and a fixed point would multiply every
input by a number fixed by its own length. For (1), count the control states of a
program of n lines: its line, the trap latch, whether the channel holds a commitment,
and for each of at most sixteen facts its property, its counter and whether it still
concerns that counter’s current version. There are at most 4(n + 1)(2n + 1)16 , and
N is four times that, so c shares no factor with any number up to N. Now suppose
a program does multiply every input by c. On a large input, a bin far fuller than
anything a CHECK names is seen only two ways: whether it’s empty, and whether
its pebbles pair off evenly. So the run breaks into stages, each a bounded cycle that
moves the small bin up by some g and the full one down by some m, both at most N.
Follow one input and the same input plus the product of the m’s through the same
stages, and compare the outputs: the growth is c times the product of the m’s on one
side and the product of the g’s on the other. A number with no factor up to N can’t
divide a product of numbers up to N unless it is 1, and c is at least 2.

Checked as tc2_no_mult (Tc2Mult.v), from am_no_multiplier (Tc2Chain.v),
which says the same for any machine with finitely many control states whose counters
are read only through zero and parity above a threshold, and tc2_plain_recurs
ion_false (Tc2Plain.v), which gives a carried-out F with no e equivalent to F (e) on
plain inputs, all closed.

The case split in the stages is decided by running for a bounded number of steps, so
no excluded middle goes in. For a long time I couldn’t read Schroeppel’s own memo.
I went looking again and found the scan. As I read it, his route is close in spirit: he
trades a two-counter machine that starts with one counter empty for a machine with
one register that can only add, multiply and divide by fixed numbers and take one
away, each of those built out of one of the program’s loops, and that’s the stages here


                                              310
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


under another name. I haven’t followed his proof line by line; this one is checked. The
c it uses is astronomically bigger than anything a real multiplier needs, and finding
the best bound is a question I leave alone.

So on two bins: Rice holds on every input. Kleene holds with inputs written as
powers of two, for the function. It fails for the facts. And with plain inputs Kleene fails
outright. The last one is the answer I didn’t see coming. The powers of two weren’t
a convenience. On two bins they’re the difference between a recursion theorem and
none.

16.19 What the universal machine covers, and what it doesn’t
Here’s what that covers, said plainly, a sentence at a time. The guests of U are this
chapter’s programs, every one of them, from every clean start start( x, y). That’s the
stated class. The whole-run theorems don’t cover a guest handed facts in its table, a
commitment in its channel or a raised flag at the start; the one-step simulation, by itself,
works from any related pair. It’s the same kind of class Turing’s universal machine
has: a fixed instruction set, and a finite program held as data, here packed into one
number the way Turing packed his into a description number. Each guest keeps its
computation, its halting, its answer, its record and its prices, exactly: the host halts
when it halts, its flag goes up when the guest’s would, on a chain of its own, and its
ledger is the guest’s.

The guests of UP are every Thiele machine whose driver, step, prices and reading
are computed by programs, with the reading decided on every state. Each keeps its
computation and its halting; its reading becomes the host’s flag as a latch, raised on an
earned chain whose claim is the guest’s own reading; and its prices become the host’s
ledger, exactly, except for a surcharge of at most two at the move where the reading
first says yes, when the reading starts at no. The surcharge is zero when that move
costs three or more, and it can’t always be avoided: when the guest certifies with a
ledger below three, no program on that host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger
exactly (Theorems 16.29 and 16.30). Picture a clerk who’ll stamp anybody’s receipt.
He copies it onto his own forms, bills at your rates to within two, and the stamp at the
bottom is one he earned by checking your own reading. He didn’t copy it.

What’s outside the class is outside the theorems. A machine whose reading no pro-
gram decides (an oracle checker, say, which the definition of Thiele-complete doesn’t
rule out) doesn’t come in. Nor does a machine whose next move is nobody’s compu-
tation. Nor does a guest that starts with a table of facts nobody checked: the guests
start where their presentation says, and the host from a clean start.

And here’s why insisting on no built-in step is the point. A plain interpreter on an
ordinary computer runs guests too, but then the guest’s record is data the interpreter’s
program updates by convention, which is exactly the position of the ordinary pro-
grammable computer from the front matter and Section 16.16. That’s a fact about how
such interpreters are built. It says nothing about what they can do: U and UP are

                                            311
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


fixed interpreters, and their record isn’t kept by convention. Nothing in them raises
the host’s flag except the host’s own CERTIFY, and the host’s step won’t let that pass
without a COMMIT, or the COMMIT without a CHECK on a slot nobody has touched.
The guest’s record isn’t data the host updates. It’s a record the host earns again, under
the same rule, on its own registers.

16.20 What it doesn’t do
Here’s where it falls short, in plain words, because a small machine is only honest if
its edges are as visible as its middle.

   • The check price is flat. CHECK costs 1 whether it’s asking “is this 0” or “is
     this at least a billion.” The property language is fixed and each property is one
     evaluation, so “pays for its work” here means that flat price, the same however
     hard the question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty of the check
     would be a different machine, and I haven’t built it.
   • DEC on zero isn’t a write. It doesn’t change the counter, so it doesn’t change the
     version. That’s the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means DEC
     on zero is a free way to move the line number without leaving any mark. The
     idle run in the window section uses exactly that.
   • After a trap, a trace still pays. On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
     traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them
     changes the core. I chose to keep charging so that the ledger stays the plain sum
     of what was issued (Theorem 16.5 has no exceptions); the price of that choice is
     that a trapped machine can still be billed for nothing.
   • “Checked” means what the property language can say. On this machine that’s
     is zero, is even and is at least n, and a live fact means one of those holds of one
     counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean the program is correct, or that anything
     follows from the property, or that the property was worth checking. So can a
     proved machine of this kind check “sorted,” the claim the opening chapter’s
     table runs on? Yes, through an encoding. A copy of this machine, instruction
     for instruction, with its property language left open, has provenance, checker
     soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once for every property
     language that comes with an exact equality test and a checker proved equal to
     its meaning. Give it “the list this counter encodes is sorted” as a property and
     it certifies a sorted list for three and refuses an unsorted one forever (sorted_
     run_certifies, sorted_run_certifies_iff and sorted_run_refus
     ed_forever, EarnedGeneric.v). The copy is written out again in its own file,
     and no theorem derives it from this one; putting the two side by side is how
     you check they’re the same machine. What makes that a check of the list is the
     proof that the checker means sortedness. Without that proof, “sorted” would be
     a number some unconstrained code wrote into a counter, and the record would
     be honest about the counter and silent about the list.


                                          312
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


   • The certificate is historical. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter
     can change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and
     committed about an edition. It says nothing about whether the claim is still true.
   • One latch, and a channel that moves on. The flag records that an earned chain
     happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing.
     The channel is the part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it
     names a fact that some earlier passing COMMIT committed (certified_ch
     annel_earned and channel_names_last_commit, EarnedCore.v). But a
     later commitment replaces it, so at the end it names the last earned commitment,
     which needn’t be the one the flag rose on. Two runs from start(0, 0) show it,
     worked from the instruction table. First run: CHECK is zero A; CHECK is zero
     B; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY; COMMIT is zero B. Second run: the same
     five instructions with the last two swapped, so COMMIT is zero B comes before
     CERTIFY. Both end in the same state: both counters 0 at version 0, both facts in
     the table, the channel holding (zero, B, 0), the trap down, a ledger of five and
     the flag up. In the first run the flag rose at step four, on the commitment about
     A. In the second it rose at step five, on the commitment about B. So the flag is
     an ever-certified latch: it says an earned chain happened at some step, and the
     end state doesn’t say which claim or which step. A receipt naming the claim
     the flag first rose on would need that claim kept where nothing can overwrite it;
     a receipt with a time on it would also need the step number kept; and several
     certifications that each last would need a record richer than one flag. None of
     those is built or proved here. They’re extensions. Several claims need a latch
     each.
   • Sixteen checks per run, ever. Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a
     run gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth
     traps. A certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but
     it’s a hard wall for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and it’s
     this machine’s small version of the opening chapter’s “you can’t keep all of it.”
     A CHECK that repeats a claim already in the table, same property, same counter,
     same edition, passes again and takes another entry. So the wall is sixteen passing
     CHECKs, and sixteen different claims is a different count. Removing duplicates,
     evicting old facts or collecting dead ones would each be a different design, and
     each would need its own invariants proved.
   • The clean start matters. Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of
     three are all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded
     with facts nobody checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems
     are about what the machine produces. What you smuggle in at the door is
     outside them. Spell the door out once: the theorems cover any list of instructions
     anybody can issue, from a clean start, on a step that runs as written, with nothing
     else writing to the machine. They say nothing about whoever sets or restores the
     start, about a reset, about a device that misbehaves, or about whoever carries

                                          313
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


      the flag’s value to you.
   • The universal programs have stated guests. U runs every one of this machine’s
     programs from every clean start start( x, y), with halting, answers, flag and
     ledger matched (the flag over the whole run, the ledger at matching points).
     UP runs every computably presented Thiele machine, with its reading decided
     by a program, its record carried as a latch, and its ledger matched to within a
     surcharge of at most two when its reading starts at no, and of three when it starts
     at yes. When the guest certifies with a ledger below three, no program on that
     host, run from a clean start, matches its ledger exactly. A machine outside that
     class, with a reading no program decides, isn’t covered by either. The simpler
     host with the built-in guest step pays one per guest step whatever the step was,
     so its ledger is at least the guest’s and usually more; U’s is exact, and UP ’s is
     exact up to the surcharge.
   • Slow, and fed directly. Universality is Minsky’s, with the inputs placed straight
     in the counters. Getting from an arbitrary Turing machine to two counters goes
     through his exponential packing, which my files don’t redo; the compiler behind
     UP uses the library’s version of it, and nothing about it is fast.
   • The step doesn’t police trivial checks. CHECK at least 0 passes on every value,
     so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for three from any start
     (the note after Theorem 16.17). A check that can’t fail establishes nothing, and
     the machine raises the flag for it anyway. The step checks order, aboutness and
     an honest checker, and it leaves “was that worth asking” to whoever reads the
     record.
   • The toll is a choice here; nothing forces it. Section 4’s argument forces a toll on
     a finite machine that pays for every merge. This machine is neither. Its counters
     have no ceiling, so it’s infinite. And its free instructions merge states: take a core
     at line ℓ with c at 1 and version w, and a core at line j − 1 with c at 0 and version
     w + 1, everything else alike, and DEC c j sends both to line j with c at 0 and
     version w + 1, for nothing. So for this machine the price of one is a design choice
     the chairs don’t force.

16.21 What this chapter adds up to
So Part IV has one machine, and it isn’t the model. It’s a Thiele machine in the front
matter’s sense, an instance of the certification system with the toll proved: earned_
cs (Theorem 16.6). It’s Thiele-complete, in the sense of Definition 16.7, the sense no
clock meets (Theorems 16.19 and 16.21): it computes whatever a Turing machine can,
its computing is free and can’t touch the record, and, from a clean start, its record is
earned. And the universal Thiele machine runs on a host made of its own kinds of
instruction: one fixed program, U, with no guest step built in, that runs every one
of its programs with halting, flag and ledger matched exactly and earns its own flag
(Section 16.13); and the same program with one paid move added, UP , that runs every


                                           314
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


computably presented Thiele machine, carrying its reading as a latch, its prices to
within two when its reading starts at no, and a flag earned on the guest’s own reading
(Section 16.14).

If you ever find yourself wondering whether a property of this machine is the model’s
or just the machine’s, hold it up against Section 3’s certification system, the latch of
Section 10 and the four clauses of Thiele-complete. What follows from those holds of
every machine that meets them; the rest (a table of sixteen facts, three properties, a flat
price of one) is this machine’s choice. Six instructions, and a seventh for a host that
has to bill somebody else’s prices. If the model needs more than that, this is where it’ll
show.

What’s left of Part IV: whether any of this depends on counters (Section 17), how
machines are built from parts (Section 18), whether any of it actually runs (Section 19),
then a check worth earning, and then what any of this costs against physics.

17 Every model
Here’s the worry I couldn’t put down after the last chapter. Everything in it was built
on Minsky’s two counters. The definition of Thiele-complete names a two-counter
window in clause (a). The universal program runs two-counter guests. So is all of this
a fact about counters? Pick a different machine to start from, a Turing machine with
its tape, a register machine, Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus, and does the record
still go on the same way, or did I just find a trick that happens to work for one toy?

I chased it with a picture: a box with a panel bolted to its front. The box computes,
with levers for moves and a window showing what clause (a) asks to see, two numbers
and a line number. The panel is the last chapter’s earned layer: version tallies that
click when the box writes, a rack for facts, the flag, and the three buttons CHECK,
COMMIT and CERTIFY at one mark each. The worry is whether that panel only bolts
onto the one box I built.

If it did, it would be a curiosity. The whole point of the opening chapter was that the
second computer is missing something any computer could have. So this chapter tries
to break that, from both directions: the panel onto other boxes, and other boxes run
inside mine.

17.1 From any base up
Start with the direction I care about most: the panel onto a box I didn’t build. The box
can be any machine at all that has a universal base in the sense of clause (a), and in the
picture that’s two things. It shows a two-counter window. And for each two-counter
instruction it has a lever that acts on the window as that instruction does. What else is
inside, what its states look like, I don’t get to know.

My first guess was to keep whatever the box came with. Plenty of machines have a
meter of their own, or a light on the front that means something’s done, so leave those

                                           315
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


where they are, bolt the panel on beside them, and see what happens. It can’t work,
and the definition says why. If a lever can cost something, computing isn’t free. If a
lever can switch on the box’s own light, a record went up with no CHECK behind
it. Thiele-complete rules out both. So the meter and the light come off, along with
everything else the box already had: its costs, its record, all of it, except the states, the
levers and what each lever does to the state.

Then bolt on a panel cut down from the small machine’s, and nothing else: one version
number for the whole box that every lever raises, which is the tally, a table with room
for at least one fact, and three new moves, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY, at one
mark each, with every lever free. Call that the lift of the machine.


Theorem 17.1 (Every universal base lifts). (1) The lift of any box with a universal base,
over a claim language with an exact equality test and a checker proved to mean what it says, is
Thiele-complete, as long as the claims its CHECK can ask include one that’s true at one loaded
state and false at another, and the fact table has room for at least one fact. (2) The claims “this
register is at least n” and “the program is at line n,” read off the window, always include such
a claim, so with those claims every universal base lifts. (3) Conversely, every Thiele-complete
machine has an interface meeting the four clauses under which its base moves, taken alone,
form a machine with a universal base. (4) The panel leaves the box alone: from a state whose
trap is down, a run of lever pulls in the lift moves the box exactly as the box’s own run does,
and the trap stays down.


The proof of (1) is the small machine’s proof with the bins swapped out for whatever
the box has. That’s the part I’d braced for, and it turned out to be nothing. The chain
CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY never looked at anything but the tally and the claim.
The levers never touched the panel. Neither side of the proof ever needed to know it
was looking at pebbles.

Checked as lift_thiele_complete, lift_window_nonvacuous, lift_windo
w_thiele_complete, lift_reduct_universal and lift_projection_run
(LiftCore.v, LiftConverse.v), all closed.

So the earned layer isn’t something two counters do. It sits on top of any machine
that can compute, and it never needed to know which one. I’d half expected to be
rewriting the proof once per model.

17.2 What never lifts
A theorem that says the panel fits every box is one I don’t trust until I’ve watched it
fail to fit something. So I went looking for boxes it won’t turn into a Thiele machine,
and the first one I tried was the one I was surest would work.

A Turing machine, with one fixed table. Each lever does one row of the table. That
looked like the obvious base to me, and it isn’t one at all. Clause (a) asks for a lever for


                                               316
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


every two-counter instruction, and there are infinitely many two-counter instructions,
since a jump can go to any line. A fixed table has finitely many rows, so it has finitely
many levers, and it runs out of levers long before it runs out of instructions. The first
two items below are that failure in two forms, and the others fail for other reasons.
Each is proved.


Theorem 17.2 (What doesn’t lift). (1) A box with only finitely many levers has no universal
base, and no box with a universal base is finitely branching, meaning that from every state all
its levers together lead to only finitely many different states. (2) The lift of a finitely branching
box is never Thiele-complete, whatever claims and fact table it gets. (3) Neither is the lift of a
box whose step ignores the state it’s in, where each lever sends every state to the same place.
(4) On a record axis where every place is at or below every other, there is no Thiele-complete
machine at all. (5) The lift’s own non-vacuity clause holds exactly when the fact table has room
and some claim is true at one loaded state and false at another.


Checked as lift_finite_moves_not_a_base, lift_ub_not_finitely_bra
nching, lift_finite_branching_not_complete, lift_stateless_not_c
omplete, lift_ax_indiscrete_no_machine and lift_canonical_nonvac_
iff (LiftConverse.v, LiftAxis.v), all closed.

So my first test case failed, and at first I read item (1) as saying a Turing machine can’t
be a base at all. It says something narrower. A Turing machine with one fixed table can’t
be one. A classic model comes in the other way round, with one lever for each whole
program, run to the end. Pull it and the box runs that program from start to stop in
a single move. That’s how the register machine below comes in, and it’s the honest
reading of “a Turing machine is a base” too. The levers are the programs. They aren’t
the rows.

Item (3) is a box with no memory. Pull a lever and it lands wherever that lever always
lands, whatever happened before. So a window on it can’t tell INC A followed by
INC A from INC B followed by INC A, and a box that can’t tell those apart can’t keep
two counters in its window.

Item (4) is the trouble with bare preorders from Section 11, where the cups stopped
telling you the place, showing up one level higher. If every place on the axis is at or
below every other, the flag has no up to go to. No step ever turns a cup over, nothing
ever has to pay, and the earned chain has nothing to earn.

17.3 The same thing, in seven models
Now the other direction, the one the worry was really about. Put boxes with different
insides in a row: one with a tape, one rewriting lambda terms, one with bins. Is a
panel riding on one of them the same as a panel riding on another? The honest way to
ask is whether the boxes agree on what they compute.



                                                317
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


My first idea was to wire the boxes to each other myself, two at a time, with a rela-
tion that says one box’s run keeps pace with another’s. I even have such a relation.
Section 10 defines weak base equivalence, and then has to admit that it never con-
nects any two of the bases it was built for. Doing that box by box would be years of
work, and somebody has already done the hard part, in a form that doesn’t need my
relation at all. The Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs, built over several years by
Yannick Forster, Dominique Larchey-Wendling, Gert Smolka and many others, proves
in Coq that seven models of computation compute the same relations on numbers:
the weak call-by-value lambda calculus L, Turing machines, two kinds of Minsky
machine, binary stack machines, John Conway’s FRACTRAN, and the µ-recursive
functions. Conway’s model I know only as a step on the library’s road to two counters
(Section 16) and by its place on that list, so I’ll say nothing about it beyond that. I
didn’t re-prove the agreement. I lean on their proof. Their proof is checked by the
same proof assistant as mine, so leaning on it costs me nothing in certainty. What I
proved is the joint where my boxes meet theirs.


Theorem 17.3 (The base doesn’t matter). (1) A relation on numbers that’s computable
in any one of those seven models is computable in all seven. (2) The box that keeps a whole
two-counter configuration in one number, with one lever for each instruction, has a universal
base, its step is computable in all seven models, and its lift, with a table of sixteen facts, is
Thiele-complete. (3) A register machine of the kind Cook and Reckhow described, where each
two-counter instruction compiles to at most six of its own instructions, has a universal base
too, and its lift is Thiele-complete. (4) Any box on numbers with a universal base lifts to a
Thiele-complete machine, and its step, computable in one model, is computable in all seven.


Checked as lift_num_models_agree, lift_ex_in_all_models, lift_ex_t
hiele_complete, lift_ram_thiele_complete, lift_numeric_base and l
ift_classic_bases (LiftModelsAll.v, LiftModels.v), all closed, with the library’s
own equivalences carrying the part about seven models.

So the answer to the worry is that the record doesn’t care. A box with a universal base,
described in any of the models people have used to say what computing is, takes the
same panel, becomes the same kind of machine, and pays the same three marks for
the same three acts.

And the trip goes back down. So far the panel went onto other boxes. Now put another
box, panel and all, inside mine. Section 16 proved that the fixed program UP on the
small machine’s host runs every computably presented Thiele machine. In terms of
the seven models, that reads: if the four relations that describe a machine (its driver,
which picks the next move or says stop, its step, its cost and its reading, on codes) are
computable in any one of the seven, then the machine is computably presented, and
UP runs it, halting when it halts, with its flag, and with a surcharge of at most two
when its reading starts at no.


                                              318
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Checked as lift_computable_runs_on_U (LiftHeadline.v).

So a Thiele machine described in lambda calculus runs, under one fixed program, on
the small machine’s host. That’s model independence in both directions: up, by lifting
any universal base, and down, by running anything presentable on one fixed program.
When I saw both arrows close I stopped worrying that I’d built a trick for one toy. A
trick for one toy wouldn’t survive being carried both ways.

17.4 Why two counters
If the box doesn’t matter, why did I build on two bins? Because I wanted the smallest
box that holds up, and the obvious smaller one has a single bin. Nothing earlier in this
book says one bin is too few. So before I’d let myself say two is the fewest, I tried one.

Watch what a program on one bin can see. While the bin isn’t empty, it can’t tell how
full it is: a stretch of lines that never finds the bin empty does exactly the same thing
from a fuller bin, with the extra pebbles riding along. So the only news a one-bin
program ever gets is the bin running dry. Between two of those moments it’s just
walking its own lines, and among more moments than there are lines, two are on the
same line, which is the pigeonhole again. Put those together and a one-bin program
either stops within a count you can write down in advance, or never stops at all.


Theorem 17.4 (One counter is too few). (1) A program P on one bin, started with n pebbles
in it, halts exactly when it has stopped within k (n + k + 1) steps, where k is the number of
lines in P. So whether it halts is decidable. (2) Halting for the book’s two-counter machine is
undecidable. (3) So no translation from two-counter programs to one-counter programs keeps
halting, unless the complement of Turing-machine halting could be listed by a program.

Proof. (1) Two facts and a count. The two facts are the walk above: the extra pebbles
ride along, and among more moments than there are lines, two are at the same line.
Counting with those two facts gives the bound. (2) The library’s undecidability of
Minsky-machine halting, carried over to the book’s instruction set line by line. (3) A
translation that kept halting would make two-counter halting decidable by (1).

Checked as lift_oc_halts_bound, lift_oc_halts_dec, lift_cm_halting
_undecidable, lift_no_oc_translation and lift_no_oc_translation_u
ndecidability (LiftOneCounter.v, LiftModels.v), all closed.

So two counters are the fewest in exactly this sense: one counter can’t compute every-
thing, because its halting can be decided, and two can. I like where the answer came
from. The pigeonhole that left no spare chair in the closed room is the same one that
says why the box has two bins.




                                             319
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


17.5 What this chapter doesn’t say
A panel that bolts onto anything is an easy picture to hear too much in, so here are four
things the chapter might be heard to say, and doesn’t. First, it doesn’t prove “a lift is
Thiele-complete exactly when its base is universal” as one equivalence. It proves the
upward direction, the converse for every Thiele-complete machine’s own base moves,
and the two kinds of base that never lift. Second, it doesn’t contain a Turing machine’s
rule table running a tape. The Turing machines here are the library’s, and they enter
through what they compute. Third, the lift’s tally is one version number for the whole
machine. It doesn’t keep one per register, the way the small machine keeps one per
counter. That’s coarser, and it’s enough for every theorem above. Fourth, it doesn’t
show that a lifted machine is computably presented in general. The trip down needs
the four relations, and for a particular machine somebody has to supply them.

All of it is one closed statement too, if you want the whole chapter in one place.
Checked as lift_model_independence (LiftHeadline.v).

I went into this chapter looking for the place where the bins were doing secret work
for the panel. I didn’t find one. Either there isn’t one, or I didn’t look hard enough,
and the four items above are where I’d send anybody who wants to look harder.

18 Built from parts
Back in Section 3 I asked a question and only got halfway: bolt two certification
systems together, and do you get one? Everything real is built out of parts. A computer
is a processor and memory and a disk, a bank is branches, a proof is lemmas. If the
record and its toll only held for one machine at a time and fell apart the moment you
put two together, they’d be a property of toys.

So put two Thiele machines on a bench, each box with its own panel, and wire them
up the three ways anybody wires machines. Side by side, with no wire between them
at all, so that every move is a lever pulled on one box or the other. End to end, with
the first box’s bins tipped into the second’s when the first is done. And one inside the
other, with the inner box running as a guest on the outer one. Some of it holds. Some
of it provably doesn’t, and the places where it doesn’t were where I learned the most.

18.1 Side by side
Two boxes on the bench, no wire between them. A move of the pair is a lever pulled
on one box or the other. The question is what the pair’s record should be, and my first
answer was the wrong one: a single count of how many certifications the bench has
made. One number, easy to read. I’ll come back to why it fails, because it’s in the list
of things that break. What works is to keep both panels showing. The pair’s record is
the pair of records, a place for the left machine and a place for the right one, compared
one side at a time.

Since that record has more than two places, “Thiele-complete” in this chapter means


                                          320
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


the definition of Section 16 with the record allowed to be a place along a direction, the
way Section 11 set it up. The old definition had a single bit there, and at two places
this one is exactly the old one. Checked as ax_tc_two_point_iff (AxTwoPoint.v).


Theorem 18.1 (Side by side). (1) The cost of any run of the pair is the left machine’s cost of
its moves plus the right machine’s cost of its moves, and the order in which levers on the two
boxes were interleaved doesn’t change where the pair ends up or what it paid. (2) The pair pays
the toll exactly when both machines do. (3) Read through “either flag is up,” two certification
systems side by side are a certification system with floor one; read through “both flags are up,”
a run that starts with both flags down and ends with both up costs at least two, and two is
reached when each part can certify for one. (4) Two Thiele-complete machines side by side are
a Thiele-complete machine. (5) In that pair, call a side’s floor the place on its record axis where
its clean states sit. A run from a clean start that ends with each side at or above a point that
isn’t at or below that side’s floor makes at least six record moves and raises the ledger by at
least six, and six is reached. (6) The pair of records is the product in the precise sense: for any
machine mapping into both, preserving records, there’s exactly one map into the pair that does
both jobs.


Most of that is what you’d guess from the bench. Each box keeps its own ledger
and nobody else pulls its levers, so the bills add, and it can’t matter which box you
happened to work on first. The six in (5) is two certifications of three marks each, one
per box, with no discount for doing them on the same bench.

Checked as cmpz_cost_prod, cmpz_interleaving_invariant, cmpz_prod
_a2_iff, cmpz_cs_or_floor, cmpz_cs_and_floor, cmpz_cs_and_tight,
cmpz_prod_tc, cmpz_prod_joint_certificate, cmpz_prod_joint_cer
tificate_tight and cmpz_prod_universal (CzProd.v, CzCounter.v, CzCS.v,
CzProdTC.v, CzCat.v), all closed. The machines that preserve cost and record form
a category with these pairs as products, and the pairing is a symmetric monoidal
structure, with the pentagon, triangle and hexagon laws checked (CzCat.v).

That last sentence is the most formal way I know of saying “side by side composes,
and nothing about the order of the parts matters.” It’s a lot of category theory to
confirm what the bench told me in a glance, and I’m glad to have it anyway. A glance
is where I’d have missed something.

18.2 One after the other
Now wire them end to end. Run the first box, and when it’s done, tip its two bins into
the second box’s start, for free, and run the second. That’s how programs get chained
everywhere, and my first thought was that the tipping couldn’t matter. It’s plumbing.
Pebbles go from one bin into another, nobody checks anything, and plumbing has no
business on a record. That turned out to be half right, and the wrong half is item (4).




                                               321
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Theorem 18.2 (One after the other). (1) Running one Thiele-complete machine and then
handing its two counters to another through free loads gives a Thiele-complete machine. (2)
For any two programs of the two-counter machine, it computes the composite: some schedule
leaves the first machine’s window where the first program takes the input, and the second’s
where the second program takes that result. (3) The hand-off keeps the toll when every state
it can load into sits at one level of the second machine’s record. (4) If some load lands the
second machine at a record that isn’t at or below another load’s, the hand-off loses the toll: it’s
a certification nobody paid for.


Checked as cmpz_seq_tc, cmpz_seq_composes, cmpz_ld_a2_if and cmpz_ld
_unclean (CzSeq.v, CzLoad.v), all closed.

Item (4) is the one to remember. The tipping is free, so it had better not tip in anything
that counts as established. If pouring pebbles into the second box can land its panel
somewhere that isn’t at or below where some other pouring would land it, the second
machine gets a raised record without ever having checked anything. That’s a forged
certificate wearing the costume of plumbing. My first thought was right about the
pebbles. It was wrong about where they land.

18.3 What doesn’t compose
Here’s the list of things I tried to build on the bench that fell apart, each with a proof
that it does. Every one of them started as a reasonable-looking wiring job.


Theorem 18.3 (What breaks). (1) Read the pair through “both flags are up” as a single flag,
and any run that raises it from a clean start makes at least six record moves; the definition
of Thiele-complete asks for a claim that three moves can certify, so through the pair’s own
interface that reading fails the non-vacuity clause. (2) Two clocks side by side are weakly
Thiele-complete. They aren’t Thiele-complete, so composing the easy notion composes nothing.
(3) Give the small machine a second writer that changes counter A without raising its version,
and the run “check that A is 0, let the other writer change A, commit, certify” raises the flag,
so the earned-record clause fails when the machine is read the small machine’s way, with the
second writer as a base move. (4) Two windows that each price their own machine exactly can
collide as a pair, so exact pricing isn’t preserved by putting machines together. (5) Count the
pair’s certifications with one number, and the count can’t tell which side certified. The pair of
records can.


Checked as cmpz_and_costs_six, cmpz_and_not_complete, cmpz_or_clo
cks_not_complete, cmpz_shared_raises, cmpz_shared_not_earned, cm
pz_exactness_not_preserved and cmpz_sum_record_loses (CzProdTC.v,
CzShared.v, CzWin.v, CzCounter.v), all closed.

Item (1) is one flag for two boxes. It costs what two certifications cost, six record moves,
and the definition wants a claim that three can settle, so a single flag over both panels,


                                               322
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


read through the pair’s interface, is too expensive to meet the definition. That’s this
interface. Nothing here shows that no other interface on the pair could meet it, and
item (4) shows the pair meeting it through a richer record.

Item (3) is the one with the most teeth, because it’s the opening chapter’s bug, the file
checked and then swapped. On the bench it’s a second hand reaching into a bin while
the box isn’t looking. Two writers, one value, and a check that’s out of date by the
time anybody leans on it. The small machine’s version rule is exactly the fix, and this
is what happens without it: the commitment goes through on a claim about a thing
that changed underneath it. Database people and the people who build processors
have been fighting this one since at least Kung and Robinson’s paper of 1981 and the
Livermore report of 1987, and the opening chapter called it time of check to time of
use. Here it’s a theorem about the record, and the version number is what makes it
go away. The second hand can still reach in. With the version, its reach shows on the
tally, and the COMMIT traps.

Item (5) is my first guess from the side-by-side wiring, coming back to fail on schedule.
It’s why the pair’s record compares one side at a time. Squash the two records into
one number and the record forgets who did the work, and a record that forgets who
did the work isn’t one anybody can lean on.

18.4 One inside another
The last way to wire the bench: put one box inside the other, as a guest on a host.
Part of this the book already has. Section 16 showed the fixed program UP runs any
computably presented Thiele machine, and the small machine’s own programs, with
the record earned again by the host. What’s new is putting those links in a row, a box
in a box in a box, and asking what the outermost one pays.

My first guess was that it could pay less. A host that’s clever about how it runs the
guest might skip some of the guest’s bills. The first item below puts a floor under that:
the host pays at least one for each step where the guest’s record went up. It’s a floor
on rises, and it doesn’t keep the guest’s whole bill.


Theorem 18.4 (Nesting). (1) If a host that pays the toll simulates a guest faithfully, with
a record map that reflects the order, then every run of the guest is matched by a run of the
host that costs at least the number of the guest’s steps that turned a cup over. (2) In each link
the surcharge is 0 while the guest’s record is down, and the bounds below hold at the points
where it’s up. A small-machine guest on UP is carried with surcharge exactly 0. A computably
presented machine whose reading starts at no is carried, through its compiled guest, with
surcharge at most 2, and exactly 2 once its reading has first said yes when moreover every
move costs at most one. One whose reading starts at yes is carried with surcharge exactly 3. (3)
Links compose, and their surcharges add: a tower of k links has surcharge between the sums of
their lower and upper bounds. (4) A tower of presented machines, each level running the next
on UP , adds exactly 2 for every level above the first, on top of the first level’s own surcharge,


                                               323
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


provided every level’s host run is itself presented by the next.


Checked as cmpz_sim_cost_ge_exits, cmpz_priced_link, cmpz_host_lin
k, cmpz_host_link_le_two, cmpz_host_link_exact, cmpz_host_link_st
art_up, cmpz_link_compose, cmpz_tower and cmpz_tower_presented_exa
ct (CzCat.v, CzLink.v, CzTower.v, CzSelf.v), all closed.

Item (1) is the cleanest sentence in the chapter. However you build the outer box, as
long as it pays its own toll and doesn’t lie about the inner box’s record, it pays at least
one for every step where the inner record climbed. That’s a floor on the climbs, and
it isn’t the inner box’s whole bill. A guest can charge a hundred for one rise while a
host charges one for the matching rise, and both pay their tolls. Keeping the whole
bill takes a further demand on the simulation, that it carry the guest’s costs too, and
for UP that’s the separate ledger theorem of Section 16.14, with its surcharge.

The premise in (4) is a real limit, and I want to say exactly what it is. Two links are
unconditional: from a presented machine to its compiled guest, and from that guest to
UP running it. Going deeper needs the host’s own run, at each level, to be presented
as a machine the next level up can run, and the host keeps a register for every whole
number, which doesn’t have a one-to-one code in a single number the way a presented
machine needs. So the box that has to fit inside the next one has more states than there
are numbers to name them. For three levels and more, the theorem says what happens
if each level is presented. It doesn’t claim that it always is.

18.5 What this adds up to
Wired side by side, end to end, or one inside the other, a Thiele machine on the bench
stays a Thiele machine, and the tolls add the way money adds. What breaks, breaks
for reasons you could name before you saw the proof: a single flag for two claims
costs two claims’ worth, a clock is still a clock, a shared value without a version
can’t be trusted, and a free hand-off can’t be allowed to carry a certificate. None of
those is a surprise in hindsight. All of them are now theorems, and the composition
question from Section 3 has an answer. Two certification systems side by side are
one under both readings I checked, “either flag” and “both flags.” The “both flags”
reading still fails the definition through the pair’s interface, the second writer breaks
the earned-record clause through the small machine’s own reading, the clocks and the
two counterexamples fail outright, and simulation in general has a proved floor.

Three of my first guesses on this bench were wrong: the single count, the harmless
tipping, and the clever host that pays less. The last two leaned toward a record that
says more than anybody paid for, and the first toward one that says less than it should.
I didn’t see any of the three coming. The proofs did.




                                               324
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele



19 Running it
Everything so far is theorems. A fair reader is entitled to ask the rude question: does
any of it run? The Coq definitions are drawings, exact to the last part, and every
theorem in this book is about the drawings. A proof that the drawn machine does
something isn’t a machine doing it, and I’d be suspicious of a book about a machine
that never once got built and switched on.

So this chapter builds it twice from the same drawings, once by Coq’s own machinery
and once by hand, switches both on, and compares them step by step. It says exactly
