19.1 Taking the coat off
The first build is made by Coq itself. Coq can turn a definition into a program in an
ordinary programming language. It calls that extraction. In the drawings every part
comes wearing a coat of proof, and extraction takes the coat off: the proof parts are
thrown away and what’s left is code that computes the same function. I extract to
OCaml, an ordinary programming language that Coq’s extraction supports directly.
Two files do it. One extracts the small machine, the host machine with a register for
every whole number, the host with PAY, both universal programs U and UP written
out instruction by instruction, and the loaders. The other extracts the compiler below
and its runner.

Two things about that build are worth knowing before you believe a word of the rest.
First, the code that runs is the code the theorems are about. Coq won’t extract some
of the files directly (a technical limit on files that rename modules), so the extracted
functions are copies with plain names, and each copy is proved equal to the original,
by computation or by a short proof, inside Coq. The two universal programs are
printed by Coq as literal lists and proved equal to the programs in the theorems.
Checked as rlz_host_program_is, rlz_phost_program_is and rlz_host_r


                                          325
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


un_prog_is (Realize.v and RealizePriced.v).

Second, whole numbers, and here my first instinct was the wrong one. The quick
way to build is to map Coq’s whole numbers onto the computer’s own machine
integers, which are fast. They’re 63 bits wide here, and the guest codes U reads go up
near 2100 , so they’d wrap around without a word of warning. Coq’s whole numbers
never overflow. A machine word does, and the book already told you what that cost
Ariane 5 (Section ). So the extraction maps Coq’s whole numbers to an OCaml library
of unbounded integers, and each arithmetic operation is mapped by hand to that
library’s version of it. Those are the hand-written substitutions in the trusted path:
one line that maps Coq’s whole numbers onto the library’s integers, a few that map
Coq’s Booleans, decisions, lists, pairs, options and its one-value type onto OCaml’s
own, two that map Coq’s “and” and “or” onto OCaml’s, two in one file that map
the hosts’ one-value property types onto OCaml’s unit, and the arithmetic operations,
seventeen in one file and thirteen in the other. Each arithmetic line carries a one-line
justification next to it: addition is addition, subtraction stops at zero the way Coq’s
does, division by zero gives zero the way Coq’s does. The rest is Coq’s own definitions.
The hand-written code outside that is two drivers, which read input, print output, and
count steps while they call the extracted step function in a loop.

What you’re trusting, if you trust a run: Coq’s extraction, the OCaml compiler and
the C tools under it, the integer library, those mapping lines, the two drivers, and the
Python code that does the comparing. None of that is proved. Coq’s extraction, the
OCaml compiler, the C tools and the integer library are old and used by a lot of people.
The mapping lines, the drivers and the comparing code are mine, and they’re small
enough to read in one sitting. That’s a reason to trust it. It isn’t a proof.

19.2 A second machine, written by hand, to check the first
Switch the first build on and let it run, and what have you learned? Less than I first
thought. A run of extracted code only tells you the extracted code agrees with itself.
If the extraction, or one of the integer mappings, or a driver had slipped somewhere,
a run on its own would never show it. So there’s a second build, made by hand: an
implementation of the small machine and both hosts written separately in Python
straight from the Coq definitions, with every function naming the definition it copies.
Then the two builds are made to argue.

They’re compared on the whole state after every step: the program line, every counter
and register and its version, the fact table in order, the channel, the trap latch, the
ledger and the flag. Against Coq itself, computing the same steps inside the proof
assistant, the Python machine is run on every small-machine program of one or
two instructions over a 26-instruction alphabet and every program of three over a
9-instruction one, 1,431 programs, each run from several starts (4,266 runs in all), 300
random ones, and a few thousand more on each host. Against the extracted OCaml,
the same exhaustive and random small-machine sets again, U and UP on tiny guests,


                                          326
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and the runs below. They agree on every step of every one. I also broke the machine
on purpose, giving it a fact table one too small, a free CHECK, a commitment that ig-
nores versions, and a write that doesn’t bump the version, and each break gets caught.
A second set pins the boundaries this book draws in words, and most of those runs
succeed: two runs that end in the same state with different first certifications, a check
that can’t fail certifying from every start, six commitments billing seven without a flag,
a write after the commitment and a flag over a claim that’s now false, sixteen copies
of one CHECK filling the table, a CERTIFY costing one at a ledger already at two, and
a merge between two yes-states that leaves the entering state alone.

That’s evidence. It isn’t proof, and Section 22 says why Dijkstra would want me to
say so. What it is, is three routes to the same numbers: Coq computing inside itself,
the code Coq extracted, and a machine written by hand from scratch. When they
agree on every step of thousands of programs, a slip in the extraction, the integer
mappings or the drivers would have to be matched by the same slip in a machine
written separately by hand to hide. I can imagine that happening. I can’t imagine it
happening often. The comparison doesn’t test whether the definitions say the right
thing, since the hand-written machine copies them. That’s what having them on the
page is for.

19.3 U on a real guest
Now the universal program, which is where I expected trouble. The guest I wanted
to run first was the obvious one, a guest that goes the whole way: CHECK, COMMIT,
CERTIFY, flag up, run inside U on the built machine. Here’s why that’s not what ran.
U keeps the whole guest program as one number, a number that grows like two raised
to the sum of the codes for the guest’s instructions (for a guest of one instruction it’s
exactly a power of two), and it reads that number the only way a counter can, one unit
at a time. So its speed depends on the code, and the code grows fast: a guest with one
CHECK in it has code 224 , and a guest with the whole chain has a code near 2100 .

So I came down to what could finish. Here’s what ran, on the extracted program,
compared against the Python guest at the end: the host stopped exactly when the
guest did, and showed the guest’s counters, latch, ledger and flag.

                     guest                  host    host steps    time
                     count A down from 2    U       25,953,317
                     one passing CHECK      U      402,654,059   618 s
                     one failing CHECK      U      201,327,155   305 s
                     one passing CHECK      UP     402,654,059   617 s
                     one failing CHECK      UP     201,327,155   313 s

The first row’s count is pinned exactly: if the build changed so that it moved by one
step, the comparison would fail. The times are from one ordinary computer and are
only there to give you the scale. That’s about twelve host steps for every unit of the
guest’s code, for every guest step, which is exponential in the size of the guest. A


                                           327
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


guest with one CERTIFY in it would have code 232 , about fifty billion host steps, and
at the measured rate of about 650,000 steps a second it would take something like
twenty-two hours, nearly a day. The guest I wanted, with the whole chain, has a code
near 2100 , which at the same twelve steps a unit is more than 1031 host steps a guest
step; at the measured rate, with this encoding on that computer, that’s around 1018
years. So U on a guest that certifies is proved. It isn’t run. I’m not going to dress that
up. Runs this long only fit in memory at all because the host’s register store can be
squeezed during the run without changing any state, which is a theorem too. Checked
as rlz_sched_sound (RealizeCompact.v).

Why so slow? Because a fixed program on a machine of counters has to keep the guest
packed into numbers, and counters only count. Whether every universal program on
counters has to pay this much is a real question, and this book doesn’t answer it. What
it claims is exactly what the table shows. I’ll admit the table stung a little. About ten
minutes to watch one CHECK pass is a long time to stare at a machine you built to be
small.

19.4 A compiler, all in Coq
Running guests one CHECK at a time doesn’t tell you whether the built machine
can do anything you’d recognise as a program. You’d want to hand it gcd, or a sort,
written the way people write them, and get the answer out, and writing gcd by hand in
INC and DEC is no way to find out. So the last piece in the drawings is a compiler. The
source is a small language you could write by hand: whole-number variables, addition,
subtraction that stops at zero, comparisons, if, while, and procedures that return several
results, with the rule that a procedure can only call ones defined before it, so there’s no
recursion. Every stage is a Coq function with a Coq proof: the procedures are inlined,
the result is flattened to assignments and jumps, that is compiled to Minsky’s counter
machine through the library’s own compiler, that to a program for the host machine,
that to a two-counter guest, and the guest to a run of UP .


Theorem 19.1 (The compiler is correct). For every source program with no recursion, and
every input: the program computes y exactly when the runner (the Coq function that gets
extracted) halts with y for some amount of fuel; exactly when the compiled host program halts
with y; exactly when the two-counter guest halts with y; and exactly when UP running that
guest halts with y, with its first counter at 0, its ledger at 0 and its flag down. So compiling a
program computes its answer and certifies nothing: the compiler is a route to answers, and a
certification has to be written into the source as a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY. The
runner also takes exactly as many steps as the host program does, with the rest of its fuel left
over, and a run that doesn’t halt has used all its fuel.


Checked as cmp_final (CmpFinal.v), with the runner as cmp_exec_machine, cmp
_exec_sound, cmp_exec_complete and cmp_exec_unhalted (CmpRun.v) and
the source language’s own interpreter as cmp_interp_sound and cmp_interp_co


                                               328
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


mplete (CmpLang.v), all closed. The statement says nothing about how many steps
the compiled program takes. It’s about answers.

The runner and the compiler are extracted, and the build has been run on a set of
programs I picked to be annoying: gcd, factorial, a primality program written with
procedures, an Ackermann tower, a sorting network on a list packed into one number,
and a tiny interpreter for another machine written in the source language. Then 220
random programs that halt, 160 random programs with loops that might not, pro-
grams that never halt run for a fixed budget, and programs mutated on purpose to
make sure the comparison notices. Each answer is compared with plain Python arith-
metic, an independent Python interpreter of the source language, Python machines
running the compiled programs step for step, and, for sixteen of them, Coq computing
the same thing itself. Ackermann’s function at (3, 5) is 253; the source program takes
64,768 operations to get there, and the compiled host program takes about 119 million
steps. The extracted runner does a few million host steps a second, so that’s well
under a minute.

That’s about 1,800 host steps per source operation for Ackermann, and up to about
a hundred thousand for multiplication by repeated addition, because every addition
copies a running total one unit at a time. Counters are unary, and unary is slow, and
the slowdown grows with the values. How it grows with the size of the program I
haven’t measured. The last two stages, the two-counter guest and UP running it, are
proved. They aren’t run, for two reasons: the files that build the guest aren’t extracted,
and even if they were, UP on a compiled guest would be slow for the same reason U
on a certifying guest is. Still, I like that 253. It came out of nothing but INC and DEC,
and a proof that they mean what the source meant.

19.5 What wasn’t built
No chip. The drawings were never cut into metal. Earlier work on this project went
into hardware, a chip design for a much bigger machine, and none of it was carried
over: there’s no circuit for the small machine, no simulation of one at the level of gates,
and no board ever ran any of this. The small machine exists as Coq definitions, as
extracted OCaml, and as a Python program written by hand, and those three agree
on every step anybody has checked. That’s the whole of what “it runs” means in this
book.

I’d love to see it in metal some day. But builds that can be held against each other on
every step are worth a lot to me. A board with nothing to hold it up against isn’t, and
that’s the trade this edition made.

20 The CHSH check
The small machine checks whether a number is zero, even, or at least something.
That’s a fine way to show the chain, and a dull thing to certify. Here’s a check worth
earning, built from zero, and then the one thing the small machine’s host does with it,


                                           329
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


which is smaller and more exact than “it checks for quantum behaviour,” a sentence
that’s tempting and wrong. The short version, so you know where this is going: the
check never computes the famous number and never writes down the famous bound.
It tests seven facts about integers in eight counts. If they pass, a certain five-by-five
table has a property called positive semidefinite, and that property forces the famous
number under the famous bound. The wall is a consequence of the check. It never
goes into it. Everything else is explaining those sentences.

But first, why is a quantum game in a book about records at all? Not for the physics.
Nothing in this section tests nature, and the check can’t tell honest play from a made-
up tally (the guarantee paragraph below says exactly how). It’s here for three reasons,
all about the record. It’s a check whose content is striking enough to tempt anyone
into thinking that certifying it should cost more than certifying something dull, and
on the small machine it doesn’t: a flag raised from a clean start costs at least three, and
exactly three at the cheapest, whatever the claim (Section 16). It sets free observation
against a priced check: a round of the game is written down for nothing, and judging
the pile is one of the three paid acts. And it’s an integer test small enough to be a
property in the small machine’s sense, a checker that’s a little program and a meaning
that’s a statement, with a proof that the two agree, which is exactly what Section 16’s
generic machine asks of any property before it lets a flag stand on it.

20.1 The game
Two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two coins and hands
Alice a question x, zero or one, and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers
a, zero or one; Bob answers b. No talking during the game. They may agree on a
plan beforehand, as detailed as they like. They win a round when their answers differ
exactly when both questions were one. In words: if either question is zero, match; if both
are one, differ.

Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what she says
to x equals one, and the same two for Bob. Four bits. Now write the four requirements
the rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals b1; a1 equals b0; a1
differs from b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1, and a0 equals b1, so
b0 equals b1. But the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1 equals b0 equals b1.
Contradiction. One of the four must break. So any plan loses at least one of the four
question pairs, and if the referee asks all four equally often, the best a plan can do is
three out of four. Seventy-five percent. Do it the long way too: there are sixteen plans
(four bits), and if you write them all out and count wins you’ll find eight win three
rounds and eight win one, and none wins four (the broken requirements always come
in odd numbers, which you can see by adding up the four equations and keeping
only whether the totals come out even or odd, with “equal” as 0 and “differ” as 1:
each of the four answers appears twice on the left, so the left sides add to an even
number, and the right sides add to one). Sharing a coin before the game to pick a
plan at random doesn’t help; a mixture of numbers no larger than three-quarters is no

                                           330
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


larger than three-quarters. Arthur Fine, a philosopher of physics at the University of
Washington, much of whose work is on the physicist Albert Einstein and the quantum
theory, proved in 1982 that the whole “pre-agreed answers, no influence between
rooms” story is exactly the mixtures of those sixteen lists, one scoreboard for all four
questions at once; the sixteen are the whole classical story. That one I don’t have to
take on his word: the form of his theorem that speaks of the four averages is checked
in this book, and the end of this section says how.

The number. Recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one. For each
question pair, let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice’s answer times Bob’s.
The CHSH quantity is S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For one fixed plan
each win adds one to S and each loss subtracts one, so S is wins minus losses: a three-
win plan has S equal to two, a one-win plan has minus two. With equal question
frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over eight. So “seventy-five percent” and
“S at most two” are the same fact, and the second is the one that got the name.

The ceiling is easy to reach and costs nothing to write down. Tally one round per
question pair with both players answering zero every time: after the recoding every
answer is plus one, so all four correlators are one. That’s the plan that answers zero
to everything, which matches on every pair and so wins the three pairs that ask for a
match, S = 1 + 1 + 1 − 1 = 2. On the small machine’s host a tally like that is a few
INCs on counters, and INC is free. Nothing in it says the rounds were played; anybody
can tally anything for nothing. The other side, that no finite mixture of plans beats
two, is Theorem F.2 in Appendix F, one direction of Fine’s result. The full equivalence,
in the form that speaks of the four averages, is checked too, as nec_e_fine_iff; the
last part of this section states it.

20.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared
So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a coin
game? The names come in a line, and the line didn’t mean much to me until I saw
that each of them moved the same thing a notch: from an argument about what’s real,
which you can only agree with or not, toward a pile of counts a referee can judge. Each
one rests on a different piece of the game above.

The trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, by then at the Institute for Advanced Study
in Princeton, and two younger colleagues there, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen,
asking whether quantum mechanics describes everything that’s real about a pair of
particles. Their argument: if measuring one particle lets you predict the other’s result
with certainty, the result must already have been fixed, and the theory leaves that out.
What they rest on is the plan in each player’s pocket, a pre-agreed list of answers,
the plan above. And the first thing worth checking is whether the paper even says
what Einstein meant. By his own account, not quite. Podolsky did the writing, and
that June Einstein wrote to Erwin Schrödinger, the Austrian physicist whose 1926
wave equation is at the heart of quantum mechanics, that the essential thing had been


                                          331
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


“smothered by formalism.” The person who lays that letter out is Arthur Fine, the
same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans above, in his encyclopedia entry on
the argument. So Fine stands at both ends of the line: he checked the founding paper
against what its author meant, and he proved exactly what the plans can do. Even the
founding paper is a lead to check. It isn’t a verdict.

For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic: if each
particle carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms, certain
averages can’t exceed a fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they do. What
that rests on took me a few reads. His inequality rules out the pair of assumptions
together, called local realism (answers exist before you ask, and no influence across the
gap). Either one alone survives it. And where does a paper like that get published? In
a brand-new journal called Physics Physique Fizika, which charged authors no page fees
and in fact paid them by the word, ten cents a word, and which folded in 1968 after
four volumes, or three. I went looking for that count, and the sources don’t agree on it:
four is the number the American Physical Society’s archive of the journal gives, and
Iulia Georgescu, writing about the journal in Physics World in 2026, says three. She’s
also where the ten cents comes from. As Andrew Whitaker tells it in his biography of
Bell, the journal gave out no free copies, so Bell spent his payment buying copies of his
own paper to mail to other physicists. A result nobody else holds a copy of hasn’t left
the room yet, and Bell paid to send his across. In 1969 four physicists, John Clauser,
then a graduate student at Columbia, Michael Horne and Abner Shimony at Boston
University, and Richard Holt at Harvard, rewrote it as the four-average form above,
S at most two, which could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment. It’s called the
CHSH inequality, after their initials. That notch rests on what a real lab can deliver.
Shimony was in philosophy and in physics at Boston University both, which is the
whole line in one man.

Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Stuart Freedman, a grad-
uate student at Berkeley, and Clauser, by then a postdoc there too, tried it in 1972. The
physicist Alain Aspect’s group at the Institut d’Optique in Orsay, with two colleagues
there, Jean Dalibard and Gérard Roger, did it in 1982 with the measurement settings
switched while the photons were in flight, which in the game’s terms, as I read it, is the
referee handing out the questions too late for any note about them to cross between
the rooms. Before that, in 1975, Aspect went to see Bell at CERN to tell him what he
planned, and by Aspect’s own account Bell heard him out in silence and then asked,
first thing, whether he had a permanent position. Aspect did. Bell’s reason, as Aspect
tells it, was that most physicists would take the experiment for a waste of time, or take
him for a crackpot. I read that as the toll in its oldest form: a check that could have
come out the other way costs somebody something to run, and Bell wanted to know
who’d pay. And in 2015 three groups of experimental physicists (Bas Hensen’s in Delft,
with electrons 1.3 kilometres apart; Marissa Giustina’s in Vienna; Lynden Shalm’s at
NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, in Boulder) closed the two



                                           332
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


main escape routes at once. In 2022 Clauser, Aspect and the Austrian physicist Anton
Zeilinger shared the Nobel Prize “for experiments with entangled photons, establish-
ing the violation of Bell inequalities and pioneering quantum information science.”
The 2015 tests came out of that line of work, and Zeilinger was one of the authors of
the Vienna one. So in under fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a
permanent job to risk to a Nobel. The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape,
that the referee’s coins were secretly correlated with the particles, is a philosophical
one and I’m not going to pretend it’s closed.

Now put this book’s check on the same line, because that’s where my position gives.
It sits past the far end, at the counts. Those fifty years went into making the counts
worth judging, rooms really apart, questions really late, escape routes really shut, and
my check starts after all of it. It’s handed eight counts and can’t tell a lab’s tally from
one somebody wrote down for free. So the check is a referee of counts, and everything
that made these counts worth refereeing happened upstream of it.

What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what to
measure from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square
root of two, about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson, a
Soviet mathematician who later taught at Tel Aviv University, in a 1980 paper called
“Quantum generalizations of Bell’s inequality,” proved that that’s a ceiling: quantum
correlations violate Bell, but only up to there. That ceiling, and the state that reaches
it, are checked for strategies in finite dimension, with real amplitudes (qs_tsirels
on and qs_tsirelson_reached, QuantumStrategies.v) and with complex ones (q
c_tsirelson and qc_tsirelson_reached, QuantumStrategiesComplex.v); and
the ceiling holds in any dimension at all, infinitely many levels included (ta_tsirel
son, TsirelsonAlgebraic.v; the next part says how). What’s checked below, besides, is
the algebra.

And the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In 1994 the physicists
Sandu Popescu and Daniel Rohrlich asked: what if you only demand that nothing can
be signalled, that Alice’s answers on their own have the same odds whatever Bob is
asked, and the other way round? Then you can write down a “box” (the PR box, after
their initials) that wins every round (its answers differ exactly when both questions
are one, by fiat, each answer alone a fair coin), S equals four, and nothing about it
lets either room send a message. So relativity alone doesn’t explain the quantum
ceiling; the PR box obeys relativity and beats 2.83. The order is: two for plans, 2.83 for
quantum, four for no-signalling.

And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: somebody
got there first. Popescu and Rohrlich’s initials stuck, but the big review of the field by
Nicolas Brunner and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall, whose 1985
paper on locality and Bell’s theorem appeared in Foundations of Physics, and, separately,
to Leonid Khalfin, a physicist at the Steklov Institute’s Leningrad branch, and Tsirelson


                                           333
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the question that really matters: if
relativity isn’t what stops things at 2.83, what is? People have tried candidates. In
2005 the computer scientist Wim van Dam, who works on the theory of quantum
computing, argued, in a paper on the implausible consequences of such boxes, that
with enough PR boxes, Bob could work out any yes-or-no function of both their inputs
after Alice sends him a single bit, which would make the whole question of how much
two parties need to talk collapse, and that’s a strong hint the boxes are too good to
be real. In 2009 Marcin Pawłowski, a physicist at the University of Gdańsk, and five
coauthors proposed a principle they called information causality: Bob can’t get more
information about Alice’s data than the bits she actually sends him. They argue that
ordinary and quantum physics both obey it, and that any theory that beats 2.83 breaks
it. How much of the rest of the quantum boundary it reaches is something I haven’t
checked. Which principle fixes the whole quantum boundary, if any one does, this
book won’t answer. The check below is a fence at the middle step.

20.3 Five sentences that are easy to say by accident
Here they are, each with what I can stand behind beside it.

“Faster than light.” Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the correlation
shows up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward. “Quantum
means random.” The average S is fixed by the state; what’s random is each single
answer; the plans are the less random side. “A Bell violation proves nonlocality.” It
rules out local realism, both assumptions together, and every real test has loopholes
with names. “A tally above two proves nonlocality.” No: S is a population average,
and one finite tally can land above two by luck. Four rounds, one per question pair,
with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one time in sixteen. That gap between
a population bound and a finite sample is the problem Yanbao Zhang, Scott Glancy
and Emanuel Knill, at NIST in Boulder, work through for real Bell tests (Physical
Review A, 2011 and 2013), and the book doesn’t solve it. The way they solve it is
worth knowing, because it has the shape of this book’s record. Turn each round into
a small bet that no local plan can expect to win, even a plan that remembers every
earlier round, multiply the bets as the rounds come in, and the French mathematician
Jean Ville’s inequality, from his 1939 thesis, one of the works that started the theory of
martingales, says the chance the product ever climbs past one over δ is at most δ. So a
flag can go up for good the moment the product crosses, with its error stated up front.
It needs one thing the small machine doesn’t have: settings drawn underneath the
program, where the program can’t choose them. And how much can one round tell
you? Wim van Dam, Richard Gill, a mathematical statistician who later held the chair
in that subject at Leiden, and Peter Grünwald (2005) measured exactly that, in bits
of evidence against every local plan. Of the two-party proofs they compare, CHSH
comes out the strongest, “much stronger” than the others in their words, at about
0.046 of a bit per round, a few hundredths, so a convincing record takes hundreds of
rounds. Four won’t do. The checked work proves only the narrow thing, that a tally


                                           334
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


above two is not explained by one fixed plan replayed every round (chsh_violation_
rules_out_locally_factorizable_coupling), and that narrow thing is what
the sentence has to stay. And “the PSD test proves the data is quantum.” (PSD is short
for positive semidefinite, the property of the five-by-five table from the short version;
the next part builds both.) It doesn’t, and the direction matters. Passing implies the
five-by-five table, pinned in a way the next part explains, is PSD, and that implies S
squared is at most eight; both are proved. The correlators of a PSD table like that are
the correlators of some quantum strategy. That’s Tsirelson’s representation theorem,
and it’s proved here: the strategy is built on two systems of eight levels each (tr_re
presentation, TsirelsonRepresentation.v). The exact edge of the quantum set for
this game was found by Lawrence Landau, whose 1969 Berkeley thesis was on the
quantum theory of local observables, and Lluís Masanes, then at the University of
Barcelona (next part), and that’s proved here too (am_arcsine, ArcsineBoundary.v).
Failing says nothing about whether the play was quantum: the check is complete for
the pinned matrix, the quantum set is wider than that, and quantum behaviour can
fail it. Every one of the sixteen plans fails it (nec_e_check_refuses_all_plans),
and I’ll show you why. What it guarantees is in one paragraph, once the check is on
the host machine.

20.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means
Here’s the mathematics the check rests on, and it’s one idea: a table of numbers could be
a table of dot products. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on the diagonal
and b off it. It’s positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least zero and a times
c minus b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on the diagonal and one
half off, the determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the diagonal and 1.2 off,
the determinant is negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the table could be the dot
products of some arrows, and 1.2 is too big a dot product for two arrows of length one.
That’s the whole idea, generalised to bigger tables.

Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice’s
two questions, Bob’s two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column zero off the
diagonal (that’s “zero marginals”: the table takes each answer alone to average to zero,
a fair coin; the counts record no marginals and the check doesn’t test this). A0 with
A1 zero, B0 with B1 zero (no round asks Alice both questions, so no tally holds that
average, and the table sets it to zero). Those zeros are choices. They pin the table to
one slice, and I’ll come back to what they cost. And the four Alice-Bob cells hold the
four correlators E. That’s a five-by-five with four free numbers in it. It splits into the
one in the corner and a four-by-four block made of an identity and the two-by-two
grid E of correlators, and PSD of that block is the same as saying E shrinks every vector
(E is a contraction), which is three inequalities: one minus E00 squared minus E10
squared at least zero; one minus E01 squared minus E11 squared at least zero; and
their product at least the square of (E00 E01 plus E10 E11).

Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two diagonal

                                           335
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below 2.83. All four
at one over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero, passes with no
slack, S equals two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry’s size up and a diagonal
goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one, one, one): first diagonal is one minus one
minus one, negative, fails, though S equals two and it’s a perfectly legal classical play.
The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the same way. A fence at the middle step,
and a fence that keeps out every one of the sixteen plans: each has all four correlators
at plus or minus one, so the first diagonal is always one minus one minus one. Of the
classical plays, only diluted mixtures of plans get through.

That point, one over root two in size in every entry, is four real numbers, and no tally
of rounds ever lands on it. A tally’s correlators are ratios of whole numbers, and
the point needs each of them to be one over root two, which would make root two a
fraction, and you killed that fraction with a pencil in Part I. That point and its mirror
image, every sign flipped, are the only places the bound is reached (Remark F.2 in the
appendix). So a passing tally always has S squared strictly below eight. It can get as
close as you like: the (17, 3) tally in the five examples below has S squared equal to
7.84, and tallies of the same shape with a fraction nearer one over root two get nearer
still. Two root two is the least bound the check can promise, and no tally the check
accepts ever reaches it. Hold on to that corner; it comes back.

Picture what quantum play can reach as a field, and every test as a fence. In 2007
Miguel Navascués, Stefano Pironio and Antonio Acín, in a paper called “Bounding
the Set of Quantum Correlations” (NPA, after their initials), came at the edge from
outside, resting on necessary conditions. In their terms a table like this one is the
first rung of a ladder: bigger tables of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary
condition for quantum behaviour when its entries are left free, each rung tighter, and
(their 2008 paper) converging to the quantum set (strictly, the set from commuting
operators, which can differ from the tensor-product set in general scenarios). Each
rung is a fence with the whole field inside it. The check’s table is the first rung with
the marginals and the two within-party entries pinned to zero. Pinning is a stronger
demand than the rung makes, so passing puts you inside the first rung, and a quantum
point can still fail. My fence cuts across the field. Lawrence Landau in 1988 and Lluís
Masanes in 2003 came at the edge itself, for this two-questions-each case only. I’d
have drawn a flat wall at 2.83. The exact boundary they found is a curved surface
(the arc-sine form) touching 2.83 at one point. It’s checked here: a table has a PSD
completion exactly when its entries lie between minus one and one and their arcsines
pass four inequalities (am_arcsine), so those are exactly the quantum tables (am_qu
antum_arcsine, ArcsineBoundary.v).

So the obvious next question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some rung
finally land exactly on the quantum set and stop? My first guess was yes, at least
here. A 2026 paper by Anubhav Chaturvedi, a quantum-information theorist at the
University of Gdańsk, says no: no finite rung of the ladder captures the whole quantum


                                           336
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


set even in this simplest case. And for the four correlators alone, a 2008 paper by the
same Navascués, Pironio and Acín works out that the first rung already lands on
Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. That looked like a contradiction until I saw what
each one fences. Landau and Masanes draw the edge for the four correlators alone.
Chaturvedi’s is the full behaviours, each room’s own odds included. So there’s the
corner again from the other side: tallies never reach it, and, if his proof holds, rungs
never close on the field. I wanted that to be one fact. It’s two. Mine is root two again,
about which points a count can hit. His is about the fences. His result backs, from
outside, the caution this book keeps about the ladder, that no finite rung may close
on the whole quantum set. It says nothing about my own check, though. My check’s
caution, that a quantum point can fail it, comes from the pinning, and his paper never
pins anything.

20.5 The check, in integers
Eight counts: for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds where the
answers matched and one where they differed. A round is one bump to one count;
nothing about the round is tested, and no marginals are recorded. Then the check
reads the eight and tests seven integer facts. For each pair, let N be same plus different
and D be same minus different (so E is D over N). The seven: the four N are strictly
positive (every pair was sampled; a pair with no rounds is rejected outright, and never
read as a correlator of zero); A, which is N00 squared N10 squared minus D00 squared
N10 squared minus D10 squared N00 squared, is at least zero; B, the same with the
other column, is at least zero; and with C equal to D00 D01 N10 N11 plus D10 D11 N00
N01, C squared is at most A times B. Those are the three contraction inequalities with
the denominators cleared. No division, no reals, no square root, no S. Try it: counts
(same, different) of (4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, minus 0.6; N is five
and D is three (minus three for the last); A is 175, B is 175, C is zero; passes. That’s the
first example above, the S equals 2.4 one, in integers.

The theorem chain, in words: a passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built from
the counts; contraction and PSD are equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces S
squared at most eight. The names are in the statements below. The underlying algebra
is one identity: four times the sum of the four correlators squared, minus S squared,
is a sum of six squares (chsh_gap_is_sum_of_squares), so if the row sums of
squares are at most one, S squared is at most eight (tsirelson_squared), and the
point one over root two reaches it (tsirelson_tight). That’s Tsirelson’s bound as
algebra, with no Hilbert space (the mathematical home of quantum states) in it.

Here is the chain as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix F; this is what
they prove.


Definition 20.1 (Correlators from the counts; the pinned matrix). For eight counts

Remark 20.1 (Sound, and incomplete). The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum
question it is usually read against. PSD of M ( E) gives the correlators a PSD completion,
since the zeros are one choice of the two free entries (zero_marginal_implies_e
lliptope, ElliptopeCompletion.v). The converse fails. The all-ones plan has a PSD
completion (deterministic_strategy_elliptope), and every deterministic
plan is a quantum strategy (qs_deterministic_plan, QuantumStrategies.v); yet
its minor on rows A0 , B0 , B1 is 1 − 1 − 1 = −1, so M( E) is not PSD there, and a tally
of one matching round per pair gives A = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 in the integer check, so
the check fails. The second failure is a named theorem on the machine: the tally of
one matching round per pair is refused forever (Proposition 20.6). Every deterministic
plan fails the same way. The tally of one round per pair fails the check for each of the
sixteen plans (nec_e_check_refuses_all_plans), so does a plan replayed over
any number of rounds once pairs 00 and 10 have been sampled (nec_e_check_refu
ses_deterministic, NecEChshInt.v), and no deterministic plan’s pinned matrix is
PSD (nec_e_deterministic_not_pinned_psd, NecEChsh.v). So a pass proves
the bound, and a failure proves only that the tally’s pinned matrix isn’t PSD or a pair
went unsampled; it says nothing about whether the play was classical or quantum.
The free tally from the start of this section is exactly such a tally: it reaches S = 2 and
the check throws it out.


None of that algebra is new, and I don’t want it to read as if it were. Tsirelson’s bound
has been formalised before, in Isabelle/HOL by Mnacho Echenim and Mehdi Mhalla,
computer scientists at Grenoble (2023), and in Lean’s mathlib, and Navascués, Pironio
and Acín already analyse this very matrix by Schur complement and discuss the level
above it. What I think is mine here is smaller: an integer decision procedure on the
counts, and a checked link from “the check passed” to PSD to the bound.

20.6 The check, earned on the host machine
Now put it on the machine. A check on the small machine is a property: a checker,
which is a little program that says yes or no, a meaning, which is a statement, and a
proof that the two agree. The version of the small machine with its property language
left open (Section 16, Theorem 16.21) takes any property language with an exact
equality test whose properties come with those three things, and for every one of
them a flag raised from a clean start stands on a passing CHECK of one claim, a
later COMMIT of the same claim with its counter untouched in between, and a later
CERTIFY, the three acts costing one each. So here’s the plan for the game. Pack the
eight counts into one counter, as a list, the way the sorted-list machine packs a list
into one number (Section 16). Let the checker be the seven integer facts read off the
unpacked counts. And let the meaning be what the facts are for: every pair was


                                           339
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


sampled, and the pinned five-by-five is positive semidefinite. Then the proof the
generic machine asks for, that the checker says yes exactly when the meaning holds,
is the chain above with the denominators cleared in both directions, and a flag raised
on that machine from a clean start means: these counts, at this edition of their counter,
passed the check, somebody committed to that with nothing changed underneath, and
the correlators they give satisfy S2 ≤ 8. Here is that, stated exactly, and it’s stronger
than the chain above in one way I want to say once and plainly. The earlier theorems
said that a passed check makes the pinned matrix PSD. The check is also complete
for it: it passes if and only if every pair was sampled and the pinned matrix is PSD,
because clearing the denominators works in both directions. The statement is over the
machine of Definition 16.8, the small machine with a counter for every number, with
PCHSH in place of its one property, Slot. A CHECK reads one counter, which is why
the eight counts have to travel in one.


Definition 20.2 (The packed tally, and the property PCHSH). Read a whole
number as a list in the list code (0 is the empty list, and 2x (2y + 1) is x fol-
lowed by the list y), and take as its tally the first eight entries, in the order
same00 , diff00 , same01 , diff01 , same10 , diff10 , same11 , diff11 , a missing entry reading 0.
Every number is some tally. The property PCHSH has the checker “the tally passes
the seven integer facts” and the meaning “every question pair was sampled, and the
pinned matrix M ( E) of the tally’s correlators is symmetric and PSD.”


Theorem 20.4 (The check is exact). (1) The seven integer facts hold of a tally if and only
if every pair was sampled and M( E) is symmetric and PSD. (2) For every whole number v,
the checker of PCHSH says yes at v if and only if the meaning holds of v’s tally. (3) Reading
the number that packs a tally gives that tally back. (4) If the facts hold, the score of the tally

satisfies S2 ≤ 8 and |S| ≤ 2 2; in fact S2 < 8 and |S| < 2 2, and passing tallies come as
close to 8 as you like.

Proof. (1) The forward half is Theorem 20.1. For the backward half, PSD gives the
three contraction inequalities (Corollary F.13); with every N positive, multiplying
them through by the squares of the denominators gives A ≥ 0, B ≥ 0 and C2 ≤ AB,
which is Lemma F.15 read the other way. (2) is (1) with the packing, since every
number is a tally. (3) is the code and its decoder being inverse. (4) is (1) forward, then
Theorem 20.2; the strict form and the closeness are Corollary 20.3.

and with v the value of c after pre: the tally of v passes the seven integer facts; every pair

          √
|S| ≤ 2 2. Conversely, from a fresh start in which a counter c holds the packing of a tally
t, the three instructions CHECK PCHSH c, COMMIT PCHSH c, CERTIFY raise the flag if
and only if t passes the check, and then the ledger reads exactly 3; if t fails, the trap goes up at

Proof. A raised flag from a clean start has the earned chain (Theorem 16.9, which

means an unchanged value. For the converse, the CHECK passes exactly when the
tally passes; if it does, COMMIT and CERTIFY find their facts and the three acts cost
three; if it fails, the trap latch goes up, and a run takes no step once the trap is up (as
in Theorem 16.17), so the flag never rises.

as a named theorem: a perfectly legal classical play with S = 2 is turned away.

What the theorem doesn’t say stays what it was. The tally is placed. Nobody plays it on
the machine: the theorem starts from a counter that already holds the packing, and no
instruction plays a round, so a program can put any code in a counter for free. There
are no marginals. The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum set, so failing says
nothing about whether the play was quantum, and there is no margin for sampling
noise at Tsirelson’s point.

A tally stays free. Each count is a counter, a round is an INC on one of them, and
INC costs nothing, so a pile of trials costs nothing to write down; the packing into
one counter is a program’s business, and in the theorem the packed counter is simply
there at the start. What costs is the claim about the pile. Statistics are free; the claim
about them is what costs.

So here, in one paragraph, is what the check guarantees. If it passes, then every ques-
tion pair was sampled, the four empirical ratios satisfy three polynomial inequalities,
hence the fixed five-by-five is PSD, hence S squared is at most eight. It does not guar-
antee that the tally came from honest play (a program can INC whatever counts it
likes for nothing, including four rounds that put S at four). It does not guarantee any
marginal is zero (no marginals are recorded and none are tested). It does not put the
players’ state behind the counts. What it does give is a quantum strategy with the
same correlators: a passing tally’s correlators have a PSD completion (zero_marg
inal_implies_elliptope), and every point with one is the correlator table of a
strategy on two eight-level systems (tr_representation). And it fails the tally
of every single plan, honest classical play included. It has no margin for sampling
noise either. Honest play at Tsirelson’s point aims at correlators of plus or minus one
over root two, and there every pair of squared correlators the check adds up comes to
exactly one, the edge of what it accepts. So an honest tally aimed at that point sits right
on the line, and ordinary luck over a finite number of rounds pushes it over a good
share of the time, and the check fails. That’s my arithmetic about where the point sits.
No theorem in the files says it. The check certifies a shape of the tally. What the shape
means is a question for whoever supplied the rounds.

And notice which way the fence faces. The most practical use anyone has found
for a Bell test, certified randomness, needs the opposite bound. Stefano Pironio and


                                              342
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


colleagues (2010) argued, and backed with an experiment, that a Bell violation, with
settings the devices can’t choose, certifies that the outputs are random, and a group
of quantum cryptographers, Rotem Arnon-Friedman, Frédéric Dupuis, Omar Fawzi,
Renato Renner and Thomas Vidick (2018), made the accounting tight with what they
call entropy accumulation. A string printed in advance passes no such test, so it’s the
cleanest case I know, outside this book, of a check that can fail, separating output that
was established from output that was printed. That needs S bounded from below, with
an error probability. This check bounds S from above and fails every single plan, so it’s
a fence that keeps out the super-quantum and the fixed plan. As a nonlocality test it’s
no use. The deployed version exists, too: Gautam Kavuri and colleagues, physicists at
NIST and the University of Colorado (2025), run a public randomness beacon whose
outputs each trace back through a Bell test to a public record, the nearest working
system I know to a certified claim written down for good. And records cut both
ways there. Jonathan Barrett, Roger Colbeck and Adrian Kent, working on quantum
cryptography (2013), pointed out that a device which keeps its own memory of earlier
rounds can leak it through outputs it makes public later, so reusing a device can undo
a guarantee the user thought was settled. A permanent record in the wrong box is an
attack.

20.7 A rational stand-in for an irrational number
One number you’ll see in the files: 5657 over 2000, which is 2.8285, and two root
two is 2.82842... It’s the four-decimal round-up, chosen so that rational code can
test “above the Tsirelson bound” without square roots, and it’s safe because 5657
squared is 32,001,649 and eight times 2000 squared is 32,000,000, so the fraction sits
above root eight by about seven hundred-thousandths (rational_tsirelson_bo
und). It’s used in a few rational theorems. It is not used in the integer check, and the
real-number theorems use root eight.

20.8 Two more tests, as mathematics
The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
products, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
entries. Its PSD is again equivalent to a contraction-like condition (q1ab_psd_if
f_column_contractive). The check for it proves something stronger, that the
matrix is positive definite, by a cascade of two Schur steps down to a four-by-four
that Sylvester’s criterion closes. Sylvester’s name on a test about matrices fits in a
way I enjoy, because the word matrix is his. In 1850, in the Philosophical Magazine, the
English mathematician James Joseph Sylvester used it for an “oblong arrangement of
terms” out of which you cut square blocks and take their determinants, and matrix
was already an old word for the place something grows from. That’s exactly what
the test does: it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the big grid, one row deep, two,
three, four (the leading minors), and asks each one’s determinant to be positive. Was
he the first to state the test? The name doesn’t settle that; names stick to people for all
kinds of reasons, and I’d treat this one as a lead. And a fact that’s easy to list without


                                           343
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


noticing what it means: with all five extra numbers at zero, the condition certifies a
strict subset of the classical set (the ball where the four correlators’ squares sum to at

bound); it can’t certify anything above the classical line. To get a point above two you
have to supply the extras (q1ab_certifies_a_superclassical_chsh_point,
S equals 2.4 with one extra at minus one half). Appendix F has the algebra.

The two sizes are one test. A single positive-semidefinite predicate takes the size as a
parameter, and the five-by-five and the nine-by-nine are it at two sizes.


Definition 20.3 (The size-generic PSD test). A claim is a top index n and a ma-
trix M indexed by naturals. It is realizable when Mij = M ji for all i, j ≤ n and
∑i≤n ∑ j≤n vi Mij v j ≥ 0 for every real vector v. The CHSH claim of E is top index
4 with the matrix M( E) of Definition 20.1; the level-1+AB claim uses top index 8 and
the nine-by-nine matrix.


Corollary 20.7 (The level-1 test is the size-five case). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : the
three contraction inequalities hold if and only if the CHSH claim of E is realizable. The same
holds at size nine for the level-1+AB contraction condition and its claim.

Proof. Realizability at top index 4 unfolds to symmetry and PSD of the five-by-five, by
computing the finite sums, and that is equivalent to contraction by Corollary F.13. At
size nine the same unfolding meets Theorem F.19. Nothing new is proved about the
matrices; the point is that one predicate covers both.

Checked as column_contractive_iff_general_realizable (GenRealizabil-
ity.v) and column_contractive_q1ab_iff_general_realizable.

The third thing: the elliptope, the set of correlators for which some choice of the two

20.9 The quantum set, checked
Three descriptions of the same set have been running through this part: the tables
some quantum strategy can produce, the tables whose five-by-five matrix has a PSD
completion, and the tables inside Landau and Masanes’s curved edge. They are the
same set, and that’s checked, for strategies on finitely many levels. Here’s how each
piece goes, because the constructions are the part worth seeing.

Quantum tables are inside the completion set. A strategy’s correlator is the inner
product of two unit vectors: Alice’s observable applied to the shared state, and Bob’s
applied to it (qs_corr_dot). Four unit vectors always have a PSD table of inner
products, so every quantum table has a completion, and Tsirelson’s bound follows
from that: S2 ≤ 8 for every strategy (qs_tsirelson, QuantumStrategies.v), and its
level-one moment matrix passes the PSD test with the marginals in (qs_npa_psd).
Quantum mechanics uses complex amplitudes, and the complex case goes through
by a plain trick: a complex vector of length n is a real vector of length 2n, its real
parts followed by its imaginary parts, and the real part of a complex inner product
is the ordinary inner product of those longer real vectors. So the real argument runs
unchanged (qc_tsirelson and qc_npa_psd, QuantumStrategiesComplex.v). The
                                                        √
two-qubit strategy from the start of this part reaches 2 2 in both readings (qs_tsir
elson_reached, qc_tsirelson_reached).

The completion set is inside the quantum tables. This is Tsirelson’s representation,
and the construction is his. Take a table with a PSD completion. A PSD matrix is a
table of inner products of vectors, always: peel off one row at a time, and a zero on
the diagonal forces its whole row to zero (tr_gram). So the completion hands over
four unit vectors in four dimensions, a0 , a1 for Alice and b0 , b1 for Bob, with a x · by
equal to the table’s entries. Now the trick. There are four real eight-by-eight matrices,
built from the two-by-two ones that swap two entries or flip the sign of one, that
each square to the identity and anticommute in pairs: multiply any two of them in
either order and the answers differ only in sign (tr_gamma_clifford, checked by
computation). Use a vector’s four components to mix those four matrices, and you
get an observable that squares to the identity, a legitimate measurement. Give Alice
and Bob a maximally entangled pair of eight-level systems, and the correlator of two
such observables comes out as exactly the inner product of their vectors (tr_corr
_inner). So the strategy built from the four vectors produces the table (tr_repre
sentation for real amplitudes and tr_representation_complex for complex,
TsirelsonRepresentation.v). Eight levels on each side is always enough.

The curved edge is the same set again. Each correlator is the cosine of an angle, the
angle between one of Alice’s vectors and one of Bob’s. Walk the loop a0 , b0 , a1 , b1


                                           345
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and back to a0 : the angle across any one leg can’t exceed the sum of the other three,
because angles on a sphere obey the triangle inequality (am_sphere_triangle,
ArcsineBoundary.v). Flip one vector to its opposite and you get the other four inequal-
ities, with 2π in them. Written in arcsines, those eight inequalities are Landau and
Masanes’s four. Going the other way, any four angles that pass them can be met by
actual vectors: put Bob’s two at the right angle to each other, build each of Alice’s from
the two angles it has to make with them, and check that the determinant that says
such a triangle exists comes out nonnegative. So a table has a PSD completion exactly
when its arcsines pass the four inequalities (am_arcsine), and those are exactly the
quantum tables (am_quantum_arcsine). The point (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) sits on the
edge, because arcsin 53 + arcsin 45 = π2 by the 3-4-5 triangle (am_pythagorean_boun
dary), and so does Tsirelson’s point (am_tsirelson_boundary).

20.10 What isn’t proved
One step on paper, and then nothing about dimension. Quantum mechanics also
allows systems with infinitely many levels, and the checks don’t need finitely many.
Whatever the dimension, a shared state v gives an expectation on the operators the
players measure with: x 7→ Re ⟨v, x v⟩. That one line is the step on paper. The proofs
use only what that expectation always has: you can add, multiply, scale and take
adjoints, the product spreads over sums, and the expectation of x ∗ x is never negative.
Each measurement is its own adjoint with the expectation of its square at most one,
which covers unsharp measurements too, and Alice’s commute with Bob’s. That last
demand is weaker than putting them on two separate systems, so the result covers
the wider, commuting model as well. On that footing Tsirelson’s sum of squares
                                                     √
goes through, and the CHSH value is at most 2 2 (ta_tsirelson). The same
nonnegative form, with each diagonal entry raised to one, completes the correlator
table to a PSD matrix (ta_realizable), so the four arcsine inequalities hold (ta_a
rcsine), and with a unit the full first-level moment matrix, marginals and all, is PSD
(ta_npa_psd, all in TsirelsonAlgebraic.v). The other direction needs no help from
infinity: every point inside the arcsine edge is reached on two eight-level systems.

Also: the finite-mixture theorem (fine_theorem in the source) proves only one
direction, that a finite local model satisfies the bound, and its converse as stated is
false: a table with S = 0 that no local model produces (nec_e_fine_converse_fa
lse). Fine’s own theorem, in the form that speaks of correlations, is proved separately
as an equivalence: a table of four correlators comes from a local model exactly when
each is between −1 and 1 and all eight CHSH inequalities hold (nec_e_fine_if
f, NecEFine.v). And one more thing about tallies, which the guarantee paragraph
above already used: a free tally is not thereby classical (the four rounds with S equal
to four). The correlators (one, one, one, minus one) are the PR box, which no classical
play produces; the classical vertex this section used, which fails the check like every
plan, is (one, one, one, one).

That’s the game, the number, the two walls, and the check. Last of the machine

sections: what all this costs against physics.

21 The counter against physics
Section 4 did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag merges
states, Landauer’s principle (a named premise) prices merges, and the toll follows.
I’m not going to do it again. This section is about what a machine’s counter, the small
machine’s µ included, has to do with any of that, and the answer is: less than the word
“Landauer” in a file name suggests, and I want you to hear the exact amount from me.

21.1 The calibration is a unit conversion
There’s a function in the source that multiplies the counter by a chosen energy per
mark, and a theorem that a state with one mark, at the scale kT ln 2 per mark, carries
kT ln 2 of energy (calibrated_mu_landauer_energy, proving the predicate mu_
landauer_calibration for every k and T). Read that for exactly what it is: a unit
conversion, true by definition, with the scale as a free input. Nothing in it picks the
scale. The theorem would be just as true with the scale set to a dollar a mark. I’d say
that out loud, so the name “Landauer” in it does no work. What would connect marks
to joules is the premise in Section 4, landauer_heat, and that one is an assumption
with a name that nothing proves. And even as a scale, k B T ln 2 a mark is the floor for
one particular squeeze, a halving. Corollary 4.9’s floor for a flip that brings k states
into a room already holding m, starting from the even spread on those m + k states, is
k B T ln mm+k , and for one newcomer into a big room that’s far below a halving, roughly
k B T/m. Price every mark at k B T ln 2 and you can overstate the floor of a single narrow
flip by a factor that grows with m.

Remember the constant from Boltzmann’s grave in Part II, the exchange rate between
a count and heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper than I can.
The k B in k B T ln 2 turns a temperature into an energy, and for most of its history it
was a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful experiments. Since
20 May 2019 it isn’t. That day the international system of units was redefined so
that Boltzmann’s constant is exactly 1.380649 × 10−23 joules per kelvin, by definition,
and the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion from temperature to
energy has been a convention since then, in the strictest sense: nobody can measure
it wrong any more. What’s still physics is everything around it, whether wiping a
bit at a temperature really sheds that much heat, which is what the Lyon bead was
measuring. The calibration theorem is the same kind of move as that redefinition. It
fixes a conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere else.


Definition 21.1 (Energy at a scale). For a real number c (joules per mark) and a state s,
the energy of s at scale c is µ(s) · c. The Landauer calibration at k B and T is the statement
that every state with µ(s) = 1 has energy k B T ln 2 at scale k B T ln 2.


Theorem 21.1 (The calibration is a unit conversion). (1) For all real k B and T, the

                                             347
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Landauer calibration at k B and T holds. (2) For any counter, there are two real-valued func-
tions of the state that give 1 and 2 on every state with one mark, so the counter alone fixes no
energy value.

Proof. (1) Substitute µ(s) = 1: 1 · k B T ln 2 = k B T ln 2, by ring arithmetic, for any k B
and T, positive or not. (2) Take the two functions to be the energy at scales 1 and 2. At
µ(s) = 1 they give 1 and 2.

Checked as calibrated_mu_landauer_energy (PricingPhysicsAudit.v), which
proves mu_landauer_calibration (PricingPhysicsTarget.v) for all k B and T, and
mu_has_no_intrinsic_joule_value (PricingPhysicsAudit.v). The physics is
the premise of Section 4, restated here once in the form the next theorems test. In
words first: a dissipation hands each instruction a whole number of heat units, each
unit worth kT ln 2. The floor premise says an instruction that takes at least one state
where some yes-or-no property is false to a state where it’s true, and never sends a
true one back to false, dissipates at least one unit. That’s a different statement from
Landauer’s principle as Premise 4.5 has it. That one depends on the spread over states,
Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H, and gives nothing for a known state. This one gives every such
instruction a floor of one whole unit, whatever the spread. To get the second from the
first you’d need more, at the least a spread with a full bit of uncertainty removed at
every such step, and the known-state theorem and the narrow squeeze of Section 4
show that isn’t automatic. So I give it its own name, structural dissipation pricing. The
calibration says no instruction dissipates more units than the counter charges it. One
word about that word: “dissipation” here means heat handed to the surroundings, in
the sense Section 4 took from Sagawa: a bill for where the forgotten bit goes. It has
nothing to do with waste, or with doing the job badly. Two premises, nothing proved
about either, and the only question is whether they can sit in the same room:


Premise 21.2 (Structural dissipation pricing). A dissipation is a function δ from instruc-
tions to naturals, counted in units of k B T ln 2. The floor, a hypothesis separate from
Premise 4.5 of Section 4: every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no property has
δ(i ) ≥ 1, where i collapses P when some state with P false is sent to a state with P true
and every state with P true is sent to one with P true. The calibration: δ(i ) ≤ cost(i )
for every instruction. Neither is proved anywhere; the theorems below ask whether
they can hold together.


21.2 The premises have to be able to hold together
Here’s the one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline, and it’s
a consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You
need two premises: that every step you’ve chosen to count dissipates at least one
unit, and an upper calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those
two hold at once? There’s a theorem saying exactly when (calibrated_model


                                              348
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


_exists_iff_positive_cost): a model satisfying both exists precisely when
every operation you’ve chosen to count (the statement below calls those eligible) costs
at least one. I should say how cheap that is. The model the proof builds takes the
dissipation to be the cost itself, so the theorem shows the two premises don’t contradict
each other. It doesn’t show that the counter tracks any dissipation. Still, it does bite
on a schedule: if you count a zero-cost step, no such model can exist. One place
the checked files show the premises holding is a one-bit reset, where resetting costs
one and idling costs nothing (bit_model_has_satisfiable_calibration); the
small machine’s flag-raising steps, below, are another.

Now point the test at the small machine of Section 16, counting every step that col-
lapses some yes-or-no property, and it fails. Its free instructions merge states (the last
item of the list at the end of that chapter has the pair: two cores that one DEC sends
to the same core, for nothing), so DEC A 2, which collapses the property “A is zero or
the line number is 2”, costs zero there, and (1) below says no dissipation can charge
it one and stay under its cost. That’s checked as nec_f_small_premise_pair_
fails, with the free merge itself as nec_f_small_free_collapse_is_merge
(NecFPhysics.v). The machine prices the certifying chain and leaves its other merges
free, so the premise pair holds for the steps the toll is about (nec_f_small_premis
e_pair_on_flag) and fails for the whole instruction set. That’s the honest shape.


Theorem 21.2 (When the premises can hold together). (1) For any set of operations, any
predicate “eligible” on them, and any cost, a dissipation with δ(i ) ≥ 1 on every eligible i and
δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) on every i exists if and only if every eligible operation costs at least one. (2) On
a one-bit machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost 0, taking “eligible” to mean “sends
two different states to one”, such a dissipation exists.

Proof. (1) If such a δ exists, 1 ≤ δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ). Conversely, take δ = cost. (2) The reset
is the only operation that sends two states to one, and it costs 1; apply (1).

Checked as calibrated_model_exists_iff_positive_cost, with the defini-
tion calibrated_positive_model, and bit_model_has_satisfiable_cali
bration (ObservationPolicy.v).

Three statements are in play, and each points its own way. Energy at a scale, µ · c,
is a conversion and points nowhere. The calibration, δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ), puts the charge
above the dissipation: an upper bound. Landauer’s principle puts the heat above
an entropy loss: a lower bound. The theorem above says the assumptions can hold
together. That’s compatibility, and it isn’t evidence. It doesn’t make the ledger the
least energy anything needs, and it doesn’t make it the heat anything gives off.

But now the history escape from Section 4, pointed at a machine. Keep the previous
state in a history list (push it onto the front each step; below, s :: h is the list h with
s put on the front) and every fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step


                                                349
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


you can see stays the same; the line number can collapse to one place while the bigger
state keeps its past. The free merge, lifted to a machine with history, isn’t a merge. So
“this step merged, therefore it dissipated” can’t be said of the visible step alone. It’s a
sentence about the whole state including whatever history is retained, and a physical
model has to say what’s retained. The permanent-certificate theorem in Section 4
supplies that for the certifying step on finite memory. For the rest of a machine’s steps
it’s unsaid.


Theorem 21.3 (Keeping history makes every step injective). Let the history step send a
pair (s, h), a state and a list of past states, to (apply(s, i ), s :: h). For any step function, the
history step with a fixed instruction is injective, and its first component is the original step.

Proof. Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two pairs
with the same image are equal.

Checked as retained_history_step_injective (ObservationPolicy.v).

21.3 The calorimeter protocol, as a specification
Here is how one would measure this, and it’s here because it makes the boundary exact.
Take a two-state register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the excited
state, and the simplest possible rate equation for how p changes in one time step (a
rate for climbing into the excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the length of the
step). For the canonical reset (population one half to zero, with the rates chosen so the
equation closes), the heat delivered to the bath is exactly half the gap (canonical_r
eset_heat_exact). Choose the gap to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT
ln 2 (selected_gap_gives_landauer_heat).

Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer’s
number and it’s the opposite. The gap was chosen to make the heat come out as
Landauer’s number. The same populations and rates with half that gap give half
the Landauer value, and there’s a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics
with different heat (master_equation_does_not_fix_heat_scale). The rate
equation fixes the shape; the energy scale is a selected Hamiltonian (the physicist’s
name for the rule that says what energy each state has), and selecting it is not deriving
it.


Definition 21.3 (The two-state protocol). For a gap ∆, the register’s mean energy at
excited population p is ∆ · p. One step of the rate equation is

                               p′ = p + δt k01 (1 − p) − k10 p ,
                                                              


and the heat to the bath over a step from p to p′ is defined as ∆p − ∆p′ . The canonical
reset takes p = 21 , δt = 1, k01 = 0, k10 = 1, ending at p′ = 0, and counts one logical


                                                350
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


event.


Theorem 21.4 (The heat is fixed by the chosen gap). (1) The canonical numbers satisfy
the rate equation. (2) For every ∆, the canonical reset’s heat is ∆/2. (3) For all k B , T, the
gap ∆ = 2k B T ln 2 gives heat k B T ln 2. (4) If k B > 0 and T > 0, the gap k B T ln 2 gives
heat strictly below k B T ln 2. (5) There are two different gaps for which the same canonical
populations satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.

Proof. All five are field arithmetic on the definitions: 12 + 1 · (0 − 12 ) = 0; ∆ · 12 − ∆ · 0 =
∆/2; and ln 2 > 0 for (4). For (5) take gaps 1 and 2.

Checked as canonical_reset_satisfies_master_equation, canonical_r
eset_heat_exact, selected_gap_gives_landauer_heat, smaller_gap_r
efutes_unconditional_landauer_floor (given k B > 0 and T > 0) and ma
ster_equation_does_not_fix_heat_scale (CalorimeterProtocol.v), with the
definitions in CalorimeterProtocolTarget.v.

What ties it to a machine: the protocol counts one logical event (the file defines that
count as the constant one), and one is what the small machine’s CERTIFY charges,
the last of the three paid acts behind a raised flag (Section 16). That’s a match of two
numbers, both one by choice, and nothing more. There is no theorem mapping the
protocol’s two register states to any machine state. The file’s “heat to the bath” is the
register’s mean energy before minus after, so it also assumes the bath receives what
the register loses, and no Coq says that. So a device test would have to measure the
gap, the populations, the rates, and the bath heat independently; separately establish
thermal admissibility and detailed balance (that the up and down rates stand in the
ratio the temperature dictates); and separately establish that the device’s physical reset
is the machine’s certify event. The protocol is an executable experimental specification.
It is not a measured device, and it is not an unconditional conversion of marks to
joules, and anyone who tells you otherwise is reading a file name.

21.4 What permanence adds to Landauer: nothing new, said plainly
Here’s a fair question: is there a prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make
that Landauer’s principle alone doesn’t? No, and the reason is short. The smallest
case, one certified state and one flipping in, is “set a bit to one whatever it held,” which
is the reset Landauer described and Bérut measured; Landauer’s own name for it is
“restore to one.” The general bound, kT ln((m plus k) over m) for squeezing m plus k
equally likely states into m, is what Landauer’s principle gives for that squeeze, at kT
ln 2 for each bit removed. What the permanence theorems add is the derivation: which
premises about a machine (finite, permanent) make the certifying step a reset, so that
Landauer applies to it. That’s a result about the machine. Physics gets nothing new
from it, and that’s the right size for it.
