The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


21.5 What this section is
A calibration that’s a unit conversion; a pair of premises, consistent on the steps the
toll is about and inconsistent on the whole instruction set; a history that makes any
step injective; and a measurement protocol that’s a specification with a selected scale.
The physics in this book is in Section 4, as a named premise with its critics named.
Here there’s accounting, and I’ve tried to call every line by its right name. That’s the
end of the machine. What’s left is what it took to check any of this, and where the
checking stops.



Part V

Checking it, and its edge

22 What Coq is, and why
Coq is a proof assistant, which is a phrase I had to go and look up. Underneath the
phrase it’s a programming language, but one whose type system is strict enough to
do a thing ordinary languages can’t: you write a proof down as a program, and the
compiler refuses it unless the program genuinely matches the statement you claimed.
You can’t talk it into a maybe.

The name is a joke three ways at once, and it’s worth knowing before you say it out
loud in English. Coq is French for rooster. It’s also a nod to Thierry Coquand, a
French computer scientist and mathematician, at the University of Gothenburg as of
2026, who worked out the logic it started from with Gérard Huet, a French computer
scientist at INRIA, and to that logic’s initials, CoC, for the Calculus of Constructions;
and there’s a French habit of naming research tools after animals. The English slang
reading did what you’d guess. By the development team’s own account, some people,
women students especially, ended up never learning the tool because of its name. So
in March 2025 it got a new one, the Rocq Prover, after Rocquencourt, the Inria site
where it was first built, and after the Roc, the giant bird of legend, so the bird stayed.
Everything in this book was checked with Coq 8.18, from before the rename, so that’s
the name I use. The rooster changes nothing about what got checked.

22.1 Types as claims
Here’s the idea, and it’s one idea. In a normal language a type says what kind of value
a variable holds: in Python, “x is an int” means x is a whole number. In Coq, types
are claims. The type “n is greater than zero” is the type of proofs that n is positive.
A function from “n is greater than zero” to “n plus one is greater than zero” is a
proof that if n is positive, n plus one is too, and the compiler checks that the function
really has that type, the way it would check that a function from integers to strings



                                           352
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


really returns strings. This correspondence between proofs and programs has a name,
Curry-Howard, after two people who noticed it separately decades apart, and Coq’s
foundation, the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, is a type system built to exploit
it. Coquand worked it out with Christine Paulin-Mohring, a logician and computer
scientist best known for developing Coq, on top of the Calculus of Constructions
he and Huet had made; their paper on it was given in 1988 and printed in 1990, so
the late 1980s is as close as I’d date it. The “inductive” part means you define your
own recursive types (numbers, lists, trees, machine states) inside the system. The
numbers, lists and states this book uses are all defined that way, inside the system, so
the foundation is explicit; nothing is smuggled.

“Decades apart” undersells it, and the gap is worth a side trip. Haskell Curry, an
American logician at Penn State best known for combinatory logic, noticed in 1934
that the type of a function from A to B reads like the claim “A implies B,” and that
the types his functions could have lined up with the claims you can prove; he and
Robert Feys, a Belgian logician at Leuven, pushed it further in 1958. William Howard,
a proof theorist at the University of Illinois at Chicago, wrote the sharper version in
1969, and then it went around as a photocopied manuscript until 1980, when it was
finally printed in a collection of essays for Curry. (The Edinburgh computer scientist
Philip Wadler’s 2015 survey, “Propositions as Types,” tells this story.) So the sharpest
statement of the idea under the tool this book is checked with spent its first eleven
years as a stack of photocopies. Is that the bottom? No. Reading a proof of “if A then
B” as a method that turns any proof of A into a proof of B is older still: the intuitionists
had it in the 1920s and 1930s, Brouwer, Heyting and Kolmogorov, which is why people
also call it the BHK interpretation. Where it really starts I can’t tell you. It changes
nothing in what the checker checks. It changes how I’d tell the story: nobody sat
down one day and invented “proofs are programs.” It kept getting noticed, by people
coming from different directions, until somebody wrote it down plainly.

The compiler checks whether the types line up. If your proof has a hole, it rejects the
proof, unless you write “trust me” (the keyword is Admitted), and then it marks the
theorem as unproved. But here’s the part that matters: the compiler checks that the
proof matches the statement. It does not check that the statement says what you meant.
Hand it a statement that means nothing and it’ll prove it for you, three characters,
no complaint. So a proof being accepted is not the same as the thing being true. It
means this proof matches this statement, and whether that’s the right statement is on
me. The machine can’t tell. The point said a short version of this and I’m saying it
again because every section since has leaned on it: the checked names in this book are
a promise that the proof is there, and the sentences around them are my claim about
what the statement says, and the second can be wrong while the first is fine, which is
why so many sections of this book stop to say exactly what a statement’s hypotheses
are.




                                            353
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


22.2 Why I used it
Not to make anything true. I used it because I don’t trust my own eye to catch a gap
in an argument I want to believe. I spent months convinced by my own reasoning,
pushed the proof through, and watched a key step come apart in my hands. The
machine caught where I’d fooled myself. That’s what it’s for. Gap-catcher. Not the
proof. The proof is the argument, and an argument has to close in a way a person can
follow, or it hasn’t closed at all, which is why this book is written in prose. A list of
theorem names can’t close an argument for anyone.

Two precedents show that a proof assistant is a serious tool. Neither of them is a
toy. CompCert, Xavier Leroy’s C compiler, written and proved correct in Coq: the
assembly it emits behaves as the source does, for programs with defined behaviour.
And Georges Gonthier’s 2005 proof of the four-colour theorem, a century-old problem
whose first proof (in 1976) needed a computer to check fewer than two thousand
configurations, by its own announcement’s count, and was distrusted for exactly
that reason. Gonthier redid it in Coq, working from a later version of the proof by
Neil Robertson, Daniel Sanders, Paul Seymour and Robin Thomas (1997), so that the
checker was the small, auditable thing and the cases were the program. That’s de
Bruijn’s criterion applied to mathematics itself: the thing you have to trust is the small
kernel. The big proof only has to get past it. The name was given by Henk Barendregt,
a Dutch logician known for his work on the lambda calculus and type theory, after
Nicolaas de Bruijn, whose Automath project, begun in 1967, kept the part of a proof
checker you have to trust small: a system meets the criterion when its proofs can be
checked by a small independent program that a person could read.

The 1976 proof deserves its own side trip. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken did
it at the University of Illinois, and the mathematics department changed the slogan
on its postage meter to “Four colors suffice.” The slogan it replaced had been on
the department’s mail since soon after 1963, and it said that 211213 − 1 is prime, a
prime Don Gillies, a professor at the same university who helped design its ILLIAC II
computer, had found in 1963 while checking that machine out. Think about that for
a second. For years on end a mathematics department stamped its mail with results
nobody could have checked by hand, first one and then the other, and both were right.
So was the distrust of the 1976 proof wrong? I don’t think so. The worry was never
that the computer lied. It was that nobody could read what had been checked, and a
check you can’t look at is hard to lean on. Gonthier’s answer was de Bruijn’s: make
the part you have to read small enough to read.

22.3 What “zero Admitted” means
“Zero Admitted” is literal. Nowhere in the proof tree did I write “trust me” and
walk on. Every step the checker could see, it saw, end to end, with no “and the rest
is obvious.” It’s a hygiene fact about the gap-catcher. It passes no verdict on the
argument: it says I didn’t let myself skip a step where the machine was watching. It



                                           354
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


does not say the statements are the right statements.

What it doesn’t mean, listed. It doesn’t mean the theorems prove physical reality; they
prove things about the machine as formalised, and whether that describes the world
is answered by experiments (Section 4, Section 21). It doesn’t mean Coq’s own founda-
tion is proved consistent; it’s believed consistent, and that can’t be proved from inside,
by Gödel (Section 13), so the foundation is trusted, and “trusted” has substance: it’s
the same kernel CompCert and the four-colour proof stand on, and a bug in it would
take all of them down together, which is a kind of safety in numbers. And it doesn’t
mean no axioms: the proofs use a handful of standard-library assumptions, and the
assumption audit names them: functional extensionality on dependent functions (two
functions that agree everywhere are equal); two decidability principles that come with
the standard library’s real numbers, used by the matrix proofs behind the game check;
and, in some theorems, the law of excluded middle (every proposition is true or false).
The count, from the full audit: the full-corpus probe covers 5,762 named theorems
across 332 files: 5,006 close under the global Coq context outright, and 756 use only
Coq standard-library assumptions. Zero project-local axioms appear in any of the
5,762 dependency trees. The small machine’s files, under minimal/, are inside that
probe too, and every one of their 1,417 probed theorems comes back closed under
Coq’s own rules, with no axiom at all. Among them are the small machine, its version
for any property language, the simpler host, the definition of Thiele-complete and
its window theorem, the host machine with a register for every whole number, the
numbers that write a guest program down, and the pigeonhole (Section 16), and the
files that run Parts II and III on that machine and the diagonal on its programs (Sec-
tions 16.17 and 16.18). Each also ends by printing the assumptions of every headline
theorem in it, and every one of those lines says the theorem is closed. A lemma a closed
theorem uses is closed with it. So for those files every headline theorem is closed under
the global context, resting on no axiom of mine or of the standard library, and two sep-
arate printouts say so. That isn’t the same as having no premises: each theorem keeps
the hypotheses written in its own statement. Only two small files under minimal/,
MuCore.v and Napkin.v, sit outside the big audit, and they are built and checked on
their own by bash scripts/verify_core.sh, which compiles each from a clean
slate with coqc, fails on any Axioms: line, and expects ten closed theorems from
MuCore.v and seven from Napkin.v. The universal program’s own files, which lean
on the vendored library’s counter-machine blocks, sit in the kernel tree with the other
link files, and they also end by printing their headline theorems’ assumptions; so do
the files of the priced host, the compiler from computable functions and the theorem
for every computably presented Thiele machine. In plain words: every theorem in the
audit either uses no axiom at all or uses only those standard-library axioms, none of
mine. The hypotheses in each statement are a separate matter, and they stay. Those
counts are of the sources at this edition. Add a theorem and the counts move. The
shape, no axiom of mine anywhere, is what every edition has to keep.



                                           355
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


22.4 What you’re trusting, in one place
If you accept every checked theorem in this book, here is what you’re still taking on
trust, all of it, so you don’t have to collect it from five chapters.

   1. The statements. The checker confirms a proof proves its statement. It doesn’t
      confirm the statement says what my sentence about it says. That’s why the book
      prints the important ones in full, premises and all, and why Appendix E prints
      the Coq text of the load-bearing ones beside a line on whether my sentence says
      exactly that, more, or less. A machine check supplements that reading.
   2. Coq’s kernel and its foundation, and the standard assumptions above.
   3. The tools under Coq. Coq’s own program, the compiler it was built with, the
      operating system it ran on and the processor under all of them are trusted. This
      is the list Ken Thompson’s lecture from Section 13 was about. I didn’t write Coq,
      or OCaml, or any of the rest, so by his moral I can’t fully trust any of them, and
      neither can you. What I can do is keep the list short and print it, so you know
      exactly which tools you’re being asked to believe have no spare key cut into
      them.
   4. The tested parts. The tests are evidence that the programs around the proofs
      do what’s claimed on the runs tried. They can’t show the programs always
      do. Edsger Dijkstra had a sentence for this, and the version in his 1976 book
      starts by admitting he’d already said it many times: program testing “can be
      quite effective for showing the presence of bugs, but is hopelessly inadequate
      for showing their absence.” (I’m quoting it as John Harrison, who was then
      proving floating-point hardware correct at Intel, quotes it in a 2007 survey, from
      that book.) That’s why this item says tested. It never says proved.
   5. The physics. Anywhere a theorem has Landauer’s principle or a calorimeter in
      it, the physical premise is named and assumed (Section 4, Section 21). Nothing
      here derives it.
   6. Whoever sets the start and whoever reads the record. Every guarantee about
      the record is about programs run from a clean start on a step that does what its
      definition says. The operator who chooses the start, a reset, a device running the
      machine, and anyone reading a report they didn’t watch being made are outside
      it (Section 25 lists the whole fence).

22.5 Thompson’s knife, again
Every link on that list is a place where Ken Thompson’s compiler from Section 13
could sit unseen: a translator that plants something and re-plants it when it translates
itself. Coq’s own binary, the compiler that built it, the operating system under both. I
don’t believe any of them does. I can’t prove it, and the discipline of this section is to
say so. “Formally verified” doesn’t cover a chain whose bottom is trust.



                                           356
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


And a planted knife isn’t the only way a trusted link goes wrong. Sometimes nobody
plants anything and the thing at the bottom is just wrong. In 1994 Thomas Nicely, a
mathematics professor at Lynchburg College who was computing with twin primes
and their reciprocals, found that his new Intel Pentium got some divisions wrong. The
standard example is 4,195,835 divided by 3,145,727, which the bad chips got wrong in
the fourth decimal place. Intel’s explanation was missing entries in a table inside the
divider: five of them, it said, dropped by a script. Intel set aside about $475 million to
cover it.

Push on the five. In 2024 Ken Shirriff, who reverse-engineers old chips from pho-
tographs of their silicon and writes them up on his blog, went to die photographs of
an affected chip, read the table’s layout off the silicon, and counted sixteen missing
entries, left out by a mistake in the table’s mathematical definition, of which only five
ever mattered. If Shirriff’s reading of the silicon is right, and I haven’t checked it,
Intel’s own explanation, repeated for thirty years, had the effect right and the cause
off, and it took somebody reading the actual silicon to say so. Floating-point arith-
metic went on to become one of the places where formal verification earned its keep
in industry; Harrison, who did that work at Intel, brings up this very bug in his 2007
survey of it. Does any of that touch this book? Only at the bottom of the list above.
Every proof here was checked by a program running on some processor, and nobody
here has read that processor’s tables off the silicon either. That’s why the processor is
on the list as trusted. I can’t give it a kinder word.

22.6 The auditor on top
Beyond the type checker, the project has a custom proof auditor I called the Inquisitor,
because a thing that reads every proof looking for ways you’ve cheated deserves a
name you won’t forget. It reads every proof file, and its source names about eighty
distinct rules. The main families: no holes (no Admitted, no admit, no give-up, no
unproved axiom or parameter in project code); vacuity heuristics (no theorem whose
conclusion is literally True or a tautology; no theorem of the shape “P implies P”;
existence claims backed by a constant witness get flagged, and a flag is a reason to
look and nothing more, since some constructions like a fixed interpreter program
are supposed to be fixed and get judged on what they compute); physics-definition
heuristics (no physical quantity defined as a placeholder constant, no physics claim
without an invariance condition); scope enforcement (the proof tree is split into tiers,
the kernel tier may not import from research-side files, and every active file must
reach the cost or semantics foundation through its imports, or it doesn’t get to claim
the kernel’s pedigree); and comment hygiene (no unfinished or historical markers in
maintained source). Its rules are heuristics. They point at places to look. They don’t
prove a theorem means what it should, and they can’t promise every empty premise
got caught.

So none of this is foolproof, the checker and the auditor included, and I don’t treat it
as if it were. That’s the reason some of the theorems are runs. The worked examples in

                                           357
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


Part IV, the earned run that pays exactly three and the one that traps for good, and the
two guests run on the simpler host, are computed by Coq from the definitions. The
demonstration machine on the priced host is different: its numbers are proved, and
nobody has run it. A proof can be hollow in a way nobody spots. A definition that
has to produce the numbers on the page, run by the checker itself, is harder to fool,
and when it disagrees, it tells you where to look.

22.7 Checking the companion formalization
The mathematical claims are the statements printed in this book, with their stated
hypotheses and the arguments given here. Running software is an additional way to
check their formal counterparts. It isn’t a prerequisite for reading the argument.

A reproducible check needs a fixed copy of the proof sources, dependencies and
probes. Changing that copy changes the object being checked; a later software result
cannot silently revise a theorem in this edition. The procedure below describes the
companion proof build. With Python 3, GNU make, Coq 8.18 and its standard library,
CSDP, OCaml with its ocamlfind tool, and MetaCoq 1.2.1 for Coq 8.18 (the vendored
lambda-calculus files need it) installed, run this from the root of a checkout of the
sources at a fixed revision. The revision this edition was checked against is this one:

23 How to break this
Every main claim in this book comes with the exact shape of the thing that would kill
it. I went to the trouble on purpose. A claim you can’t break is a claim that wasn’t
saying anything. So I’m handing you a loaded gun pointed at my own work, with
every sentence sharp enough to aim at. These are written as instructions: here is the
trace to find, the object to build, the theorem to exhibit. Build one and the proof tree
falls, and I mean that as an invitation.

The invitation is an old one, and people have put prices on it. Donald Knuth gives the
first person to find each error in his books one hexadecimal dollar, 0x$1.00, which is
$2.56, deposited these days at the Bank of San Serriffe, a bank that doesn’t exist, since
real checks turned out to be an open door for fraud. Why pay strangers to find your
mistakes? His own page says it plainly enough: a careful reader makes the book better
for everyone who reads it next. This chapter doesn’t come with a bank, real or made
up. What it comes with is, for every claim, a description of the exact object that would
make it fall, so you know before you start what counts as winning.

Before the list, the honest part about it. Most targets below are theorems Coq has
checked, and knocking one of those over head-on would take a bug in Coq’s kernel.
That can happen, but it isn’t where I’d put my money. The places a reader can actually
win are aimed at me, and there are three. None of them goes through Coq. A sentence
of mine that says more than the Coq statement it cites (Appendix E puts the load-
bearing ones side by side to make that easy). A Coq definition that doesn’t capture
the English word it’s named for: on the small machine, “is at least 0” is a check that
can’t fail, and the step certifies it anyway, so “certified” there doesn’t mean “found
something out” (Section 16 says so, and that’s the kind of gap to hunt). And a list of
premises that only its own example satisfies.




                                          360
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


23.1 The abstract claims (Parts II and III)
The universal floor (Section 3). Build a certification system that satisfies the one-step toll
and give a run from uncertified to certified with total cost zero. universal_nfi_
any_substrate falls. If you instead drop the toll, you’ve built a free-certification
system. That’s a different system, and it counts for nothing against the theorem.

The toll from premises (Section 4). Exhibit a finite, duplicate-free list of every state, a
certificate no step revokes, and an injective step that switches it on. permanent_f
lip_is_not_injective falls, and the derivation of the toll with it. An infinite
state space, a revocable certificate, or an unpriced merge is not a counterexample; the
file already builds one of each. For the squeeze bound, a finite permanent machine
with a cost meeting the halving premise where one step switches k states on beside m
certified ones and two to the cost times m is less than m plus k; permanent_flips
_compression_bound falls. For merge-or-revoke, a finite machine and an injective
instruction that switches a reading on without switching it off anywhere; flip_merg
es_or_revokes falls. A move that merges and also revokes counts against nothing.
It’s the three cards. For the eight-state machine, a move of it that merges two states
and costs nothing; fin_merging_priced falls.

The bill in bits (Section 4). Exhibit a finite machine with a permanent certificate, a
move that switches k states on beside m certified ones (k at least one), and a spread of
probability over those m plus k states whose image under the move has entropy above
log base two of m. permanent_step_entropy_ceiling falls. For the general
form, a step and a spread on a finite list of every state under which two different states,
each with some probability, land on the same state while the entropy doesn’t drop; en
tropy_drop_pos_of_support_merge falls. A heat measurement on a real device
below what the bound asks doesn’t touch either theorem. It refutes the premise lan
dauer_heat for that device, which is Landauer’s principle, and that’s a fight with
physics. The counting stays where it was. And a certifying step from a state already
known that gives off no heat isn’t a counterexample: known_state_flip_forces
_no_heat says the premise sets no positive floor there.

Learning is free (Section 5). Show that the four-state demon’s measure step merges two
states, or that its observer’s candidate list doesn’t shrink. observer_narrowing_ca
n_be_free falls. A different price schedule that charges the measure step is allowed
and isn’t a counterexample. The claim is “not forced.” It never says “always free.”

The counter (Section 6; on the small machine, Section 16). Find a state of the small machine
and an instruction such that the ledger after is anything other than the ledger before
plus that instruction’s cost; the loud version is a ledger that goes down. mu_cons
ervation falls. The uniqueness half, that only one bookkeeping starts at zero and
follows the schedule, is checked over any counter machine as nec_f_initiality
(Section 6); a reachable state where two such bookkeepings disagree makes it fall.

Windows (Section 7). Exhibit a window and a price computed from the observed before

                                             361
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


and after that meets the floor and never overcharges, on a machine where two steps
share their before and after pictures and only one certifies. shadow_cannot_pri
ce_exactly falls. A window that shows certification is not a counterexample; the
theorem says exactly that such a window prices exactly. For the three escapes, a
verifier of one of the three kinds that’s wrong about the pair, under its own relation;
the argument after Definition 7.1 falls.

Entitlement (Section 8). Produce a strict narrowing of a candidate list, with a distin-
guishing observation, that does not yield a strictly stronger membership test; the card
argument falls. Or exhibit a run with a tree no deeper than its paid steps, covering
the narrowing, whose counter rose by less than the index bits lost; Theorem 8.2 falls.
On every Thiele-complete machine: a run from a clean start that ends with the record
up, meets the hypotheses of Theorem 16.39, and has fewer record moves than the
index bits it narrowed, or has no earned chain in it; ent_representation falls,
and the weighted form (ent2_weighted_representation) falls the same way. A
narrowing with a big drop and a small bill is not a counterexample unless a tree no
deeper than the record moves covers it: the covering is a hypothesis, and ent2_unco
vered_claim_false says why it has to stay one. On the host machine, a run from
a clean start that raises the record only after more than sixteen CHECKs; ent2_ques
tions_cap falls. On the small machine, a program of INC and DEC that runs fewer
than m moves and whose final line number and B determine whether A ≥ m at every
start; ent2_free_cannot_decide_fast falls.

The latch (Section 10). Exhibit an extension of a base whose record is driven by the
computation and never switches off, and which is not a latch on any event. record_
axis_is_latch_holds falls. A record that switches off, or one driven by a hidden
clock, is the file’s own pair of counterexamples. The file built those already.

The diagonal (Section 13). Two routes. A decider for some substrate with a shortcut
predicate whose flip the substrate can represent and which answers correctly on every
program; the generic proof fails at a named step. For the nat family, a d that correctly
decides the predicate of the substrate built from d. L has its recursion theorem by
proof, so it gets a target of its own: a map on L’s terms, computable by an L term, with
no term that behaves like its own image; L_recursion_theorem falls. On the host
machine: a host program that decides an extensional property of host programs that
some program has and some lacks, or a map of host programs that a host program
carries out, with no host program that computes the same function as its image; sm
_host_rice or sm_kleene falls. On the small machine: a decider for a property
of what two-counter programs do from the clean start that some program has and
some lacks; sm_guest_rice falls. A decider for such a property over every input of
two-counter programs; tc_rice falls. A two-counter program that multiplies every
plain input by the number of Theorem 16.54; tc2_no_mult falls. A map of host
programs that a host program carries out, with no host program that stops when its
image stops and agrees with it on register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the


                                          362
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


number of facts and whether the channel is empty, is a counterexample to sm2_klee
ne_obs. A map whose fixed point disagrees with its image on some other register is
not one: some computable map has no fixed point that agrees with its image on every
register (sm2_no_exact).

The pointer conjecture (Section 15). It’s a conjecture, so the three routes are its own: a
deployed discipline pricing a non-proliferating event; a rival event proliferating as
well as certification in a real ecosystem; an honest formalisation with independence
defined where certification fails the test.

One concession goes with it, and I make it in full. The window results, the separation
of the two runs, and the counter’s uniqueness don’t single out certification. Their
proofs use only that the step carries something the classical picture doesn’t determine,
so the same shape of result holds for any such field. Nothing in Parts II to IV proves
that certification is the one event a model is forced to price; Section 4 forces a price on
every merge, certifying or not. That’s the conjecture, and Section 15 is the case I make
for it.

The five models (Section 14). Each fragment has a theorem with a named falsifier: a
finality fork with nobody slashable; a gas schedule meeting floor and no-overcharge
whose charging predicate differs from the commit predicate on some step; one of the
RFC’s own example proofs that the transcribed inclusion check rejects, or an input
with leaf index equal to tree size that it accepts; a program the bounds checker accepts
whose verification condition fails. Each kills one fragment. None of them, and I want
this clear, says anything about the real system beyond the fragment.

23.2 The machine claims (Part IV)
The small machine (Section 16). Four targets. From a clean start, a run that raises the
flag without an earlier passing CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY of the same claim,
with the counter’s version unchanged between the CHECK and the COMMIT; earne
d_certification_provenance falls, and earned_commitment_provenance
for a COMMIT alone. From a clean start, a trace that leaves a fact in the table nobody
checked; no_forging falls. From a clean start, a run that ends certified for a total
charge under three; certified_run_min_cost falls, and a run at exactly three is
not a counterexample: CHECK “A is 0”, COMMIT, CERTIFY from a start where A
is 0 is one, and the same program from any other start is refused forever (earned_
run_check_can_fail, earned_run_refused_forever). A check that can’t fail
certifying for three isn’t a counterexample either; the step doesn’t police trivial checks,
and the book says so. A two-counter machine and a program whose run on the small
machine disagrees with it step for step, or halts when it doesn’t; simulation_step
or halting_correspondence falls.

Thiele-complete (Section 16). A machine that charges at least one for every move and still
meets the four clauses; complete_has_free_move falls, and with it clock_not_
thiele_complete, whose proof uses it. A Thiele-complete machine and a function

                                           363
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


of its window that gives its record at the end of every run from every loaded state; co
mplete_no_record_oracle falls. A clause none of the excluded machines needs:
drop it and show the paid latch or the silent machine still fails, and paid_latch_n
ot_thiele_complete or silent_not_thiele_complete has been proved by
the wrong clause, which is worth a letter.

The universal program (Section 16.13). A program of the small machine and a start on
which U halts and the guest doesn’t, or the other way round; universal_halting
falls. One on which the flags disagree, or the ledgers differ at a matching point; uni
versal_flag_iff or universal_ledger_exact falls. A run of U whose raised
flag doesn’t stand on a passing CHECK, then COMMIT, of one slot, then CERTIFY; u
niversal_earned falls.

Every computably presented machine (Section 16.14). A computably presented Thiele
machine and a start on which UP ’s flag goes up while the machine’s reading never
says yes, or the other way round; presented_universal_flag_iff falls. With
the reading starting at no, a step the machine reaches at which every point of UP ’s run
that matches it has a ledger more than two above the machine’s; presented_unive
rsal_surcharge_le_two falls. A program on the host machine, from a clean start,
that matches exactly a guest certified with its whole ledger below three; presented_
universal_no_exact_below_three falls. A machine whose reading no program
decides isn’t a counterexample. It’s outside the class, and the book says so.

The classical CHSH bound (Section 20). Exhibit four fixed bits and a tally consistent with
that one plan, every pair sampled, scoring above two. chsh_violation_rules_o
ut_locally_factorizable_coupling falls, and so does known mathematics. A
randomised plan landing past two by luck doesn’t count; the theorem is about one
fixed plan, and Section 20’s coin-flip example shows the luck.

The integer check (Section 20). The game check has two walls, and here’s how to knock
each one over. A correlator that passes the three contraction inequalities whose five-
by-five is not PSD (forward), or a PSD five-by-five of that shape whose correlators
aren’t contractive (reverse); npa_psd_iff_column_contractive falls. A correla-
tor whose pinned five-by-five is PSD (contractive, by the equivalence) with S squared
above eight; npa_psd_implies_tsirelson_bound falls. The PR box and the clas-
sical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) are not counterexamples to any of these. Both fail contraction
by plain arithmetic (the table in Appendix F.4), which is exactly what the theorems
need them to do. On the machine: a raised flag from a clean start with no passing
CHECK of the packed-counts property before it, or whose counts give S2 > 8; small
_chsh_flag_implies_tsirelson falls. A tally that passes the seven facts while
its pinned matrix isn’t PSD, or one with every pair sampled and a PSD pinned matrix
that fails them; small_chsh_check_iff falls. The all-ones tally and the PR box
being refused are not counterexamples; those refusals are the point.

The nine-by-nine (Section 20). A point and five extra numbers where the contraction-like


                                           364
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


condition holds and the nine-by-nine isn’t PSD, or the other way round; q1ab_psd
_iff_column_contractive falls. A point where the condition holds with all five
extras at zero and S is above two; q1ab_check_at_gzero_implies_classical_
bound falls.

The elliptope completion (Section 20). This one’s a shape, so you’re trying to push a
point in or out of it. Three targets, one per theorem, plus the decider beside it. Signs
a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 , each squaring to one, and a vector on which the completed matrix of that
plan goes negative; deterministic_strategy_elliptope falls. A correlator
with some positive semidefinite completion and S squared above eight; elliptope
_tsirelson falls. Real numbers x and y that make the PR box’s completed matrix
positive semidefinite; pr_box_not_elliptope falls. And for the decider that sits
beside it: inputs on which it says yes while the correlators have no PSD completion
at all (S squared above eight is one way to show that); elliptope_check_full
_sound falls. The all-ones plan and (1, 0, 1, 0) aren’t counterexamples here either,
from the other side: the completion admits them (turing_point_elliptope for
the second), which is what the theorems require.

The audit (Section 22). Run the assumption probe on any theorem the book cites and
find a project-local axiom or parameter in its dependencies, and the claim of zero of
them falls. For the small machine, its hosts and the universal programs, compile any
of their files and find a printed assumption line that isn’t closed. Run the Inquisitor
and read what it says; it fails on high and medium findings. A new finding means
somebody looks. It doesn’t automatically mean a theorem is false.

23.3 What’s mine and what isn’t
This is not a claim to have been first. Appendix C does the sorting item by item, with
sources: what was known, what’s added, and what kind of addition it is. Here’s the
short form, and I’d welcome correction on any boundary.

Borrowed, with names. As the opening chapter warned, I usually had the hunch first
and found these names after, and that order doesn’t make any of it mine. Everything
in Part I (every source is cited where it’s used), the category theory (Eilenberg, Mac
Lane) included. Minsky’s two-counter machines and the Coq library that proves their
halting undecidable and compiles computable functions into them (Forster, Larchey-
Wendling and coauthors). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice, Cantor, Gödel, the diagonal
pattern, Lawvere’s unification, and the mechanized versions of them: Michael Nor-
rish’s in HOL4, Mario Carneiro’s in Lean, and Yannick Forster, Fabian Kunze and Gert
Smolka’s in Coq. Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Stephanie Wehner’s semidefinite proof of
Tsirelson’s bound (2006), NPA, Landau, Masanes, Fine, the elliptope, and the machine-
checked proofs of Tsirelson’s bound that came before mine (Echenim and Mhalla in
Isabelle, and Lean’s mathlib). Landauer, Bennett, Szilard, Maxwell, and their critics.
The potential method (Tarjan) and its mechanizations (Nipkow, Charguéraud and
Pottier), Lamport’s clocks, Floyd and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley, Shannon,


                                            365
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Rissanen. Zurek. The guarantee about every program: the reference monitor (Ander-
son), execution monitors (Schneider), and monitors checked at every instruction and
verified in Coq (Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors). The counting under the per-
manence results: Poincaré’s recurrence, as Zermelo used it. The seL4 and CompCert
discipline. The facts under the permanence results are Landauer’s own example and
Shannon’s bounds, and “set a bit to one whatever it held” is my way of saying his
RESTORE TO ONE.

Formal reconstructions. The Coq development defines the state types, transition sys-
tems, real-matrix predicates, encodings, and proof terms this book uses. When I say a
theorem is checked, I mean the stated proposition has a kernel-checked proof under
its printed premises. That doesn’t make the underlying idea mine, and it doesn’t make
it new.

What this project proved, inside its stated interfaces. The abstract floor, which is the poten-
tial method with one particular potential. The derivation of the toll from finiteness,
permanence, and a named price, in counted states and in bits, with each premise’s
counterexample built. The eight-state machine on which every one of those premises
is a theorem. The window that can’t price the flag exactly, and the small machine’s
own colliding pair. The latch form over any base, with its two counterexamples and
converse. The small machine’s earned record from a clean start (checked, then com-
mitted, then certified, about the same edition, nothing forged, three at least), its exact
ledger, its universality through Minsky, the definition of Thiele-complete that every
clock fails and the window blindness of every machine meeting it, the universal pro-
gram U with its guest’s halting and flag matched exactly, its ledger equal to the guest’s
at every matching point, and its own flag earned, the priced program UP that runs
every computably presented Thiele machine with its reading latched, its flag earned
on the guest’s own reading and its ledger within two of the guest’s when the reading
starts at no, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid
when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three, and the simpler host’s
mirror, its isolation and its refusal to certify for free. The substrate diagonal and the
L results, with Rice’s and Kleene’s theorems on the machine’s host and Rice’s from
the clean start on the two-counter machine. The integer check, exact for every pair
being sampled and the pinned matrix being PSD (and so a sufficient test for the bound,
which tells you nothing about quantum behaviour), the equivalence with contraction,
Tsirelson’s bound from PSD, which is known mathematics checked again here, and the
check earned on the host, a raised flag standing on it. Structural entitlement for every
Thiele-complete machine, with its worked members, its floor that takes no supplied
tree and its proof that the covering can’t be dropped; the eight-state machine run by
the small machine; the time a check saves; and the collision of every bare-transcript
verifier on every Thiele-complete machine. All of it with premises printed. Of that
list, the toll derivation as a rule on a ledger (Ouldridge and Wolpert priced the same
merge in entropy first), the pricing form of the window fact, and the latch form are



                                             366
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


the only pieces I’d call new statements, and only in the sense that I didn’t find them
stated where I looked. The fourth thing I’d name is built and checked, and its idea
isn’t new: a record that’s priced, and on the small machine earned, under the reference
monitor’s every-program move, which is old and isn’t mine. Appendix C names the
same four the same way, with the prior work beside each.

Interpretation, which is mine and not proved. That structure is what a computation
establishes and the toll is the right thing to price. That certification is the pointer event.
That the record axis “belongs in the step.” Those are proposals, with the arguments
I’ve given, and the proposals are where I’d aim first if I were you.

24 The claim ledger
Here’s everything this book claims, one line each: what kind of claim it is, and where it
lives. “Proved” means proved under the premises printed in that section, and nothing
more. If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right and the
line is wrong. “By unfolding” after it means the proof does little more than read the
answer off the definitions, a case split whose every branch is a line: true, checked, and
carrying almost nothing the definitions didn’t already say. If you’re counting results,
count those differently. I mark them so they don’t pad the list.

Ledger is a good word for it, and it’s older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a ledger
was a book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from the old
verb leggen, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. A book that stays
put. That’s the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is
the one place where every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you
left it.

24.1 Claims about the model
First the model. Every line in this table is about any system that has the pieces the
line names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading and the toll,
a counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about my machine,
except the lines that run these results on it, which say so and point to Section 16.17.
The table runs over several pages, in reading order.

Here’s one way to use it, and it takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you
trust least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the
home section and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says
more, you’ve found my mistake, and the end of this section says what I’d like done
about it.
