24.3 What I propose
And then there’s what I’m proposing. These are mine. They reach further than any
theorem in here, and nothing in the tables puts an unavoidable physical price on every
observable change.


                                               387
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


   • That the axis belongs in the step (Section 25, Section 26).
   • That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step (Section 26).
   • That certification is the event worth recording, which is the pointer conjecture
     (Section 15).
   • That this is a structural account of computation, with a cost model as one part of
     it (Section 25).
   • That the toll is the right thing to price. The alternatives are a wall or a penalty
     for contradiction (Section 14, Section 26).

And three things this book doesn’t settle, with what would settle each. Whether
Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every theorem standing and one
premise unowned by the world: that takes measurements of real devices (Section 4).
Whether certification really is the pointer event: that takes a definition of the systems
the conjecture is about, and Section 15 gives three ways to kill it. And whether there’s
a smaller start than a partition: that takes a ruler someone can state and a smaller
structure measured by it (Section 2).

That’s the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn’t on it, or a line that
says more than its home does, that’s my mistake, and I’d want to hear about it.

25 Scope
This is the line around what I’ve proved. Inside it: an accounting law for one event,
a derivation of that law from premises each with its own counterexample, a set of
windows that provably lose it, a record axis that’s a latch over any base, a diagonal
that holds by proof on L, a machine of six instruction kinds on which commitments
are earned and which computes what two counters can, one fixed program in its
instruction kinds, run on a host with more counters and one paid move, that runs
every computably presented Thiele machine, and an integer check that implies a
bound by algebra. Outside it: everything that follows. This is the fence. I built it
myself, so lean on it before you trust it.

G. K. Chesterton, the English writer who has been called the prince of paradox, has a
famous fence, in a 1929 book called The Thing. A reformer finds a fence across a road,
can’t see what it’s for, and wants it cleared away; the wiser one tells him to go off and
find out why it was put there, and only then come back and argue for tearing it down.
This section runs the other way round. Every post below comes labelled with what
it’s there for, the overclaim it stops, so you don’t have to go off and find out first. Pull
up any post you like. Just look at what walks through the gap when you do.

Physical interpretation of the counter. The ledger is unique once the start and schedule
are chosen. That doesn’t make it entropy, and it doesn’t make it energy. A physical
bridge needs a model of which states carry information, premises that can all hold



                                            388
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


at once, and a real argument tying the formal charge to dissipation. The permanent-
certificate theorems supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent
reading. The two premises are shown able to hold together whenever every counted
step costs at least one, and for a one-bit reset. The small machine’s free steps merge
states and are charged nothing, which breaks the bridge for its whole instruction set
(Section 21), and the calorimeter protocol shows that population dynamics don’t fix
the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one mark without thermal and device
premises (Section 4, Section 21). Once you pick the start and the price list, the number
is forced by arithmetic, and it isn’t energy. What I’d need before it could be is the list
at the top of this paragraph.

Class separation. The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They
don’t stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No
separation of standard complexity classes follows from the collisions (Section 7, Sec-
tion 16). I’ll be blunt about why I’m careful here. Whether P equals NP is one of the
seven problems the Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on, at a meeting
in Paris in May 2000. One of the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture,
by the mathematician Grigori Perelman, who posted the proof as preprints in 2002
and 2003. P versus NP hasn’t. If a two-state collision on my machine settled it, I’d
be owed a million dollars. Nobody owes me anything. A window that loses a field
is a fact about that window. A complexity class is a fact about what every possible
program can do within a budget, and nothing in these collisions reaches that far.

Trace initiality, and what it doesn’t settle. The universal property of the trace fold is about
evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there’s exactly one
way to fold a list into it (Section 6, checked as nec_f_fold_unique). The counter’s
uniqueness assumes a schedule. Rise-only pricing assumes an event, and a reference
count that says what charging too much means (Section 7). Those results make the
construction precise. None of them shows that the schedule I chose, or the event I
chose, is physically necessary.

Other observables. Certification is one worked example. A family of other observations
might turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own events, its own
evidence, and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The window and oracle
results are about what specific maps keep, and nothing more.

Program predicates versus state observations. The state-level collision (Section 7’s wall)
and the program-level diagonal (Section 13’s wall) live in different domains. Linking
them would take a theorem of its own. The nat family and L (Section 13) keep their
explicit quantifiers and representability premises.

Entitlement bounds. The count is handed its tree and its covering, along with the
payment condition. It doesn’t dig the tree out of an arbitrary run, and it isn’t a
Shannon bound on every trace (Section 8). On every Thiele-complete machine the
payment is the record moves, each exactly one mark, and a floor that takes no tree


                                             389
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


exists when the questions are the run’s own CHECKs; but its answers are taken at the
rivals as they start, a free branch can still narrow for nothing, the lists, tree and fibres
are supplied except in the worked members, and the covering can’t be dropped. The
search through n bits is capped at 16 questions by the machine’s fact table, and the
time tax is a lower bound for programs of INC and DEC only. Nothing here extends it
to every Thiele-complete machine (Section 16.17).

Quantum behaviour. The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with zero
marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party mo-
ments move, at the level of correlators. Full behaviours with marginals, and operator
realisations, need identifications this book doesn’t make. A sound check isn’t com-
plete for those bigger sets, and the elliptope decider is mathematics. None of the small
machine’s properties is it (Section 20).

The record axis. The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a base
computation is a latch on an event; on a finite machine its write merges states; and
the named windows don’t recover it. Certification is one instance. No theorem selects
it as the unique event every system must record (Section 10, Section 15). A finite
monotone multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches. One Boolean latch
can’t hold it. Revocation, including revocation priced from the other side as in Casper,
lies outside the permanent-record axis; a price on revocation doesn’t transfer to a price
on the write (Section 14). Probabilistic records don’t inherit the uniqueness result
either. Two honest random records can have the same branches and the same charges
and still give those branches different weights, one choosing evenly and one two to
one, so the schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities (schedule_determines_proba
bilities_refuted). And no single deterministic latch explains a record that can
branch both ways from the same observation (deterministic_latch_handles_
branching_refuted). Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence; no
two of the three bases of Definition 10.3, and none of them and the small machine, are
related by it in the checked work, and the latch form holds on each separately, so it
doesn’t tell them apart (Section 10). A record driven by the computation that stays up
is a latch, and on a finite machine its write merges states; which event deserves the
latch isn’t proved; records that can come back down lie outside all of this (they’re limit
computability’s, and Section 10 points at Ershov’s ladder), and random ones lose the
uniqueness.

Who it’s safe against. Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any list of
instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says, one
writer stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It
doesn’t cover whoever sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts
nobody checked), a reset or a power cycle, whoever picks the program, the wire that
carries the report, someone who flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the step,
or a second writer that changes a counter without bumping its edition. Those are the
operator, the device and the tool chain, and they’re outside this fence. A record read


                                            390
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


by someone who didn’t watch it being made is only as good as their reason to believe
the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote over measured state and
a proof that travels on its own, are in Section 7 and Section 14, and this book builds
neither. What the guarantee gives inside the fence is safety: no program forges the
chain. Availability is a different promise, and it isn’t given. A hostile program can put
the trap up or fill the table, and after that nothing useful gets done. The proofs also use
Coq’s whole numbers, which never overflow, so versions and the ledger grow without
bound. A build with fixed-width counters, versions or ledger has to stop before any of
them wraps, failing safe with the trap up, because a wrapped version could make an
old fact look live again and a wrapped ledger would fall. Starting, restoring, resetting
and that overflow stop belong to the implementation, and none of them is proved
here.

The diagonal on the machine. What’s proved for the small machine’s programs is that
halting is undecidable in the library’s synthetic sense, for them and for the univer-
sal program (Section 16). L has its recursion theorem, Rice and halting by proof
(Section 13). On the host machine, the one with a counter for every number, Rice’s
theorem holds for properties that depend on everything a program ends with (every
register, the table, the channel, the trap, the ledger and the flag; the line number and
the versions are left out), for programs run on an input in register 1; s-m-n holds with
no premise on register 2; and Kleene’s recursion theorem holds for the transforma-
tions a host program carries out on numbers, with a fixed point that agrees with its
image on stopping, register 0, the trap latch, the ledger, the flag, the number of facts
and whether the channel is empty; for some of these transformations no fixed point
agrees on every register. On the two-counter machine itself Rice’s theorem is proved
on every input, with facts compared by what they’re about, their versions left out of
the comparison; Kleene’s is proved with inputs written as powers of two and refuted
with plain inputs (Section 16.18).

The five models. Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice;
the gas fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures;
the transparency verifier covers control flow and leaves collision resistance out; the
proof-carrying checker is a three-instruction memory-bounds language. None is a
claim about the real system beyond its fragment (Section 14).

The machine. Part IV has one small machine, with the hosts that run it, and here’s its
fence. The small machine of Section 16 (two counters, six instruction kinds) is where
commitments are earned: from a clean start, a raised flag went through a passing
check, a commitment and a certification of the same claim, nothing is forged, and
the cheapest such run adds exactly three to the ledger, a price reached by a check
that could have failed (the step doesn’t police trivial checks: a check that can’t fail
certifies for three too). It’s also where universality is proved, by matching Minsky’s
two-counter machines step for step and borrowing their undecidable halting from the


                                           391
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Coq library. It’s Thiele-complete under a definition every clock-style machine fails,
and every machine meeting that definition hides its record and ledger from its own
window. The universal Thiele machine is one fixed program, U, on a host with the
small machine’s instruction kinds and more counters, with no guest step built in: it
runs every program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts when
the guest halts, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and
only if the guest’s flag rises somewhere in the guest’s run, and keeps a ledger equal to
the guest’s at every matching point. With one paid move added, one fixed program,
UP , runs every computably presented Thiele machine: its step, prices and reading
computed by programs, the reading decided on every state, the run fixed by a driver.
The host halts when the guest stops, its flag is the latch of the guest’s reading, raised
on its own earned chain whose claim is that reading, and its ledger is the guest’s plus a
surcharge of at most two when the reading starts at no, a surcharge no program on that
host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger
below three. A machine whose reading no program decides is outside. A simpler host
with a guest step built in runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest’s
flag; its ledger only covers the guest’s. The small machine’s check price is flat, its fact
table holds sixteen, and its certificate is historical (Section 16 lists the rest).

The comparison machines. The small machines I built to compare against are fragments
too. The random-access memory result covers an addressed list memory with load,
increment and decrement on cells (concrete_ram_write_reads_back and its
neighbours), and it’s about that machine. The register machine Section 10 puts the
latch on (record_axis_is_latch_on_ram_holds) is a different small machine,
the one with indirect addressing, and that theorem is about it. The reversible-machine
result covers arithmetic update cores: add and subtract, each undone by the other,
with or without wrapping at a modulus (janus_like_unbounded_inverse, j
anus_like_bounded_inverse). None is a theorem about real memories or full
reversible languages. The cost-semantics results are local correspondences, short of
full cost-framework embeddings: the trace’s cost is a writer cost and a grade, and
the toll is the potential method with one potential (Section 6). Nobody’s whole type
system gets embedded either.

Outward consequences. I looked for results about real systems that would need the
record axis. Five narrow ones are proved, each as a two-state countermodel: a
certificate-transparency client’s local tree head can’t decide whether the world’s log is
consistent (ct_local_view_insufficient); a quote check that matches only the
composite digest accepts a mismatched selection (tpm_selection_binding_is_
necessary); a local suffix can’t decide a trusted anchor (weak_subjective_suff
ix_insufficient); an acknowledgement without a durable commit record can be
lost (wal_ack_requires_durability); and a current local log can’t decide what
happened before it (audit_local_snapshot_insufficient). Each reduces to a
known indistinguishability or durability argument. Five stronger candidates would



                                           392
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


need protocol or hardware semantics I haven’t formalised, and I’ve proved nothing
about them. So none of this yields a new outside result that both needs the record axis
and is ready to use.

Where each result lives. Every system that follows the toll, whatever its states: the floor,
at most as many certifications as cost, and the potential-method reading. Every finite
machine whose price covers merges: the toll for permanent records, and, when its
move names can be decided equal or different, which instructions every such price
must charge. Every finite machine paying per halving: the machine’s own narrowing
bound. Every machine extending a base with a driven, permanent record: the latch.
Every window through which a certifying and a non-certifying step look alike: no
exact price from the window. Every machine meeting the definition of Thiele-complete:
a free move, at least three marks on any run from a clean state that ends certified, and
a final window that doesn’t determine the record or the ledger. Any eight counts:
the integer check and its PSD bridge, which are mathematics. This machine only: its
six instruction kinds and their prices, its sixteen slots, its own colliding pair, and the
encodings its universal programs use.

What I’m proposing beyond that. That the axis belongs in the step; that certification is
the event worth recording; that this is a structural account of computation, with a cost
model as one part of it. Those reach further than any theorem here, and no theorem
here puts an unavoidable physical price on every observable change. They’re the
argument, and the argument is what the rest of the book was. What kind of claim is
that? A proposal about which distinctions an account of computation ought to draw,
and no proof settles an “ought”. The proofs show the proposal hangs together, follows
from premises I’ve named, and costs little (six instruction kinds on the small machine);
whether anyone should adopt it is something I argue for and can’t prove. Here’s what
would weaken it: if every use people have for the record turned out to be recoverable
from a log the program writes plus a correctness proof about the program, or if the
real systems keep choosing walls over tolls for good reasons, as the five in Section 14
mostly did.

26 Conclusion
I started with one word and a machine I couldn’t explain. Here’s where the word
ended up, and where the machine did.

Structure, by the end of Part I, was relations among things, kept under chosen changes,
carried by whatever stuff, always relative to a frame. The start I chose, the smallest
one by the count of names, was a sorting of a pile, and the thing nobody I read had
priced was the moment you stand behind the sorting. That was Part I, and it ended
with a question.

The question got an exact form in Part II: five parts, one rule, one theorem you proved
at the table. Then the rule stopped being only my preference. With finitely many yes-


                                            393
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


states and a flag that stays up, every move that raises it merges states, and if forgetting
is charged for, the way Landauer’s principle charges for it in its worst case, the toll
follows. That’s a derivation under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each
with its counterexample built. It isn’t a proof that every computation has to adopt the
rule; and the charge on forgetting is a named premise with its critics named. Learning
can be free; committing to a record that stays put can’t be, on those premises. That’s
as far as physics goes in this book, and I’ve tried to keep it exactly that far.

Part III was the logic, and here’s what it earned, in the order it was earned. The counter
is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a raising step and a
quiet one look the same can’t price the raise exactly, by a fact about functions far older
than the machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked relation, and a paid
event; given lists, a tree and a covering somebody supplies, a run that paid a charged
step for every level of the tree has paid for the index bits it commits to (no run is shown
to have to pay them, the run doesn’t recover the tree, the lists count repeats, and the
index bits aren’t the questions anybody asked); on every Thiele-complete machine the
same count, for a run from a clean start, is a theorem about its record moves, with the
earned chain inside the run, and the count can’t do without the covering; and it is a
license to lean on a claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true. Insight, in the sense the toll
prices, is a committed relation. A feeling doesn’t count. Its floor is flat: at least one,
however deep. The claim behind the flag is something a check could have refused,
and in the bare model nothing makes the commit wait for the check. Over any base,
an honest record is a latch, with two free choices, the event and the price list; “only one
substrate” is false and “one structure, many price lists” is true once the event is fixed.
No procedure the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a
recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege’s floor, and the machine’s
answer is to record the commitment. It leaves the judgement unautomated. Of five
record disciplines I modelled in fragments, one prices the write. And which event to
record is a conjecture, with its refutations listed.

Part IV built one small machine, two counters and six instruction kinds, with hosts
to run it, and on it the model stands whole: from a clean start, a raised flag was
checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition of the same counter,
nothing gets forged, the cheapest run to a raised flag adds exactly three to the ledger,
and a run whose check could have failed reaches that three (the step doesn’t police
trivial checks), and it computes everything Minsky’s two-counter machines can, so
its halting is undecidable. Earned commitments and universality are proved there.
So is what Thiele-complete has to mean: a universal base that’s free and can’t touch
the record, a record that stays up once it’s up, an earned record, one mark for each
check, commit and certificate, and some claim whose check can fail. Every clock, every
machine that charges for computing, fails it; the small machine meets it; and every
machine that meets it hides its record and its ledger from its own window. And so is a
universal Thiele machine, with its scope said plainly: one fixed program, U, written



                                           394
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction on a host with more counters,
with no guest step built in, that runs every small-machine program from every clean
start start( x, y), halts exactly when its guest halts, raises its own flag by its own check,
commit and certificate if and only if the guest’s rises somewhere in its run, and keeps
a ledger equal to the guest’s at every matching point. And then the bigger version
of the same thing: with one paid move added, one fixed program, UP , runs every
computably presented Thiele machine, a machine from anywhere whose driver, step,
prices and reading are computed by programs. It halts when the guest stops, raises its
own flag on its own earned chain exactly when the guest’s reading has said yes, with
the guest’s own reading as the claim it checked, and, when the guest’s reading starts
at no, keeps the guest’s prices to within a surcharge of at most two, which no program
on that host, run from a clean start, can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole
ledger below three. An ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t do that
for the programs it runs; U and UP show a fixed interpreter can. All of it is proved
in Coq with no axioms: each file prints the assumptions of every headline theorem,
and every line comes back closed. Then a check worth earning, the two-player game
with an integer test whose pass forces Tsirelson’s bound for the tally it’s handed, and
what the counter has to do with physics, which is less than the word Landauer in a
file name suggests. The places where the machine came up short of the idea stayed
on the page: its free steps merge states, so the toll on it is a choice the chairs don’t
force, and a check that can’t fail certifies for three like any other. Part V was how to
check it and how to break it. Every result carries the shape of the thing that would kill
it, gathered in one place (Section 23): a state of the small machine and an instruction
after which the ledger goes down; a contractive correlator whose pinned matrix isn’t
positive semidefinite; a certification system that follows the toll and certifies at total
cost zero; a function on numbers that correctly decides the shortcut predicate of the
substrate built from it. Any one of them brings down the theorem it matches. I hunted.
I came up empty. For a theorem Coq has checked, that’s no surprise: finding one
would take a bug in the checker. The places a reader can really win are where my
sentence says more than the statement does, or a definition doesn’t catch the word it’s
named for, and Section 23 starts with those.

If you asked what’s new here, I wouldn’t give you one thing, because there isn’t one.
There are four, and each comes with its fence and its neighbours. First, the toll isn’t
only my preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can only be turned
on by a step that merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it costs (Theorem 4.1,
Theorem 4.2). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the recurrence argument
Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the price on a merge is Landauer’s, as a
premise. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) had already put a physical price on that merge
for finite automata, so what’s here is the toll as a rule on a ledger. Second, a window
that shows a raising step and a quiet one the same can’t price the raise exactly (Theo-
rem 7.2); that a price computed from what a window shows can’t tell apart two steps
the window shows the same is elementary, and what’s here is the pricing form. Third,


                                            395
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


a record driven by the computation that never switches off is a latch on one event, over
any base (Theorem 10.1); latches and history variables are old, and the theorem covers
only records that never come down. Fourth, a record that’s priced, and on the small
machine earned (Theorem 16.9), under the move of guaranteeing something about
every program. That move isn’t mine at all. It’s the reference monitor’s (Anderson,
1972), made precise for monitors that watch a run (Schneider, 2000), and verified in
Coq for monitors checked at every instruction (Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors,
2015). What’s put together under it here is built and checked, and its idea isn’t new:
the check bound to the edition it looked at, the toll paid on top, and universal pro-
grams that carry both to every program of the small machine and to every computably
presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag as they go. Appendix C sorts all four
with sources.

And two things I’d point at if you asked how far the checking reaches. Neither is a
fifth new thing.

In the game: an integer check on eight counts forces a five-by-five matrix to be positive
semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows, and the chain never once
reaches for physics. No Hilbert space, no operators, no observables. The route through
the matrix is the first rung of a ladder Navascués, Pironio and Acín built in 2007. None
of that route is mine, and the semidefinite road to Tsirelson’s bound is older than
that. What’s here is the check that runs in whole numbers, and the checked link
from “the check passed” to the bound. It’s algebra you can follow line by line, and
the assumption audit on that link finds exactly three standard axioms from Coq’s
own library (two that come with its real numbers, and functional extensionality) and
nothing of mine, which is how anyone can see that no physics was smuggled in. And
on the small machine’s host a raised flag can stand on that check: from a clean start
a raised flag contains a passing CHECK of the packed counts, a COMMIT and a
CERTIFY, and the check passes exactly when every pair was sampled and the five-by-
five is positive semidefinite (Section 20).

In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be ex-
pressed inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the fixed
point is proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice’s theorem. On the
small machine’s host, Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem are proved for
its own programs, so the wall stands there by proof, with its premise a theorem: no
host program decides a property of what a program computes that some program has
and some lacks; such a property is undecidable in the library’s sense (Section 16.18).

What this book doesn’t settle, by my count. Whether the toll is the right thing to
price. The five real systems mostly built a wall or a penalty for contradiction. Whether
certification is the pointer event. Whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would
leave every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world. And the
question I’d most like someone to take from me: is there a smaller start than a partition,


                                           396
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


by a ruler they can state? I said in Section 2 it would change this book. It would.

And the two computers from the first pages, the sorter and the copier, holding the
same bits. Walk the warehouse again. On an ordinary machine there’s still no lamp
for what the sorter did, and nothing in this book changes that. On the small machine
there is one: a flag and a counter you can read off the state, and a theorem that, from
a clean start, the flag can’t be up unless some claim went through a passing check, a
commit about the same edition and a certificate, in that order, where a claim can be
any property, in a language with an exact equality test, whose checker is proved to
mean what it says, “this counter, read as a list, is sorted” among them (sorted_run_
certifies_iff and sorted_run_refused_forever, EarnedGeneric.v). That’s
the one lamp I set out to light. It’s a lamp for whoever can read this machine’s state.
A “tests passed” sheet fits it only when the test is a checker proved to mean what it
says; the sticker and the very sure AI from the first pages ask something else, whether
to believe a report you didn’t watch being made, and nothing in this book answers
that (Section 25). Whether every machine ought to have that lamp is the argument.
No proof here settles it.

So that’s the Thiele Machine. An abstract model with five parts and one rule, an
argument made with it that the usual account of a computation is a shadow and the
axis it leaves out belongs in the step, and one small machine to check the argument
against, with one fixed program, written in its instruction kinds plus one paid move
and run on a host with more counters, that runs every machine of the model whose
workings a program can present. The theorems are what they are, with their premises
printed. The interpretation is mine, and I’ve tried to say at every turn which is which,
because the first time through I was the only one checking, and I’ve met me, and that’s
not enough people. Now there’s you.

A Things I had to learn first
I came in with none of the formal fields this work turned out to need. By the time the
proofs compiled I’d needed enough of half a dozen of them that I had to put down
somewhere what those fields had words for. This appendix is that place. None of it
is the argument. It’s what I needed to be able to make it. Everything below is what I
understood after I went and read about it; I’m not claiming to teach you these subjects,
and if you already know a part, skip it.

A.1 Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees
A bit is one digit that’s either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold. Every-
thing else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any number
from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the same byte is
also a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the letter A, 48 the digit
0, 32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The meaning is a convention laid
on top.


                                            397
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


You can see the convention’s seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001. Knock
off the first two digits and what’s left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B is 66, which
ends in 00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the same pattern with
one more bit switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its small letter differ in
exactly that bit. That’s on purpose. The first version of the code, in 1963, had no lower
case at all; when lower case arrived, in the 1967 revision, it was placed so the two cases
differ by one bit, which made matching them, and building keyboards and printers,
simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it’s a letter, but somebody made the letters easy
for a circuit to tell apart.

Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs. None of it belongs to the abstract
model, which has a kind of state and a step rule and nothing about widths or slots,
and the small machine of Part IV needs very little of it: its two counters have no width
at all, and hold any whole number.

A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit, in 2026 usually 64 bits (0 to
about 18 quintillion) on a desktop or server and 32 (0 to about 4 billion) on many small
devices. The abstract model doesn’t care which width.

A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word, the fastest
place to read or write. Memory is a longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index,
the address. The program counter is one specific register that tracks where in the
program the machine is; after every instruction it moves on to the next instruction
unless the instruction says jump. On the small machine it’s called the line number. A
stack pointer is a register pointing at the top of a region used for nested calls. A port
is a named channel for talking to the outside world.

Modular arithmetic means counting wraps around: counting modulo 16, the numbers
run 0 to 15, and 17 wraps to 1. Bitwise operations work on the bits of a value one
position at a time: AND is 1 only when both bits are, OR when either is, XOR (exclusive
or) exactly when they differ. A shift moves every bit left or right, which multiplies or
divides by a power of two. Popcount is the count of one-bits in a value. Hexadecimal
is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written with a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.

A trap, on a CPU, means execution jumps to a fixed handler and the program stops
advancing, the chip’s “this went wrong.” On the small machine a trap is one bit
that goes up when an instruction refuses, and then the core stops moving. An ISA,
instruction set architecture, is the list of every instruction a CPU recognises, each
identified by an opcode, a numeric tag the CPU decodes. The small machine’s has six.
The abstract model has none; it has a step rule.

A.2 The notation the formal parts use
I don’t think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers
are 0, 1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives;
the reals are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written


                                              398
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


with an arrow. For a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its
absolute value. A big sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a
quantity means the change in it. An upside-down A means “for every”; a backwards
E means “there exists.” A double arrow is implication; a double-headed one is “if
and only if.” A small circle between two functions is composition, apply the right one
first. Angle brackets mean one of three things, and the sentence around them says
which: a pair of numbers packed into one, ⟨m, n⟩ (Section 16.13); a dot product of two
vectors; or, around a random quantity, its long-run average, which I picked up from
the Bell-test papers. The quantum sense of a circled times never appears, because the
game section does its work in plain integer arithmetic. A superscript T on a matrix
is its transpose, rows and columns swapped, and I with a subscript n is the identity
matrix.

A.3 Coq, in just enough detail
Coq is a proof assistant: a programming language whose type system is expressive
enough that proofs are programs and the compiler checks them (Part V has the long
version). A Theorem is a named statement followed by a proof; a Lemma is the
same thing used for an intermediate result; a Definition introduces a named value;
an Inductive type is one with a finite list of constructors, the only ways to build a
value of it (Coq’s natural numbers have two: zero, and successor of another natural).
A tactic is a step inside a proof: induction (base case, then step), destruct (split into
cases), reflexivity (prove a thing equals itself), simpl (compute), lia and lra and nra
(arithmetic solvers for integers, linear reals, and polynomial reals), psatz (a certificate
search for polynomial inequalities). Qed ends a proof and asks Coq to check the
whole chain. Admitted is the keyword for “I claim this without proof,” and it appears
nowhere in the active tree. A Hypothesis inside a Section is a named premise that
becomes an argument of every theorem that uses it when the Section closes; “closed
under the global context” doesn’t make it go away. Print Assumptions lists the global
axioms a theorem depends on; on the kernel tier it shows only standard-library ones.
A total function always returns a value, and Coq requires every function to be total;
the small machine’s step function is, traps included. “Parametric in K” means the
proof works for any K; the small machine’s table size, sixteen, is a literal constant, and
the proofs are about that literal.

A.4 Category theory beyond Part I
Section 2 sketches objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, and the iden-
tity laws. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one category to
another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting composition
and identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds of structure. An
embedding is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is the precise version
for arrows: two distinct arrows never land on one. Conservative is the version for
inverses: if the image of an arrow has an inverse, the arrow already had one, so the
functor can’t manufacture an isomorphism (an arrow with an inverse) that wasn’t


                                           399
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


there. The two properties are different, and neither gives the other. Read the natural
numbers under addition as a category with one object and an arrow for each number,
and the same for the integers. The inclusion of the first into the second is faithful, since
distinct naturals stay distinct integers. It isn’t conservative: 1 has no inverse among
the naturals, and its image has one, minus 1. The other way round, the functor from
the integers onto the trivial one-arrow group is conservative, since every arrow of the
integers already has an inverse. It isn’t faithful: it sends every integer to the same
arrow. An embedding needs faithfulness specifically. A monoidal product combines
two objects or two arrows into one, with a unit and laws that make the combining
behave. An initial object has exactly one arrow into every object; the counter’s unique-
ness in this book is a uniqueness-on-reachable-states fact, and no category-theoretic
initial object is involved. Yoneda’s lemma is where the categorical engine first clicked
for me, the night I quit borrowing other people’s runtimes (Section 1), and nothing in
the formal development uses it.

A.5 Bell-test vocabulary
A correlation between two outcomes is the average of their product; with outcomes
plus or minus one it lies between minus one and one, plus one meaning always match,
minus one always differ. A correlator is one such average in a labelled setting, E00 for
Alice’s setting 0 and Bob’s 0. The marginal of a joint distribution is the distribution of
one side alone with the other averaged out; zero-marginal means each side’s outcome
is plus or minus one equally often on average. A local hidden-variable model is one
where both outcomes are fixed by a shared random variable agreed before the game
plus each side’s own setting; Bell’s theorem says no such model produces certain
correlations quantum mechanics does. No-signalling means neither side’s marginal
depends on the other’s setting. Quantum-realisable means compatible with some
quantum state and measurements; the NPA hierarchy gives a ladder of necessary tests,
each a positive-semidefiniteness condition on a moment matrix, and no single rung is
known to be sufficient in general (Chaturvedi’s 2026 preprint argues none is, even for
this game). The PR box is the no-signalling correlation that wins the game every time,
stronger than quantum mechanics allows. Cauchy-Schwarz is the inequality that a
dot product is bounded by the product of the lengths. The Tsirelson bound is two root
two, the largest game score quantum mechanics allows; the classical bound is two and
the PR bound is four. (If you go looking for Boris Tsirelson’s 1980 paper, look under
Cirel’son, the spelling the journal printed, or you may not find it.) The elliptope is the
set of correlators that can be filled out into a positive-semidefinite matrix.

A.6 Other terms I use without rebuilding
Provenance is the recorded chain of where an object came from; on the small ma-
chine, a commitment’s provenance is the passing check that came before it (Section 16).
Simulation, in computer science, is one system imitating another’s input-output be-
haviour; a Turing machine simulates any system of the model whose step a program
can compute, my machine included, by writing the whole state out on its tape, and


                                            400
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


the difference this book is about is what a window on that tape shows. That’s real,
and it raises a fair question: if a tape can stand in for the state, what was the differ-
ence? The tape carries a picture of the state, the way a photograph carries a fire, and a
photograph of a fire keeps you exactly as warm as any other photograph. The counter
and the toll live in the step rule. An encoding copies the bytes, and the step rule isn’t
in them. A Turing machine built with the toll in its own transition table is a different
case: it’s an instance of the model, and it simulates nothing. What no machine can do
is make a simulated rule binding just by writing it down on tape.

Projection is a function that drops information on purpose. The window on the small
machine keeps three things, the line number and the two counters, which are what
Minsky’s machine already has, and that’s why projecting lands you back in ordinary
computation. It drops everything else, including the parts doing the new work: the
versions, the table of checked facts, the channel, the ledger and the flag. Nothing is
wrong with it. It’s a perfectly good function. It just costs you what made the state more
than a pair of counters. A quotient is the operation of declaring two things the same
when they agree on what you chose to look at and working with the classes instead.
A projection does exactly that. Dropping fields one at a time also glues together states
that the dropped fields kept apart. The fibre of a function over a value is everything
the function sends to that value. An injection sends no two inputs to the same output;
a surjection covers every output. Decidable means an algorithm always halts with a
yes-or-no answer; keep the claim and the algorithm apart, since the algorithm decides
the claim only once there’s a proof that its answer matches. Polynomial time means
running time bounded by a power of the input size; P is the problems solvable that
way, NP the problems where a candidate solution can be checked that way, and whether
the two are the same is open.

“Kernel” wears three hats in this book, so here they are before one of them ambushes
you. First, mathematics: the kernel of a map is what it sends to the identity, and for a
projection the useful version is the relation “these two states project to the same thing.”
Second, the proofs, where the hat comes in two sizes: the kernel tier, the part of the Coq
development where the model is written down and its main theorems live (Section 22),
with the link files that tie the small machine to them; and Coq’s own kernel, the small
checker that accepts or rejects every proof. Third, the operating-system kernel, which
I never use and mention only so you know it isn’t meant. The sentence around the
word always says which one is.

A.7 Matrices
A matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD) when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every vector v; the game
check is all about one matrix being PSD. The determinant of a square matrix is a single
number that is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat. For a two-
by-two matrix with rows ( a, b) and (c, d) it’s ad − bc. For a bigger one, expand along
a row: for each entry, delete its row and column, take the determinant of what’s left,
multiply by the entry, alternate the signs, and add up; the recursion bottoms out at

                                           401
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


two by two. A principal submatrix is what you get by choosing some of the indices
and keeping only those rows and the same columns; its determinant is a principal
minor. A symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when every principal minor is at least zero,
every one of them, and the game check uses the three-by-three ones (Appendix F.4).
The Schur complement turns a question about a block matrix into a question about
a smaller one. For a symmetric block matrix with corner block P, off-diagonal block
Q and other corner R, it’s R − QT P−1 Q, and when P is positive definite the whole
matrix is PSD exactly when that complement is (Lemma F.8). Positive definite matters;
invertible isn’t enough. Take P = −1 and every other entry zero: the complement is
zero, which is PSD, and the whole matrix isn’t.

A.8 Borrowed ideas the book pushes on
These get their full story in the chapter that uses them; here’s the one-line version for
when you’ve forgotten which one Landauer was.

The pigeonhole principle: put more pigeons than holes and some hole holds two. Sec-
tion 4’s room with too few chairs is that, and so is the proof that a permanent flag can
only be raised by a step that forgets something. Landauer’s principle (Rolf Landauer,
1961): a step that wipes information, lowering the entropy of what a machine holds
by some number of bits, gives off at least Boltzmann’s constant times the temperature
times the natural log of two in heat per bit. In this book it’s always a premise with
its name on it. Nothing here derives it (Section 4, Section 21). Entropy, in Claude
Shannon’s sense: for a spread of chances over states, roughly the average number
of yes-or-no questions you’d need to pin the state down, so an even spread over n
states has log2 n bits. A spread, in this book, is just a list of chances that add up to
one. Maxwell’s demon (Section 5): a little creature that watches molecules and sorts
fast from slow, seemingly for free; Charles Bennett’s answer was that the measuring
can be free and the wiping of the demon’s notes is what costs. The potential method
(Robert Tarjan, 1985): pay for a run with a quantity stored in the state, so a step’s bill
plus the change in the stored quantity is what you count; Section 6 reads the toll as
that method with one particular potential.

The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936, who essentially proved it without stating
it in this form; Stephen Kleene stated it in 1952, and Martin Davis seems to have
been the first to name it, in 1958, Section 13): no program decides, for every program
and input, whether it stops. Kleene’s recursion theorem (Stephen Kleene, 1938): for
any transformation of programs that can itself be computed, some program behaves
exactly like its own transform. Rice’s theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that
depends only on what a program does, and isn’t true of all programs or of none,
can’t be decided by a program. The diagonal is the move under all three: build
the thing that does the opposite of what the table says about it (Section 13). L is a
small lambda calculus, a language made of nothing but functions applied to functions,
which Yannick Forster and Gert Smolka built in Coq and which Section 13 uses as a
tool. A hash is a short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so that finding two

                                           402
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


inputs with the same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash chain folds each new
record into the fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds them pairwise into one
root (Section 3, Section 14).

A.9 Words this book builds
These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is
built properly in the chapter named; this is only a reminder.

A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly one
meaning. The model (or the abstract model) is a kind of state and a rule for stepping,
plus exactly the extra pieces a given theorem asks for: a certification reading and the
toll, or a counter and a price list, or a window, or programs written as states and a
recursion theorem. The name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I to III
live there, and every claim in them is about any system with the pieces it names. A
substrate is the model’s shape with whatever extension a theorem names, and nothing
else; the word never means my machine, and never the side of a simulation that does
the stepping (Let me be straight with you). My machine (also the machine I build,
the build, the small machine, the smallest honest machine, Section 16) is the concrete
machine of Part IV that fills in those pieces at once: two counters with their versions,
a table of checked facts, a channel, a trap, a ledger and a flag, six instruction kinds
and their prices, with its hosts and universal programs. The scaffolding is that machine
and everything built on it, and Part IV lives there. A Thiele machine, lower case, is any
system proved to be an instance of the certification system (Definition 3.1), five parts
and the toll; the paper toys are, and so is the small machine. Weakly Thiele-complete
means a Thiele machine whose base is Turing-universal; that bar is nearly empty, since
a clock that charges one for every move pays the toll for any record. Thiele-complete
means more (Definition 16.7): a universal base whose moves are free and can’t touch
the record, a record that stays up once it’s up and is raised from a clean state only after
a passing check, a commitment to the same claim and a certificate, one mark for each
of those three acts, and a claim whose check, commit and certificate raise the record
on some loaded starts and leave it down on others. Every clock-style machine fails
it; the small machine meets it; and every machine that meets it hides its record and
ledger from its own window. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed program that
runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s record earned again and
its toll paid by the host’s own steps. The ones in this book are U (Section 16.13), a fixed
program in the small machine’s instruction kinds, with no guest step built in, that
runs every small-machine program with halting and flag exact and its ledger equal to
the guest’s at every matching point, and UP (Section 16.14), the same program with
one paid move added, that runs every computably presented Thiele machine, one whose
driver, step, prices and reading are computed by programs with the reading decided
on every state, keeping its reading as a latch and, when the reading starts at no, its
prices to within two, a surcharge no program on that host, run from a clean start, can
avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three. The simpler host


                                           403
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


with a built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror of the guest’s
flag. A computer running the small machine isn’t a Thiele machine; it implements one,
inside bounds, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine. When a word below
belongs to only one of the two layers, the entry says which.

A partition is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing left
over (Section 2). A certification system is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per move,
and a yes-or-no reading, plus one rule, the toll: a move that turns the reading from no
to yes costs at least one (Section 3). The files call that rule A2 in the numbering their
certification records use (Appendix B). A move merges when two different starting
states land on the same end; one that never does is injective, it forgets nothing. A
reading is permanent when no move turns it from yes back to no (Section 4).

The counter, which I also call the ledger: in the model, a number carried in the state
that starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step’s charge (Section 6).
My machine has exactly one, the ledger µ (Section 16). Two other things get called
counters, and each chapter says which: Minsky’s two bins on the small machine, and
the eight counts that tally the game’s rounds (Section 20). Neither is the ledger. A price
list says what each move costs; the model takes it as given, and my machine’s table of
what each instruction costs is in Section 16. A receipt is a total that lives in the state,
only climbs, equals the sum of the charges on every path including the failures, and is
the only such total for its price list (Section 6 proves it for any system with a counter
and a price list, nec_f_conservation, nec_f_counter_monotone and nec_f_
initiality; on my machine the sum is a checked theorem too, Section 16). In the
model there is just a certification reading, yes or no (Section 3); on the small machine
it’s the flag, set by a CERTIFY that passes and never cleared.

These belong to the small machine only (Section 16). A two-counter machine is Minsky’s:
two counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and two instructions: add
one, and subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero, or else go on to the next
line; already enough that nobody can decide in general whether one halts. The small
machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and three instructions for the record,
six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. A counter’s version is
its edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by one every time the counter is written,
so an edition never comes back. A fact is a property, a counter and a version together,
such as “A is even, as of edition 3”; the properties come from a fixed language of three,
is zero, is even and is at least n. The same theorems also hold for any property language
with an exact equality test whose checker is proved to mean what it says, and one
such language reads a counter as a list and asks whether it’s sorted (sorted_run_c
ertifies_iff and sorted_run_refused_forever, EarnedGeneric.v). The fact
table holds up to sixteen facts, and the only way in is a CHECK that passed; nothing
ever leaves it. The small machine’s channel holds one committed fact or nothing, and
COMMIT puts a fact there only if the table has it about the counter’s current edition.
With the flag up from a clean start it names a commitment earned that way, and a later


                                           404
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


COMMIT replaces it, as a two-commit run shows (certified_channel_earned
and channel_names_last_commit, EarnedCore.v). The trap is a bit that goes up
when an instruction refuses, and then nothing in the core moves again. A commitment
is earned when a passing check put its fact in the table first, about the same edition,
with no write to that counter in between; on the small machine every flag raised from
a clean start is earned, and that’s a theorem. CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost
one each and everything else costs nothing, so from a clean start a run ending with the
flag up adds at least three to the ledger, and a run whose check could have failed adds
exactly three: CHECK is zero on A, COMMIT, CERTIFY, from a start where A is 0. The
step doesn’t police trivial checks; is at least 0 passes every value and certifies for three
too. The host machine is the small machine with a counter, called a register, for every
whole number, and one property, Slot, true of a number that packs a property of the
small machine together with a value it holds of. A slot is a register of the host used for
nothing but holding one checked fact about the guest, and its mirror is a register beside
it, safe to read, that says which claim the slot holds while its fact is live. U is the fixed
program of 3728 host instructions that runs every small-machine program; it reads
guest instructions out of one register, keeps the guest’s counters in two others, and
puts every checked fact in a slot, because on this machine reading a counter writes it.
The universal program’s guest is a program of the small machine, held as one number
in a register of the host and run one instruction at a time by U’s fetch and decode. UP
is U with one more handler, for PAY, an instruction that costs one and does nothing
else; its guests are programs compiled from computably presented Thiele machines
(Section 16.14).

A window is any function that shows you part of a state (Section 7); a shadow, said
loosely, is what a window leaves you with. A collision is two steps that look the same
through a window, before and after, where one raises the flag and the other doesn’t
(Section 7). Entitlement is what a run has when it carries an object, a checked relation
between that object and a claim, and a paid event that put the object in place: a license
to lean on the claim. It doesn’t prove the claim true (Section 8). A latch is a record
that switches on the first time some event holds and never switches off (Section 10).
The diagonal’s substrate (Section 13) is the model’s shape extended with programs, a
run that may give nothing back, a counter that never falls, a way to write programs
as states, the transformations the substrate counts as its own, and its own recursion
theorem for those; the proof of the diagonal uses neither the counter nor the toll.

B Every assumption in one place
This book leans on a small number of rules that nothing proves, plus a handful of
record types that carry rules as fields. I’ve named each one where it’s used. Here they
are side by side, because a reader who wants to break this book should be able to see
every place where it says “suppose,” in one list, with what each “suppose” buys.

One thing to undo first, and it’s my fault. The checked work numbers the rules its


                                            405
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


records carry with bare labels, A2, A3 and so on, as if they were axioms. The book
uses “the toll” for the rule that matters and avoids the bare labels; this appendix maps
the labels for anyone reading the files.

B.1 The records that carry a rule
Definition B.1 (Certification system). The record CertificationSystem (Univer-
salCertificationCost.v) has five data fields, a state type, a move type, a step function, a
cost per move in N, and a yes/no reading, and one proof field, cs_cert_costs: a
move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. This proof field is the
toll of Section 3, and in this record’s numbering it is called A2. Every result stated “for
any certification system” assumes it, because the record cannot be built without it.


Definition B.2 (Quantitative certification system). The record QuantitativeCerti
ficationSystem (QuantitativeNoFI.v) extends a certification system with a witness,
a function W from states to N, and a threshold N ∈ N, and adds two proof fields: (A3,
qcs_cost_bounds_witness) W (s) + cost(i ) ≥ W (step(s, i )), the witness grows by
at most what the move cost; and (A5, qcs_cert_threshold_witness) a state that
reads yes has W (s) ≥ N. An optional extension, QuantitativeCertificationSy
stem_full, adds (A4, qcsf_witness_nondecreasing) W (s) ≤ W (step(s, i )).


Theorem B.1 (The floor raised to a threshold). In a quantitative certification system, every
run from a state with witness 0 (this starting condition is called A6) to a state that reads yes
has total cost at least N.

Proof. Adding A3 along the run telescopes: the witness at the end is at most the
witness at the start plus the total cost, so at most the total cost. A5 says the end witness
is at least N. Neither A4 nor the toll is used.

Checked as universal_nfi_quantitative (QuantitativeNoFI.v). A3 and A4
bound opposite directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1, cost 0, witness
0 satisfies A3 and breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does the reverse. The
record is a general shape. The small machine’s own floor of three is proved directly
(Theorem 16.16) and never goes through it.
