Three remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise holds by construction for
the nat family and by proof for L (Section 13) and for the programs of the small
machine’s host (Section 16.18). Second, the class Substrate (Substrate.v) carries a
different rule from the toll, mu_monotone: the counter never goes down on a step.
Neither implies the other, and the diagonal uses neither. Third, merge pricing is
Landauer’s principle taken in its worst case over what the machine might be holding:
it charges every merging move, while the principle in its general form charges only for
uncertainty actually removed, when the step can be driven by a protocol timed from
outside it (Theorem 4.12). Under time-symmetric control, Riechers, Boyd, Wimsatt
and Crutchfield (2020) argue, even a known state pays for a move that doesn’t undo
itself.

B.3 The axioms of the checker itself
Beyond the premises above, the checked proofs rest on Coq’s own foundation and
on a handful of standard-library axioms, which the assumption audit lists theorem
by theorem: functional extensionality on dependent functions; two decidability prin-
ciples for the real numbers (used wherever real analysis is, for example in the game
check of Section 20); and the law of excluded middle, in some theorems. No axiom or
parameter of the project’s own appears in the audited theorems. Section 22 says what
that does and doesn’t mean.

C What’s mine, and what isn’t
Every chapter of this book leans on somebody, and I’ve named them where I lean.
This appendix does a different job, and it’s the one where I’d most like to be caught
out, and caught out early. For each thing the book could be accused of claiming as its
own, it says what was already known, what this work actually defines, builds, proves,
or connects, and what kind of contribution that is. Six kinds, and they aren’t the
same claim: a new result (a statement nobody had); a new proof of something known;
a mechanization (a known result checked by a machine, here Coq); an implementation
(something built that runs); a synthesis (known pieces put together under one question);
and a conjecture. Every kind can be worth doing. None of them is the others. And if
you read down the list and notice that “new result” hardly shows up, good. You’re
reading it right.

Two warnings about my own evidence before the list. First, “I didn’t find it” is a fact
about my searches. The literature is bigger than my searches. I searched with every


                                          408
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


tool I had, and some tools will cheerfully invent a citation if you let them, so where it
matters I say where I looked, and you should assume it may well be sitting in a paper
I’d need a few more lifetimes of homework to read. Second, nothing below is inferred
from how many theorems there are, from the audit’s clean bill, or from a good story
about who came before. Those tell you the work was checked. They don’t tell you
it’s new. Thousands of checked theorems could, in principle, be thousands of careful
ways of agreeing with Tarjan.

C.1 The universal floor and the potential method
Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose drop
bounds the cost of a run, is Tarjan’s (1985), and it has been mechanized more than once
(Nipkow in Isabelle/HOL, 2015 and 2019; Charguéraud and Pottier’s time credits in
Coq, 2019), built into type systems for automatic resource analysis (Hoffmann and
coauthors, 2011 onward), and recast in cost-aware type theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin
and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing the potential that is one when a designated reading
says no and zero when it says yes, so that “the crossing costs” (the toll) and “every
run that crosses paid” (the floor) are the potential method’s two halves (Section 6).
Kind: a mechanization of a known technique with a particular choice of potential. The
choice is the point: it makes “was certified” something the account must carry. The
theorem is not new mathematics. If it looks clever, that’s Tarjan’s cleverness; my part
was picking which number to plug in.

Go back to Tarjan’s paper and there’s a sentence that sits right on the line this book
draws. He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at intervals,
as in a sinking fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the banker’s view
the computer is coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits to spend or save;
in the physicist’s view, which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every state has a potential
and you count its changes. Then he stops to say that the credits are only an accounting
device: the programs that actually run contain no mention of credits or debits. That’s
exactly right for what he wanted, a bound proved about a program from outside. It’s
also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in the proof. The one move I chose
was to put them in the step, where no program takes a step without it being counted.
Same arithmetic, different place.

C.2 The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges
Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer’s
principle charges for is Landauer’s (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003; the
words “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths” are from the 2003
abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input distribution are Maroney’s
(2009), Sagawa’s (2014), Wolpert’s; the critique is Earman and Norton’s and Norton’s.
Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest and Shamir, 1982), where
the question is reuse and price never comes up, and Chris Heegard (1985) worked
out the capacity of permanent memory with noise, again a question of how much fits.



                                          409
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


What it costs doesn’t come into it. Statisticians priced permanence on finite memory
in their own currency: in Hellman and Cover’s analysis of hypothesis testing with
finite memory (1970), a machine that settles its answer by falling into states it never
leaves does worse than one that doesn’t, so a decision held for good costs memory
states. Heat never enters their analysis. And the counting under the theorem is older
than any of that, twice over. Theorem 4.1 is the finite, discrete cousin of the recurrence
argument Zermelo, using Poincaré’s theorem of 1890, turned on Boltzmann in 1896,
here aimed at a reading. Zermelo aimed it at entropy, and Bocchieri and Loinger gave
the quantum recurrence in 1957. In automata form it is classical: a finite machine
whose moves are all one-to-one reshuffles recognises only group languages, and the
inputs that raise a permanent reading form a language that is never one of those
unless it is empty (Pin’s 1992 paper on reversible automata is the reference I’d check;
automata theorists treat the step as folklore), and going quantum doesn’t change it
(Brodsky and Pippenger, 2002: quantum finite automata that measure once, at the
end, accept with bounded error exactly the group languages). The closest of all is
recent. Ouldridge and Wolpert (2023) give a proof that if the smallest automaton
for a language has a step that merges states, every automaton for it does, and argue
that recognising it on a device that repeats one local step produces entropy, while a
language whose smallest automaton only reshuffles can be recognised for free; one of
their worked examples is the strings with no b, the complement of the latch’s language.
That’s the core with a physical price already on it. And the logarithm in the heat
floor matches the absolute-irreversibility bound of Murashita, Funo and Ueda (2014),
which Manzano, Kardeş, Roldán and Wolpert (2024) carried over to computation. The
match is a mirror image. It isn’t a special case of their bound: the squeeze is ordinary
Landauer heat, whose logarithm equals their bound for the free expansion that undoes
it, and absolute irreversibility reaches the commit itself only on a fixed-rate device
starting from a known state. Constructor theory states a cousin of the same core for
devices that run in a cycle: Marletto, Vedral and coauthors (2022) and Violaris and
Marletto (2022) built an irreversible task out of the quantum homogeniser and argued
that erasure may cost more than Landauer’s bound. Section 4 tells all of it. Mine: the
price as a named rule on a ledger, a premise that merges cost at least a mark, which
turns “the flip merges” into “the flip costs” on any machine whether or not anybody’s
physics is right, and the toll derived from it (Theorem 4.2); what comes with that
form, namely the characterisation of the moves every merge-pricing schedule must
charge, when move names can be decided equal or different (the merging moves, so
the core again in pricing words), the merge-or-revoke dichotomy for a single move,
the squeeze and entropy forms for a permanent flip, and a built counterexample for
each premise; and the mechanization of all of it (Section 4). Kind: the core is classical,
and somebody else’s: Zermelo’s in physics, folklore in automata theory, with Pin’s
paper as the place to check it. The pricing form isn’t wholly mine either: priced in
entropy, for automata, it’s Ouldridge and Wolpert’s. They derive the price from the
physics. I assume mine. What’s mine is the price as a named rule on a ledger, the
toll derived from it, its single-move and counted forms, the counterexamples, and the

                                           410
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


mechanized proofs, and the physics is a named premise and is Landauer’s. Searches:
the core turned up in the places just named, and its physical price in Ouldridge and
Wolpert; I didn’t find the ledger form or the derived toll stated anywhere I looked,
and nobody’s search covers a whole field, mine least of all; I found no mechanization
of Landauer’s principle in Coq, Isabelle, or Lean.

C.3 Learning free, committing priced
Known: that measurement can be done at no fundamental cost and the cost sits in
erasing the record is Bennett’s resolution of Maxwell’s demon (1982), with the quan-
titative trade-off by Sagawa and Ueda (2009). The closest physics I found to the line
between learning and committing is Ouldridge and ten Wolde’s fundamental costs
of persistent copies (2017; with Govern, 2017), copies that stay correlated with their
originals after the two come apart; theirs is heat for a correlation in chemistry, and
Section 5 says how it differs. The sharp chemical form, that a persistent copy grown
at equilibrium carries no information about its template, is Poulton, ten Wolde and
Ouldridge’s (2019), and that the bill can be split between measuring and erasing in
more than one way is Fahn’s (1996). Mine: the four-state demon and the three-state
ring as checked models, and the two-state impossibility (Section 5). Kind: mechaniza-
tion and illustration of a known physical point inside my ledger. Not a new physical
claim. Bennett did the hard part in 1982; I built a toy with four dots on it and got Coq
to agree with him.

C.4 Windows that can’t price what they hide
Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation’s fibres; that’s ele-
mentary, and the systems version of it is Moore’s distinguishing experiments (1956),
Kalman’s observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract interpreta-
tion (Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000); in control
theory it is diagnosability and opacity of discrete-event systems (Sampath and coau-
thors, 1995; Saboori and Hadjicostis, 2007), where a collision is a hidden event no
observer can diagnose without delay; in economics it is the hard-evidence view of
mechanism design (Green and Laffont, 1986; Bull and Watson, 2007), where what a
mechanism can tell apart is limited by the evidence on offer; and its sharp form for
fingerprints is Naor and Rothblum’s lower bound for checking a stored file (2005); in
distributed systems it is Haeberlen and Kuznetsov’s (2009), that only omission and
commission faults can be detected from outside, and in philosophy it is Easwaran’s
transferability (2009). Mine: stating the pricing version (no window price is exact
across a collision), exhibiting a colliding pair for the small machine’s window, and
the theorem that every Thiele-complete machine has two runs from one clean start
that end looking the same through the window its base shows, one certified and one
not (complete_hides_record; Section 7, Section 16). Kind: mechanization of an
elementary lemma, plus specific facts about the machine and the definition.




                                          411
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


C.5 Structural entitlement and its bound
Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells N cases apart has depth at
least log2 N); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the gap
between justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition of
entitlement as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and the
count that, given lists, a tree and a covering, a run that paid for the tree’s depth pays
at least the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Kind: synthesis; the counting idea
is standard, the assembly and its vocabulary are this work’s, the pricing policy is
assumed (nothing derives it), and the count is mechanized: in its bill form over any
certification system, and for the record moves of every Thiele-complete machine on
a run from a clean start, with the earned chain in the run, a floor that takes the run’s
own checks in place of a tree, and a counterexample showing the covering can’t be
dropped (Section 16.17).

C.6 The record axis is a latch
Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, 1918), sticky
bits (Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated data types (Shapiro and coauthors),
history variables and stuttering in refinement (Abadi and Lamport, 1991), append-
only authenticated sets for transparency logs, which fit revocation as a once-only
event (Tomescu and coauthors, 2019), and, in program logic, monotonic state, where a
property witnessed once on state that only moves forward can be recalled at any later
point, with a soundness proof and a working home in F⋆ (Ahman, Fournet, Hriţcu,
Maillard, Rastogi and Swamy, 2018): the type-theory name for a record that stays up.
Past the finite case, inductive and quasi-inductive definitions (Richter and Aczel, 1974;
Burgess, 1986) and the flag trick of infinite time Turing machines (Hamkins and Lewis,
2000) are the transfinite versions of a record that only grows and a toggle, and Danos
and Krivine’s (2005) reversible calculus needs an action declared irreversible in order
to commit. Mine: the exact statement that a record driven by the computation that
never switches off is, over any base, a latch on one event, with its converse and a
counterexample for each of the two conditions, and the argument that honest records
agree up to the price list while the stronger uniqueness fails (Section 10). Kind: a small
structural lemma, I think not stated before in this form (I found no prior statement in
the searches I ran), built from old notions; the latch form is mechanized, and so is the
agreement up to the price list (nec_w_billed_same_up_to_schedule).

C.7 The diagonal and L
Known: Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem; Lawvere’s fixed-point form
(1969) and Yanofsky’s retelling (2003); mechanized recursion theorems and Rice (Nor-
rish in HOL4, 2011; Carneiro in Lean; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors in Coq,
including L itself, 2017, and the Coq Library of Undecidability). Mine: the diago-
nal stated once over any substrate that supplies a recursion theorem; and Rice and
halting proved again for L from its reduction rules (Section 13); and the same two


                                           412
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


theorems built for the small machine’s host, with Rice’s on every input of the two-
counter machine and Kleene’s with inputs written as powers of two, and Kleene’s
refuted for plain inputs (Section 16.18). Kind: checked instances of known theorems
of computability. They hold for any model with universality and s-m-n, and the work
is in building those for this machine.

C.8 The game check
Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson
bound is Tsirelson’s (1980) and Stephanie Wehner’s semidefinite proof (2006), from
a paper on Tsirelson bounds for generalized CHSH inequalities; the moment-matrix
hierarchy, the Schur-complement analysis of this very level-one matrix and the level
1 + AB are Navascués, Pironio and Acín’s (2007, 2008); that every point with a PSD
completion is the correlator table of a quantum strategy, built from anticommuting
observables in a maximally entangled state, is Tsirelson’s too (1980); the arcsine charac-
terization is Landau’s (1988) and Masanes’s (2003); and Tsirelson’s bound has already
been checked by machine, in Isabelle/HOL (Echenim and Mhalla, 2023) and in Lean’s
mathlib. Rational sum-of-squares certificates are Helfried Peyrl and Pablo A. Parrilo’s
(2008), from a paper on computing sum-of-squares decompositions with rational co-
efficients. Mine: a decision procedure in integer arithmetic on outcome counts; a
checked chain from “the counts pass” to “the pinned level-one matrix is positive semi-
definite” to “S2 ≤ 8”; checked proofs of the representation in finite dimension, real
or complex, on two eight-level systems, and of the arcsine characterization; proofs
of the contraction equivalence by explicit test vectors; and the level-1 + AB cascade
and an elliptope gate in whole numbers, with a soundness proof (Section 20 and its
derivation appendix). Kind: mechanization, with a new proof of a known equivalence
in one slice. I found no prior formalization taking counts as input, and that’s a report
on where I looked, and the literature is bigger than where I looked. The same check
earned on the small machine’s host, a raised flag standing on it, is built and checked;
the idea isn’t new (Section 20).

C.9 Five record disciplines, one question
Known: each system and its guarantee belongs to its designers: Casper (Buterin and
Griffith, 2017), Ethereum’s storage gas and refunds (EIP-2200, EIP-3529), extend-only
TPM registers, Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162), proof-carrying code. Mine: asking
all five whether the write is priced, with a small checked fragment of each (Section 14).
Kind: synthesis and an organizing reading; the fragments are not verifications of those
systems.

C.10 The pointer conjecture
Known: Zurek’s quantum Darwinism (2009), with Ollivier, Poulin and Zurek (2004)
and Blume-Kohout and Zurek (2006): preferred states are the ones whose records
proliferate redundantly in the environment. Mine: borrowing that shape for the
question of which event deserves a record, with definitions, a toy, and refutations of


                                           413
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


two stronger forms (Section 15). Kind: conjecture. No claim about quantum physics.

C.11 The counter as a receipt
Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing’s 1949 note
on checking a large routine, Floyd’s ranking functions (1967), Lamport’s clocks (1978).
Carrying a run’s cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner, Licata and Ramyaa
(2015) and of Danner and Licata (2022), and the graded effect semantics of Katsumata
(2014), with a working-language version in Orchard, Liepelt and Eades (2019). The
receipt side of time credits is Mével, Jourdan and Pottier’s (2019): in their Coq-checked
extension of the Iris logic every step uses up a credit and produces a receipt, receipts
prove lower bounds, and enough of them prove that a counter can’t overflow in any
feasible time, which is the closest published neighbour of a total that only climbs.
Mine: putting three properties side by side (the total only climbs, it equals the sum
of the charges on every path including the failures, and it is the only such total for
a given price list), the argument for any system with a counter and a price list, and
the checked sum on the small machine (Section 6, Section 16). Kind: synthesis; the
abstract statements are checked over any counter machine (nec_f_conservation,
nec_f_counter_monotone and nec_f_initiality), and on the small machine
the sum is too. Against the graded frameworks the answer is split: the counter is their
writer exactly (run_writer_is_run_and_cost), and their type systems, bounding
relations and before-the-run checking of grades are not embedded, because the grade
here is written by the step during the run (Section 6). On loop-free programs the
counter agrees with a fixed grade exactly, and where a run’s cost depends on its data
it holds the exact number that a fixed grade can only bound; that’s argued in Section 6,
with no checked theorem behind it, and cost-aware type theories such as calf get
exactness back with grades that depend on the inputs.

C.12 The small machine
Known: two-counter machines are Minsky’s (1961, 1967), and the undecidability
of their halting is checked in the Coq Library of Undecidability (Forster, Larchey-
Wendling and coauthors, 2019, 2020). The guarantee about every program is older
than any of this, and it isn’t mine either. It’s the reference monitor (Anderson, 1972): a
check that sits in the path of every operation, so no program gets around it. Schneider
(2000) worked out what a monitor that watches a run can enforce: only safety proper-
ties, the kind a bad run breaks at some finite moment, and “no CERTIFY without an
earlier earned COMMIT” is one of those. Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors (2015)
verified, in Coq, monitors that check tags at every instruction. The shape of “earned,”
a certificate nothing can make except through the rules, is Milner’s LCF, where a theo-
rem is a value only the logic’s rules can build (Gordon, Milner and Wadsworth, 1979;
Gordon, 2000); the small machine is that architecture at the level of single instructions.
“No certify without an earlier commit” is also a correspondence assertion in the sense
of Woo and Lam (1993), which Gordon and Jeffrey (2003) check with a type system,
and a store of commitments that the rules of a dialogue keep, each speaker’s updated


                                           414
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


by the rules as the moves are made, is Hamblin’s (1970, chapter 8, on formal dialectic);
the difference from all three is again that here the step enforces it. A check that blesses
a value and a write that takes the blessing away is close kin to dynamic taint tracking,
whose labels go back to Denning’s lattice model of information flow (1976), with the
blessing itself, controlled endorsement, given a type system and a security theorem
by Cecchetti, Myers and Arden (2017), and what a monitor can enforce with bounded
memory is Talhi, Tawbi and Debbabi’s question (2008). A small monotone record
inside each replica of a replicated service is A2M (Chun and coauthors, 2007), TrInc
(Levin and coauthors, 2009), MinBFT (Veronese and coauthors, 2013) and Damysus
(Decouchant and coauthors, 2022), and Clement, Junqueira, Kate and Rodrigues (2012)
worked out, with proofs, what such a record buys and what it doesn’t. The signature
route to the same goal, which needs no trusted step, is IA-CCF (Shamis and coauthors,
2021): replicas sign and log their protocol messages in the ledger, so blame lands on
individual members however many of them misbehave. And “check once, issue a ca-
pability the system trusts, rely on it later” is built and deployed in Garg and Pfenning’s
proof-carrying file system (2010), whose logic lets a policy’s consequences change with
time and state, and in Sirer and coauthors’ logical attestation for the Nexus operating
system (2011), unforgeable statements about programs used as credentials; those are
the closest systems I’ve found to check, commit, certify. Mine: a machine of six instruc-
tion kinds on two counters, with a version for each counter, a bounded fact table and a
channel; its theorems that, from a clean start, a committed fact was checked first about
the same edition, that nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted, that with the flag up
from a clean start the channel names a fact an earlier passing COMMIT committed,
and a later commit can replace it, as a two-commit run shows (certified_channel
_earned and channel_names_last_commit, EarnedCore.v), and that a run from
a clean start to a raised flag adds at least three to the ledger, with three reached by a
run whose check could have failed (the step doesn’t police trivial checks, so one that
can’t fail costs three too); the same theorems for any property language with an exact
equality test whose checker is proved to mean what it says, a sorted list read out of a
counter included (sorted_run_certifies_iff and sorted_run_refused_fo
rever, EarnedGeneric.v); and the step-for-step match with the library’s machine, so
halting is undecidable for it (Section 16). Kind: an instance of monitor enforcement,
implemented and mechanized, with two things on top that I didn’t find put together
where I looked: the check is bound to the edition of the thing it checked, and a toll is
paid for the commitment. The universality and the undecidability are borrowed, and
the other properties are short consequences of the step rule. Whether the design is
new I can’t say, and I make no claim beyond the proofs.

C.13 The universal host
Known: Turing’s universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data,
and the universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Keeping a guest
and the code running beside it out of each other’s state is what a virtual machine
monitor promises (Popek and Goldberg, 1974). Compiling computable functions into


                                           415
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


counter machines is checked in the Coq Library of Undecidability. Mine: one fixed
program, U, written in the small machine’s own six kinds of instruction on a host
with a register for every whole number, with no guest step built in, that runs every
program of the small machine from every clean start start( x, y), halts exactly when
its guest does, raises its own flag by its own check, commit and certificate if and only
if the guest’s rises somewhere in its run, and keeps a ledger equal to the guest’s at
every matching point; its host machine is Thiele-complete, and whether U halts on a
loaded guest is undecidable (Section 16.13). Two small facts force its shape, and they’re
stated there: reading a counter on this machine writes it, and a finite program can’t
keep the guest’s facts on a copy of the guest’s counter, by the pigeonhole. Beside it, a
simpler host with a built-in guest step runs guests by construction and keeps a mirror
of the guest’s flag, with the mirror, isolation and earned-chain theorems. An ordinary
programmable computer, as built, doesn’t do this for the programs it runs, because
the code beside a program shares its memory and can flip anything; U is a fixed
interpreter that does. Kind: implementation and mechanization of a design whose
shape is Turing’s universal machine, with the record and the toll carried through. The
universality is borrowed from the small machine and from Minsky. And the same
program with one paid move added, UP , runs every computably presented Thiele
machine, with its halting matched, its reading carried as a latch on the host’s own
earned flag whose claim is that reading, and its prices to within a surcharge of at most
two when the reading starts at no, which no program on the host, run from a clean start,
can avoid when the guest certifies with its whole ledger below three (Section 16.14);
the compiler that carries the guest onto two counters is the library’s. Kind for that
part: implementation and mechanization again. That a universal machine runs any
computable machine is Turing’s; what’s carried through here is the record, earned
again, and the prices, exact up to the surcharge, and I didn’t find that put together
where I looked.

C.14 Thiele-complete, defined so a clock fails
Known: Turing completeness, and the observation every theorist makes in four sec-
onds, that a toll alone is cheap: a machine that charges for every step pays any toll.
Enforcement mechanisms have been compared and sorted before, and they aren’t
one notion seen several ways: James Morris (1973) separated access limitation from
authentication in programming languages, and Kevin Hamlen, Greg Morrisett and
Fred Schneider (2006) classified which policies execution monitors, program rewriters
and static analysis can each enforce, and they differ; Wai Wong (1995), on a neighbour-
ing track, recorded and checked HOL proofs so a theorem could carry its derivation.
Mine: a definition of Thiele-complete with four clauses (a free universal base that can’t
touch the record and a record that stays up once it’s up, an earned record, an exact
toll on the three record acts, and some claim whose check can fail), the proofs that
every clock-style machine and a paid latch and a silent machine fail it while the small
machine, the same machine over any property language with an exact equality test, a
proved checker and a property that holds of one number and fails of another, and the


                                          416
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


universal program’s host meet it, and the theorem that every machine meeting it hides
its record and ledger from its own window (Section 16). Kind: a definition with short
consequences. The window theorem is the fibre fact of item 4 plus one observation,
that a universal base prints any window for free. I’m not claiming the definition is
the only reasonable one, or that LCF kernels, reference monitors and proof-carrying
code are all Thiele-complete machines in disguise; Hamlen, Morrisett and Schneider’s
sorting says such mechanisms genuinely differ, and the book doesn’t have a theorem
showing the definition holds up across such differences.

C.15 What that adds up to
Read straight down the list. The mathematics underneath this book is mostly known,
and some of it is very old. What’s mine is the question (should an account of computa-
tion carry what was certified and what certifying cost, as part of how it steps), and the
answer isn’t one result. It’s four, and I name them the same way wherever they come
up. The toll derived from finiteness, permanence and a price on merges (item 2; the
counting is classical, the finite cousin of Zermelo’s recurrence objection and folklore
about permutation automata, and Ouldridge and Wolpert already priced it in entropy
for automata, so what’s mine is the price as a rule on a ledger and the toll it gives, and
the price is Landauer’s, as a premise). The pricing form of the window fact (item 4;
the fact itself is elementary). The latch form of a record that never comes down (item 6;
latches and history variables are old). And a record that’s priced, and on the small ma-
chine earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move (items 12, 13 and 14;
the move is Anderson’s, Schneider’s and the micro-policy authors’, and what’s added
is the check bound to its edition, the toll on top, a definition of Thiele-complete that a
clock fails, and universal programs that carry both to every small-machine program
and to every computably presented Thiele machine, earning their own flag). The first
is a ledger form of a core that’s classical and already priced in physics; the second and
third are small exact statements I didn’t find stated where I looked; the fourth is built
and checked, and its idea isn’t new. Under all four sits a large body of mechanized
proof that ties those statements to one small machine and the programs that run on
it. Around it is my best attempt at saying which is which, which you should check as
hard as anything else in here. Item 2’s core, the finite cousin of Zermelo’s recurrence
objection, was folklore among automata theorists, with Pin’s paper as the place to
check it, long before I found it, and its price in physics was Ouldridge and Wolpert’s.
If someone shows me its ledger form, the pricing form in item 4, or item 6 stated
earlier, I’ll move it up the list and be glad to, and a little embarrassed, in that order.

D Every result and where it is checked
Every numbered result in this book is in the table below, in the order it appears, with
the Coq names that carry it, the file each lives in, and what the last full assumption
audit printed for it. Four groups of rows are placed out of that order, beside the rows
they belong with: Definition 16.11 and Theorems 16.37 and 16.38 beside the eight-
state machine of Section 4, the rows from Theorem 16.39 to Theorem 16.44 beside

                                           417
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Theorem 8.3, Theorem 16.29 and the two rows after it below the host’s rows, and
Remark 20.1 below the small machine’s five tallies. “none” means the theorem is
closed: its proof uses nothing beyond Coq’s own rules. The other entries name the
standard-library assumptions it uses: FE is functional extensionality on dependent
functions, RD is one or both of the two decidability principles that come with the real
numbers, and EM is excluded middle. “def” marks a definition, which has nothing
to assume. The audit covers every file the project builds, the small machine’s files
under minimal/ and the kernel tree under coq/kernel alike; only MuCore.v and
Napkin.v, which are built and checked on their own, sit outside it. The small machine’s
files, the universal program’s files and the priced host’s files also end by printing the
assumptions of their own headline theorems, and every one of those lines says closed.
“+N” after a file means N other files under coq/ and minimal/ define or declare a
name spelled the same way, section variables and hypotheses included (notations,
module aliases and record fields aren’t counted); the row gives the file this result uses.
A premise is assumed and never proved, so its row gives at most the Coq definition
that states it, marked “def”. A conjecture has no Coq name, because the book states it
and doesn’t claim it. The section that states each one says so.

This table is an index of companion formalizations. The statements, hypotheses and
arguments are in the numbered sections it points to. An audit status reports the
recorded check; running a later version does not change a claim in this book. Each row
has one of three relations to its Coq names. Most are equivalent: one Coq statement, or
one per numbered part, says what the numbered statement says. A few are assembled:
the numbered statement follows from the listed Coq results by a step done in the text,
and the row says so, as Corollary 20.3’s does with “the composition of.” No row is
meant to say more than its Coq names, and where the prose does, the prose is wrong.
A name and its file fix the constant, the revision is the one in Section 22, and Section E
prints twenty-one of the statements with their premises and that comparison made.
