E The exact words of twenty-one results
This book states its theorems in its own words, and Section 22 says why that’s a risk:
the checker confirms a proof matches its statement. Whether my sentence matches the
statement is a question the checker never asks. So here are the statements themselves
for twenty-one of the results the argument leans on hardest. Each is copied from its
file with the comments taken out and a few long lines broken to fit the page, which
Coq doesn’t notice, and nothing else changed, and each comes with its file, a plain
reading, and a line on whether the book’s printed version says exactly that, more, or
less. You don’t need to read Coq to use this. Put the printed theorem next to the block
and check that every premise in the block turns up in the sentence. That’s the whole
test. These are the statements this book was checked against; if a file differs later, the
book means the one printed here.

E.1 The universal floor
universal_nfi_any_substrate, coq/kernel/nfi/UniversalCertificationCost.v,
with the record it quantifies over.

Record CertificationSystem := mk_cert_system {
   cs_state : Type;
   cs_instr : Type;
   cs_step : cs_state -> cs_instr -> cs_state;
   cs_cost : cs_instr -> nat;
   cs_cert : cs_state -> bool;
   cs_cert_costs :
     forall (s : cs_state) (i : cs_instr),
       cs_cert s = false ->
       cs_cert (cs_step s i) = true ->
       cs_cost i >= 1;
}.

Theorem universal_nfi_any_substrate :
  forall (CS : CertificationSystem)
         (trace : list (cs_instr CS))
         (s0 : cs_state CS),
    cs_cert CS s0 = false ->
    cs_cert CS (cs_run CS trace s0) = true ->
    cs_total_cost CS trace >= 1.

In plain words: a certification system is a record of a state type, a move type, a step,
a cost and a yes-or-no reading, plus one more field, cs_cert_costs, which is the
toll: a move that takes the reading from false to true costs at least one. Since the toll
is a field, every system the theorem talks about has it. The theorem: start at a state
reading false, run any list of moves (cs_run applies them in order, cs_total_co
st adds their costs), end at a state reading true, and the costs add up to at least one.
Theorem 3.1 says exactly this; the rule that Definition 3.1 calls the toll is the record’s
last field here.



                                           458
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


E.2 A permanent flip merges
permanent_flip_is_not_injective, coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertification.v,
inside a section that fixes the states, the moves, the step and the reading.

Variables (S I : Type).
Variable step : S -> I -> S.
Variable cert : S -> bool.

Definition finite_states (all : list S) : Prop :=
  NoDup all /\ forall s, In s all.

Definition permanent : Prop :=
  forall s i, cert s = true -> cert (step s i) = true.

Definition step_injective (i : I) : Prop :=
  forall a b, step a i = step b i -> a = b.

Theorem permanent_flip_is_not_injective :
  forall all s i,
    finite_states all ->
    permanent ->
    cert s = false ->
    cert (step s i) = true ->
    ~ step_injective i.

In plain words: finite_states all says the list all has no repeats and every state is
on it, so there are finitely many. permanent says once the reading is true, every move
keeps it true. step_injective i says move i never sends two different states to the
same one. The theorem: on a finite machine with a permanent reading, a move that
takes some state from false to true isn’t injective, so it merges two states. Theorem 4.1
says exactly this, with “merges” meaning “isn’t injective”.

E.3 The toll from finiteness, permanence and merge pricing
a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence, the same file and section, with a
cost on moves added.

Variable cost : I -> nat.

Definition merging_steps_priced : Prop :=
  forall i, ~ step_injective i -> cost i >= 1.

Definition a2_holds : Prop :=
  forall s i, cert s = false -> cert (step s i) = true -> cost i >= 1.

Theorem a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence :
  forall all,
    finite_states all ->
    permanent ->
    merging_steps_priced ->
    a2_holds.



                                          459
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


In plain words: merging_steps_priced says every move that isn’t injective costs
at least one, and a2_holds is the toll. The theorem: finite, permanent and merges
priced give the toll. Theorem 4.2 says this and one thing more, that the machine with
that cost is then a certification system the universal floor applies to. That second half
isn’t in this statement. It’s the definition right after it in the file (certification_s
ystem_from_merging_price), which fills the record’s toll field with this theorem,
so the printed form is true, and it leans on two Coq items: this theorem and that
definition.

E.4 No exact window price across a collision
shadow_cannot_price_exactly, coq/kernel/nfi/ShadowPricing.v, inside a
section that fixes the states, moves, step, reading and a window obs.

Variables (S I O : Type).
Variable step : S -> I -> S.
Variable cert : S -> bool.
Variable obs : S -> O.

Definition flips (s : S) (i : I) : bool :=
  negb (cert s) && cert (step s i).

Definition shadow_cost (price : O -> O -> nat) (s : S) (i : I) : nat :=
  price (obs s) (obs (step s i)).

Definition meets_floor (cost : S -> I -> nat) : Prop :=
  forall s i, flips s i = true -> cost s i >= 1.

Definition never_overcharges (cost : S -> I -> nat) : Prop :=
  forall s i, flips s i = false -> cost s i = 0.

Definition shadow_collision : Prop :=
  exists s1 i1 s2 i2,
    obs s1 = obs s2 /\
    obs (step s1 i1) = obs (step s2 i2) /\
    flips s1 i1 = true /\
    flips s2 i2 = false.

Theorem shadow_cannot_price_exactly :
  shadow_collision ->
  forall price,
    ~ (meets_floor (shadow_cost price) /\
       never_overcharges (shadow_cost price)).

In plain words: flips s i says move i takes s from false to true. A shadow price is
any function of what the window shows before and after a step. meets_floor says
every flip costs at least one, never_overcharges says every step that isn’t a flip
costs nothing, and a shadow_collision is two steps that look the same through the
window, before and after, one a flip and one not. The theorem: given a collision, no
shadow price does both. Theorem 7.2 bundles this with three neighbours from the


                                          460
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


same file: that a price meeting the floor charges some non-flip at least one (shadow_
floor_overcharges), that a window showing the reading prices exactly (window
_showing_reading_prices_exactly), and that such a window has no collision
(window_showing_reading_has_no_collision). This statement is the second
of the four clauses, and the book says exactly what it says.

E.5 The record is a latch
record_axis_is_latch_holds, coq/kernel/foundation/StructuralRecordAxis.v;
the definitions come from StructuralCoreAnyBase.v and StructuralCoreCover.v.
Definition record_permanent (M : RCM) : Prop :=
  forall s, rc_cert M s = true -> rc_cert M (rc_next M s) = true.

Definition computation_driven (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
  : Prop :=
  exists f : b_state B -> bool -> bool,
    forall m, rc_cert M (rc_next M m) = f (base_state M B C m) (rc_cert M m).

Definition HonestBaseExtension (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
  : Prop :=
  computation_driven M B C /\ ledger_carried M /\ rc_a2 M /\
  record_permanent M /\ reachable_record_write M.

Definition latch_next (B : BaseMachine) (h : b_state B -> bool)
    (x : b_state B * bool) : b_state B * bool :=
  (b_next B (fst x), orb (snd x) (h (fst x))).

Definition latch_factorization (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
    (h : b_state B -> bool) : Prop :=
  forall m,
    (base_state M B C (rc_next M m), rc_cert M (rc_next M m)) =
    latch_next B h (base_state M B C m, rc_cert M m).

Definition record_axis_is_latch : Prop :=
  forall M B C, HonestBaseExtension M B C ->
    exists h, latch_factorization M B C h.

Theorem record_axis_is_latch_holds : record_axis_is_latch.


In plain words: here a machine M steps by itself (rc_next gives the one next state),
carries a reading rc_cert and a ledger, and sits over a base B through a cover C, a
map down to the base’s states that commutes with the step. computation_drive
n says the reading’s next value is some function f of the base state and the reading’s
current value. Honest means driven, a ledger that never falls, the toll, a permanent
reading, and some reachable step that writes it. latch_next is the latch of an event
h: the base steps, and the record becomes “already on, or h holds now.” The theorem:
every honest extension evolves exactly as the latch of some event. Theorem 10.1
says a little more than this statement: it names the event, h(b) = f (b, off), where the
statement only says one exists. The proof builds exactly that event (its first move
is exists (fun b => f b false)), so it shows the theorem’s stronger form too.
And the proof uses two of the five honesty conditions, driven and permanent; the
other three are carried along and never used.


                                          461
The Thiele Machine                                                                            Devon Thiele


E.6 A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified
earned_certification_provenance, minimal/EarnedCore.v.
Theorem earned_certification_provenance : forall s0 tr,
  clean_start s0 -> cert (run tr s0) = true ->
  exists pre1 p c mid1 mid2 post,
    tr = pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ COMMIT p c :: mid2 ++ CERTIFY :: post /\
    check_ok (core_of (run pre1 s0)) p c = true /\
    commit_ok (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1) s0)) p c = true /\
    certify_ok (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ COMMIT p c :: mid2) s0))
      = true /\
    ver (core_of (run pre1 s0)) c = ver (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1) s0)) c /\
    untouched (run (pre1 ++ [CHECK p c]) s0) mid1 c.



In plain words: the clean-start premise on s0 says the fact table and the channel are
empty and the flag is down, and run tr s0 runs a list of instructions. The theorem:
from a clean start, if the flag is up at the end, the list splits as some start, CHECK
p c, a middle, COMMIT of the same p c, another middle, CERTIFY, and the rest;
the CHECK, the COMMIT and the CERTIFY each pass where they run; the counter’s
version at the CHECK equals its version at the COMMIT; and nothing in the first
middle touched that counter. Theorem 16.9 says exactly this.

E.7 Checker soundness
checker_soundness, minimal/EarnedCore.v.
Theorem checker_soundness : forall s0 tr f,
  clean_start s0 ->
  let k := core_of (run tr s0) in
  In f (facts k) -> f_ver f = ver k (f_ctr f) -> holds (f_prop f) (val k (f_ctr f)).


In plain words: from a clean start, after any list of instructions, every fact in the table
that’s about its counter’s current version is true of that counter’s current value, where
holds is the property’s meaning written without the checker. Theorem 16.11 says
exactly this in its first sentence; its “in particular” is the next corollary in the file, comm
itted_claim_holds.

E.8 No forging
no_forging, minimal/EarnedCore.v, with the two definitions it uses.
Definition earned (s0 : state) (tr : list instr) (f : fact) : Prop :=
  exists pre mid,
    tr = pre ++ CHECK (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) :: mid /\
    check_ok (core_of (run pre s0)) (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) = true /\
    f = claim (core_of (run pre s0)) (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) /\
    (f_ver f = ver (core_of (run tr s0)) (f_ctr f) ->
     untouched (run (pre ++ [CHECK (f_prop f) (f_ctr f)]) s0) mid (f_ctr f)).

Definition no_forgery (s0 : state) (tr : list instr) : Prop :=
  forall f, In f (facts (core_of (run tr s0))) -> earned s0 tr f.

Theorem no_forging : forall s0 tr, clean_start s0 -> no_forgery s0 tr.


In plain words: a fact is earned when a passing CHECK of exactly that property
and counter wrote it somewhere in the list, it is exactly the claim that CHECK made,
and, if it’s still about the counter’s current version, nothing touched the counter since.


                                                      462
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


no_forgery says every fact in the table at the end is earned. The theorem: from
every clean start, every list of instructions leaves no forgery. That’s the last clause
of Theorem 16.12, with Definition 16.6 saying the same as earned; the two one-step
clauses before it are facts_step (one instruction at a core) and no_forging_step
(a trace with no forgery stays that way when one instruction is added).

E.9 The minimum price of a certificate
certified_run_min_cost, minimal/EarnedCore.v.

Theorem certified_run_min_cost : forall s0 tr,
  clean_start s0 -> cert (run tr s0) = true ->
  total_cost tr >= 3 /\ mu (run tr s0) >= mu s0 + 3.

In plain words: from a clean start, a list of instructions that ends with the flag up cost
at least three in total, and the ledger rose by at least three. Theorem 16.16 says exactly
this in its first sentence; its form for stored programs is program_certified_min_
cost.

E.10 Three, reached by a check that could have failed
earned_run_check_can_fail and earned_run_refused_forever,
minimal/EarnedCore.v, with the program they run.
Definition earned_run : list instr := [CHECK PZero CA; COMMIT PZero CA; CERTIFY].

Theorem earned_run_check_can_fail : forall a b,
  (a = 0 ->
     cert (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = true /\
     mu (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = 3) /\
  (a <> 0 ->
     cert (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = false /\
     err (core_of (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b))) = true).

Theorem earned_run_refused_forever : forall n a b,
  a <> 0 -> cert (run_prog n earned_run (start a b)) = false.


In plain words: earned_run is CHECK “A is 0”, COMMIT the same, CERTIFY, and
start a b puts a in A and b in B with an empty table. The first theorem: run it for
four program steps; if a is 0 the flag is up and the ledger is exactly 3, and if a isn’t 0
the flag is down and the trap is up. The second: if a isn’t 0, the flag is down after any
number of steps. So three is reached by a check that could have failed, and when it
fails nothing ever certifies. Theorem 16.17 says this. The older witness in the same file,
min_cost_tight, reaches three with “A is at least 0”, a check that can’t fail; the step
doesn’t police that, and Section 16 says so.

E.11 Thiele-complete, the four clauses
thiele_complete, minimal/ThieleComplete.v, with the clauses it is made of.
load a b is the interface’s loaded state for the start (1, a, b), written inside a section
that fixes I; run M runs a list of moves from a state.
Definition universal_base_clause : Prop :=



                                           463
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


  (forall i, ti_kind I (ub_compile (ti_base I) i) = KBase) /\
  (forall a b, ti_clean I (load a b)) /\
  (forall s m, ti_kind I m = KBase -> m_record M (m_step M s m) = m_record M s) /\
  (forall s m, m_record M s = true -> m_record M (m_step M s m) = true).

Definition earned_chain (s0 : m_state M) (tr : list (m_move M)) : Prop :=
  exists pre c chk mid1 cmt mid2 crt post,
    tr = pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: mid2 ++ crt :: post /\
    ti_kind I chk = KCheck c /\ ti_kind I cmt = KCommit c /\
      ti_kind I crt = KCertify /\
    ti_check I (run M pre s0) c = true /\
    (forall t1 t2, mid1 = t1 ++ t2 ->
       ti_same I c (run M pre s0) (run M (pre ++ chk :: t1) s0)) /\
    m_record M (run M (pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: mid2) s0) = false /\
    m_record M (run M (pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: mid2 ++ [crt]) s0) = true.

Definition earned_record_clause : Prop :=
  (forall s, ti_clean I s -> m_record M s = false) /\
  (forall s0 tr, ti_clean I s0 -> m_record M (run M tr s0) = true ->
    earned_chain s0 tr) /\
  (forall s c, ti_check I s c = true -> ti_meaning I c s) /\
  (forall c s s’, ti_same I c s s’ -> ti_meaning I c s -> ti_meaning I c s’).

Definition record_move (m : m_move M) : nat :=
  match ti_kind I m with KBase => 0 | _ => 1 end.

Definition exact_toll_clause : Prop :=
  (forall m, m_cost M m = record_move m) /\
  (forall s m, ti_ledger I (m_step M s m) = ti_ledger I s + m_cost M m).

Definition non_vacuity_clause : Prop :=
  exists c chk cmt crt,
    ti_kind I chk = KCheck c /\ ti_kind I cmt = KCommit c /\
      ti_kind I crt = KCertify /\
    (forall a b, m_record M (run M [chk; cmt; crt] (load a b)) = true <->
                 ti_meaning I c (load a b)) /\
    (exists a b, ti_meaning I c (load a b)) /\
    (exists a b, ~ ti_meaning I c (load a b)).

Definition thiele_complete_with : Prop :=
  universal_base_clause /\ earned_record_clause /\ exact_toll_clause /\
    non_vacuity_clause.

Definition thiele_complete (M : machine) : Prop :=
  exists I : thiele_interface M, thiele_complete_with I.

Theorem clock_not_thiele_complete : forall rd, ~ thiele_complete (clock rd).


In plain words: M is a machine (states, moves, step, cost, record) and I an interface
for it (a universal base, claims with meanings, a checker, “unchanged,” clean states,
a ledger, and a kind for each move). The first clause says the compiled two-counter
moves are base moves, loaded states are clean, base moves leave the record alone,
and the record never comes down; the universal base’s own fields, not printed here,
say the compiled moves act on the window exactly as the two-counter instructions
act. earned_chain is a passing check of a claim, then a commit of the same claim
with the thing it’s about unchanged at every point between, then the certify that raises
the record. The earned-record clause says clean states have the record down, every


                                          464
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


run from a clean state that raises it contains that chain, a passing check means the
claim holds, and a claim that holds keeps holding while its thing is unchanged. The
exact toll: base moves cost 0, record moves 1, and the ledger adds each move’s cost.
Non-vacuity: some claim’s bare chain raises the record from a loaded state exactly
when the claim holds there, and the claim holds at one loaded state and fails at another.
thiele_complete asks for one interface meeting all four. clock is the two-counter
machine with every move costing 1 and any reading of its configuration as the record.
Definition 16.7 says this and adds the weaker notion, weakly Thiele-complete (weakl
y_thiele_complete, not printed here). Theorem 16.19 says the last line and more:
the clock is weakly Thiele-complete (clock_weakly_thiele_complete), a flag
that switches on at the first yes behaves the same way (latch_clock_weakly_t
hiele_complete and latch_clock_not_thiele_complete), and no machine
whose every move costs at least 1 is Thiele-complete, which comes from complete_
has_free_move.

E.12 The universal program’s flag and ledger
universal_halting, universal_flag_iff, universal_ledger_exact and
universal_thiele_complete, coq/kernel/foundation/UniversalRun.v.
Theorem universal_halting : forall P x y,
  (exists m, E.halted P (E.core_of (grun P x y m))) <->
  (exists n, M.halted U (M.core_of (hrun P x y n))).

Theorem universal_flag_iff : forall P x y,
  (exists m, E.cert (grun P x y m) = true) <->
    (exists n, M.cert (hrun P x y n) = true).

Theorem universal_ledger_exact : forall P x y,
  (forall m, exists n,
     ((rel P (grun P x y m) (hrun P x y n) /\ m <= n) \/
      rel_halt P (grun P x y m) (hrun P x y n)) /\
     M.mu (hrun P x y n) = E.mu (grun P x y m)) /\
  (forall n, exists m,
     E.mu (grun P x y m) <= M.mu (hrun P x y n) <= E.mu (grun P x y (S m))).

Theorem universal_thiele_complete : TC.thiele_complete host_machine.


In plain words: grun P x y m is m program steps of the small machine’s program P
from start x y; hrun P x y n is n program steps of the one fixed host program
U from the host loaded with P, x and y. The first theorem: the guest halts at some step
exactly when U does. The second: the guest’s flag is up at some step exactly when
the host’s is. The third: for every guest step count there’s a host step count where the
two are related, with the host count at least the guest count, or both stopped, with
equal ledgers; and every host point’s ledger lies between the guest’s at some step and
at the step after. rel and rel_halt are the relations Theorem 16.24 spells out. The
fourth: the host machine, the small machine with a register for every whole number
and the one property PSlot, read one move per instruction, is Thiele-complete in the
sense of the previous subsection. Theorem 16.26 says exactly the second and the third.
Theorem 16.25 says the first and more: at halting the registers, the traps, the ledgers


                                          465
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and the flags match too (universal_output, not printed here). Theorem 16.28 says
the fourth and more: U’s run is a run of the host, the floor on the cost of a run that
raises the flag, and the undecidability of U’s halting, each with its own Coq theorem
in the table of Section D.

E.13 The universal reading checker
cg_run_check, cg_ueval and cg_ueval_iff,
coq/kernel/foundation/CompilerChecker.v.
Definition cg_run_check (rc : cg_routine_code) (v : nat) : bool :=
  match rc with
  | (ig, R, xS, xB, xT, m) =>
       let st := cg_mme_run_fuel (cg_expo (qs xT) v) (ig, R) (ig, cg_env_chk m v) in
       cg_out_codeb (ig, R) (fst st) && Nat.eqb (get_env (snd st) xB) 1
  end.

Definition cg_ueval (p : cg_uprop) (v : nat) : bool :=
  match p with
  | UBase q => G.ceval q v
  | URun r =>
       match cg_rdec r with
       | Some rc => cg_run_check rc v
       | None => false
       end
  end.

Theorem cg_ueval_iff : forall p v, cg_ueval p v = true <-> cg_uholds p v.


In plain words: a claim is either one of the counter language’s words, checked as
before, or a number r naming a reading routine. For the second kind the checker
decodes r; a code that names no routine gets false. Otherwise it reads the registers
and a fuel number t out of the value, runs the routine for at most t steps, and says yes
exactly when the routine has left its code with 1 in its answer register. The theorem
says the checker’s yes is the claim’s meaning, which for a routine is that bounded run.
Section 16.14 says exactly this. The checker answers on every input because it’s a Coq
function that always returns (cg_ueval_total).

E.14 The surcharge can’t always be avoided
presented_universal_no_exact_below_three,
coq/kernel/foundation/PresentedUniversal.v.
Theorem presented_universal_no_exact_below_three :
  forall (Mp : presented_machine) (s0 : T.cs_state (pm_sys Mp)) (n : nat),
  mlatch Mp s0 n = true -> mledger Mp s0 n < 3 ->
  forall (h0 : hstate) (tr : list (@M.pu_instr pu_hprop)),
  M.pu_clean_start h0 ->
  ~ (M.cert (hrun_l tr h0) = mlatch Mp s0 n /\
     M.mu (hrun_l tr h0) = M.mu h0 + mledger Mp s0 n).


In plain words: if a presented machine’s latch is up after n moves while its ledger is
below three, then no list of host instructions, run from a clean host start, ends with
the host’s flag equal to that latch and the host’s ledger raised by exactly that ledger.


                                          466
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Theorem 16.30(3) says exactly this. It’s about the guest’s whole ledger at that point. A
guest whose one raising move is cheap but whose earlier moves already paid three or
more isn’t covered.

E.15 Nesting pays for every rise
cmpz_sim_cost_ge_exits, coq/kernel/foundation/CzCat.v.
Theorem cmpz_sim_cost_ge_exits : forall {X Y} (f : cmpz_hom X Y),
  (forall a b, bp_le (ob_P Y) (h_rec f a) (h_rec f b) -> bp_le (ob_P X) a b) ->
  ax_a2 (X := am_axsys (ob_M Y)) ->
  forall (tr : list (am_move (ob_M X))) s, exists tr’ : list (am_move (ob_M Y)),
    h_state f (am_run (ob_M X) tr s) = am_run (ob_M Y) tr’ (h_state f s) /\
    cmpz_cost (ob_M Y) tr’ >= cmpz_exit_count (ob_M X) tr s.


In plain words: take a simulation f of a guest X inside a host Y, whose record map
reflects the order, and let Y pay its toll. Then every list of the guest’s moves, from any
state, is matched by a list of the host’s moves that lands on the image of the guest’s
end state and costs at least the number of guest steps whose new record isn’t at or
below the old one. Theorem 18.4(1) says exactly this, with “faithfully” meaning that f
is a simulation. It bounds the host’s cost by the guest’s rises. It says nothing about the
guest’s other charges.

E.16 The copy is the record, on the simpler host
record_agreement, minimal/UniversalThiele.v.

Definition agrees (h : hstate) : Prop := mrec h = E.cert (gst h).

Theorem record_agreement : forall tr h, agrees h -> agrees (hrun tr h).

In plain words: the host keeps a mirror bit mrec beside the guest’s state gst, and
agrees h says the mirror equals the guest’s own flag. The theorem: a host state
that agrees still agrees after any list of host moves, whatever they are. Theorem 16.32
says this for lists of moves and adds single moves, stored programs, loading, and the
mirror after n moves GSTEP 1, which are record_agreement_step, record_agr
eement_program, hload_agrees and simulated_record.

E.17 No free host certification, on the simpler host
no_free_host_certification, minimal/UniversalThiele.v, with the host’s
moves and their costs.
Inductive hinstr : Type :=
| OWN (i : E.instr)
| GSTEP (b : nat).

Definition hcost (i : hinstr) : nat :=
  match i with OWN j => E.cost j | GSTEP b => b end.

Definition crossing (g g’ : E.state) : bool := negb (E.cert g) && E.cert g’.

Theorem no_free_host_certification : forall tr h,
  mrec h = false -> mrec (hrun tr h) = true ->



                                           467
The Thiele Machine                                                                         Devon Thiele


  exists pre b post, tr = pre ++ GSTEP b :: post /\ b >= 1 /\
    crossing (gst (hrun pre h)) (gst (hexec (hrun pre h) (GSTEP b))) = true.


In plain words: a host move is either OWN i, one of the small machine’s own instruc-
tions on the host’s core, or GSTEP b, one guest step with budget b, which costs b
whatever the guest instruction cost. crossing g g’ says the guest’s flag went from
down to up. The theorem: if the mirror is down before a list of host moves and up
after it, then somewhere in the list there’s a GSTEP b with b at least one at which the
guest’s flag crossed. Theorem 16.34 prints the one-move form, no_free_host_ce
rtification_step, which also says the host wasn’t trapped and the guest’s next
instruction was CERTIFY; this is the form for whole lists that it lifts to. The printed
theorem says two things more, each with its own Coq theorem: a trace of OWN moves
alone leaves the mirror and the guest state where they were (guestless_runs_lea
ve_mirror), and the host’s own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY that passes (ow
n_record_only_by_certify). Neither the one-move form nor the list form says
what the guest did before its CERTIFY. That, after a run from a loaded host, a raised
mirror means the guest’s own run checked and committed first is the next theorem.

E.18 A raised mirror stands on the guest’s own earned chain, on the simpler host
host_mirror_earned, minimal/UniversalThiele.v.
Theorem host_mirror_earned : forall tr a b P x y,
  mrec (hrun tr (hload a b P x y)) = true ->
  exists n gtr pre1 p c mid1 mid2 post,
    gtr = E.trace_of n P (E.start x y) /\
    gst (hrun tr (hload a b P x y)) = E.run gtr (E.start x y) /\
    gtr = pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ E.COMMIT p c :: mid2 ++ E.CERTIFY :: post /\
    E.check_ok (E.core_of (E.run pre1 (E.start x y))) p c = true /\
    E.commit_ok (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1) (E.start x y))) p c
      = true /\
    E.certify_ok (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ E.COMMIT p c :: mid2)
                               (E.start x y))) = true /\
    E.ver (E.core_of (E.run pre1 (E.start x y))) c
      = E.ver (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1) (E.start x y))) c /\
    E.untouched (E.run (pre1 ++ [E.CHECK p c]) (E.start x y)) mid1 c.



In plain words: load the host with a guest program P and a guest start (x, y) (hloa
d gives the guest a clean start), run any list of host moves, and suppose the mirror is up
at the end. Then for some number of steps n, the guest’s state is its own program’s run
of n steps, and the instructions that run executed split exactly the way Theorem 16.9
splits a trace: a passing CHECK, a COMMIT of the same claim at the same version
with the counter untouched between, then a passing CERTIFY. So the host’s mirror
can’t be up unless the guest’s own program earned it. The book’s sentences citing h
ost_mirror_earned say this in words; the Coq says a little more than they need,
since the chain sits inside the instructions the guest program itself executed. Any list
containing the chain would have been enough for them.

E.19 Structural entitlement, represented
ent_representation, minimal/EntitlementSmall.v, with the definitions it leans
on.
Definition ent_strict_sublist (post prior : list X) : Prop :=
  incl post prior /\ exists x, In x prior /\ ~ In x post.




                                                      468
The Thiele Machine                                                                           Devon Thiele



Definition ent_distinguishes (obs : X -> O) (w : X) (post : list X) : Prop :=
  forall t, In t post -> obs w <> obs t.

Definition ent_member (eqb : O -> O -> bool) (obs : X -> O) (L : list X) (o : O) : bool :=
  existsb (fun t => eqb (obs t) o) L.

Definition ent_stronger (P Q : O -> bool) : Prop :=
  forall o, P o = true -> Q o = true.

Definition ent_strictly_stronger (P Q : O -> bool) : Prop :=
  ent_stronger P Q /\ exists o, P o = false /\ Q o = true.

Definition ent_reduction (r : X -> O) (T : ent_tree) (prior post : list X) : Prop :=
  exists F : X -> list X,
    (forall x, In x prior -> exists t, In t post /\ In x (F t) /\ r x = r t) /\
    length prior <= fold_right Nat.add 0 (map (fun t => length (F t)) post) /\
    (forall t, In t post -> length (F t) <= ent_leaves T).

Definition ent_certified {M : machine} (I : thiele_interface M) {O : Type}
    (s0 : m_state M) (tr : list (m_move M))
    (d : list (m_move M) -> O) (P : O -> bool) : Prop :=
  m_record M (run M tr s0) = true /\ P (d tr) = true.

Theorem ent_representation :
  forall (M : machine) (I : thiele_interface M) (X O : Type)
         (s0 : m_state M) (tr : list (m_move M))
         (d : list (m_move M) -> O) (obs r : X -> O) (eqb : O -> O -> bool)
         (prior post : list X) (T : ent_tree),
    thiele_complete_with I ->
    (forall o1 o2, eqb o1 o2 = true <-> o1 = o2) ->
    ent_strict_sublist post prior ->
    (exists w, In w prior /\ ~ In w post /\ ent_distinguishes obs w post) ->
    ti_clean I s0 ->
    ent_certified I s0 tr d (ent_member eqb obs post) ->
    ent_depth T <= record_moves I tr ->
    0 < length post ->
    ent_reduction r T prior post ->
    ent_strictly_stronger (ent_member eqb obs post) (ent_member eqb obs prior) /\
    earned_chain I s0 tr /\
    (exists pre c chk mid1 cmt rest,
       tr = pre ++ chk :: mid1 ++ cmt :: rest /\
       ti_kind I chk = KCheck c /\ ti_kind I cmt = KCommit c /\
       ti_meaning I c (run M pre s0) /\ ti_meaning I c (run M (pre ++ chk :: mid1) s0)) /\
    Nat.log2_up (length prior) - Nat.log2_up (length post) <= record_moves I tr /\
    record_moves I tr = ti_ledger I (run M tr s0) - ti_ledger I s0 /\
    ti_ledger I s0 + 3 <= ti_ledger I (run M tr s0).



In plain words: take a machine and an interface through which it is Thiele-complete,
any type of rivals X and of observations O with an exact equality test, a run t from
a clean state s0 , and a decoder d that reads the run’s receipts, its list of moves. Hy-
potheses in order: the posterior list is inside the prior and drops at least one rival;
some dropped rival shows an observation no survivor shows; the start is clean; the
run ends with the record up and the posterior’s membership test accepts the decoded
run; the tree is no deeper than the number of record moves in the run; the posterior is
non-empty; and the covering is by fibres, as ent_reduction spells out. Conclusions
in order: the posterior’s test is strictly stronger; the run contains the earned chain;
some CHECK of a claim and a later COMMIT of the same claim appear in the run,
with the claim holding at both; the index bits are at most the record moves; the record
moves are exactly the ledger’s rise; and the rise is at least 3. Theorem 16.39 says this,
with the hypotheses numbered (M1) to (M6) and the conclusions numbered (1) to (5),
and it says one thing more in (2): there the meanings hold at the chain’s own CHECK
and COMMIT. The Coq’s third conclusion is a separate existential that doesn’t name
the chain; the printed form follows from it with the last two parts of clause (b), a
passing check means the claim holds and an unchanged thing keeps it holding.


                                                      469
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


E.20 A raised flag stands on the CHSH check
small_chsh_flag_implies_tsirelson,
coq/kernel/quantum/SmallChshMachine.v, over the host machine with the one
property small_chsh_PCHSH.
Theorem small_chsh_flag_implies_tsirelson :
  forall (s0 : @state small_chsh_prop) (tr : list (@instr small_chsh_prop)),
  clean_start s0 ->
  cert (run small_chsh_prop_eqb small_chsh_eval tr s0) = true ->
  exists pre1 c mid1 mid2 post,
    tr = pre1 ++ CHECK small_chsh_PCHSH c :: mid1
           ++ COMMIT small_chsh_PCHSH c :: mid2 ++ CERTIFY :: post /\
    let v := vals (core_of (run small_chsh_prop_eqb small_chsh_eval pre1 s0)) c in
    let t := small_chsh_tally_of v in
    small_chsh_check t = true /\
    small_chsh_meaning t /\
    (small_chsh_score t * small_chsh_score t <= 8)%R /\
    (Rabs (small_chsh_score t) <= 2 * sqrt 2)%R /\
    vals (core_of (run small_chsh_prop_eqb small_chsh_eval
                    (pre1 ++ CHECK small_chsh_PCHSH c :: mid1) s0)) c = v.


In plain words: start from a clean start and run any list of instructions of the host
machine whose only property is the CHSH one, and suppose the flag is up at the end.
Then the list splits as some instructions, a CHECK of the property at some counter
c, some more, a COMMIT of the same property at the same counter, some more, a
CERTIFY, and the rest. Take the value v that counter c held just before the CHECK,
and read it as a tally of eight counts. That tally passes the seven integer facts (small_
chsh_check); it means what the check is for: every question pair sampled and the
pinned five-by-five symmetric and positive semidefinite (small_chsh_meaning);
                                   √
its score S has S2 ≤ 8 and |S| ≤ 2 2; and counter c still held v when the COMMIT ran.
Because that tally passes the check, its score is in fact strictly below the bound, S2 < 8
(nec_e_check_strict), and passing tallies come as close to 8 as you like (nec_e_
check_sharp), both in NecEChsh.v. Theorem 20.5 says exactly this in its first part. It
says more in two places that have their own Coq theorems, the stored-program form
and the converse that the three instructions certify exactly when the check passes, and
the real numbers in the statement are why it carries FE and RD, three standard-library
assumptions in all, as printed in Section D.

E.21 The recursion theorem up to the record, and no better
sm2_kleene_obs and sm2_no_exact, coq/kernel/foundation/SmFixedPoint.v
and coq/kernel/foundation/SmNoExact.v, with the relation they use. Here M is the
host machine’s module, hendsPxs says program P, started with x in register 1 and
everything else clean, stops (a trap counts as stopping) in state s, and sm_computes
_mapTF says that on the number of every program p, T stops with the number of Fp.
Definition sm2_obs (s t : hstate) : Prop :=
  M.vals (M.core_of s) 0 = M.vals (M.core_of t) 0 /\
  M.err (M.core_of s) = M.err (M.core_of t) /\
  M.mu s = M.mu t /\ M.cert s = M.cert t /\
  length (M.facts (M.core_of s)) = length (M.facts (M.core_of t)) /\



                                           470
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


  (M.chan (M.core_of s) = None <-> M.chan (M.core_of t) = None).

Definition sm2_obs_equiv (P Q : list hinstr) : Prop :=
  forall x,
    (forall s, hends P x s -> exists t, hends Q x t /\ sm2_obs s t) /\
    (forall t, hends Q x t -> exists s, hends P x s /\ sm2_obs s t).

Theorem sm2_kleene_obs : forall (F : list hinstr -> list hinstr) (T : list hinstr),
  sm_computes_map T F -> exists e, sm2_obs_equiv e (F e).

Theorem sm2_no_exact :
  exists (F : list hinstr -> list hinstr) (T : list hinstr),
    sm_computes_map T F /\ forall e, ~ hequiv e (F e).


In plain words: sm2_obsst says two final states agree on register 0, the trap latch, the
ledger, the flag, the number of facts and whether the channel is empty, and nothing else.
sm2_obs_equivPQ says that on every input, any state P ends in has a state Q ends
in that agrees in that sense, and the same the other way round, which includes that P
stops on an input exactly when Q does. The first theorem: for every transformation F of
host programs that some host program T carries out on numbers, there is a program e
that agrees with Fe in that sense. T is any host program, and may itself check, commit
and certify. The second: there is a transformation F, carried out by a host program,
such that no program e behaves the same as Fe in the sense of Definition 16.12, which
compares every register, the fact table, the channel, the trap latch, the ledger and the
flag. Theorems 16.49 and 16.50 say these two. The book’s printed version says exactly
this, with the line number and versions left out of both comparisons, as the definition
does.

F The CHSH derivation, in full
This appendix supports Section 20. That section tells the story; this one does the
algebra. Each item gives the exact statement with all its hypotheses, the steps a reader
needs to check it, and the Coq name with its file; the file paths in this appendix are
under coq/. Nothing here identifies any matrix with a quantum state. Where the
reading “quantum” appears, it is a cited result from outside the kernel.

F.1 Setting and notation
Definition F.1 (Settings, outcomes, correlators). Alice receives a setting x ∈ {0, 1} and
Bob a setting y ∈ {0, 1}. Each answers a bit, recoded as an outcome a, b ∈ {+1, −1}
(bit 0 becomes +1, bit 1 becomes −1). The correlator Exy is the average of the product
ab over the rounds with settings ( x, y). The CHSH quantity is

                               S = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .

I collect the four correlators into the 2 × 2 matrix
                                                    !
                                            E00 E01
                                     E=               ,
                                            E10 E11


                                           471
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


whose rows are indexed by Alice’s setting and whose columns by Bob’s. The rows of
E are ( E00 , E01 ) and ( E10 , E11 ); the columns are ( E00 , E10 ) and ( E01 , E11 ).


The     same    polynomial   S   appears  under    three     names in  the
source:        CHSH     (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v),    CHSH_val
ue      (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v)    and     chsh_S     (ker-
nel/quantum/ElliptopeCompletion.v).


Definition F.2 (Counters). Eight counts sit in the record WitnessCounts (ker-
nel/quantum/CHSHColumnCheck.v): for each setting pair, samexy counts rounds
whose two answer bits matched and diffxy counts rounds whose bits differed. A round
adds one to exactly one of the eight. Write

                                                                               Dxy
          Nxy = samexy + diffxy ,        Dxy = samexy − diffxy ,       Exy =       .
                                                                               Nxy


A matched round contributes ab = +1 and a differing round ab = −1, so Dxy is the
sum of the products and Dxy /Nxy is their average. Since | Dxy | ≤ Nxy , every correlator
from counters lies in [−1, 1]. In Coq the integers are chsh_n_z and chsh_d_z (ker-
nel/quantum/CHSHColumnCheck.v). When a bucket is empty, the real-valued corre-
lator state_bucket_correlation (kernel/quantum/CHSHColumnCheck.v) and
the rational one chsh_correlator_q (kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v)
both return 0 by convention. The CHSH score of a tally, chsh_stat_from_wc
(CHSHStatisticalBridge.v), adds the first three correlators and obtains − E11 by swap-
ping the two counters of the last bucket.

F.2 The classical bound
Lemma F.1 (Deterministic strategies). Let a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {+1, −1}. Then −2 ≤ a0 b0 +
a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 ≤ 2.

Proof. Factor: a0 b0 + a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 = a0 (b0 + b1 ) + a1 (b0 − b1 ). If b0 = b1 then
b0 + b1 = ±2 and b0 − b1 = 0; if b0 ̸= b1 the other way round. In both cases exactly
one of the two brackets is ±2 and the other is 0, so the expression is ±2 times a sign,
which is +2 or −2. There are sixteen sign choices, and every one of them gives exactly
±2. None gives 0 or ±4.

The Coq proofs do not factor; they split into the sixteen sign cases and compute. The
rational statement is local_S_2_deterministic (kernel/quantum/BoxCHSH.v):
for f A , f B : N → Q with every value ±1, the absolute value of f A (0) f B (0) +
f A (0) f B (1) + f A (1) f B (0) − f A (1) f B (1) is at most 2. The real statement is determi
nistic_strategy_chsh_bounded (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v), with
conclusion −2 ≤ · · · ≤ 2.



                                             472
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


Definition F.3 (Finite factorizable model, is_factorizable). A real-valued correla-
tion function E( a, b, x, y) is factorizable (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v) when
there exist response functions A( x, λ), B(y, λ), weights p(λ) and a natural number
λmax such that: 0 ≤ p(λ) ≤ 1 for λ ≤ λmax ; ∑λλmax    =0 p ( λ ) = 1; every A ( x, λ ) and every
B(y, λ) is −1 or +1; and for all a, b, x, y, E( a, b, x, y) = ∑λλmax
                                                                  =0 p ( λ ) A ( x, λ ) B ( y, λ ). The
outcome arguments a, b are dummies; only correlations are modelled.


Theorem F.2 (fine_theorem, one direction only). If E is factorizable,
then −2 ≤ E(0, 0, 0, 0) + E(0, 0, 0, 1) + E(0, 0, 1, 0) − E(0, 0, 1, 1) ≤ 2 (ker-
nel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v; restated as factorizable_CHSH_classical
_bound).

Proof. Substitute the factorization: S = ∑λ p(λ)Sλ , where Sλ is the deterministic
expression of Lemma F.1 at the signs A(·, λ), B(·, λ). Each Sλ ∈ [−2, 2], the weights
are nonnegative and sum to 1, so −2 = ∑λ p(λ)(−2) ≤ S ≤ ∑λ p(λ) · 2 = 2.


Remark F.1 (What the name does and does not cover). Fine’s 1982 theorem is an equiv-
alence between several descriptions of local models and the Bell inequalities. fine_
theorem proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys the bound. Its con-
verse, as it’s stated, is false (nec_e_fine_converse_false); the equivalence in the
form Fine meant, for correlations, with each correlator between −1 and 1 and all eight
inequalities, is nec_e_fine_iff. And fine_theorem covers only finitely many
hidden states (λ ≤ λmax ). An arbitrary probability space is outside it. The transfer to
rational boxes is local_box_CHSH_bound (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v):
if box_correlations B is factorizable then the real image of |S( B)| is at most 2.


The finite-tally statement concerns one fixed strategy replayed on every recorded
round.


Definition F.4 (WCLocallyConsistent). For bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {0, 1} and a counter
record w (kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v), w is locally consistent with
( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ) when, for each setting pair ( x, y): if a x = by then diffxy = 0, otherwise
samexy = 0; and every bucket is sampled, N00 , N01 , N10 , N11 > 0.


Theorem F.3 (A tally above 2 is not one replayed strategy). Let w be a counter
record whose rational score chsh_stat_from_wc w is greater than 2. Then
for all bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 , w is not locally consistent with ( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ). This is
chsh_violation_rules_out_locally_factorizable_coupling (ker-
nel/quantum/CHSHCouplingBridge.v). A stronger companion, locally_consisten
t_classical_bound, states that a locally consistent record has score of absolute value at
most 2; read through its contrapositive, it gives the first statement.



                                                 473
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


Proof. Under local consistency each sampled bucket is pure: if a x = by every round
in the bucket matched, so Exy = Nxy /Nxy = +1; otherwise every round differed and
Exy = −1. In signs, Exy = α x β y with α x = (−1) ax and β y = (−1)by . The score is then
the deterministic expression of Lemma F.1, which is at most 2 in absolute value. A
score above 2 contradicts this.

The theorem rules out one explanation, a single four-bit plan used on every round. It
says nothing about a local model that redraws its hidden state every round; Section 20
gives a four-round coin-flip tally with score 4.

F.3 Tsirelson’s bound from algebra
Lemma F.4 (The six-square identity, chsh_gap_is_sum_of_squares). For all real
a, b, c, d,

          4( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − ( a + b + c − d )2
             = ( a − b )2 + ( a − c )2 + ( a + d )2 + ( b − c )2 + ( b + d )2 + ( c + d )2 .

(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v, closed by ring.)

Proof. Expand the square on the left: ( a + b + c − d)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 + 2ab + 2ac −
2ad + 2bc − 2bd − 2cd. So the left side is

               3( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − 2ab − 2ac + 2ad − 2bc + 2bd + 2cd.

On the right, each variable appears in exactly three of the six brackets (a in a − b, a − c,
a + d; b in a − b, b − c, b + d; c in a − c, b − c, c + d; d in a + d, b + d, c + d), so the
squared terms add to 3( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ). The cross terms are −2ab from ( a − b)2 ,
−2ac from ( a − c)2 , +2ad from ( a + d)2 , −2bc from (b − c)2 , +2bd from (b + d)2 and
+2cd from (c + d)2 . Both sides agree term by term.

Since the right side is a sum of squares, S2 ≤ 4 ∑ xy Exy
                                                       2 for any four reals; this is cauc

hy_schwarz_chsh (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v).

Remark F.2 (Where equality can happen). The step about where equality happens is
checked as nec_e_equality_forces_point and nec_e_equality_two_poin
ts, and the fact that no ratio of whole numbers solves 2a2 = 1 as nec_e_no_rati
onal_half_square (NecEChshEquality.v); the conclusion about tallies at the end
is checked as nec_e_no_sqrt8, nec_e_check_strict, nec_e_check_never_
tsirelson and nec_e_check_sharp (NecEChsh.v). Equality S2 = 8 under the
row bounds forces equality in both steps of the proof above: the six squares must all
vanish, which gives a = b = c = −d, and the rows must be tight, which gives 2a2 = 1.
So the point of Theorem F.6 and its negative are the only places the bound is reached.
A tally’s correlators are ratios of whole numbers and 2a2 = 1 has no such solution, so
no tally reaches the bound; the integer check’s passing tallies stay strictly below it and
come as near as you like.

Lemma F.8 (Schur complement, the!standard form). Let P be symmetric positive definite.
                           P Q
The symmetric block matrix         is PSD if and only if R − QT P−1 Q is PSD.
                           QT R

Proof. For u, w of the right sizes,
        !T           !       !
    u        P Q         u
                                 = (u + P−1 Qw)T P (u + P−1 Qw) + wT ( R − QT P−1 Q) w.
    w        QT R        w

The first term is never negative because P is positive definite, and it is zero at u =
− P−1 Qw. So the form is nonnegative for all (u, w) exactly when the second term is
nonnegative for all w.

The lemma is checked in general form, for finite index sets and any symmetric P with
a symmetric inverse, as schur_identity and schur_complement_psd (Schur-
Complement.v); the forward direction needs no positivity at all, and the converse
needs P positive semidefinite. The proofs of the checks don’t invoke it abstractly. They
carry out its one instance with P = I2 , Q = E, R = I2 , where the complement is

Remark F.3 (What PSD of the pinned matrix means). M ( E) is the level-1 moment
matrix with the two within-party entries ⟨ A0 A1 ⟩ and ⟨ B0 B1 ⟩ pinned to zero. Its PSD is
sufficient for the correlators to admit some PSD completion (item G, zero_margina
l_implies_elliptope), and it is not necessary: the all-ones plan has a completion
but fails here. So a check built on M( E) is sound for the completion set and not
complete for it, and it rejects some honest classical tallies. That correlators with a
PSD completion are exactly those reachable by quantum measurements is Tsirelson’s
theorem, and both halves are proved here in finite dimension. For real and for complex
amplitudes, a strategy’s correlators are inner products of unit vectors (qs_corr_dot,
qs_uvec_unit and qs_vvec_unit; with complex amplitudes, qc_corr_dot, qc
_uvec_unit and qc_vvec_unit, the vectors read as real ones of twice the length)
and its level-1 moment matrix is PSD (qs_npa_psd, qc_npa_psd), so they have a
PSD completion (tr_quantum_elliptope, tr_complex_elliptope). The other
half, that every PSD completion comes from a quantum strategy, is tr_represent
ation: the strategy is built on two eight-level systems from the completion’s Gram
vectors (item H).

F.6 Level 1+AB
The source’s comments index Alice’s observables A1 , A2 and Bob’s B1 , B2 , so its ⟨ A1 B1 ⟩
is E00 here. The Coq variables themselves are already named in the book’s order,
from e00 to e11 . The five extra parameters are named in the record Q1ABMoments
(kernel/quantum/QuantumPartitionPSD_1AB.v): γ1 for ⟨ A0 A1 B0 ⟩, γ2 for ⟨ A0 A1 B1 ⟩,

Lemma F.20 (Fraction-free Schur step). For a symmetric n × n matrix h and any vector v,
with Sij = h11 hij − h1i h1j for i, j ≥ 2 (here S is the Schur matrix; the score plays no part in
this lemma),
                                                    2

                                                  j              i,j≥2

So if h11 > 0 and the (n − 1) × (n − 1) matrix S gives a nonnegative form, then h does too.

qf_nonneg_from_pd.

Proof. Expand the square: h211 v21 + 2h11 v1 ∑ j≥2 h1j v j + (∑ j≥2 h1j v j )2 . The left side is
h211 v21 + 2h11 v1 ∑ j≥2 h1j v j + h11 ∑i,j≥2 hij vi v j . The difference is ∑i,j≥2 (h11 hij − h1i h1j )vi v j .
Dividing by h11 > 0 keeps the sign.

Remark F.4 (Interior only). Every test in the cascade is strict, so a passing check
certifies that H is positive definite, which is stronger than semidefinite. A point
where H is PSD but singular cannot pass, and neither can a moment with |γk | = 1.
For example, the tally of item E with correlators (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) has H11 =
1 − 9/25 − 16/25 = 0, so the full 1+AB check fails on it for every choice of γ, though
the level-1 check of item E accepts it (nec_e_singular_full_fails and nec_e
_singular_level1_passes, NecEChshEquality.v). The source proves soundness
only; no converse is stated.

                                                486

tope). (ElliptopeCompletion.v) If a20 = a21 = b02 = b12 = 1, then ( a0 b0 , a0 b1 , a1 b0 , a1 b1 ) is
elliptope realizable, with x = a0 a1 and y = b0 b1 .

Proof. With these entries the form equals v20 + ( a0 v1 + a1 v2 + b0 v3 + b1 v4 )2 . Expanding
the second square gives a20 v21 + · · · on the diagonal, which is v21 + · · · by the unit
squares, and the cross terms 2a0 a1 v1 v2 = 2xv1 v2 , 2a0 b0 v1 v3 = 2E00 v1 v3 , and so on for
all six pairs. A sum of two squares is never negative.

The all-ones plan is the instance classical_tightness_witness_elliptope,
and the classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) is turing_point_elliptope, at x = 1, y = 0,
with form v20 + (v1 + v2 + v3 )2 + v24 .


Theorem F.25 (Convexity and finite mixtures). For 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, if E and F are elliptope
realizable, so is λE + (1 − λ) F (elliptope_convex, ElliptopeCompletion.v). For finitely
many members with nonnegative weights summing to at most 1, the weighted sum is realizable
(elliptope_finite_mixture). Every finite mixture of deterministic plans is realizable
(lhv_mixture_elliptope).

Proof. The form is affine in ( E, x, y) for each fixed v. Take the completion (λx1 + (1 −
λ) x2 , λy1 + (1 − λ)y2 ); the form at the mixture is the same mixture of two nonnegative
forms. The finite version is induction on the number of members, with the shortfall in
weight absorbed by the zero point (elliptope_zero). The last statement combines
this with Theorem F.24.


Theorem F.26 (Tsirelson’s bound holds on the completion set, elliptope_tsirels
on). (ElliptopeCompletion.v) If E is elliptope realizable then S2 ≤ 8.

Proof. For a symmetric PSD matrix the bilinear form obeys Cauchy-Schwarz,
B(u, w)2 ≤ Q(u) Q(w) (psd_cauchy_schwarz), because Q(u + tw) = Q(u) +
2t B(u, w) + t2 Q(w) ≥ 0 for all t and Lemma F.11 applies. Take u1 = e A0 and
w+ = e B0 + e B1 : B(u1 , w+ ) = E00 + E01 , Q(u1 ) = 1, Q(w+ ) = 2 + 2y. Take
u2 = e A1 and w− = e B0 − e B1 : B(u2 , w− ) = E10 − E11 , Q(w− ) = 2 − 2y. So
c21 ≤ 2 + 2y and c22 ≤ 2 − 2y with c1 = E00 + E01 , c2 = E10 − E11 , and both bud-
gets are nonnegative. Then c21 c22 ≤ (2 + 2y)(2 − 2y) = 4 − 4y2 ≤ 4, so c1 c2 ≤ 2, and
S2 = (c1 + c2 )2 = c21 + 2c1 c2 + c22 ≤ (2 + 2y) + 4 + (2 − 2y) = 8.

The completion can make a row of E longer than 1 (the all-ones plan has rows of
squared length 2), which is why this proof does not use the row bounds of item D.

tion.v) (1, 1, 1, −1) is not elliptope realizable, since its S2 = 16 > 8.

The gate (kernel/quantum/ElliptopeGate.v) is an integer decider with a soundness

Definition F.12 (The two branches). elliptope_pd_check (ElliptopeGate.v): with
the completion supplied as buckets and all entries scaled to integers by a positive com-

buckets and any certificate, then the four correlators of the record are elliptope realizable. And
elliptope_full_gate_never_accepts_pr_box: on the PR box tally the gate
returns false for every choice of the remaining arguments.

Proof. The first branch reduces to Lemma F.21 through the same fraction-free identity
(elliptope_pd_check_sound). The second is a weighted sum of squares: given
the ten equations, the form is ∑k dk Pk2 with dk ≥ 0 (elliptope_ldl_check_soun
d). The PR statement is soundness followed by Corollary F.27.

The gate is a decider with a soundness proof, and that’s all it is: no property of the

F.8 What is not proved
The following are cited results and open questions. Where part of one is proved, the
paragraph names the theorem and the part that stays cited.

The arcsine boundary. For two settings and two outcomes per side, Tsirelson, Landau
(1988) and Masanes (2003) give theorems characterizing the correlators reachable by
quantum measurements: | arcsin E00 + arcsin E01 + arcsin E10 − arcsin E11 | ≤ π and
its sign variants. The characterization is checked in ArcsineBoundary.v as an if and
only if with the completion set (am_arcsine) and, through Tsirelson’s representation,
with the quantum set (am_quantum_arcsine). The point (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5)
is on the boundary: arcsin 35 + arcsin 54 = π2 by the 3-4-5 triangle, so the sum is π
(am_pythagorean_boundary); Tsirelson’s point is on it too (am_tsirelson_b
oundary). The necessary direction holds in any dimension, for any expectation
on an algebra of observables in which Alice’s commute with Bob’s (ta_arcsine,
TsirelsonAlgebraic.v).

Equality with the quantum set. That the completion set of item G is exactly the
set of quantum correlators is Tsirelson’s representation theorem, and it is proved
in finite dimension: tr_representation for real amplitudes and tr_represe
ntation_complex for complex ones (TsirelsonRepresentation.v), with two eight-
level systems enough for every point. That PSD of the level-1 moment matrix is
necessary for quantum behaviour is proved for strategies in finite dimension, with
real amplitudes (qs_npa_psd, QuantumStrategies.v) and with complex ones (qc_n
pa_psd, QuantumStrategiesComplex.v), and in any dimension, marginals included,
for any expectation on an algebra of observables (ta_npa_psd, TsirelsonAlgebraic.v).

Achievability. Theorem F.6 is a point of R4 . A state and measurements that reach it
                                                                    √
are built in QuantumStrategies.v: the two-qubit state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/ 2 with A0 = Z,
                         √                           √                   √      √
A1 = X, B0 = ( Z + X )/ 2 and B1 = ( Z − X )/ 2 has correlators 1/ 2, 1/ 2,
   √        √          √
1/ 2, −1/ 2 and S = 2 2 (qs_tsirelson_reached), and every strategy in finite
dimension has S2 ≤ 8, with real amplitudes (qs_tsirelson) and with complex
ones (qc_tsirelson, QuantumStrategiesComplex.v). No experiment stands behind
either.

Completeness of the checks. The 1+AB cascade and the elliptope gate are proved
sound, and neither has a proved converse. The level-1 integer check is the exception:
on the small machine the same seven integer facts hold exactly when every pair was
sampled and the pinned matrix is positive semidefinite (small_chsh_check_iff,
Theorem 20.4), so that check is complete for what it tests. The 1+AB cascade is strict
and misses boundary points. The comment in ElliptopeGate.v that the second branch
accepts every point with a rational PSD completion is a mathematical remark about
LDLT factorizations, and the file has no theorem for it; nor is there a theorem that the

                                          489
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


four 1+AB checks accept nested sets.

Finite levels. For full behaviours, marginals included, the NPA levels are relaxations.
Chaturvedi (arXiv 2607.14569, 2026) argues, in a preprint, that no finite NPA level
characterizes the complete quantum set even in this simplest Bell scenario. Nothing
in this book checks that proof.

Statistics and physics. Nothing here says how many rounds make a tally informative,
and nothing says the counters came from honest play; a program can INC whatever
counts it likes.

F.9 Prior work
                                           √
Tsirelson’s 1980 paper gives the bound 2 2 for quantum correlations, and his theorem
says that quantum two-outcome correlators are inner products of real unit vectors.
Landau (1988) and Masanes (2003, arXiv quant-ph/0309137) each give a condition
that, by their proofs, characterizes the quantum correlators exactly for two settings
and two outcomes. Wehner (2006, arXiv quant-ph/0510076) gets Tsirelson bounds,
CHSH among them, from a semidefinite program on the 4 × 4 Gram matrix of those
vectors. Navascués, Pironio and Acín (2007, arXiv quant-ph/0607119; 2008, arXiv
0803.4290) built the hierarchy of moment-matrix tests; their 2008 paper applies a Schur
complement to the level-1 matrix of this scenario, recovers the arcsine condition, and
discusses the 1+AB level. I went back to each of those papers for these points, and
that is what I found in them. The results are theirs. Two of them are proved again
here in Coq, in finite dimension: Tsirelson’s representation (TsirelsonRepresentation.v)
and the arcsine characterization (ArcsineBoundary.v); the rest of their proofs are not
redone. Formal proofs of Tsirelson’s bound already exist, by Echenim and Mhalla
in Isabelle/HOL (arXiv 2306.12535) and in Lean’s mathlib (tsirelson_inequality in
Mathlib.Algebra.Star.CHSH), and exact rational sum-of-squares certificates go back at
                                                                   √
least to Peyrl and Parrilo (2008). So the moment-matrix route to 2 2 is standard. What
is specific here is narrower: an integer certificate computed from outcome counts, and
a mechanized chain from “the counts pass” to PSD of the pinned matrix and on to
S2 ≤ 8. I did not find that chain elsewhere, and I make no claim beyond it. On the
host machine, the same chain is earned: a raised flag from a clean start stands on a
passing check of the packed counts, and the check passes exactly when the pinned
matrix is positive semidefinite and every pair was sampled (Section 20, Theorems 20.4
and 20.5). The converse direction of the integer check, integers from PSD, is checked
there too, and there too I make no claim beyond the chain.

G Constructing the quoting operation
The proof in Section 13 uses a program that takes the code of a term and returns the
code of that code. Here is its construction. Nothing in the operation lets a program
inspect itself by magic: its input is an ordinary tree encoded as a closed lambda term.




                                          490
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


G.1 Numerals and syntax as data
For readability, the formulas below give names to bound variables. Renaming a
bound variable changes nothing; the underlying syntax uses the de Bruijn indices
of Definition 13.3. Applications associate to the left. Write X ⇓ Y here for a finite
sequence of the weak call-by-value steps ending in the value Y.

Scott numerals are the following closed values:

                           0 = λz.λs.z,      n + 1 = λz.λs.s n.

Thus a numeral selects either the supplied zero case or the supplied successor case,
passing its predecessor to the latter. The cases below are values, so choosing one does
not prematurely run the other.

The three syntax constructors, operating on already encoded children, are

                                V = λn.λv.λa.λl.v n,
                                A = λp.λq.λv.λa.λl.a p q,
                                L = λp.λv.λa.λl.l p.

The builder L is a term of the language L of Definition 13.3, and the two share only the
letter. For a variable of index n, an application and an abstraction, respectively, define
their codes by the following resulting values:

                               ⌜#n⌝ = λv.λa.λl.v n,
                               ⌜ p q⌝ = λv.λa.λl.a ⌜ p⌝ ⌜q⌝,
                               ⌜λp⌝ = λv.λa.λl.l ⌜ p⌝.

In particular, V n, A ⌜ p⌝ ⌜q⌝ and L ⌜ p⌝ reduce to these three codes. A code is closed
even when the term it describes has a free variable: the index of that variable is stored
as a numeral. It is data inside the code, and the code itself has no free variable.

G.2 Recursion without running under a lambda
The usual self-application trick has to delay its recursive call in a call-by-value lan-
guage. Use

               W = λx.λ f .λv. f (λa.x x f a) v,     rec( F ) = λv.W W F v.

When F and u are closed values, beta reduction gives

             rec( F ) u −→ W W F u −→∗ F (λa.W W F a) u = F (rec( F )) u.

The recursive argument is a lambda, hence already a value. It starts work only when
F applies it to an argument. That is the whole reason this construction survives the
call-by-value rule.


                                            491
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


G.3 Quoting numerals
Let Ej = ⌜#j⌝ for j = 0, 1, 2, and let Z = ⌜0⌝, obtained directly from the finite syntax
of 0 = λλ.1. Write Lk ( X ) for k nested applications of the syntax builder L to X; it
is an abbreviation for constructing k lambda nodes, and the language gains no new
operation from it.

Define
                FN = λr.λn. n Z (λk.L2 ( A E0 (r k))),           Q N = rec( FN ).

Then Q N n ⇓ ⌜n⌝, by induction on n. At zero the Scott numeral selects Z. At a
successor it passes n to the second case; the induction hypothesis supplies the code of
n, and the builders produce the code of λλ.(#0 n), which is exactly the syntax of n + 1.

G.4 Quoting terms
For a proposed recursive call r, define three handlers:

                               HV = λn.L3 ( A E2 ( Q N n)),
                            H A (r ) = λp.λq.L3 ( A ( A E1 (r p)) (r q)),
                            HL (r ) = λp.L3 ( A E0 (r p)).

Now set
                     FQ = λr.λt.t HV ( H A (r )) ( HL (r )),    Q = rec( FQ ).

The handlers are lambdas and so are values. The Scott code of the input chooses one
of them and hands it the encoded children. Induction on the represented term proves
Q ⌜t⌝ ⇓ ⌜⌜t⌝⌝:

   • For t = #n, the first handler constructs three lambda nodes over an application
     of variable 2 to the quoted numeral. That is the syntax of λλλ.(#2 n), the code of
     #n.
   • For t = p q, the induction hypotheses quote both child codes. The second handler
     constructs three lambdas over variable 1 applied to those two codes. That is the
     syntax of the application code.
   • For t = λp, the last handler constructs three lambdas over variable 0 applied to
     the quoted child code. That is the syntax of the abstraction code.

Each recursive call works on a proper child of the finite input tree, or on a smaller nu-
meral. Each builder takes finitely many beta steps. The induction therefore establishes
termination as well as the value returned.

The mkapp used in Section 13 is the builder A here. That proof also has a term of
its own called A, and it is a different term. With Q and that builder written out, its
self-referential term has every piece on the page. The companion names are mk_app_
enc, rec_spec, Qn_spec and Q_spec (LRecursion.v); the construction above is the


                                                 492
The Thiele Machine                                                         Devon Thiele


argument those names identify.

H Sources and mathematical dependencies
These works identify the principal mathematical dependencies and the intellectual
background named in the book. The definitions, statements and worked exam-
ples remain on its pages. A published result about thermodynamic cost, quantum
correlations or universal computation is not an additional theorem proved by this
manuscript.

The universal programs and the compiler that puts every computably presented Thiele
machine on the universal host use effective computability and counter-machine simu-
lation; their construction is given in Section 16.13 and Section 16.14, and the counter
and lambda references identify the established machinery under them. The thermo-
dynamic references do not remove the explicit physical premise of the heat bound.
The environmental-record papers motivate Section 15; they do not prove this book’s
pointer conjecture.
